\] The last identity is the natural one retained in D.34A, so its image in \(\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2\) is still \(V\).

Apply \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-more-algebra-lemma-geometrically-regular-over-field]{F.109} using the selected differential basis. It gives a flat map \(P'_{\mathfrak p'}\to L\) and a regular quotient \(L/\mathfrak p'L\). Its written conormal square identifies the image of the source cotangent space with the preceding first-homology image \(V\). Append the global elements \(\lambda_{s+i}=c_id_i^{r_i-1}\) to form \(P=k[y_1,\ldots,y_m]\to\Lambda\). Their cotangent classes are the originally chosen complementary classes multiplied by the nonzero scalars \(\bar d_i^{r_i}\), and therefore still form a complementary basis. Their residues are zero. Hence \(P_{\mathfrak p}\) is the localization of \(P'_{\mathfrak p'}[y_{s+1},\ldots,y_m]\) at the prime generated by \(\mathfrak p'\) and these variables.

Polynomial local regularity is proved in \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/d02d0a3669f42579db037cd44de1d113fdd770a1/docs/courses/AG-CA/src/regular-local-rings.md}{AG-CA-14, Proposition 3.3}. The old regular parameters and the appended variables are a regular parameter list for this source: its maximal ideal is generated by them and its cotangent space is the old cotangent space plus one independent class for each new variable. Their images are a regular sequence in \(L\). The old list remains regular by the flat map from \(P'_{\mathfrak p'}\), applying flat base change to each successive multiplication injection. The new list is a minimal parameter list on the regular local quotient \(L/\mathfrak p'L\), hence is regular by \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/d02d0a3669f42579db037cd44de1d113fdd770a1/docs/courses/AG-CA/src/regular-sequences-depth-and-cohen-macaulay-modules.md}{AG-CA-12, Theorem 6.1}. Concatenating these lists proves the assertion. \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-flat-over-regular]{F.46} now makes \(P_{\mathfrak p}\to L\) flat. Their cotangent classes span \(\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2\); Nakayama \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-NAK]{F.10} gives \(\mathfrak pL=\mathfrak m\). This proves (1).

All polynomial generators have their classes in \(A'\), so the map to \(B\) factors through \(A'\). An element outside \(\mathfrak p\) has nonzero residue and maps to a unit of this local ring. Moreover \(\mathfrak p^n\) maps to zero in \(B\), hence in \(A'\subset B\). We obtain \[
R=P_{\mathfrak p}/\mathfrak p^nP_{\mathfrak p}
\longrightarrow A'\longrightarrow B.
\] The ring \(R\) is Artinian: it is Noetherian local with nilpotent maximal ideal, and its finite ideal-power quotients have finite dimension over its residue field. Its composite map to \(B\) is the flat base change of (1). Since \(A'\to B\) is faithfully flat, \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-flatness-descends-more-general]{F.48} makes \(R\to A'\) flat. The ideals \(\mathfrak pA'\) and \(\mathfrak m_{A'}\) become equal in \(B\); faithful flatness detects equality by tensoring their quotient, so they are equal. The residue extension is the finite separable extension \(F'/K_0\) just proved. \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-essentially-of-finite-type-into-artinian-local]{F.40} makes \(A'\) a finite \(R\)-module. Since \(R\) is Noetherian, it is a finitely presented algebra, by taking finite module generators and a finite kernel in their polynomial presentation. Its only fibre is the finite separable residue field. The proved étale criterion \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-characterize-etale]{F.16} therefore makes \(R\to A'\) étale, in particular essentially smooth. Take \(D=A'\). It retains \(E\subset A\), proving (2) and (3). ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-smoothing-lemma-enlarge-solution-modulo}

\subsubsection{Lemma D.36: enlarge solution modulo}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-d.36-enlarge-solution-modulo}

Reading source: \href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/07FI}{Stacks, Tag 07FI}.

Use the notation and a local Artinian factorization of D.35: \[
R=k[y_1,\ldots,y_m]_{\mathfrak p}/\mathfrak p^n
\longrightarrow D\longrightarrow
B=\Lambda_{\mathfrak q}/\mathfrak q^n\Lambda_{\mathfrak q},
\] where \(R\to D\) is essentially smooth and \(D\to B\) is flat. For every \(\lambda\in\Lambda\setminus\mathfrak q\), there are a positive \(p\)-power \(q\) and a local Artinian factorization \(R\to D\to D'\to B\) with \(D\to D'\) essentially smooth, \(D'\to B\) faithfully flat, and \(\lambda^q\) in the image of \(D'\).

\textbf{Proof.} The polynomial-source maximal ideal extends to that of \(B\), by D.35(1). We verify that the maximal ideal of \(D\) does also, even for a factorization other than the particular étale one constructed there. The closed fibre \(D/\mathfrak m_RD\) is Artinian local and essentially smooth over the field \(R/\mathfrak m_R\). The regularity theorem \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/d02d0a3669f42579db037cd44de1d113fdd770a1/docs/courses/AG-CA/src/smooth-algebras-over-a-field-and-the-jacobian-criterion.md}{AG-CA-18, Theorem 2.1}, followed by localization, makes it regular. An Artinian local ring has dimension zero. For a regular local ring of dimension zero its cotangent dimension is zero; its finite maximal ideal equals its square, and Nakayama makes that ideal zero. Thus this fibre is a field and \(\mathfrak m_D=\mathfrak m_RD\). Extending to \(B\) gives \(\mathfrak m_DB=\mathfrak m_B\).

All rings required by D.34A are Noetherian. The source \(R\) is Noetherian, and the essentially smooth algebra \(D\) is a localization of a finitely presented \(R\)-algebra, so the Hilbert basis theorem and localization make it Noetherian. The ring \(B\) is the displayed Artinian quotient of the Noetherian local ring \(\Lambda_{\mathfrak q}\), and \(\mathfrak m_B^n=0\). The flat local map \(D\to B\) is faithfully flat by the local criterion. The image of \(\lambda\) is a unit because its residue is nonzero. Apply the one-unit case of \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-smoothing-artinian-denominator-enlargement]{D.34A}. It supplies \(D\subset D'\subset B\), an essentially smooth first map, a faithfully flat last map, and the exact power containment \(\lambda^q\in D'\). Composition with \(R\to D\) gives the required factorization. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-smoothing-lemma-resolve-general}

\subsubsection{Lemma D.37: resolve general}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-d.37-resolve-general}

Reading source: \href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/07FJ}{Stacks, Tag 07FJ}.

Let \(k\) have characteristic \(p>0\). In \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-smoothing-situation-local]{D.27}, suppose that \(\Lambda\) is Noetherian and geometrically regular over \(k\), and that \(\mathfrak q\) is minimal over \(\mathfrak h_A\). Then the problem has a resolution.

\textbf{Proof.} Put \(L=\Lambda_{\mathfrak q}\), \(\mathfrak m=\mathfrak qL\), \(d=\dim L\), and \(H=H_{A/k}=(a_1,\ldots,a_r)\). These generators exist by the Hilbert theorem \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/d02d0a3669f42579db037cd44de1d113fdd770a1/docs/courses/AG-CA/src/noetherian-and-artinian-rings.md}{AG-CA-03, Theorem 2.1}. The ring \(L\) is regular by geometric regularity. As in D.33, minimality and a finite maximal-ideal generating list give \(N>0\) with \(\mathfrak m^N\subset HL\).

Over \(P_0=k[x_1,\ldots,x_d]\) form \[
B=A[x_1,\ldots,x_d,z_{ij}]/(x_i^{2N}-\sum_j a_jz_{ij}).
\] Eliminating \(z_{ij}\) on an \(a_j\)-chart proves smoothness there; the equation makes those charts cover \(B_{x_i}\). By \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-locally-smooth]{F.67}, \(B_{x_i}/P_0\) is smooth. Apply \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-smoothing-lemma-improve-presentation]{D.9} to obtain \(B\to C\) with retraction \(C\to B\). The smooth charts of \(C\) have finite free differentials. Since \(C/P_0\) is finitely presented by the Hilbert theorem, \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-smoothing-lemma-compare-standard]{D.15(e)} gives one \(c>0\) for which all \(x_i^c\) are strictly standard. If \(d=0\), take \(c=1\). Fix, before making any Artinian approximation, \[
e=8c,\qquad n=\max\{N+dc,\ d(e-1)+1\}.
\tag{D.37a}
\]

Apply \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-smoothing-lemma-solution-modulo]{D.35} to the images of a finite \(k\)-algebra generating list of \(A\) in \(\overline L=L/\mathfrak m^n\). It gives a polynomial algebra \(P=k[y_1,\ldots,y_m]\) mapping to \(\Lambda\), its contracted prime \(\mathfrak p\), and local maps \[
S_0=P_{\mathfrak p}/\mathfrak p^nP_{\mathfrak p}
\longrightarrow D\longrightarrow\overline L.
\] The first map is essentially smooth, the second is flat, and the generator images belong to \(D\). Also \(P_{\mathfrak p}\to L\) is flat and \(\mathfrak pL=\mathfrak m\). Its closed fibre is a field, so the dimension formula \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/d02d0a3669f42579db037cd44de1d113fdd770a1/docs/courses/AG-CA/src/dimension-theory-of-noetherian-local-rings.md}{AG-CA-11, Theorem 5.1} gives \(\dim P_{\mathfrak p}=d\).

Choose \(\pi_1,\ldots,\pi_d\in\mathfrak p\) representing a regular parameter list of \(P_{\mathfrak p}\). Polynomial local rings are regular by iteration of \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/d02d0a3669f42579db037cd44de1d113fdd770a1/docs/courses/AG-CA/src/regular-local-rings.md}{AG-CA-14, Proposition 3.3}, starting with the field. The minimal-parameter theorem \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/d02d0a3669f42579db037cd44de1d113fdd770a1/docs/courses/AG-CA/src/regular-sequences-depth-and-cohen-macaulay-modules.md}{AG-CA-12, Theorem 6.1} makes their minimal generating list regular. Their images generate \(\mathfrak m\) and form a regular parameter list of \(L\), by the same theorem and \(\dim L=d\). Let \[
R=P[t_1,\ldots,t_d],\qquad \gamma_i=\pi_it_i.
\] Throughout, localization of this polynomial ring at the coefficients means \[
R_S=(P\setminus\mathfrak p)^{-1}R=P_{\mathfrak p}[t_1,\ldots,t_d].
\] It is distinct from localization at a prime of \(R\).

First arrange the source kernel conditions. By \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-regular-sequence-in-polynomial-ring]{F.75}, the \(\gamma_i\) form a regular sequence in \(R_S\). Powers of earlier entries preserve regularity by \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/d02d0a3669f42579db037cd44de1d113fdd770a1/docs/courses/AG-CA/src/regular-sequences-depth-and-cohen-macaulay-modules.md}{AG-CA-12, Proposition 1.3}. Inductively, on the finite \(R\)-module \(R/(\gamma_1^e,\ldots,\gamma_{i-1}^e)\), the localized kernels for \(\gamma_i\) and \(\gamma_i^2\) are zero. \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-smoothing-lemma-ogoma]{D.31} supplies \(s_i\in P\setminus\mathfrak p\) such that replacing \(\pi_i\) by \(s_i\pi_i\) makes these kernels equal globally. Earlier equalities are unchanged, because their entries and quotient ideals have not changed. Such scaling is by local units, so both local parameter lists remain regular. Continue through all \(i\), using the modified \(\pi_i\) from now on.

Next construct units \(\delta_i\in\Lambda\setminus\mathfrak q\), coefficients \(\lambda_{ij}\in\Lambda\), and an essentially smooth Artinian enlargement \(D\to D'\) with flat local map \(D'\to\overline L\), such that \[
(\delta_i\pi_i)^{2N}=\sum_j a_j\lambda_{ij}
\quad\hbox{in }\Lambda,
\tag{D.37b}
\] and both \(\delta_i\) and \(\lambda_{ij}\) have images in \(D'\). We additionally require equal kernels for \(\delta_i\pi_i\) and its square modulo the earlier \((\delta_h\pi_h)^e\). A flat local map into the nonzero local ring \(\overline L\) is faithfully flat, and hence injective, by \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/d02d0a3669f42579db037cd44de1d113fdd770a1/docs/courses/AG-CA/src/faithful-flatness-and-the-local-criterion-for-flatness.md}{AG-CA-08, Theorem 2.2}. Thus every ring in this construction may be regarded as a subring of \(\overline L\). In particular all relations among the chosen \(A\)-generator images already hold in \(D\), so there is a map \(A\to D\).

Suppose the construction has reached \(i-1\). The element \(\pi_i^N\) lies in \(H\overline L\); faithful flatness contracts this ideal to \(HD'\). Write \(\pi_i^N=\sum_j a_jd_j\) in \(D'\), and lift the \(d_j\) to \(u_j\in L\). The error lies in \(\mathfrak m^n\subset H\mathfrak m^{n-N}\), since \(n\ge N\). Thus choose \(v_j\in\mathfrak m^{n-N}\) with \[
\pi_i^N=\sum_j a_j(u_j+v_j)\quad\hbox{in }L.
\] Set \(w_j=\pi_i^N(u_j+v_j)\). Then \(\pi_i^{2N}=\sum_j a_jw_j\), and the residue of \(w_j\) in \(\overline L\) is \(\pi_i^Nd_j\), because \(\pi_i^Nv_j\in\mathfrak m^n\).

Here is the global denominator calculation. Choose \(s_0\notin\mathfrak q\) so that every \(s_0^{2N}w_j\) is represented by \(\widetilde\mu_j\in\Lambda\). The error \[
r_i=(s_0\pi_i)^{2N}-\sum_j a_j\widetilde\mu_j
\] vanishes in \(L\). Hence some \(v\notin\mathfrak q\) annihilates \(r_i\), by the fraction-zero criterion of \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/main/docs/courses/AG-RG/AG-RG-S01.md}{S01, Lemma 1.1}. Set \(s=s_0v\) and \(\mu_j=v^{2N}\widetilde\mu_j\). Now \((s\pi_i)^{2N}=\sum_j a_j\mu_j\) in \(\Lambda\), and \(\mu_j/s^{2N}=w_j\) in \(L\).

Use \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-smoothing-lemma-enlarge-solution-modulo]{D.36} to put \(s^h\) in a further \(D'\), for some \(h>0\). Replace \(s\) by \(s^h\) and \(\mu_j\) by \(s_{\rm old}^{2N(h-1)}\mu_j\). The exact equation survives, and the new coefficient residue is \(s^{2N}\pi_i^Nd_j\in D'\). In \(L/((\delta_1\pi_1)^e,\ldots,(\delta_{i-1}\pi_{i-1})^e)\), multiplication by \(s\pi_i\) is injective, because the preceding entries are powers of a regular parameter list scaled by units. Apply D.31 on the corresponding finite \(\Lambda\)-module to obtain \(s'\notin\mathfrak q\) for which every \((s')^q s\pi_i\), \(q>0\), has equal global kernels with its square. D.36 puts one such \((s')^q\) in an enlargement of \(D'\). Take \[
\delta_i=(s')^qs,\qquad \lambda_{ij}=(s')^{2Nq}\mu_j.
\] This proves (D.37b), the residue assertions, and the required target kernel equality. Later enlargements retain all earlier assertions. The finite induction constructs the full list; when \(d=0\) this construction is empty and \(D'=D\).

Map \(R\to\Lambda\) by the given \(P\)-map and \(t_i\mapsto\delta_i\). Give \(R\) its \(P_0\)-structure by \(x_i\mapsto\gamma_i\). Equation (D.37b) defines \(B\to\Lambda\) by \(x_i\mapsto\delta_i\pi_i\) and \(z_{ij}\mapsto\lambda_{ij}\). The retraction defines \(C\to\Lambda\), and these maps induce \[
C_R=C\otimes_{P_0}R\longrightarrow\Lambda.
\] Every \(a_j\)-chart of \(C_R/R\) is smooth, so the singular radical of this new input contains \(\mathfrak h_A\). A resolution over \(R\) returns to one over \(k\): finite presentation composes with the polynomial base, and smooth composition gives \(H_{T/R}\subset H_{T/k}\).

Let \(I=(\gamma_1^e,\ldots,\gamma_d^e)\subset R\). \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-smoothing-lemma-strictly-standard-base-change]{D.7} transports the strictly standard elements \(x_i^c\) to \(\gamma_i^c\). The arranged source and target kernel equalities hold also for their \(c\)-th powers, by the kernel induction in D.33. \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-smoothing-lemma-lift-solution]{D.28} therefore lifts a resolution modulo \(I\) to an \(R\)-resolution. For \(d=0\), \(I=0\) and this lifting step is unnecessary.

We construct the quotient resolution explicitly. Put \(J=(\pi_1^e,\ldots,\pi_d^e)\subset P\), and let \(\mathfrak r\) be the inverse image of \(\mathfrak q\) in \(R\). Each \(t_i\notin\mathfrak r\), since \(\delta_i\notin\mathfrak q\). Consequently \[
IR_{\mathfrak r}=JR_{\mathfrak r},
\qquad IL=JL.
\tag{D.37c}
\] The parameters generate \(\mathfrak pP_{\mathfrak p}\) and \(\mathfrak m\). The bound \(n\ge d(e-1)+1\) in (D.37a) gives, by expansion into monomials, \[
\mathfrak p^nP_{\mathfrak p}\subset JP_{\mathfrak p},
\qquad\mathfrak m^n\subset JL.
\tag{D.37d}
\] For \(d=0\), both maximal ideals are zero, so these containments hold as well.

Set \(S_1=S_0[t_1,\ldots,t_d]\). Bars below denote elements in \(D'\subset\overline L\). Each \(\overline\delta_i\) is a unit of \(D'\): its image is a unit and the map is local. Define \[
B\longrightarrow D'[t_1,\ldots,t_d],
\qquad
x_i\longmapsto\overline\pi_it_i,\quad
z_{ij}\longmapsto
\overline\lambda_{ij}\overline\delta_i^{-2N}t_i^{2N}.
\tag{D.37e}
\] Injectivity of \(D'\to\overline L\) transports (D.37b) to \(D'\). The image of the \(i\)-th defining equation in (D.37e) is therefore \[
t_i^{2N}\left(\overline\pi_i^{2N}
-\overline\delta_i^{-2N}\sum_j\overline a_j\overline\lambda_{ij}\right)=0.
\] Its restriction to \(P_0\) is exactly the prescribed \(x_i\mapsto\pi_it_i\) in \(S_1\), so the map extends to \(B\otimes_{P_0}S_1\). Evaluation \(t_i\mapsto\overline\delta_i\) recovers the prescribed images \(\delta_i\pi_i,\lambda_{ij}\) in \(\overline L\).

The map \(S_0\to D'\) is essentially smooth by construction and composition. Express it as a localization of a smooth finitely presented \(S_0\)-algebra. Localization is the filtered colimit of its principal localizations at finite products of the inverted elements. These stages are smooth, and adjoining the \(t_i\) gives smooth \(S_1\)-stages with colimit \(D'[t_i]\). Finite presentation and \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-when-colimit]{F.90} factor (D.37e) through one smooth \(S_1\)-stage \(T\), followed by the specified map to \(\overline L\). Composing with \(C\to B\) gives the same smooth factorization for \(C\otimes_{P_0}S_1\).

By (D.37d) there are quotient maps \(S_1\to P_{\mathfrak p}[t_i]/J\) and \(\overline L\to L/JL\). Base changing \(T\) gives a smooth factorization over \(P_{\mathfrak p}[t_i]/J\). Localize further at \(\mathfrak r\). Every denominator then has a unit image in the local target, so its map extends. By (D.37c) this is a smooth factorization of the localized problem modulo \(I\).

The target \(L/JL\) has nilpotent maximal ideal: degree \(d(e-1)+1\) monomials vanish. Thus its dimension is zero. If the singular radical of the unlocalized quotient input escapes the image of \(\mathfrak q\), the identity factorization resolves that quotient. Otherwise this prime is minimal over the radical, and \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-smoothing-lemma-delocalize-height-zero]{D.30} delocalizes the smooth factorization just obtained. D.28 then lifts it before quotienting by \(I\). Finally the polynomial change of base returns the resolution to \(k\). All constructions above include \(d=0\), empty parameter lists, and the specified target maps. ∎

\subsection{The main theorem}\label{AG-RG-S05-the-main-theorem}

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-smoothing-section-main}

The final argument selects a maximal unsuccessful singular radical and uses the local resolutions to enlarge it, giving a contradiction.

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-smoothing-theorem-popescu}

\subsubsection{Theorem D.38: popescu}\label{AG-RG-S05-theorem-d.38-popescu}

Reading source: \href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/07GC}{Stacks, Tag 07GC}.

If \(R\to\Lambda\) is a regular map between Noetherian rings, then \(\Lambda\), as an \(R\)-algebra, is a filtered colimit of smooth \(R\)-algebras.

\textbf{Proof.} The reduction \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-smoothing-lemma-reduce-to-field]{D.26} reduces the assertion to a field \(k\) and a Noetherian geometrically regular \(k\)-algebra \(\Lambda\). By \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-smoothing-lemma-final-solve]{D.8}, it is enough that every finite type factorization \(k\to A\to\Lambda\) can be followed by \(A\to B\to\Lambda\) with \(B\) finite type and \(\mathfrak h_B=\Lambda\). All such algebras are finitely presented by the Hilbert theorem.

Assume some factorization has no such successor. Among the singular radicals of all these unsuccessful factorizations choose a maximal one, say \(\mathfrak h_A\). A nonempty collection of ideals in a Noetherian ring has a maximal member: otherwise successive strict enlargements would contradict the ascending chain condition. The ideal \(\mathfrak h_A\) is proper, since if it were \(\Lambda\), \(A\) itself would be a successor.

There is a prime \(\mathfrak q\) minimal over \(\mathfrak h_A\). Here are the existence details. Zorn's lemma first gives an ideal maximal among the proper ideals containing \(\mathfrak h_A\): a chain union is still proper, since it cannot contain \(1\). Such an ideal is prime, because if \(a\) is outside it, the ideal and \(a\) generate \(1\), and multiplication of that relation by \(b\) shows that \(ab\) in the ideal forces \(b\) into it. Now order all primes containing \(\mathfrak h_A\) by reverse inclusion. A chain intersection is a proper ideal containing \(\mathfrak h_A\), and is prime: if \(ab\) belongs to the intersection while \(a,b\) do not, two members excluding them have a smaller member excluding both, contradicting its primality. Zorn's lemma therefore supplies the desired minimal prime.

Geometric regularity makes \(\Lambda_{\mathfrak q}\) regular local. In positive characteristic \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-smoothing-lemma-resolve-general]{D.37} resolves this problem. In characteristic zero every field extension is separable in the sense of \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-definition-separable-field-extension]{F.5}: each finitely generated subextension has a finite transcendence basis followed by a finite algebraic extension, whose irreducible polynomials have nonzero derivatives and hence distinct roots. Thus \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-smoothing-lemma-resolve-special]{D.33} resolves it in that case.

In either case obtain \(A\to C\to\Lambda\) with \[
\mathfrak h_A\subset\mathfrak h_C,\qquad
\mathfrak h_C\not\subset\mathfrak q.
\] Because \(\mathfrak h_A\subset\mathfrak q\), the first inclusion is strict. Maximality of the unsuccessful ideal \(\mathfrak h_A\) means that \(C\) has a successor with unit singular radical. Composing its factorization with \(A\to C\) supplies the forbidden successor of \(A\), a contradiction. Hence every finite type input has the required successor. D.8 supplies the smooth filtered presentation, and D.26 returns the assertion to the original regular map. ∎

\section{5. Foundation statements and their free-source proofs}\label{AG-RG-S05-foundation-statements-and-their-free-source-proofs}

The flatness arguments use projective resolutions, the two ways of computing Tor, and the connecting maps of a short exact sequence. These constructions are proved for arbitrary modules in \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/main/docs/courses/AG-RG/AG-RG-S01.md\#tor-calculus}{Algebra and sheaf cohomology before reductive groups, Lemma 1.A (Reductive group schemes)}.

We begin with the two-term conormal complex and the field and dimension conventions used below. The numbered arguments then establish the presentation, flatness, regularity and completion results needed in Section 4. Section 6 collects the earlier algebra lessons used along the way.

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-cotangent-context}

\textbf{The two-term conormal complex.} A polynomial presentation \(P=R[X_s]\twoheadrightarrow S\) with kernel \(I\) gives the complex \([I/I^2\to\bigoplus_s S\,dX_s]\), in degrees \(-1\) and \(0\); the map sends the class of \(f\) to \(df\). We denote it by \(\operatorname{NL}(P\to S)\). One presentation is always available: take a variable \(X_s\) for each \(s\in S\) and send it to \(s\). For maps \(R\to R'\) and \(S\to S'\) forming a commuting square, a map of presentations is a compatible map of their polynomial algebras lifting \(S\to S'\). The comparison and homotopy formulas below prove that the resulting two-term object does not depend on the presentation. The localization argument concerns this complex itself.

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-inseparable-exponent-context}

\textbf{The inseparable exponent calculation.} Let \(\alpha\) be algebraic over a field \(F\) of characteristic \(p\). Its irreducible polynomial is \(f(T)=g(T^{p^s})\) for a maximal \(s\geq0\). Such \(s\) exists because \(f\) has finite positive degree. Maximality gives \(g'\ne0\). Any factorization of \(g\) would give a factorization of \(f\), so \(g\) is irreducible, and its relatively prime derivative makes it separable. The element \(\alpha^{p^s}\) is a root of \(g\), hence is separable over \(F\). This proves the field-theoretic exponent choice used in the enlargement argument.

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-dimension-context}

\textbf{Dimension conventions.} The dimension of a ring is the supremum of the lengths of its finite chains of primes. For a prime \(\mathfrak p\), its height is \(\dim R_{\mathfrak p}\). In a Noetherian local ring of dimension \(d\), a system of parameters consists of \(d\) elements whose ideal has radical the maximal ideal. Existence is proved in AG-CA-11, Theorem 2.1. Minimal primes and irreducible components are treated in AG-CA-01, Theorem 4.1, Lemma 4.2 and Theorem 4.3. Polynomial-ring dimension and the finite-type domain height formula are AG-CA-11, Theorem 6.1 and AG-CA-09, Theorem 4.3, respectively.

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-definition-lci}

\subsubsection{Definition F.1: lci}\label{AG-RG-S05-definition-f.1-lci}

Reading sources: \href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/00SL}{Stacks, Tag 00SL}; \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/unofficial-stacks-project-ai-drafts/blob/565b10e987aba5969b21145a0833f42d69f96790/algebra.tex\#L37874-L37881}{AI Integrated Stacks, pinned Algebra, lines 37874--37881}.

For an arbitrary ring map \(R\to S\), the word \emph{syntomic} means that the following three requirements hold together: \(S\) is a finitely presented \(R\)-algebra, it is flat as an \(R\)-module, and, for every \(\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Spec}R\), the fibre algebra \[S(\mathfrak p)=S\otimes_R\kappa(\mathfrak p)\] is a local complete intersection over \(\kappa(\mathfrak p)\) in the sense of \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-definition-lci-field]{F.2}. The phrase \emph{flat local complete intersection over \(R\)} has this same meaning.

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-definition-lci-field}

\subsubsection{Definition F.2: lci field}\label{AG-RG-S05-definition-f.2-lci-field}

Reading sources: \href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/00S9}{Stacks, Tag 00S9}; \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/unofficial-stacks-project-ai-drafts/blob/565b10e987aba5969b21145a0833f42d69f96790/algebra.tex\#L37249-L37264}{AI Integrated Stacks, pinned Algebra, lines 37249--37264}.

Let \(S\) be a finite-type algebra over a field \(k\). To call \(S\) a \emph{global complete intersection over \(k\)} is to require a finite presentation \[S=k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/(f_1,\ldots,f_c)\] for which its Krull dimension is exactly \(n-c\). A \emph{local complete intersection over \(k\)} means that one can cover \(\operatorname{Spec}S\) by principal opens \(D(g_i)\), with each algebra \(S_{g_i}\) satisfying this global condition. The zero algebra is included among the global complete intersections by convention; it therefore causes no exception when an open or a fibre is empty.

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-definition-lci-local-ring}

\subsubsection{Definition F.3: lci local ring}\label{AG-RG-S05-definition-f.3-lci-local-ring}

Reading sources: \href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/00SD}{Stacks, Tag 00SD}; \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/unofficial-stacks-project-ai-drafts/blob/565b10e987aba5969b21145a0833f42d69f96790/algebra.tex\#L37446-L37458}{AI Integrated Stacks, pinned Algebra, lines 37446--37458}.

Suppose \(S\) is a local \(k\)-algebra essentially of finite type, where \(k\) is a field. The condition \emph{complete intersection over \(k\)} asks for a regular local \(k\)-algebra \(R\), itself essentially of finite type, together with a regular sequence \[f_1,\ldots,f_c\in\mathfrak m_R\] and a \(k\)-algebra isomorphism \(R/(f_1,\ldots,f_c)\cong S\). Thus the presenting ring is local and regular, and the equations lie in its maximal ideal. All these requirements belong to the definition.

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-definition-relative-global-complete-intersection}

\subsubsection{Definition F.4: relative global complete intersection}\label{AG-RG-S05-definition-f.4-relative-global-complete-intersection}

Reading sources: \href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/00SP}{Stacks, Tag 00SP}; \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/unofficial-stacks-project-ai-drafts/blob/565b10e987aba5969b21145a0833f42d69f96790/algebra.tex\#L37943-L37951}{AI Integrated Stacks, pinned Algebra, lines 37943--37951}.

For a ring map \(R\to S\), a \emph{relative global complete-intersection presentation} consists of \[S=R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/(f_1,\ldots,f_c)\] such that, for each \(\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Spec}R\) with nonempty fibre, the ring \(S\otimes_R\kappa(\mathfrak p)\) has dimension \(n-c\). The map is a \emph{relative global complete intersection} if it has at least one such presentation. When a particular displayed presentation is called a relative global complete intersection, the fibre condition refers to its displayed values of \(n\) and \(c\). Empty fibres impose no dimension condition.

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-definition-separable-field-extension}

\subsubsection{Definition F.5: separable field extension}\label{AG-RG-S05-definition-f.5-separable-field-extension}

Reading sources: \href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/030O}{Stacks, Tag 030O}; \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/unofficial-stacks-project-ai-drafts/blob/565b10e987aba5969b21145a0833f42d69f96790/algebra.tex\#L10135-L10146}{AI Integrated Stacks, pinned Algebra, lines 10135--10146}.

Consider a field extension \(K/k\). It is \emph{separably generated} when there is a transcendence basis \((x_i)_{i\in I}\) such that \[K/k(x_i\mid i\in I)\] is algebraic and separable. The index set may be infinite. The condition \emph{separable over \(k\)} used here is tested on every intermediate field \(K'\) finitely generated over \(k\): each extension \(K'/k\) must be separably generated in the preceding sense. These are the two field-extension conditions used in the separable and inseparable arguments.

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-definition-smooth}

\subsubsection{Definition F.6: smooth}\label{AG-RG-S05-definition-f.6-smooth}

Reading sources: \href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/00T2}{Stacks, Tag 00T2}; \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/unofficial-stacks-project-ai-drafts/blob/565b10e987aba5969b21145a0833f42d69f96790/algebra.tex\#L38526-L38533}{AI Integrated Stacks, pinned Algebra, lines 38526--38533}.

Smoothness of \(R\to S\) requires finite presentation together with the following condition on the naive cotangent complex: \[H_1(\operatorname{NL}_{S/R})=0,\qquad
\Omega_{S/R}\text{ is a finite projective }S\text{-module}.\] Equivalently, that two-term complex is quasi-isomorphic to a finite projective module concentrated in degree zero. To verify this equivalence directly, map the two-term complex to its degree-zero cokernel. This map induces an isomorphism on degree-zero homology; it is a quasi-isomorphism exactly when the degree-minus-one kernel, denoted \(H_1\), vanishes. Its cokernel is \(\Omega_{S/R}\). Presentation independence is proved in \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-NL-homotopy]{F.11}.

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-definition-smooth-at-prime}

\subsubsection{Definition F.7: smooth at prime}\label{AG-RG-S05-definition-f.7-smooth-at-prime}

Reading sources: \href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/00TB}{Stacks, Tag 00TB}; \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/unofficial-stacks-project-ai-drafts/blob/565b10e987aba5969b21145a0833f42d69f96790/algebra.tex\#L38953-L38960}{AI Integrated Stacks, pinned Algebra, lines 38953--38960}.

Given \(R\to S\) and \(\mathfrak q\in\operatorname{Spec}S\), \emph{smoothness at \(\mathfrak q\)} means that some principal neighbourhood of this point has a smooth coordinate algebra over \(R\). Explicitly, there must be \[g\in S\setminus\mathfrak q\quad\text{with}\quad R\to S_g\text{ smooth}.\] This definition applies to any ring map; finite presentation is required of the witnessing localization through \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-definition-smooth]{F.6}.

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-definition-unramified}

\subsubsection{Definition F.8: unramified}\label{AG-RG-S05-definition-f.8-unramified}

Reading sources: \href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/00UT}{Stacks, Tag 00UT}; \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/unofficial-stacks-project-ai-drafts/blob/565b10e987aba5969b21145a0833f42d69f96790/algebra.tex\#L42897-L42912}{AI Integrated Stacks, pinned Algebra, lines 42897--42912}.

For \(R\to S\), both unramified conditions require \(\Omega_{S/R}=0\). Their finiteness requirements differ: \emph{unramified} requires finite type, whereas \emph{G-unramified} requires finite presentation.

At a prime \(\mathfrak q\) of \(S\), each condition means that it holds on some principal neighbourhood \(D(g)\) of \(\mathfrak q\). Thus \emph{unramified at \(\mathfrak q\)} requires \(g\notin\mathfrak q\) with \(S_g/R\) of finite type and \(\Omega_{S_g/R}=0\); \emph{G-unramified at \(\mathfrak q\)} requires such a \(g\) with \(S_g/R\) finitely presented and the same differential-module vanishing.

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-CM-over-regular-flat}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.9: CM over regular flat}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.9-cm-over-regular-flat}

Reading source: \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/unofficial-stacks-project-ai-drafts/blob/565b10e987aba5969b21145a0833f42d69f96790/algebra.tex\#L34036-L34074}{AI Integrated Stacks, pinned Algebra, lines 34036--34074}.

Let \(R\to S\) be local, with both rings Noetherian and local. Suppose \(R\) is regular, \(S\) is Cohen--Macaulay, and \[\dim S=\dim R+\dim(S/\mathfrak m_RS).\] Then \(S\) is flat as an \(R\)-module.

\textbf{Proof.} We reduce the dimension of the regular source by one while preserving the dimension equality. Write \(d=\dim R\). If \(d=0\), regularity says \(\mathfrak m_R/\mathfrak m_R^2=0\). Nakayama, \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-NAK]{F.10}, applies to the finite ideal \(\mathfrak m_R\) and gives \(\mathfrak m_R=0\). Thus \(R\) is a field, and a basis makes every \(R\)-module free, hence flat.

For \(d>0\), consider the finitely many associated primes of \(S\). The Cohen--Macaulay component theorem AG-CA-12, Theorem 4.1, says that they are its minimal primes \(\mathfrak q_i\) and that \(\dim(S/\mathfrak q_i)=\dim S\). None contains \(\mathfrak m_RS\). Indeed that containment would give a surjection \(S/\mathfrak m_RS\to S/\mathfrak q_i\), forcing the dimension of the latter to be at most that of the former, whereas the hypothesis gives \[\dim(S/\mathfrak m_RS)=\dim S-d<\dim S.\] Consequently every contraction \(\mathfrak p_i=R\cap\mathfrak q_i\) is strictly smaller than \(\mathfrak m_R\).

The prime-avoidance calculation \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-silly]{F.80} now chooses \[x\in\mathfrak m_R\setminus\bigl(\mathfrak m_R^2\cup\textstyle\bigcup_i\mathfrak p_i\bigr).\] To check its hypotheses, \(\mathfrak m_R\) is not contained in any \(\mathfrak p_i\), and is not contained in \(\mathfrak m_R^2\), since otherwise Nakayama would again give \(d=0\). There is just one nonprime ideal in this avoidance list.

The element \(x\) avoids all associated primes of \(S\), so it is a nonzerodivisor on \(S\). The complete regular-sequence and Cohen--Macaulay arguments of AG-CA-12, Sections 2 and 4, make \(S/xS\) Cohen--Macaulay with dimension \(\dim S-1\). AG-CA-14, Theorem 1.1 and Corollary 1.2, make \(x\) a nonzerodivisor of \(R\) and \(R/xR\) regular of dimension \(d-1\). The quotient map is still local, and its closed fibre is \(S/\mathfrak m_RS\). Hence it satisfies \[\dim(S/xS)=\dim(R/xR)+\dim(S/\mathfrak m_RS).\] Induction gives flatness of \(S/xS\) over \(R/xR\).

The two-term free resolution of \(R/xR\) has differential multiplication by \(x\). Its tensor with \(S\) therefore has zero first homology, because \(x\) is a nonzerodivisor on \(S\). Thus \(\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(R/xR,S)=0\). Apply the entire proper-ideal local criterion AG-CA-08, Corollary 4.4, with ideal \((x)\) and module \(S\), which is finite over the stipulated Noetherian local overring \(S\). The quotient is flat and its required Tor vanishes. This proves flatness over \(R\) and completes the induction. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-NAK}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.10: NAK}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.10-nak}

Reading sources: \href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/00DV}{Stacks, Tag 00DV}; \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/unofficial-stacks-project-ai-drafts/blob/565b10e987aba5969b21145a0833f42d69f96790/algebra.tex\#L3732-L3813}{AI Integrated Stacks, pinned Algebra, lines 3732--3813}.

For a ring \(R\), an ideal \(I\), and an \(R\)-module \(M\), the following twelve forms of Nakayama's lemma hold. Write \(\operatorname{rad}(R)\) for the Jacobson radical.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  If \(M\) is finite and \(M=IM\), some \(f\in1+I\) annihilates \(M\).
\item
  Under the conditions of (1), \(I\subset\operatorname{rad}(R)\) implies \(M=0\).
\item
  If \(N,N'\subset M\), \(M=N+IN'\) and \(N'\) is finite, some \(f\in1+I\) satisfies \(fM\subset N\) and \(M_f=N_f\).
\item
  Under the conditions of (3), \(I\subset\operatorname{rad}(R)\) implies \(M=N\).
\item
  For a module map \(N\to M\) with \(M\) finite, surjectivity of \(N/IN\to M/IM\) implies surjectivity of \(N_f\to M_f\) for some \(f\in1+I\).
\item
  Under the conditions of (5), \(I\subset\operatorname{rad}(R)\) makes the original map \(N\to M\) surjective.
\item
  If \(M\) is finite and the images of \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) generate \(M/IM\), these same elements generate \(M_f\) over \(R_f\) for some \(f\in1+I\).
\item
  Under the conditions of (7), \(I\subset\operatorname{rad}(R)\) implies that \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\) generate \(M\).
\item
  If \(I\) is nilpotent, \(M=IM\) implies \(M=0\), with no finiteness requirement on \(M\).
\item
  If \(I\) is nilpotent and \(M=N+IN'\) for submodules \(N,N'\), then \(M=N\), with no finiteness requirement on \(N'\).
\item
  If \(I\) is nilpotent and \(N/IN\to M/IM\) is surjective, then \(N\to M\) is surjective, without module finiteness assumptions.
\item
  If \(I\) is nilpotent and a possibly infinite family \((x_\alpha)\) generates \(M/IM\), it generates \(M\).
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Proof.} The determinant assertion \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-NAK]{F.10 / nakayama}, namely (1), supplies all finite-module cases. Choose a generating column \(y=(y_1,\ldots,y_r)^{\mathsf t}\) of \(M\). The equality \(M=IM\) expresses each \(y_i\) as an \(I\)-linear combination of the \(y_j\), so for a matrix \(Z\) with entries in \(I\) we have \((1_r-Z)y=0\). By the proved adjugate identity \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-matrix-left-inverse]{F.70}, \[\operatorname{adj}(1_r-Z)(1_r-Z)=\det(1_r-Z)1_r.\] Consequently \(f=\det(1_r-Z)\) kills every generator. Reduction modulo \(I\) gives \(f\equiv1\), as required. An empty generating list uses \(f=1\).

If \(I\subset\operatorname{rad}(R)\), \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-contained-in-radical]{F.34} proves that every element of \(1+I\) is a unit. Multiplying \(fM=0\) by its inverse proves (2).

For (3) and (4), put \(Q=M/N\). Since the image of \(N'\) generates \(Q\) and \(N'\) is finite, \(Q\) is finite. The hypothesis \(M=N+IN'\) gives \(Q=IQ\). Apply (1) to obtain \(fQ=0\), equivalently \(fM\subset N\), and apply (2) for the equality \(Q=0\) when the radical condition holds. Once \(fM\subset N\), any fraction \(m/f^a\) in \(M_f\) equals \((fm)/f^{a+1}\) and comes from \(N_f\). The inclusion \(N_f\subset M_f\) follows from exact localization. Thus the stated equality of localized modules is proved as well.

For a map \(u:N\to M\), let \(Q=\operatorname{coker}u\). Right exactness identifies its quotient \(Q/IQ\) with the cokernel of \(N/IN\to M/IM\). The assumed surjectivity therefore gives \(Q=IQ\). If \(M\) is finite, so is \(Q\). Assertion (1) makes \(Q_f=0\), and exact localization makes \(u_f\) surjective, proving (5). Assertion (2) gives \(Q=0\) in the radical case, proving (6). Apply these conclusions to \(R^n\to M\), \((r_i)\mapsto\sum r_ix_i\), to get (7) and (8).

Finally suppose \(I^a=0\). Repeated substitution into \(M=IM\) yields \(M=I^aM=0\), proving (9) for an arbitrary module. In (10), \(Q=M/N\) satisfies \(Q=IQ\), whether or not the image of \(N'\) is finite, so (9) gives \(Q=0\). For (11), take the same cokernel \(Q\) of the given map and use its zero quotient modulo \(I\). For (12), quotient by the submodule generated by all \(x_\alpha\); its quotient modulo \(I\) is zero, so (9) kills it. This proves all twelve assertions, including empty generating lists and arbitrary nilpotent ideals. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-NL-homotopy}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.11: NL homotopy}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.11-nl-homotopy}

Reading sources: \href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/00S1}{Stacks, Tag 00S1}; \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/unofficial-stacks-project-ai-drafts/blob/565b10e987aba5969b21145a0833f42d69f96790/algebra.tex\#L36700-L36815}{AI Integrated Stacks, pinned Algebra, lines 36700--36815}.

Let \(u:R\to R'\) and \(\phi:S\to S'\) be compatible with the structure maps \(R\to S\) and \(R'\to S'\). Choose polynomial presentations \(\alpha:P\twoheadrightarrow S\) and \(\alpha':P'\twoheadrightarrow S'\), allowing arbitrary sets of variables. Then:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  There is a map \(\psi:P\to P'\) whose restriction to \(R\) is \(u\) and for which \(\alpha'\psi=\phi\alpha\).
\item
  Any two such maps induce chain-homotopic maps \(\operatorname{NL}(\alpha)\to\operatorname{NL}(\alpha')\).
\item
  Composing presentation maps composes their induced complex maps.
\item
  If \(u\) and \(\phi\) are isomorphisms, every induced map is a homotopy equivalence and a quasi-isomorphism.
\end{enumerate}

In particular the comparison with the \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-cotangent-context]{canonical presentation} identifies \(\operatorname{NL}(\alpha)\) with \(\operatorname{NL}_{S/R}\) up to homotopy, and these identifications respect the stated functorialities up to homotopy.

\textbf{Proof.} Write \(P=R[x_a\mid a\in E]\), \(I=\ker\alpha\) and \(I'=\ker\alpha'\). For each \(a\), choose a polynomial in \(P'\) lifting \(\phi(\alpha(x_a))\). Sending the variables to these choices and the coefficients through \(u\) gives \(\psi\) by the polynomial universal property. Each polynomial uses only finitely many variables, so this construction also works when \(E\) is infinite. It proves (1).

The two terms of the complex are \[C_1=I/I^2,\qquad C_0=\bigoplus_{a\in E}S\,dx_a,\qquad
d:C_1\to C_0,\quad [f]\mapsto df.\] The map is well-defined because \(d(fg)=f\,dg+g\,df\) vanishes modulo \(I\) when \(f,g\in I\). Its target counterpart is \(C'_1=I'/(I')^2\to C'_0=\Omega_{P'/R'}\otimes_{P'}S'\). Regard these target modules as \(S\)-modules through \(\phi\). The induced maps are \[\psi_1([f])=[\psi(f)],\qquad
\psi_0(dx_a)=d\psi(x_a).\] The map on \(I/I^2\) is well-defined since \(\psi(I)\subset I'\). On a monomial the product rule gives \(\psi_0(df)=d\psi(f)\), since differentiation over \(R'\) kills the transformed coefficient from \(R\). Addition gives this identity for every polynomial. Thus these are complex maps.

For another choice \(\chi\), both evaluations of any \(p\in P\) have the same residue in \(S'\). Set \[D(p)=\psi(p)-\chi(p)\pmod{(I')^2}\in I'/(I')^2.\] Both choices give the same action of \(P\) on this module: their difference lies in \(I'\), which kills \(I'/(I')^2\). That action factors through \(S\), because the image of \(I\) is in \(I'\). The exact product identity \[\psi(pq)-\chi(pq)
=\psi(p)\bigl(\psi(q)-\chi(q)\bigr)
 +\bigl(\psi(p)-\chi(p)\bigr)\chi(q)\] therefore becomes the derivation rule for \(D\). It is additive and vanishes on \(R\). Define the \(S\)-linear map \[h:C_0\longrightarrow C'_1,\qquad h(dx_a)=D(x_a).\] Expanding a monomial by the derivation rule shows \(h(dp)=D(p)\) for every polynomial \(p\), including constant and empty-variable cases.

Both homotopy identities can now be checked without a diagram omission. For \(f\in I\), \[h(d[f])=D(f)=\psi_1([f])-\chi_1([f]).\] For each free differential generator, \[d'h(dx_a)=d\bigl(\psi(x_a)-\chi(x_a)\bigr)
=\psi_0(dx_a)-\chi_0(dx_a).\] The first identity holds on all relation classes and the second on a free basis, so \[\psi_1-\chi_1=hd,\qquad \psi_0-\chi_0=d'h.\] These are exactly a chain homotopy, proving (2).

For a subsequent presentation map \(\eta:P'\to P''\), the relation-class map sends \([f]\) successively to \([\psi(f)]\) and \([\eta\psi(f)]\). The differential map sends \(dx_a\) to \(d\psi(x_a)\) and then to \(d(\eta\psi(x_a))\), by the same monomial product-rule calculation. Thus the composite equals the map of the composite presentation, proving (3).

If the two structural square maps are isomorphisms, apply (1) to their inverse square to get a presentation map in the reverse direction. Both composites lie over identity squares. By (2), their complex maps are homotopic to the respective identity maps. This is the required homotopy equivalence. A homotopy changes a degree-one map by \(hd\) and a degree-zero map by \(d'h\); the former is zero on the kernel and the latter has zero class in the cokernel. Thus homotopic maps act equally on both homology modules. The two reverse maps consequently induce inverse isomorphisms on kernel and cokernel, proving the quasi-isomorphism assertion. Taking identity structural maps and the canonical polynomial presentation proves the last assertion, with composition compatibility already established. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-Noetherian-field-extension}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.12: Noetherian field extension}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.12-noetherian-field-extension}

Reading source: \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/unofficial-stacks-project-ai-drafts/blob/565b10e987aba5969b21145a0833f42d69f96790/algebra.tex\#L6331-L6347}{AI Integrated Stacks, pinned Algebra, lines 6331--6347}.

If \(A\) is a Noetherian algebra over a field \(k\), then extending scalars from \(k\) to a finitely generated field extension \(K\) leaves it Noetherian.

\textbf{Proof.} Select a finite field-generating list \(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_r\) for \(K/k\), and put \(B=k[\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_r]\subset K\). The field of fractions of \(B\) is \(K\), since it contains both \(k\) and all chosen field generators. Therefore \[K=(B\setminus\{0\})^{-1}B.\] A polynomial surjection \(k[T_1,\ldots,T_r]\to B\) gives a surjection \(A[T_1,\ldots,T_r]\to A\otimes_kB\). The Hilbert-basis and quotient arguments in AG-CA-03, Theorem 2.1, make the latter algebra Noetherian.

Localizing it at the images of the nonzero elements of \(B\) gives \(A\otimes_kK\): the maps in both directions send a pure tensor with a fraction to that fraction of the corresponding pure tensor. They are inverse by the tensor and localization universal properties. AG-CA-03, Theorem 2.1, also proves that a localization of a Noetherian ring is Noetherian, giving the result. For a finite extension the same conclusion follows from its finite \(k\)-basis, which makes the tensor algebra a finite free \(A\)-module; its ideals are then finite \(A\)-submodules. The argument requires finite field generation, rather than finite degree. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-another-variant-local-criterion-flatness}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.13: another variant local criterion flatness}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.13-another-variant-local-criterion-flatness}

Reading source: \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/unofficial-stacks-project-ai-drafts/blob/565b10e987aba5969b21145a0833f42d69f96790/algebra.tex\#L24942-L24990}{AI Integrated Stacks, pinned Algebra, lines 24942--24990}.

Consider a commutative square of local homomorphisms between Noetherian local rings \[
\begin{array}{ccc}
R&\longrightarrow&R'\\
\downarrow&&\downarrow\\
S&\longrightarrow&S'.
\end{array}
\] Let \(I\subsetneq R\) and let \(M\) be a finite \(S\)-module. Put \(I'=IR'\) and \(M'=M\otimes_SS'\). Assume \(S'\) is a localization of \(B=S\otimes_RR'\), the module \(M/IM\) is flat over \(R/I\), and the natural map \[\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(M,R/I)
\longrightarrow\operatorname{Tor}_1^{R'}(M',R'/I')\] is zero. Then \(M'\) is flat over \(R'\).

\textbf{Proof.} We prove the needed Tor surjection and then apply the proper-ideal criterion. All free-resolution comparisons, naturality and balance used here are the complete arbitrary-module calculus of \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/main/docs/courses/AG-RG/AG-RG-S01.md\#tor-calculus}{AG-RG-S01, Lemma 1.A}.

Choose an \(R\)-free presentation \(0\to K\to F\to M\to0\), with no finiteness requirement on \(F\). Set \(T=\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(M,R/I)\), and let \(U\) be the image of \(K/IK\) in \(F/IF\). The free-presentation kernel formula gives exact sequences \[0\to T\to K/IK\to U\to0,\qquad
0\to U\to F/IF\to M/IM\to0.\] Since the last quotient is flat, the proved flat-syzygy criterion AG-CA-07, Theorem 6.1, makes \(U\) flat over \(R/I\). Tensoring the first sequence with an \(R/I\)-module \(N\) is consequently left exact. Tensoring the second is left exact because its last quotient is flat. Their kernel comparison gives the natural identity \[\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(M,N)=T\otimes_{R/I}N.\] This uses only the kernel formula for a free presentation; it does not assume that \(K\) is flat.

Take \(N=R'/I'\). In \(F_0=F\otimes_RR'\) let \(K_0\) be the image of \(K\otimes_RR'\). Then \(F_0\) is \(R'\)-free and \(F_0/K_0=M_0=M\otimes_RR'\). The surjection \(K\otimes_RR'\to K_0\) remains surjective after tensoring with \(R'/I'\). A cycle in \[\ker\bigl(K_0\otimes_{R'}R'/I'\to F_0\otimes_{R'}R'/I'\bigr)\] therefore has a lift in \(K\otimes_RR'/I'\). That lift maps to zero in the same free-module target, so is already a source cycle. Thus \[\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(M,R'/I')
\twoheadrightarrow\operatorname{Tor}_1^{R'}(M_0,R'/I').\] The preceding natural identity identifies its source with \(T\otimes_RR'\).

Write \(S'=V^{-1}B\), so \(M'=V^{-1}M_0\). We justify localization of the last Tor group with its natural \(B\)-action. Choose an \(R'\)-free resolution of \(R'/I'\). Balance identifies Tor with the homology after tensoring this resolution with \(M_0\); multiplication by \(B\) acts on each tensor term. Exact localization of \(B\)-modules commutes with kernels and images, and tensoring the same resolution with \(V^{-1}M_0\) is the localization of each term. Hence \[\operatorname{Tor}_1^{R'}(M',R'/I')
=V^{-1}\operatorname{Tor}_1^{R'}(M_0,R'/I').\] The preceding surjection is \(B\)-linear: multiplication by \(S\) acts by the functorial module maps on \(M\), while \(R'\) acts by scalar extension; the comparison calculus in Lemma 1.A makes these actions compatible. Localizing that surjection consequently gives \[V^{-1}(T\otimes_RR')\twoheadrightarrow
\operatorname{Tor}_1^{R'}(M',R'/I').\] The hypothesis says the original natural map from \(T\) to this target is zero. Its \(R'\)-linear extension is zero, and its extension across \(V\) is still zero, because the target is a module over \(V^{-1}B\). The displayed surjection is therefore the zero map, forcing its target to vanish.

Finally \(M'/I'M'\) is obtained from the flat \(R/I\)-module \(M/IM\) by scalar extension to \(R'/I'\) and localization at \(V\). Scalar extension preserves flatness. For the localization, an injection of \(R'/I'\)-modules remains injective after tensoring with the unlocalized flat module, and remains injective after exact localization of the resulting \(B\)-modules. This proves flatness of the localized quotient. The ideal \(I'\) is proper because \(R\to R'\) is local and \(I\subset\mathfrak m_R\). The module \(M'\) is finite over the stipulated Noetherian local ring \(S'\). AG-CA-08, Corollary 4.4, applies with this quotient flatness and the Tor vanishing just proved, and gives \(R'\)-flatness. No flatness assumption on \(R\to R'\) was added. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-base-change-relative-global-complete-intersection}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.14: base change relative global complete intersection}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.14-base-change-relative-global-complete-intersection}

Reading sources: \href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/00SS}{Stacks, Tag 00SS}; \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/unofficial-stacks-project-ai-drafts/blob/565b10e987aba5969b21145a0833f42d69f96790/algebra.tex\#L38076-L38106}{AI Integrated Stacks, pinned Algebra, lines 38076--38106}.

For a relative global complete-intersection presentation \[S=R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/(f_1,\ldots,f_c),\] all three of the following presentations have the same property:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  For any \(R\to R'\), the coefficientwise base change \(S\otimes_RR'=R'[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/(f_1,\ldots,f_c)\).
\item
  If \(g\in S\) is represented by \(h\in R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\), the principal localization \[S_g=R[x_1,\ldots,x_n,Z]/(f_1,\ldots,f_c,hZ-1).\]
\item
  If \(f\in R\) already has a unit image in \(S\), its presentation over \(R_f\) obtained by viewing the same equations in \(R_f[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\).
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Proof.} The fibre condition of \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-definition-relative-global-complete-intersection]{F.4} is a dimension condition. We first prove the field-extension calculation it requires. Let \(A\) be a finite-type \(k\)-algebra and \(K/k\) any field extension. Its nilradical is nilpotent and has finitely many minimal primes, by AG-CA-03, Proposition 2.2. Nilpotence persists after tensoring with \(K\) and does not affect dimension, since every prime contains every nilpotent element.

For the reduced quotient, let its minimal primes be \(\mathfrak q_1,\ldots,\mathfrak q_r\). Their product is zero, being contained in their zero intersection. After field extension the product of their extended ideals is still zero. Every prime contains one of these extended ideals: otherwise choose one element outside the prime from each ideal and multiply, contradicting primality. Thus the extended spectrum is the finite union of the closed spectra of \[(A/\mathfrak q_i)\otimes_kK.\] Every prime chain belongs to one of these closed sets, by choosing an ideal contained in its smallest prime. Dimension is therefore the maximum of their dimensions.

For each domain \(A/\mathfrak q_i\), Noether normalization AG-CA-09, Corollary 3.2, supplies an injective finite polynomial subalgebra \(k[t_1,\ldots,t_{d_i}]\). Exact field tensor preserves its injection and finite module generators. The corresponding \(K\)-algebra is thus integral and injective over \(K[t_1,\ldots,t_{d_i}]\). The entire integral-dimension theorem AG-CA-05, Theorem 5.1, gives dimension \(d_i\). Taking the maximum proves \(\dim(A\otimes_kK)=\dim A\). The zero algebra has empty spectrum and causes no nonempty-fibre case.

For (1), a fibre at a prime of \(R'\) is the scalar extension of the original fibre at its contraction, by associativity of tensor products and the induced residue-field inclusion. A nonempty new fibre therefore has the original dimension \(n-c\) by the calculation above. The displayed coefficientwise presentation proves (1).

For (2), the field case of \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-relative-global-complete-intersection-conormal]{F.77} proves that each original nonempty fibre is equidimensional of dimension \(n-c\). Indeed its minimal-prime height calculation applies to its polynomial presentation over the fibre field, without any Noetherian assumption on \(R\). A principal open in a surviving irreducible component has the same dimension as that component: its coordinate domain has unchanged fraction field, and AG-CA-09, Theorem 4.2, computes dimension by its transcendence degree. The localized nonempty fibre therefore still has dimension \(n-c\). Adjoining \(Z\) and \(hZ-1\) adds one variable and one equation, preserving the difference \(n-c\). Evaluation at \(Z=g^{-1}\) and adjoining that inverse give both directions of the claimed algebra isomorphism.

For (3), multiplication gives \(S\otimes_RR_f\cong S\), because the image of \(f\) already has an inverse. Its inverse sends \(s\) to \(s\otimes1\); the forced inverse of \(f\) verifies the other composite on fractions. Apply (1) to this base localization. All three arguments apply over arbitrary base rings and to empty fibres. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-change-base-NL}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.15: change base NL}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.15-change-base-nl}

Reading sources: \href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/00S4}{Stacks, Tag 00S4}; \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/unofficial-stacks-project-ai-drafts/blob/565b10e987aba5969b21145a0833f42d69f96790/algebra.tex\#L36963-L36981}{AI Integrated Stacks, pinned Algebra, lines 36963--36981}.

Let \(\alpha:P\twoheadrightarrow S\) be a polynomial presentation over \(R\), with an arbitrary variable set, and let \(R\to R'\) be flat. Put \(P'=P\otimes_RR'\), \(S'=S\otimes_RR'\), and let \(\alpha':P'\twoheadrightarrow S'\) be the resulting presentation. There is an isomorphism of two-term complexes \[\operatorname{NL}(\alpha)\otimes_RR'
=\operatorname{NL}(\alpha)\otimes_SS'
\cong\operatorname{NL}(\alpha').\] Consequently the canonical comparison \[\operatorname{NL}_{S/R}\otimes_SS'\longrightarrow
\operatorname{NL}_{S'/R'}\] is a homotopy equivalence.

\textbf{Proof.} Write \(I=\ker\alpha\). Tensoring \(0\to I\to P\to S\to0\) with the flat \(R'\) identifies \(I'=\ker\alpha'\) with \(I\otimes_RR'\). The square \((I')^2\) is the image of \(I^2\otimes_RR'\): a product of two elementary tensors from \(I'\) is the image of the product of their \(I\)-entries, and every product generator of \(I^2\) is obtained this way. Tensoring the quotient therefore gives \[I'/(I')^2\cong(I/I^2)\otimes_RR'.\] For any \(S\)-module \(E\), the pure-tensor maps \[E\otimes_SS'\longrightarrow E\otimes_RR',
\quad e\otimes(s\otimes r')\longmapsto se\otimes r',
\qquad e\otimes r'\longmapsto e\otimes(1\otimes r')\] are inverse. They give the other tensor description of the conormal term.

The polynomial differential term is free on the same \(dx_a\) over \(S\) and over \(S'\). Differentiating a polynomial commutes with changing its coefficients, since every monomial derivative multiplies by the same integer exponent and lowers the same variable degree. Thus both differentials agree on every relation class, proving the complex isomorphism. Each polynomial has finite support, so no finite-variable assumption enters.

Apply \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-NL-homotopy]{F.11} to compare each presentation with the canonical one. Tensoring its explicit homotopy identities with \(S'\) preserves those identities. The complex isomorphism just proved, between these comparison homotopy equivalences, therefore identifies the displayed canonical map up to homotopy and supplies its inverse up to homotopy. This proves the final assertion without assuming that \(S\) is flat over \(R\). ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-characterize-etale}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.16: characterize etale}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.16-characterize-etale}

Reading source: \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/unofficial-stacks-project-ai-drafts/blob/565b10e987aba5969b21145a0833f42d69f96790/algebra.tex\#L40942-L40975}{AI Integrated Stacks, pinned Algebra, lines 40942--40975}.

Let \(\mathfrak q\in\operatorname{Spec}S\) lie over \(\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Spec}R\). The map \(R\to S\) is étale at \(\mathfrak q\) if the following four hypotheses hold: it is finitely presented; \(R_{\mathfrak p}\to S_{\mathfrak q}\) is flat; the ideal \(\mathfrak pS_{\mathfrak q}\) is the maximal ideal of \(S_{\mathfrak q}\); and \(\kappa(\mathfrak q)/\kappa(\mathfrak p)\) is finite separable.

\textbf{Proof.} Write \(k=\kappa(\mathfrak p)\) and \(L=\kappa(\mathfrak q)\). The stipulated maximal-ideal equality identifies the local fibre ring with the field \(L\). Since \(L/k\) is finite, the complete isolated-fibre argument \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-isolated-point-fibre]{F.56} supplies a principal neighbourhood of \(\mathfrak q\) having no other point in this fibre. Its finite presentation is preserved by \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-cover-upstairs]{F.35}. On this neighbourhood the fibre algebra \(B=S\otimes_Rk\) has exactly one prime. It is local: every nonunit lies in a maximal ideal, and there is only one such ideal. Therefore its localization at that prime is \(B\) itself. This localization is the given local fibre \(L\), so \(B=L\).

We prove directly the smoothness and differential vanishing of this finite separable field fibre. A finite \(k\)-basis generates \(L\) as a field; adjoining its entries gives a finite tower \(k=E_0\subset E_1\subset\cdots\subset E_t=L\), with \(E_i=E_{i-1}(\alpha_i)\). Let \(p_i(T)\) be the monic minimal polynomial of \(\alpha_i\) over \(E_{i-1}\). The complete monic-division and Bezout arguments \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/main/docs/courses/AG-RG/AG-RG-S02.md}{AG-RG-S02, Lemma 4.A} give \(E_i=E_{i-1}[T]/(p_i)\). Each \(p_i\) divides the separable minimal polynomial of \(\alpha_i\) over \(k\), now regarded over \(E_{i-1}\), so \(p_i'(\alpha_i)\ne0\).

Choose polynomial representatives in the preceding variables for all coefficients of \(p_i\), obtaining \(P_i(T_1,\ldots,T_i)\). Successive monic division gives \[L=k[T_1,\ldots,T_t]/(P_1,\ldots,P_t).\] The Jacobian over \(L\) is triangular with diagonal \(p_i'(\alpha_i)\), so is invertible. The equation classes give a surjection \(L^t\to I/I^2\), where \(I=(P_1,\ldots,P_t)\), and its composite with the conormal differential to \(L^t\) is this invertible Jacobian. The surjection must also be injective, and the conormal differential is an isomorphism. Hence its kernel and cokernel vanish. \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-definition-smooth]{Definition F.6} and presentation comparison give smoothness of \(L/k\) and \(\Omega_{L/k}=0\). For \(L=k\), use the empty tower and the two zero modules.

The local flatness hypothesis and the finite presentation now meet every condition of \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-flat-fibre-smooth]{F.45}, giving a smooth principal neighbourhood of \(\mathfrak q\). The complete arbitrary-base chart result \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-smooth-syntomic]{F.83} gives a further neighbourhood with a standard smooth presentation \[S=R[X_1,\ldots,X_n]/(f_1,\ldots,f_c).\] Every inverted element has nonzero residue in \(L\), so the fibre remains exactly \(L\). By \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-standard-smooth]{F.85(2)}, the differential module is free on \(dX_{c+1},\ldots,dX_n\). The full differential scalar-extension calculation AG-CA-15, Theorem 2.1, identifies its fibre with \(\Omega_{L/k}=0\). Thus \(L^{n-c}=0\), forcing \(n=c\).

We check the lifting definition of étaleness on this final chart. Given a map to \(D/J\) with \(J^2=0\), lift its variable tuple to \(a\in D^n\). The error vector \(f(a)\) lies in \(J^n\). The square Jacobian \(A(a)\) is invertible: its determinant is a unit modulo \(J\), a lift of an inverse gives a product \(1+j\) with inverse \(1-j\), and the adjugate identity \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-matrix-left-inverse]{F.70} gives the matrix inverse. Take \[b=a-A(a)^{-1}f(a).\] Expanding each monomial and dropping terms with two entries from \(J\) gives \(f(b)=f(a)+A(a)(b-a)=0\). Thus \(b\) defines a lift. A second lifting root has the form \(b+\epsilon\) for \(\epsilon\in J^n\). The same expansion gives \(A(b)\epsilon=0\), and \(A(b)\) is invertible by its unchanged reduction modulo \(J\), so \(\epsilon=0\). Every square-zero test therefore has exactly one lift. With finite presentation this is étaleness by the programme definition. The chart contains \(\mathfrak q\), proving the claim for the original map. Empty variable lists use the unique empty tuple and determinant \(1\); no Noetherian or perfect-field hypothesis was introduced. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-characterize-formally-smooth-field-extension}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.17: characterize formally smooth field extension}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.17-characterize-formally-smooth-field-extension}

Reading source: \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/unofficial-stacks-project-ai-drafts/blob/565b10e987aba5969b21145a0833f42d69f96790/algebra.tex\#L45959-L45969}{AI Integrated Stacks, pinned Algebra, lines 45959--45969}.

For any field extension \(K/k\), the vanishing of \(H_1(\operatorname{NL}_{K/k})\) is equivalent to formal smoothness of \(K\) as a \(k\)-algebra.

\textbf{Proof.} Choose a polynomial surjection \(P=k[X_a\mid a\in E]\to K\), allowing an infinite set \(E\), with kernel \(I\). By \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-NL-homotopy]{F.11}, the homology in question is the kernel of \[d:I/I^2\longrightarrow\Omega_{P/k}\otimes_PK.\] Its cokernel is \(\Omega_{K/k}\), by the conormal calculation. When this kernel is zero, the sequence with these three modules is short exact. A vector-space basis of \(\Omega_{K/k}\) can be lifted to the middle module. Extending those lifts \(K\)-linearly splits the surjection, and hence the sequence.

The entire arbitrary-variable criterion AG-CA-17, Theorem 3.1, proves that this split conormal sequence is equivalent to formal smoothness. Its hypotheses apply to the chosen polynomial presentation over \(k\) with target \(K\) and impose no finite generation. Conversely, formal smoothness gives a split exact conormal sequence by that same complete theorem, so its left map has zero kernel. F.11 identifies that kernel with the presentation-independent first cotangent homology, also denoted \(H_1(L_{K/k})\) in the reading source. This proves both directions for arbitrary field extensions. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-characterize-smooth-kbar}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.18: characterize smooth kbar}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.18-characterize-smooth-kbar}

Reading sources: \href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/00TS}{Stacks, Tag 00TS}; \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/unofficial-stacks-project-ai-drafts/blob/565b10e987aba5969b21145a0833f42d69f96790/algebra.tex\#L39962-L40064}{AI Integrated Stacks, pinned Algebra, lines 39962--40064}.

Let \(S\) be a finite-type algebra over an algebraically closed field \(k\), and let \(\mathfrak m\) be a maximal ideal. Write \[d=\dim S_{\mathfrak m},\qquad
e=\dim_{\kappa(\mathfrak m)}
\bigl(\Omega_{S/k}\otimes_S\kappa(\mathfrak m)\bigr).\] The following four conditions are equivalent: \(S_{\mathfrak m}\) is regular local; \(e\leq d\); \(e=d\); and some \(g\in S\setminus\mathfrak m\) has \(S_g/k\) smooth.

\textbf{Proof.} The complete rational-point result AG-CA-18, Proposition 3.1, gives \(\kappa(\mathfrak m)=k\) and \[\Omega_{S/k}\otimes_Sk\cong\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2.\] The embedding-dimension theorem of AG-CA-14, Section 1, says \(d\leq\dim_k\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2\), with equality exactly for regularity. Thus the first three conditions are equivalent. The same complete AG-CA-18 proposition proves that smoothness at this closed rational point implies regularity, giving the implication from the fourth to the first.

For the converse we construct a smooth chart and identify its entire relation ideal. Suppose \(S_{\mathfrak m}\) is regular. Choose a finite polynomial presentation \(S=k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/I\), shifting each generator by its residue so that the preimage of \(\mathfrak m\) is \(\mathfrak n=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\). The exact conormal sequence at this point is \[I/\mathfrak nI\longrightarrow\mathfrak n/\mathfrak n^2
\longrightarrow\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2\longrightarrow0.\] Since the middle dimension is \(n\) and the last is \(d\), select \(c=n-d\) elements \(f_1,\ldots,f_c\in I\) whose linear classes form a basis of the kernel. Put \(J=(f_1,\ldots,f_c)\) and \(T=k[x]/J\), with maximal ideal \(\mathfrak m'=\mathfrak n/J\). The corresponding conormal sequence shows that the cotangent space of \(T_{\mathfrak m'}\) has dimension \(d\). This local ring surjects onto \(S_{\mathfrak m}\), so its dimension is at least \(d\); its embedding dimension bounds it above by \(d\). It is therefore regular of dimension \(d\).

By AG-CA-14, Theorem 1.1, \(T_{\mathfrak m'}\) is a domain. The surjection to \(S_{\mathfrak m}\) has zero kernel. To prove this, a nonzero kernel would put every lifted quotient prime strictly above \((0)\). A prime chain of length \(d\) in the quotient exists because its dimension is the finite integer \(d\). Prepending \((0)\) to the lifted chain would give length \(d+1\) in \(T_{\mathfrak m'}\), a contradiction. Thus the local surjection is an isomorphism.

The independent linear coefficient rows of the \(f_i\) have a nonzero \(c\)-variable Jacobian minor \(\Delta\) at this point. Existence of such a minor follows from the explicit pivot induction in \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-smoothing-lemma-find-strictly-standard]{D.2}; for \(c=0\) take \(\Delta=1\). Reorder the pivot variables first. The presentation \[T_\Delta=k[x_1,\ldots,x_n,u]/(f_1,\ldots,f_c,u\Delta-1)\] has a selected Jacobian determinant \(\Delta^2\): the last column is zero in the first \(c\) rows, its last entry is \(\Delta\), and the first square block has determinant \(\Delta\). This determinant is a unit in the quotient. The complete principal-localization standard-smooth calculation \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-standard-smooth]{F.85} therefore proves \(T_\Delta/k\) smooth.

It remains to pass from \(T\) to \(S\). The kernel of \(T\to S\) is finite since \(T\) is Noetherian, and becomes zero at \(\mathfrak m'\) by the local isomorphism. For each of its finite generators take a localization annihilator outside \(\mathfrak m'\). Their product \(a\) still avoids \(\mathfrak m'\) and kills the entire kernel. Exact localization of the surjection then gives \(T_a\cong S_{\bar a}\), hence \[T_{a\Delta}\cong S_{\overline{a\Delta}}.\] The left side is a principal localization of the smooth algebra \(T_\Delta\), and F.85(4) supplies its smooth presentation. On the right \(g=\overline{a\Delta}\) avoids \(\mathfrak m\). This gives the fourth condition, with the exact kernel eliminated on the whole neighbourhood. Empty equation lists obey the same construction. The algebraically closed ground-field assumption is retained throughout. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-charpoly}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.19: charpoly}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.19-charpoly}

Reading source: \href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/00DX}{Stacks, Tag 00DX}.

For a square matrix \(M\) of size \(n\) over any commutative ring \(R\), let \(P(T)=\det(T1_n-M)\). Then \(P(M)=0\) as an endomorphism of \(R^n\).

\textbf{Proof.} Define determinants by the signed permutation formula. Grouping its terms according to the entry in a fixed row gives the cofactor expansion. If that row is replaced by another row, the same expansion is zero: permutations pair with the transposition of the two equal rows, and the paired terms have opposite signs. The column calculation is identical. Thus, for every square matrix \(C\), the transpose of its signed cofactor matrix, denoted \(\operatorname{adj}(C)\), satisfies \[
C\operatorname{adj}(C)=\operatorname{adj}(C)C=(\det C)1_n.
\] This argument uses addition and multiplication only, so it applies over \(R[T]\) as well.

Assume \(n>0\), write \[
\operatorname{adj}(T1_n-M)=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}C_jT^j,
\qquad P(T)=\sum_{j=0}^n p_jT^j,\quad p_n=1.
\] The degree bound follows because each cofactor is a determinant of size \(n-1\). Comparing coefficients in the first adjugate identity gives \[
-MC_0=p_0 1_n,\qquad
C_{j-1}-MC_j=p_j1_n\ (1\leq j<n),\qquad C_{n-1}=1_n.
\] Multiply the equation indexed by \(j\) on the left by \(M^j\), the constant equation by \(1_n\), and the last equation by \(M^n\). Adding them cancels every \(M^{j+1}C_j\) against its next occurrence. The result is \(\sum_{j=0}^n p_jM^j=0\). No substitution into a polynomial with noncommuting matrix coefficients, and no division, is involved. If \(n=0\), the empty determinant gives \(P=1\); its value is the identity of the zero module, which is the zero endomorphism. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-codimension}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.20: codimension}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.20-codimension}

Reading source: \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/unofficial-stacks-project-ai-drafts/blob/565b10e987aba5969b21145a0833f42d69f96790/algebra.tex\#L29578-L29596}{AI Integrated Stacks, pinned Algebra, lines 29578--29596}.

Let \(S'\twoheadrightarrow S\) be a surjection of finite-type algebras over a field \(k\). For a prime \(\mathfrak p\subset S\), let \(\mathfrak p'\subset S'\) be its inverse image, and let \(x,x'\) denote the corresponding points. Then \[\dim_{x'}\operatorname{Spec}S'-\dim_x\operatorname{Spec}S
=\operatorname{ht}_{S'}\mathfrak p'-\operatorname{ht}_S\mathfrak p.\]

\textbf{Proof.} The induced map \(S'/\mathfrak p'\to S/\mathfrak p\) is an isomorphism: surjectivity descends, and the definition of \(\mathfrak p'\) makes its kernel zero. Its fraction-field map therefore identifies \(\kappa(\mathfrak p')\) with \(\kappa(\mathfrak p)\) as extensions of \(k\). Call their common transcendence degree \(e\).

The complete point-dimension argument AG-CA-09, Theorem 6.1, applies separately to the two finite-type algebras and gives \[\dim_{x'}\operatorname{Spec}S'=\dim S'_{\mathfrak p'}+e,\qquad
\dim_x\operatorname{Spec}S=\dim S_{\mathfrak p}+e.\] Here point dimension is the minimum of the dimensions of open neighbourhoods. Localization identifies chains of primes in \(S'_{\mathfrak p'}\) with chains in \(S'\) ending below \(\mathfrak p'\); taking their supremum gives \(\dim S'_{\mathfrak p'}=\operatorname{ht}_{S'}\mathfrak p'\). The same chain correspondence gives \(\dim S_{\mathfrak p}=\operatorname{ht}_S\mathfrak p\). All dimensions are finite by that earlier finite-type theorem. Subtract the two displayed equalities; the identical terms \(e\) cancel and give the assertion. No equidimensionality assumption is needed. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-colimit-eventually-flat}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.21: colimit eventually flat}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.21-colimit-eventually-flat}

Reading source: \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/unofficial-stacks-project-ai-drafts/blob/565b10e987aba5969b21145a0833f42d69f96790/algebra.tex\#L34105-L34145}{AI Integrated Stacks, pinned Algebra, lines 34105--34145}.

Consider a directed system of local maps \(R_\lambda\to S_\lambda\) between Noetherian local rings, with local transition maps, and let \(R=\operatorname*{colim}_\lambda R_\lambda\) and \(S=\operatorname*{colim}_\lambda S_\lambda\). Suppose that for \(\mu\geq\lambda\), \(S_\mu\) is the specified localization of \(S_\lambda\otimes_{R_\lambda}R_\mu\). Let \(M_\lambda\) be finite \(S_\lambda\)-modules with \(M_\mu=M_\lambda\otimes_{S_\lambda}S_\mu\), and put \(M=\operatorname*{colim}_\lambda M_\lambda\). These are exactly the kinds of models supplied by \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-limit-essentially-finite-presentation]{F.59} and \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-limit-module-essentially-finite-presentation]{F.60}. If \(M\) is \(R\)-flat, then \(M_\mu\) is \(R_\mu\)-flat at some stage.

\textbf{Proof.} Fix \(\lambda\), write \(\mathfrak m=\mathfrak m_\lambda\), and form \[T=\operatorname{Tor}_1^{R_\lambda}(M_\lambda,R_\lambda/\mathfrak m)
=\ker\bigl(\mathfrak m\otimes_{R_\lambda}M_\lambda\longrightarrow M_\lambda\bigr).\] The free-resolution and ideal-kernel calculation is AG-RG-S01, Lemma 1.A. The ideal \(\mathfrak m\) is finite over \(R_\lambda\), so its tensor with the finite \(S_\lambda\)-module \(M_\lambda\) is finite over \(S_\lambda\). Since \(S_\lambda\) is Noetherian, its kernel \(T\) is finite as well. Choose generators \(\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_a\) over \(S_\lambda\).

For \(\nu\geq\lambda\), put \(I_\nu=\mathfrak mR_\nu\). The transition of each \(\xi_i\) lies in \[\ker(I_\nu\otimes_{R_\nu}M_\nu\longrightarrow M_\nu)
=\operatorname{Tor}_1^{R_\nu}(M_\nu,R_\nu/I_\nu).\] The colimit of the ideals \(I_\nu\) is \(\mathfrak mR\): a finite sum of images of generators has a representative at a common stage, and equality of two representatives holds at a later stage. The same finite sums and the finitely many tensor relations show \[\operatorname*{colim}_{\nu\geq\lambda}
(I_\nu\otimes_{R_\nu}M_\nu)
\cong(\mathfrak mR)\otimes_R M.\] Multiplication from the last module into \(M\) is injective, because tensoring the inclusion \(\mathfrak mR\subset R\) with the flat module \(M\) preserves injectivity. Each \(\xi_i\) consequently has zero image in this colimit. The definition of a directed colimit says that its representative is already zero at some later stage. Choose a common successor \(\mu\) for these finitely many witnesses. The entire natural map \[T\longrightarrow\operatorname{Tor}_1^{R_\mu}(M_\mu,R_\mu/\mathfrak mR_\mu)\] is now zero, since it is compatible with the scalar map \(S_\lambda\to S_\mu\) and kills every chosen generator.

Apply the full local-square criterion \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-another-variant-local-criterion-flatness]{F.13} to \((R_\lambda,S_\lambda,R_\mu,S_\mu)\) and \(I=\mathfrak m\). This ideal is proper and its extension is proper because \(R_\lambda\to R_\mu\) is local. The module \(M_\lambda/\mathfrak mM_\lambda\) is flat over the field \(R_\lambda/\mathfrak m\): any vector-space basis expresses it as a free module, without a finite-dimensional assumption. The localized tensor description and finite \(S_\lambda\)-module hypothesis are exactly those stipulated above. The zero Tor map just proved supplies the last hypothesis of F.13, giving \(R_\mu\)-flatness of \(M_\mu\). ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-colimit-formally-etale}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.22: colimit formally etale}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.22-colimit-formally-etale}

Reading source: \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/unofficial-stacks-project-ai-drafts/blob/565b10e987aba5969b21145a0833f42d69f96790/algebra.tex\#L42732-L42747}{AI Integrated Stacks, pinned Algebra, lines 42732--42747}.

Let \((S_i)\) be a filtered system of formally étale \(R\)-algebras. Then \(\operatorname*{colim}_iS_i\) is formally étale over \(R\).

\textbf{Proof.} Set \(S=\operatorname*{colim}_iS_i\). Test the formal lifting property on an \(R\)-algebra \(A\), an ideal \(J\subset A\) with \(J^2=0\), and an \(R\)-map \(u:S\to A/J\). The restriction \(u_i:S_i\to A/J\) has exactly one lifting \(v_i:S_i\to A\), by the assumed formal étaleness.

If \(\phi_{ij}:S_i\to S_j\) is a transition map, then \(v_j\phi_{ij}\) and \(v_i\) both lift \(u_i\). Uniqueness on \(S_i\) forces \(v_j\phi_{ij}=v_i\). The colimit universal property therefore gives a map \(v:S\to A\) whose restrictions are all \(v_i\). Its reduction agrees with \(u\) on every stage and hence on \(S\). If \(v'\) is another lifting, its restriction to each \(S_i\) equals \(v_i\), so the same universal property gives \(v'=v\).

For a general nilpotent ideal \(J\) with \(J^N=0\), apply the square-zero test successively to \(A/J^{n+1}\to A/J^n\) for \(1\leq n<N\). Its kernel \(J^n/J^{n+1}\) has square zero because \(2n\geq n+1\). Each lifting step exists uniquely; induction reaches \(A\) and also proves uniqueness there. Thus either formulation of the formal étale test holds. No finite-presentation condition on any stage or on the colimit enters the proof. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-colimit-syntomic}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.23: colimit syntomic}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.23-colimit-syntomic}
