Reading source: \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/unofficial-stacks-project-ai-drafts/blob/565b10e987aba5969b21145a0833f42d69f96790/algebra.tex\#L46090-L46123}{AI Integrated Stacks, pinned Algebra, lines 46090--46123}.

Every extension of fields \(K/k\) is a filtered union of \(k\)-subalgebras that are global complete intersections. If \(K/k\) is separable, it is a filtered union of smooth \(k\)-subalgebras.

\textbf{Proof.} We first place an arbitrary finite set \(E\subset K\) in one of the asserted complete intersections. The subfield \(L=k(E)\) has a finite transcendence basis \(t_1,\ldots,t_d\) and is finite over \(F=k(t_1,\ldots,t_d)\). Choose a finite tower \[F=L_0\subset L_1\subset\cdots\subset L_r=L,\qquad L_i=L_{i-1}(y_i).\] Write \(e_i\) for the degree of the monic minimal polynomial of \(y_i\) over \(L_{i-1}\). Successive monic division, proved in AG-RG-S02, Lemma 4.A, makes the products \(\prod_{j<i}y_j^{a_j}\) with \(0\leq a_j<e_j\) an \(F\)-basis of \(L_{i-1}\). Expand each coefficient of the minimal polynomial in this basis. Its basis coefficients belong to \(F\); finitely many rational-function denominators occur.

Choose one nonzero \(h\in k[t_1,\ldots,t_d]\) clearing these denominators, and put \(B=k[t_1,\ldots,t_d,1/h]\). The expansions give monic polynomials \[P_i\in B[Y_1,\ldots,Y_i],\qquad
C=B[Y_1,\ldots,Y_r]/(P_1,\ldots,P_r).\] At each successive quotient monic division gives a free module on \(1,Y_i,\ldots,Y_i^{e_i-1}\). Hence \(C\) is finite free over \(B\) on the corresponding product monomials. Multiplication by a monic polynomial in a polynomial ring is injective even over a ring with zero divisors: in a nonzero product, the leading coefficient of the other factor survives unchanged as the leading coefficient. Applying this fact at each stage proves that the displayed equation list is a regular sequence.

After tensoring with \(F\), these same quotients are the chosen minimal-polynomial tower, so \(C\otimes_BF=L\). Freeness over the domain \(B\) makes the map \(C\to C\otimes_BF\) injective: a nonzero element of \(B\) cannot kill a nonzero coordinate in a free basis. We may thus regard \(C\) as a subalgebra of \(L\). Expand the finitely many elements of \(E\) in its product basis over \(F\), and enlarge \(h\) to clear their coefficients as well. The construction with this enlarged \(B\) then contains \(E\).

The coefficient ring \(B\) has dimension \(d\) by the finite-type-domain dimension theorem AG-CA-09, Theorem 4.2; its fraction field is \(F\). The finite injective integral map \(B\to C\) preserves dimension by AG-CA-05, Theorem 5.1. Encoding \(1/h\) by a variable \(Z\) gives \[C\cong k[t_1,\ldots,t_d,Y_1,\ldots,Y_r,Z]/
(P_1,\ldots,P_r,hZ-1),\] where the coefficients of the \(P_i\) are polynomial representatives modulo \(hZ-1\). This presentation has \(d+r+1\) variables, \(r+1\) equations, and dimension \(d\), so it satisfies the global complete-intersection definition \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-definition-relative-global-complete-intersection]{F.4} over \(k\).

If the extension is separable, \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-definition-separable-field-extension]{F.5} makes the finitely generated subfield \(L\) separably generated. The entire forward construction in \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-localization-smooth-separable]{F.64} supplies a smooth finite-type domain \(D\subset L\) with fraction field \(L\). For every element of \(E\) choose a numerator and a nonzero denominator in \(D\). Localizing at their finite product gives a smooth algebra containing \(E\), by the principal-localization calculation \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-standard-smooth]{F.85}.

Finally, in either case two constructed subalgebras have finite sets of algebra generators over \(k\). Apply the corresponding construction to the union of those generator sets. The resulting subalgebra contains both, proving directedness under inclusion. Applying the construction to a singleton includes each element of \(K\). The union, and thus its filtered colimit, is exactly \(K\). Empty towers and transcendence bases use the same argument with their empty products equal to one. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-colimits-NL}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.24: colimits NL}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.24-colimits-nl}

Reading source: \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/unofficial-stacks-project-ai-drafts/blob/565b10e987aba5969b21145a0833f42d69f96790/algebra.tex\#L36983-L36999}{AI Integrated Stacks, pinned Algebra, lines 36983--36999}.

For a filtered system of ring maps \(R_\lambda\to S_\lambda\), put \(R=\operatorname*{colim}R_\lambda\) and \(S=\operatorname*{colim}S_\lambda\). The canonical two-term conormal complexes satisfy \[\operatorname{NL}_{S/R}\cong
\operatorname*{colim}_\lambda\operatorname{NL}_{S_\lambda/R_\lambda}.\]

\textbf{Proof.} Use the canonical presentation \(P_\lambda=R_\lambda[X_s\mid s\in S_\lambda]\twoheadrightarrow S_\lambda\), with kernel \(I_\lambda\). A transition sends coefficients along the base map and sends \(X_s\) to the variable named by the image of \(s\). Thus distinct variables may become equal; injective transition maps are not assumed. Let \(P=R[X_s\mid s\in S]\) and \(I=\ker(P\to S)\).

Every element of \(P\) uses finitely many coefficients, variables and monomials. They all have representatives at one common stage, giving surjectivity of \(\operatorname*{colim}P_\lambda\to P\). If a representative polynomial is zero in \(P\), the finitely many identifications among its variable labels and the finitely many coefficient equalities hold at a common later stage. The representative is zero there. This proves injectivity and identifies the two polynomial rings.

A representative polynomial belongs to \(I\) precisely when its evaluation becomes zero in \(S\). That one finite equality holds at a later stage, so the polynomial can then be represented in \(I_\mu\). If an element of \(I_\lambda\) becomes zero in \(I\subset P\), it is zero at a later polynomial stage, and hence at a later ideal stage. Therefore \(I=\operatorname*{colim}I_\lambda\). An element of \(I^2\) is a finite sum of products of two elements of \(I\). Choose a common stage for all those factors and their kernel equalities; their products lie in \(I_\mu^2\). Vanishing is again detected in a later polynomial ring. This proves \(I^2=\operatorname*{colim}I_\lambda^2\).

Filtered colimits of the relevant modules preserve short exact sequences. Indeed, if a left representative maps to zero in the middle colimit, it is zero in the middle at a later stage, where injectivity makes it zero on the left. If a middle representative maps to zero on the right, at a later stage exactness expresses it as an image from the left. A right representative has a middle preimage at its own stage. These arguments also work for modules over the varying rings: the actions of the colimit rings are defined using common representatives. Applying them to \(I_\lambda^2\subset I_\lambda\) gives \[I/I^2\cong\operatorname*{colim}_\lambda I_\lambda/I_\lambda^2.\]

The degree-zero term is \(\bigoplus_{s\in S}S\,dX_s\). Its vectors have finite support; a common-stage argument for their coefficients and labels, with later-stage detection of zero, identifies it with the colimit of \(\bigoplus_{s\in S_\lambda}S_\lambda\,dX_s\). Formal differentiation of a polynomial is a finite coefficient calculation and respects every transition, including variable identifications. Consequently the two module identifications intertwine the maps \([f]\mapsto df\). They give the asserted isomorphism of entire two-term complexes. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-complete-local-Noetherian-domain-finite-over-regular}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.25: complete local Noetherian domain finite over regular}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.25-complete-local-noetherian-domain-finite-over-regular}

Reading source: \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/unofficial-stacks-project-ai-drafts/blob/565b10e987aba5969b21145a0833f42d69f96790/algebra.tex\#L46654-L46712}{AI Integrated Stacks, pinned Algebra, lines 46654--46712}.

Every complete Noetherian local domain \(A\) contains a regular complete local subring \(A_0\) such that \(A\) is finite over \(A_0\) and the residue fields agree. The subring can be chosen as a power-series ring over a field or over a Cohen ring.

\textbf{Proof.} Write \(\mathfrak m\) for the maximal ideal and \(D=\dim A\). The complete coefficient-ring construction is AG-CA-19S, Theorem 5.1. Its arbitrary-residue-field step uses \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-more-algebra-lemma-p-basis]{F.119}, including the full degree-\(p\) argument: \(T^p-a^p=(T-a)^p\), and the coefficient \(-da\) of a proper monic factor, with \(1\leq d<p\), forces the claimed degree. Thus this construction applies without a perfect-residue-field assumption.

In equal characteristic it embeds a coefficient field \(k\subset A\). Choose a system of \(D\) parameters \(x_1,\ldots,x_D\) by AG-CA-11, Theorem 2.1. In mixed characteristic the coefficient ring is a Cohen DVR \(C\) with uniformizer \(p\) and residue field \(k\). It embeds in \(A\): a nonzero kernel ideal in this DVR would contain a power of \(p\), whereas the domain \(A\) has characteristic zero. The element \(p\) is consequently a nonzerodivisor in \(A\), and AG-CA-11, Theorem 3.2, gives \(\dim A/pA=D-1\). Choose parameters \(x_1,\ldots,x_{D-1}\) in that quotient and lift them to \(A\).

In the respective cases put \[B=k[[X_1,\ldots,X_D]]
\quad\hbox{or}\quad
B=C[[X_1,\ldots,X_{D-1}]],\] and let \(\mathfrak n\) be its maximal ideal. The ideal \(I\) generated by the proposed images of \(\mathfrak n\) is \((x_1,\ldots,x_D)\) or \((p,x_1,\ldots,x_{D-1})\). The parameter property gives \(\sqrt I=\mathfrak m\). AG-CA-03, Proposition 2.2, supplies an integer \(b\) with \(\mathfrak m^b\subset I\), while \(I\subset\mathfrak m\). Hence \[\mathfrak m^{bn}\subset I^n\subset\mathfrak m^n\qquad(n\geq1).\] The two filtrations are cofinal. Completeness and separatedness of \(A\) for its maximal-ideal filtration therefore imply the same properties for its \(I\)-adic filtration. Evaluation \(X_i\mapsto x_i\) defines a ring map \(B\to A\): the tail of a power series of degree at least \(n\) evaluates into \(I^n\), and finite truncation followed by a separated limit respects addition and multiplication. This is the evaluation calculation of AG-CA-19S, Theorem 6.1.

The local quotient \(A/I\) has nilpotent maximal ideal and residue field \(k\). Each maximal-ideal layer is finite-dimensional over \(k\), since \(\mathfrak m\) is finite and its powers are generated by finitely many products. The finite-layer proof in AG-CA-03, Theorem 4.2, therefore makes \(A/I\) finite-dimensional. Choose elements \(a_1,\ldots,a_s\in A\) lifting a \(k\)-basis of this quotient.

These elements generate \(A\) over \(B\). To verify this directly, approximate any \(a\in A\) modulo \(I\) by \(\sum_jc_{j1}a_j\) with coefficients lifted from \(k\) to \(B\). If coefficients have been chosen through order \(n\), the error lies in \(I^n\). Express it as a finite sum of degree-\(n\) products of the generators of \(I\) times elements of \(A\). Replace each latter element modulo \(I\) by its residue-basis expansion. Lifting those coefficients to \(B\) gives corrections in \(\mathfrak n^n\) and leaves an error in \(I^{n+1}\). Induction constructs compatible coefficients \(c_{jn}\) modulo \(\mathfrak n^n\). The complete ring \(B\) supplies limits \(c_j\); continuity of evaluation and \(I\)-adic separatedness give \(a=\sum_jc_ja_j\). Thus \(A\) is a finite \(B\)-module.

The ring \(B\) is the maximal-ideal completion of the polynomial local ring over \(k\) or \(C\): their quotients by each maximal-ideal power have the same finite polynomial truncations, including the coefficient reductions modulo powers of \(p\) in the second case. AG-CA-14, Proposition 3.3, proves regularity of that polynomial local ring, and AG-CA-11, Theorem 5.1, gives its dimension \(D\). Completion preserves this dimension and regularity by AG-CA-19, Theorem 4.1. Hence \(B\) is a regular local domain of dimension \(D\).

Let \(J\) be the evaluation kernel. If it contains a nonzero element \(f\), the one-equation theorem AG-CA-11, Theorem 3.2, gives \(\dim B/(f)=D-1\), and the further quotient \(B/J\) has dimension at most \(D-1\). But \(B/J\) embeds in the finite integral extension \(A\), so AG-CA-05, Theorem 5.1, gives \(\dim B/J=\dim A=D\), a contradiction. Therefore \(J=0\). Take \(A_0\) to be the resulting embedded copy of \(B\). Its residue map is the coefficient identification with \(k\), and the finiteness has already been proved. If \(D=0\), the Noetherian local domain is its own residue field, so \(A_0=A\) gives the empty-variable case directly. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-completion-at-quasi-finite-prime}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.26: completion at quasi finite prime}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.26-completion-at-quasi-finite-prime}

Reading source: \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/unofficial-stacks-project-ai-drafts/blob/565b10e987aba5969b21145a0833f42d69f96790/algebra.tex\#L32412-L32464}{AI Integrated Stacks, pinned Algebra, lines 32412--32464}.

Let \(R\) be Noetherian, let \(R\to S\) be finite type, and let \(\mathfrak q\subset S\) be quasi-finite over \(\mathfrak p=\mathfrak q\cap R\). There is an algebra \(D\) with \[\widehat{R_{\mathfrak p}}\otimes_RS
\cong\widehat{S_{\mathfrak q}}\times D,\] whose first projection is the natural map to the completed local ring.

\textbf{Proof.} The full affine conductor theorem \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/main/docs/courses/AG-RG/AG-RG-S04.md}{Zariski Main, Theorem C4.3} produces an integral subalgebra \(C\subset S\) and \(g\in C\setminus\mathfrak q\) such that \(C_g=S_g\). Choose a finite set of \(R\)-algebra generators of \(S_g\). Each is a fraction with numerator in \(C\) and denominator a power of \(g\). Let \(S'\subset C\) be generated over \(R\) by those numerators and by \(g\). All these generators are integral. Repeated monic reduction, as in AG-CA-05, Section 1, shows that their bounded product powers generate \(S'\) as an \(R\)-module. Thus \(S'\) is finite over \(R\), and the chosen generators give \(S'_g=S_g\).

Put \(\mathfrak q'=\mathfrak q\cap S'\). Localizing the last equality at the corresponding primes gives \(S'_{\mathfrak q'}=S_{\mathfrak q}\), including their maximal ideals, so their maximal-adic completions are naturally identified. By \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-completion-finite-extension]{F.27}, \[T'=\widehat{R_{\mathfrak p}}\otimes_RS'
\cong A\times D',\qquad A=\widehat{S_{\mathfrak q}}.\] Let \(e\in T'\) be the idempotent \((1,0)\). Its image in \(T=\widehat{R_{\mathfrak p}}\otimes_RS\) gives an explicit product map \[T\longrightarrow eT\times(1-e)T,\qquad t\longmapsto(et,(1-e)t),\] with inverse addition. The structural map \(A=eT'\to eT\) is unital. The image of \(g\) in \(A\) is a unit because \(g\notin\mathfrak q'\), and remains a unit in \(eT\).

Localizing \(T'\to T\) at \(g\) gives an isomorphism, by \(S'_g=S_g\) and the tensor/localization universal properties. Its \(e\)-factor is \[A=A_g\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }(eT)_g=eT.\] This identifies the first factor with the required completion, and the second is \(D=(1-e)T\).

It remains to determine the projection on all of \(T\). On \(\widehat{R_{\mathfrak p}}\) and \(S'\) it agrees with the completed-local structural maps by the construction in F.27. Given \(s\in S\), the equality \(S'_g=S_g\) writes \(s/1=b/g^n\) with \(b\in S'\). Equality of these fractions means that some \(g^a\) kills \(g^ns-b\) in \(S\). Therefore \(g^{n+a}s=g^ab\in S'\). Both the factor projection and the natural map \(S\to\widehat{S_{\mathfrak q}}\) have the same value on this element and on the unit \(g\). Multiplying by the inverse of \(g^{n+a}\) makes their values on \(s\) equal. The values on all pure tensors are now equal, proving the assertion about the first projection. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-completion-finite-extension}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.27: completion finite extension}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.27-completion-finite-extension}

Reading source: \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/unofficial-stacks-project-ai-drafts/blob/565b10e987aba5969b21145a0833f42d69f96790/algebra.tex\#L24144-L24184}{AI Integrated Stacks, pinned Algebra, lines 24144--24184}.

For a finite map of Noetherian rings \(R\to S\) and a prime \(\mathfrak p\subset R\), let \(\mathfrak q_1,\ldots,\mathfrak q_r\) be all primes of \(S\) above \(\mathfrak p\). Then \[\widehat{R_{\mathfrak p}}\otimes_RS
\cong\prod_{i=1}^r\widehat{S_{\mathfrak q_i}},\] where each local ring is completed at its own maximal ideal.

\textbf{Proof.} Replace the base by \(R_{\mathfrak p}\) and the finite algebra by \(S_{\mathfrak p}\); tensor associativity gives the same left side, and localizing at each prime gives the same right side. Write \(\mathfrak m\) for the resulting base maximal ideal. The integral lying-over and maximal-ideal results AG-CA-05, Theorems 3.3--3.4, show that the maximal ideals of this finite algebra are precisely the finitely many \(\mathfrak q_i\), and all contract to \(\mathfrak m\).

For \(n\geq1\), the ring \(R/\mathfrak m^n\) has a finite filtration whose successive quotients are finite-dimensional over the residue field: each \(\mathfrak m^j/\mathfrak m^{j+1}\) is generated by finitely many products of generators of \(\mathfrak m\). It is therefore Artinian. The finite module \(S/\mathfrak m^nS\) has finite length over this ring, by the finite-module argument AG-CA-03, Theorem 3.3, and consequently is itself Artinian. Its primes are the images of the \(\mathfrak q_i\): every prime over \(\mathfrak m^n\) contracts to \(\mathfrak m\) and is maximal by integrality.

The entire Artinian product theorem AG-CA-03, Theorem 4.2, now gives the canonical localization decomposition \[S/\mathfrak m^nS
\cong\prod_{i=1}^r S_{\mathfrak q_i}/\mathfrak m^nS_{\mathfrak q_i}.\] These maps commute with reduction from order \(n+1\) to order \(n\), because every projection is the corresponding localization map. Inverse limits of a finite product are computed componentwise: a compatible tuple sequence is exactly a tuple of compatible sequences. Hence the \(\mathfrak mS\)-adic completion of \(S\) is \[\varprojlim_n S/\mathfrak m^nS
\cong\prod_i\varprojlim_n
S_{\mathfrak q_i}/\mathfrak m^nS_{\mathfrak q_i}.\]

In the \(i\)th local ring the radical of \(\mathfrak mS_{\mathfrak q_i}\) is its maximal ideal \(\mathfrak q_iS_{\mathfrak q_i}\): a prime containing the former corresponds to a prime above \(\mathfrak m\), and localization leaves only \(\mathfrak q_i\). AG-CA-03, Proposition 2.2, supplies \(b_i\) such that \[(\mathfrak q_iS_{\mathfrak q_i})^{b_in}
\subset\mathfrak m^nS_{\mathfrak q_i}
\subset(\mathfrak q_iS_{\mathfrak q_i})^n.\] These cofinal filtrations have canonically identical completions. The right-hand limits are thus \(\widehat{S_{\mathfrak q_i}}\). Finally AG-CA-19, Theorem 3.1, identifies the left-hand limit with \(\widehat R\otimes_RS\), because \(S\) is a finite \(R\)-module. Every identification respects the maps from \(R\) and \(S\), giving the asserted natural product. If there are no primes above \(\mathfrak p\), then \(S_{\mathfrak p}=0\), and both sides are the zero ring, with the empty product interpreted as that ring. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-compose-finite-type}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.28: compose finite type}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.28-compose-finite-type}

Reading source: \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/unofficial-stacks-project-ai-drafts/blob/565b10e987aba5969b21145a0833f42d69f96790/algebra.tex\#L547-L571}{AI Integrated Stacks, pinned Algebra, lines 547--571}.

Finite-type maps compose, and finitely presented maps compose. Given \(R\to S'\to S\), if \(S/R\) is finite type then \(S/S'\) is finite type. If \(S/R\) is finitely presented and \(S'/R\) is finite type, then \(S/S'\) is finitely presented.

\textbf{Proof.} Choose generators \(y_1,\ldots,y_a\) for \(S'\) over \(R\) and \(x_1,\ldots,x_b\) for \(S\) over \(S'\). Each coefficient of a polynomial expression in the \(x_j\) is itself a polynomial in the \(y_i\) with coefficients in \(R\). Substitution shows that the combined finite list generates \(S\) over \(R\), proving the first claim.

For the second claim take finite presentations \[S'=R[Y_1,\ldots,Y_a]/(u_1,\ldots,u_c),\qquad
S=S'[X_1,\ldots,X_b]/(v_1,\ldots,v_d).\] Lift the finitely many coefficients of the \(v_j\) through \(R[Y]\twoheadrightarrow S'\) to obtain \(\widetilde v_j\in R[Y,X]\). Then \[R[Y,X]/(u_1,\ldots,u_c,\widetilde v_1,\ldots,\widetilde v_d)
\cong S.\] Indeed quotienting first by the \(u_i\) gives \(S'[X]\), where the remaining equations are exactly the \(v_j\). This is a finite presentation of the composite.

If \(S\) is generated by a finite list over \(R\), every element is already an \(R\)-coefficient polynomial in that list, hence also an \(S'\)-coefficient polynomial. This proves the third claim without a finiteness assumption on \(S'\).

For the fourth claim write \[S=R[X_1,\ldots,X_b]/(f_1,\ldots,f_d),\qquad S'=R[Y_1,\ldots,Y_a]/J.\] The ideal \(J\) need not be finite. For each \(i\) choose \(h_i(X)\) representing the image of \(\bar Y_i\) in \(S\). Form the finitely presented \(S'\)-algebra \[Q=S'[X_1,\ldots,X_b]/
(f_1,\ldots,f_d,\bar Y_1-h_1(X),\ldots,\bar Y_a-h_a(X)).\] Evaluation at the specified elements of \(S\) defines \(Q\to S\). Conversely the images of the \(X_j\) in \(Q\) satisfy every \(f_j\), giving an \(R\)-map \(S\to Q\). Their composite on \(S\) fixes its \(R\)-algebra generators. The other composite fixes each \(X_j\), and it fixes every coefficient from \(S'\) because it fixes \(\bar Y_i=h_i(X)\) and \(S'\) is generated by those elements over \(R\). Both composites are identities, so \(Q\cong S\) as \(S'\)-algebras. This proves finite presentation over \(S'\) without making any extra assumption on \(J\). ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-compose-smooth}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.29: compose smooth}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.29-compose-smooth}

Reading source: \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/unofficial-stacks-project-ai-drafts/blob/565b10e987aba5969b21145a0833f42d69f96790/algebra.tex\#L39039-L39053}{AI Integrated Stacks, pinned Algebra, lines 39039--39053}.

If \(R\to S\) and \(S\to T\) are smooth ring maps, then \(R\to T\) is smooth.

\textbf{Proof.} First translate the cotangent condition into the earlier lifting criterion. For a polynomial presentation of \(S/R\), F.11 identifies its conormal complex with the canonical one. F.6 gives zero kernel and a projective differential cokernel, so the conormal sequence is split exact. AG-CA-17, Theorem 3.1 then proves that \(S\) is formally smooth over \(R\). The same argument proves that \(T\) is formally smooth over \(S\).

In a lifting problem \(T\to C/J\) over \(R\), where \(J\) is nilpotent, first lift its restriction \(S\to C/J\) to an \(R\)-map \(S\to C\). This supplies an \(S\)-algebra structure on \(C\) whose reduction is exactly the given one. Formal smoothness of \(T/S\) now lifts the original map to an \(S\)-map \(T\to C\). In particular it is an \(R\)-map. Thus \(T/R\) is formally smooth, by an explicit composition of the two lifts.

Finite presentation is equally explicit. Write \(S=R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/(f_1,\ldots,f_r)\) and \(T=S[y_1,\ldots,y_m]/(g_1,\ldots,g_s)\), and lift each coefficient in the \(g_j\) to a polynomial in the \(x_i\). The resulting polynomials \(\widetilde g_j\) give \(T=R[x_i,y_l]/(f_i,\widetilde g_j)\): the two maps fixing the generators are inverse by the quotient universal property. Applying the same entire conormal criterion AG-CA-17, Theorem 3.1 to this finite presentation gives zero first homology and finite projective differentials. F.11 transports them to the canonical complex, so F.6 proves that \(R\to T\) is smooth. The lifting and presentation arguments include zero algebras and empty lists. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-compose-standard-smooth}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.30: compose standard smooth}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.30-compose-standard-smooth}

Reading source: \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/unofficial-stacks-project-ai-drafts/blob/565b10e987aba5969b21145a0833f42d69f96790/algebra.tex\#L38815-L38878}{AI Integrated Stacks, pinned Algebra, lines 38815--38878}.

A composite of standard smooth ring maps is standard smooth.

\textbf{Proof.} Take standard smooth presentations \[S=R[X_1,\ldots,X_n]/(f_1,\ldots,f_c),\qquad
T=S[Y_1,\ldots,Y_m]/(g_1,\ldots,g_d).\] Reorder the variables in each list so that the first \(c\) and first \(d\) variables respectively give the chosen square Jacobian minors. Denote their determinants by \(\Delta_f\) and \(\Delta_g\); they are units in \(S\) and \(T\). Choose polynomial representatives \(\widetilde g_j\in R[X,Y]\) for the coefficients of every \(g_j\). Quotienting first by \((f)\) and then by the remaining equations gives \[T\cong R[X_1,\ldots,X_n,Y_1,\ldots,Y_m]/
(f_1,\ldots,f_c,\widetilde g_1,\ldots,\widetilde g_d).\]

Use the pivot variables \(X_1,\ldots,X_c,Y_1,\ldots,Y_d\) and write Jacobian rows by equations. In \(T\) its selected matrix has the form \[\begin{pmatrix}A&0\\ B&C\end{pmatrix},\qquad
A=(\partial f_i/\partial X_j),\quad
C=(\partial g_i/\partial Y_j).\] The upper-right entries are zero because the \(f_i\) contain no \(Y\) variables. Reduction of the derivatives of \(\widetilde g_i\) with respect to \(Y_j\) equals the derivatives of \(g_i\): changing polynomial coefficients commutes with the monomial differentiation rule.

In the permutation expansion of this determinant, a nonzero term must assign the first \(c\) rows to the first \(c\) columns; otherwise one of those rows uses a zero upper-right entry. The remaining rows then use the remaining columns. Factoring the two independent permutation sums gives \(\det A\det C=\Delta_f\Delta_g\). The image of the first unit and the second given unit are units in \(T\), so their product is a unit. The displayed finite presentation is therefore standard smooth.

If a presentation includes a principal localization at \(h\), replace it by one more variable \(Z\) and equation \(hZ-1\). With \(Z\) added last to the pivot list, the old equation rows have zero \(Z\) entry and the new last diagonal entry is \(h\). The selected determinant is the old determinant times \(h\), which is invertible in the localized quotient. This calculation encodes all the stated localized presentations before applying the preceding composition argument. Empty equation lists use determinant one and the same permutation calculation. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-composition-essentially-of-finite-type}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.31: composition essentially of finite type}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.31-composition-essentially-of-finite-type}

Reading source: \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/unofficial-stacks-project-ai-drafts/blob/565b10e987aba5969b21145a0833f42d69f96790/algebra.tex\#L13129-L13138}{AI Integrated Stacks, pinned Algebra, lines 13129--13138}.

Composites of essentially finite-type ring maps are essentially finite type. Composites of essentially finitely presented ring maps are essentially finitely presented.

\textbf{Proof.} Let \(R\to S\to T\) be the maps. Write \(S=U^{-1}A\), where \(A\) is a finite-type \(R\)-algebra, and write \(T=V^{-1}(S[Y_1,\ldots,Y_m]/J)\). Set \(P=A[Y_1,\ldots,Y_m]\) and let \(K\) be the kernel of \(P\to S[Y]/J\). Its quotient \(B=P/K\) is finite type over \(R\), even if \(J\) and \(K\) have infinitely many generators.

The map \(U^{-1}P\to S[Y]/J\) has kernel exactly \(U^{-1}K\). Indeed every element of \(U^{-1}P\) is \(f/u\); its image is zero precisely when the image of \(f\) is zero, because the image of \(u\) is a unit. This identifies \(U^{-1}B\) with \(S[Y]/J\). For each \(v\in V\), choose a fraction \(b_v/u_v\) representing it in \(U^{-1}B\). Let \(W\subset B\) be generated multiplicatively by the images of \(U\) and all the \(b_v\). Since the \(u_v\) are already inverted, inverting \(b_v/u_v\) is equivalent to inverting \(b_v\). The localization universal property in both directions gives \(T\cong W^{-1}B\), proving the finite-type assertion. No single denominator for all relations has been assumed.

For finite presentation, choose \(A\) finitely presented over \(R\) and \(J=(j_1,\ldots,j_d)\) in \(U^{-1}P\). Each \(j_i\) has the form \(f_i/u_i\) with \(f_i\in P\) and \(u_i\in U\). The images of \(f_1,\ldots,f_d\) generate the same ideal after localizing at \(U\), since all their denominators are units there. Therefore \[S[Y]/J\cong U^{-1}\bigl(A[Y]/(f_1,\ldots,f_d)\bigr).\] The algebra in parentheses is finitely presented over \(R\): combine the finite presentation of \(A\) with these finitely many polynomial equations, as in \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-compose-finite-type]{F.28}. As before, incorporate the numerator representatives of \(V\) into the final multiplicative set. Thus \(T\) is a localization of a finitely presented \(R\)-algebra. The two arguments also cover empty variable lists and the zero algebra. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-composition-syntomic}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.32: composition syntomic}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.32-composition-syntomic}

Reading source: \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/unofficial-stacks-project-ai-drafts/blob/565b10e987aba5969b21145a0833f42d69f96790/algebra.tex\#L38404-L38453}{AI Integrated Stacks, pinned Algebra, lines 38404--38453}.

For arbitrary ring maps \(R\to S\to T\):

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  If both maps are syntomic, their composite is syntomic.
\item
  If both maps admit relative global complete-intersection presentations, their composite admits such a presentation.
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Proof.} Begin with (2). Choose presentations \[S=R[X_1,\ldots,X_n]/(f_1,\ldots,f_c),\qquad
T=S[Y_1,\ldots,Y_m]/(h_1,\ldots,h_d).\] Lifting each coefficient of \(h_j\) to \(R[X]\) gives polynomials \(\widetilde h_j\) and the exact presentation \[T\cong R[X,Y]/(f_1,\ldots,f_c,\widetilde h_1,\ldots,\widetilde h_d).\] To check \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-definition-relative-global-complete-intersection]{F.4}, fix \(\mathfrak p\subset R\) and let \(k=\kappa(\mathfrak p)\), \(A=S\otimes_Rk\) and \(B=T\otimes_Rk\). Empty \(B\) imposes no dimension condition. If \(B\ne0\), then \(A\ne0\), and \(\dim A=n-c\). Every nonempty fibre of \(A\to B\) has dimension \(m-d\): it is a field extension of a corresponding fibre of \(S\to T\), so the coefficient-change calculation \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-base-change-relative-global-complete-intersection]{F.14} applies.

We prove both dimension inequalities for \(B\). Given a minimal prime \(\eta\) of \(B\), let \(\mathfrak a=\eta\cap A\), \(F=\kappa(\mathfrak a)\) and \(L=\kappa(\eta)\). The finite-type domain \(A/\mathfrak a\) has dimension \(\operatorname{trdeg}_kF\leq\dim A=n-c\), by AG-CA-09, Theorem 4.2. The prime induced by \(\eta\) in \(B\otimes_AF\) has residue field \(L\). That fibre has dimension \(m-d\), so applying the same domain dimension theorem to its prime quotient gives \(\operatorname{trdeg}_FL\leq m-d\). Transcendence degrees add here. To check this, choose a finite transcendence basis \(U\) of \(F/k\) and one \(V\) of \(L/F\). The elements of \(V\) are independent over \(F\), hence over \(k(U)\); together with the independence of \(U\) this proves independence of \(U\cup V\) over \(k\). Algebraicity of \(F/k(U)\) and \(L/F(V)\), and transitivity of algebraicity, show that \(L/k(U,V)\) is algebraic. Thus \[\dim(B/\eta)=\operatorname{trdeg}_kL
=\operatorname{trdeg}_kF+\operatorname{trdeg}_FL
\leq n-c+m-d.\] The Noetherian finite-type algebra \(B\) has finitely many minimal primes, and its dimension is the maximum of their quotient dimensions. This proves the upper bound.

For the lower bound, the polynomial presentation of \(B\) has \(n+m\) variables and \(c+d\) equations. A prime minimal over its equation ideal has height at most \(c+d\), by the full height theorem \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/d02d0a3669f42579db037cd44de1d113fdd770a1/docs/courses/AG-CA/src/dimension-theory-of-noetherian-local-rings.md}{AG-CA-11, Theorem 3.1}. The polynomial domain dimension formula AG-CA-09, Theorem 4.3, makes its quotient dimension at least \(n+m-c-d\). Such a prime exists because \(B\ne0\). Consequently \(\dim B\geq n+m-c-d\). Equality follows, proving (2) over arbitrary \(R\).

For (1), first suppose that \(R\) is Noetherian. Finite presentation of both syntomic maps makes \(S\) and \(T\) Noetherian by the Hilbert basis theorem. At \(\mathfrak q\subset T\), with contraction \(\mathfrak r\subset S\), the entire neighbourhood criterion \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-syntomic]{F.87} supplies \(g\in S\setminus\mathfrak r\) and \(h\in T\setminus\mathfrak q\) such that \(R\to S_g\) and \(S\to T_h\) have relative global complete-intersection presentations. By F.14, \(S_g\to T_{gh}\) has one too. Assertion (2) gives such a presentation for \(R\to T_{gh}\). These opens cover \(\operatorname{Spec}T\). Its quasi-compactness \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/d02d0a3669f42579db037cd44de1d113fdd770a1/docs/courses/AG-CA/src/spectra-of-rings.md}{AG-CA-01, Proposition 2.3} gives a finite subcover. Each chart is syntomic by F.87, and the complete gluing proof \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-local-syntomic]{F.62} gives syntomicity of \(T/R\).

Now let \(R\) be arbitrary. Finite presentation follows from F.28, and flatness follows by composing the two exact tensor functors, as in AG-CA-07, Proposition 3.2. For \(\mathfrak p\subset R\) use the same \(k,A,B\) as above. The map \(k\to A\) is syntomic: finite presentation and flatness survive base change, and its only field fibre is the given local complete intersection. The map \(A\to B\) is also syntomic. Its finite presentation and flatness are the base changes of those of \(S\to T\). At a prime \(\mathfrak a\subset A\) over \(\mathfrak r\subset S\), its fibre is \[B\otimes_A\kappa(\mathfrak a)
\cong\bigl(T\otimes_S\kappa(\mathfrak r)\bigr)
\otimes_{\kappa(\mathfrak r)}\kappa(\mathfrak a).\] Choose the principal global complete-intersection cover of the original field fibre, as in \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-definition-lci-field]{F.2}. Scalar extension carries that cover to a cover, and F.14 carries each of its presentations to a global complete-intersection presentation. Thus the displayed fibre is a local complete intersection. Since the base \(k\) is Noetherian, the case already proved applies to \(k\to A\to B\). It makes \(B/k\) syntomic, in particular a local complete intersection. Every field fibre of \(T/R\) has now been checked. Together with flatness and finite presentation, the syntomic definition \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-definition-lci]{F.1} proves (1) for arbitrary bases. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-conormal-module-localize}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.33: conormal module localize}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.33-conormal-module-localize}

Reading source: \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/unofficial-stacks-project-ai-drafts/blob/565b10e987aba5969b21145a0833f42d69f96790/algebra.tex\#L37203-L37225}{AI Integrated Stacks, pinned Algebra, lines 37203--37225}.

Suppose that \(R[X_1,\ldots,X_n]\twoheadrightarrow S\) and \(R[Y_1,\ldots,Y_m]\twoheadrightarrow S_g\) have kernels \(I\) and \(J\). There is an isomorphism of \(S_g\)-modules \[(I/I^2)_g\oplus S_g^{\oplus m}
\cong J/J^2\oplus S_g^{\oplus n}.\]

\textbf{Proof.} Put \(C=S_g\), \(P=R[X]\) and \(Q=R[Y]\). Choose \(f\in P\) mapping to \(g\). Exact localization gives \(P_f\twoheadrightarrow C\) with kernel \(I_f\). Lift the image of each \(Y_j\) to \(u_j\in P_f\), and lift the image of each \(X_i\) to \(v_i\in Q\).

The simultaneous evaluation \(W=P[Y]=Q[X]\to C\) has kernel \(L=(J,X_i-v_i(Y))\): quotienting by the graph equations eliminates \(X\) and leaves exactly \(Q/J\). Translation by \(v_i(Y)\) makes \(W=Q[Z_1,\ldots,Z_n]\) and \(L=(J,Z_1,\ldots,Z_n)\). In this polynomial ring \[L^2=(J^2,\ JZ_1,\ldots,JZ_n,\ Z_iZ_j\mid1\leq i,j\leq n).\] Therefore reading the constant term modulo \(J^2\) and each linear coefficient modulo \(J\) gives an isomorphism \(L/L^2\to J/J^2\oplus C^n\). Its inverse sends a relation class to its constant representative and each coordinate to the class of the corresponding \(Z_i\). Changes of representatives lie in the displayed square, so both maps are well defined and inverse.

The image of \(f\) is a unit in \(C\), and \(L/L^2\) is a \(C\)-module. Multiplication by \(f\) on it is consequently invertible. Localizing thus gives the same module, namely \[L/L^2\cong L_f/L_f^2.\] On \(W_f=P_f[Y]\), the same evaluation has kernel \((I_f,Y_j-u_j)\): eliminating \(Y\) leaves \(P_f/I_f=C\). Translate \(Y_j\) by \(u_j\). The identical constant-and-linear calculation now gives \[L_f/L_f^2\cong I_f/I_f^2\oplus C^m.\] The ideal-product fraction formulas identify \(I_f/I_f^2\) with \((I/I^2)_g\). Combining these isomorphisms gives the assertion. No free summand was cancelled, and no flatness of \(C\) over \(R\) was used. Empty variable lists and \(C=0\) satisfy the same formulas. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-contained-in-radical}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.34: contained in radical}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.34-contained-in-radical}

Reading source: \href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0AME}{Stacks, Tag 0AME}.

For an ideal \(I\) of a commutative ring \(R\), the inclusion \(I\subset\operatorname{Jac}(R)\) is equivalent to invertibility of every \(1+i\), \(i\in I\). Under either condition, every element invertible modulo \(I\) is already invertible in \(R\). Here the Jacobson radical is the intersection of all maximal ideals.

\textbf{Proof.} We first justify the maximal-ideal test for a unit. A nonunit \(a\) generates a proper ideal. The partially ordered set of proper ideals containing \((a)\) has an upper bound for every chain, its union: that union cannot contain \(1\), since then a member would contain \(1\). Zorn's lemma supplies a maximal proper ideal containing \(a\). Conversely no unit belongs to a proper ideal. Therefore an element is a unit exactly when it belongs to no maximal ideal.

Suppose \(I\) is contained in every maximal ideal. If a maximal ideal contained \(1+i\), it would contain its difference with \(i\), namely \(1\). This is impossible, so the unit test makes every \(1+i\) invertible. Conversely, if a maximal ideal \(\mathfrak m\) fails to contain \(I\), maximality gives \(I+\mathfrak m=R\). Write \(1=i+b\) with \(i\in I\) and \(b\in\mathfrak m\). The element \(b=1-i\) has the stipulated form, yet is not a unit. This contradiction proves the inclusion.

If \(a\bmod I\) is a unit, lift one inverse to \(b\in R\). Then \(ab=1+i\) for some \(i\in I\). The element \(b(ab)^{-1}\) is an actual inverse of \(a\), proving the last assertion. In the zero ring the empty intersection is the whole ring and its unique element is its identity and a unit; the conclusions hold there too. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-cover-upstairs}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.35: cover upstairs}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.35-cover-upstairs}

Reading source: \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/unofficial-stacks-project-ai-drafts/blob/565b10e987aba5969b21145a0833f42d69f96790/algebra.tex\#L4346-L4405}{AI Integrated Stacks, pinned Algebra, lines 4346--4405}.

Let \(g_1,\ldots,g_r\in S\) generate the unit ideal. The \(R\)-algebra \(S\) is finite type, respectively finitely presented, if and only if every \(S_{g_i}\) has that property.

\textbf{Proof.} We will use a finite-cover calculation for arbitrary modules. In a ring \(A\), suppose \(\sum_i c_it_i=1\) and \(N_{t_i}=0\) for all \(i\). For \(n\in N\), choose positive \(e_i\) with \(t_i^{e_i}n=0\). In the expansion of \((\sum_i c_it_i)^b\) with \(b=1+\sum_i(e_i-1)\), every monomial has an exponent at least \(e_i\) in one of the \(t_i\). Multiplication by \(n\) kills every monomial. Since the expanded element is one, \(n=0\). Thus \(N=0\) without a finiteness hypothesis.

Choose \(h_i\) with \(\sum_i h_ig_i=1\). If every \(S_{g_i}\) is finite type, choose a finite \(R\)-algebra generator list for each, written as fractions \(a_{ij}/g_i^{b_{ij}}\). Let \(S_0\subset S\) be generated over \(R\) by all \(a_{ij},g_i,h_i\). The map \((S_0)_{g_i}\to S_{g_i}\) is surjective by the chosen generators. It is injective: a numerator from \(S_0\) whose fraction vanishes in \(S_{g_i}\) is killed by a power of \(g_i\) in \(S\), hence also in the subring \(S_0\). Therefore \((S/S_0)_{g_i}=0\) as a module over \(S_0\). The \(g_i\) generate one in \(S_0\), so the cover calculation gives \(S=S_0\). This proves finite type.

If every chart is finitely presented, the finite-type case supplies \(S=P/J\) for a finite polynomial ring \(P=R[X_1,\ldots,X_n]\). Choose lifts \(u_i,v_i\in P\) of \(g_i,h_i\). The kernel of \[P[Z]\longrightarrow S_{g_i},\qquad Z\longmapsto g_i^{-1},\] is \(JP[Z]+(u_iZ-1)\), since its quotient is exactly \((P/J)[Z]/(g_iZ-1)\). The entire presentation-independence proof \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-finite-presentation-independent]{F.44} makes this kernel finitely generated. Express each of its finite generators as a finite sum of multiples of elements of \(J\) and of \(u_iZ-1\). Collect the finitely many coefficients \(a_{ij}\in J\) used in those sums. They, together with \(u_iZ-1\), generate the same kernel: they belong to it and generate each chosen generator.

Set \[J_0=\bigl(\sum_i v_iu_i-1,\ a_{ij}\text{ for all }i,j\bigr)\subset J,\qquad A=P/J_0.\] The images of \(u_i\) generate one in \(A\). The preceding kernel equalities give isomorphisms \(A_{u_i}\cong S_{g_i}\). Indeed adjoining \(Z\) with \(u_iZ-1\) identifies both quotients with the same localization, and every element of \(J_0\) also belongs to the original kernel. The kernel \(J/J_0\) of \(A\twoheadrightarrow S\) therefore vanishes on this cover. The arbitrary-module calculation gives \(J=J_0\), so the original finite polynomial presentation has a finite relation ideal.

Conversely, localization adds only \(g_i^{-1}\) to a finite generating list. For a finite presentation \(S=P/(f_1,\ldots,f_d)\) and a lift \(u_i\) of \(g_i\) it gives the exact finite presentation \(S_{g_i}=P[Z]/(f_1,\ldots,f_d,u_iZ-1)\). If the cover is empty, its unit-ideal condition forces \(S=0\); the presentation \(R/(1)\) handles both assertions directly. Empty generator lists cause no exception. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-criterion-flatness-fibre}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.36: criterion flatness fibre}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.36-criterion-flatness-fibre}

Reading source: \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/unofficial-stacks-project-ai-drafts/blob/565b10e987aba5969b21145a0833f42d69f96790/algebra.tex\#L34374-L34496}{AI Integrated Stacks, pinned Algebra, lines 34374--34496}.

Let \(R\to S\to S'\) be local maps of local rings and write \(\mathfrak m=\mathfrak m_R\). Suppose that both \(S/R\) and \(S'/R\) are essentially finitely presented, that \(M\ne0\) is a finitely presented \(S'\)-module, that \(M\) is \(R\)-flat, and that \(M/\mathfrak mM\) is flat over \(S/\mathfrak mS\). Then \(S\) is \(R\)-flat and \(M\) is \(S\)-flat. The original rings need not be Noetherian.

\textbf{Proof.} We construct compatible Noetherian local models, then apply the Noetherian fibre criterion twice through the two flatness hypotheses. The full finite-expression construction \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-limit-essentially-finite-presentation]{F.59} writes \(R=\operatorname*{colim}R_\lambda\), where the \(R_\lambda\) are local rings essentially of finite type over \(\mathbf Z\), with maximal ideals \(\mathfrak p_\lambda\) and local transitions. Their maximal ideals have colimit \(\mathfrak m\).

An essentially finitely presented algebra that is local is a localization at one prime of a finitely presented algebra: all elements outside the inverse image of its maximal ideal are units, so the two localization universal properties identify the rings. Choose such finite presentations for \(S\) and \(S'\). To model their intervening map, choose images in \(S'\) of the finite generators of \(S\), represented by polynomials with finitely many denominators. Put those denominators among the inverted elements, and impose the finite graph equations equating the chosen source generators with their images. Eliminating the graph variables recovers the presentation of \(S'\) over \(R\) after localization. The source relations vanish there; any vanishing of their finitely many representatives is witnessed by finitely many additional denominators. Include these witnesses too. All the coefficients and finite equality witnesses can be placed at one stage of F.59.

For later stages we consequently have presentations \[S_\lambda=(R_\lambda[X]/(f_\lambda))_{\mathfrak q_\lambda},\qquad
S'_\lambda=(R_\lambda[X,Y]/(f_\lambda,g_\lambda))_{\mathfrak q'_\lambda},\] where the primes are contracted from the actual local target rings. The two maps are local. The coefficient lists are fixed and finite, so the Hilbert basis theorem makes all these model rings Noetherian. For \(\mu\geq\lambda\), tensoring the displayed polynomials and relations gives exactly \[S_\lambda\otimes_{R_\lambda}R_\mu\longrightarrow S_\mu,\qquad
S'_\lambda\otimes_{S_\lambda}S_\mu\longrightarrow S'_\mu\] as localizations. The same description holds with the final rings \(R,S,S'\).

Write a finite module presentation \((S')^a\xrightarrow{A}(S')^b\to M\to0\). By \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-limit-module-essentially-finite-presentation]{F.60}, its finitely many matrix entries occur at a common stage. Define \(M_\lambda=\operatorname{coker}((S'_\lambda)^a\xrightarrow{A_\lambda}(S'_\lambda)^b)\). Right exactness of tensor gives \[M_\mu\cong M_\lambda\otimes_{S'_\lambda}S'_\mu,\qquad
M\cong M_\lambda\otimes_{S'_\lambda}S'.\] In particular every \(M_\lambda\) is nonzero, because a zero one would make the final tensor zero. It is finite over the stipulated Noetherian local overring \(S'_\lambda\).

The \(R\)-flatness of \(M\) and the localized tensor descriptions allow \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-colimit-eventually-flat]{F.21} to be applied to \(R_\lambda\to S'_\lambda\) and \(M_\lambda\). It gives a stage where \(M_\lambda\) is \(R_\lambda\)-flat. At every later stage this persists: scalar extension preserves the exact tensor functor, and localization of an algebra-module preserves its injection tests. The final module and the later ones have precisely these two forms.

Next put \[A_\lambda=S_\lambda/\mathfrak p_\lambda S_\lambda,\qquad
B_\lambda=S'_\lambda/\mathfrak p_\lambda S'_\lambda,\qquad
N_\lambda=M_\lambda/\mathfrak p_\lambda M_\lambda.\] These are local Noetherian algebra models with finite target modules. The local transitions and right exactness give their colimits \(S/\mathfrak mS\), \(S'/\mathfrak mS'\) and \(M/\mathfrak mM\). Reduction of the same polynomial presentations along the residue-field maps \(R_\lambda/\mathfrak p_\lambda\to R_\mu/\mathfrak p_\mu\) shows that \[B_\lambda\otimes_{A_\lambda}A_\mu\longrightarrow B_\mu\] is a localization, and that \(N_\mu=N_\lambda\otimes_{B_\lambda}B_\mu\). Thus this quotient system has every model property required by F.21. The assumed flatness of its limit over \(S/\mathfrak mS\) gives a later stage where \(N_\lambda\) is \(A_\lambda\)-flat. Passing to a common successor retains the first flatness assertion as well.

At that stage the local maps \(R_\lambda\to S_\lambda\to S'_\lambda\) and the nonzero finite module \(M_\lambda\) satisfy the full criterion \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-criterion-flatness-fibre-Noetherian]{F.37}. It gives \(R_\lambda\)-flatness of \(S_\lambda\) and \(S_\lambda\)-flatness of \(M_\lambda\). Finally \(S\) is a localization of \(S_\lambda\otimes_{R_\lambda}R\), so it is \(R\)-flat. The module \(M\) is a localization of \(M_\lambda\otimes_{S_\lambda}S\), so it is \(S\)-flat. These conclusions use the exact scalar-extension and localization functors and impose no new hypothesis on the original rings. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-criterion-flatness-fibre-Noetherian}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.37: criterion flatness fibre Noetherian}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.37-criterion-flatness-fibre-noetherian}

Reading source: \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/unofficial-stacks-project-ai-drafts/blob/565b10e987aba5969b21145a0833f42d69f96790/algebra.tex\#L24999-L25045}{AI Integrated Stacks, pinned Algebra, lines 24999--25045}.

Let \(R\to S\to T\) be local maps of Noetherian local rings, let \(\mathfrak m=\mathfrak m_R\), and let \(M\ne0\) be finite over \(T\). If \(M\) is \(R\)-flat and \(M/\mathfrak mM\) is flat over \(S/\mathfrak mS\), then \(M\) is faithfully flat over \(S\) and \(S\) is flat over \(R\).

\textbf{Proof.} Set \(I=\mathfrak mS\). Locality gives \(I\subset\mathfrak m_S\), so it is proper. The map \[u:\mathfrak m\otimes_RM\longrightarrow I\otimes_SM,\qquad
x\otimes z\longmapsto x\otimes z\] is surjective: write an element of \(I\) as a finite sum of products \(sx\) and move each \(s\) to the module factor. Its composite with multiplication \(I\otimes_SM\to M\) is injective by \(R\)-flatness. Therefore \(u\) is injective as well as surjective, and multiplication from \(I\otimes_SM\) is injective. The ideal-kernel Tor calculation of AG-RG-S01, Lemma 1.A, gives \(\operatorname{Tor}_1^S(S/I,M)=0\).

Apply the full proper-ideal criterion AG-CA-08, Corollary 4.4, to the source \(S\), local overring \(T\), finite \(T\)-module \(M\) and ideal \(I\). Its flat quotient condition is exactly the assumed flatness of \(M/IM\) over \(S/I\), and the Tor condition has just been proved. Thus \(M\) is \(S\)-flat. Since \(M\) is finite and nonzero over the local ring \(T\), Nakayama \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-NAK]{F.10} gives \(M/\mathfrak m_TM\ne0\). The quotient \(M/\mathfrak m_SM\) surjects onto it, by locality of \(S\to T\), so this closed fibre is nonzero too. The complete flat-module criterion AG-CA-08, Theorem 1.1, gives faithful flatness over \(S\).

Let \(L=\operatorname{Tor}_1^R(R/\mathfrak m,S)\). The ideal sequence over \(R\) and its Tor-kernel calculation give the exact sequence of \(S\)-modules \[0\longrightarrow L\longrightarrow\mathfrak m\otimes_RS
\longrightarrow I\longrightarrow0.\] Tensor with the flat \(S\)-module \(M\). Tensor associativity identifies its middle term with \(\mathfrak m\otimes_RM\), and its final term is \(I\otimes_SM\). Their map is the isomorphism \(u\) already proved, so \(L\otimes_SM=0\). Faithfulness forces \(L=0\). AG-CA-08, Theorem 4.2, applied to the local map \(R\to S\) and the module \(S\), finite over its own Noetherian local overring, gives \(R\)-flatness of \(S\). Both conclusions are established with the stated target-module finiteness, without assuming \(M\) finite over \(R\) or \(S\). ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-descent-regular}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.38: descent regular}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.38-descent-regular}

Reading source: \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/unofficial-stacks-project-ai-drafts/blob/565b10e987aba5969b21145a0833f42d69f96790/algebra.tex\#L48353-L48371}{AI Integrated Stacks, pinned Algebra, lines 48353--48371}.

If \(R\to S\) is faithfully flat and \(S\) is a regular ring, then \(R\) is regular. In particular the source is Noetherian even if this is not separately assumed.

\textbf{Proof.} First prove that \(R\) is Noetherian. For an ideal \(I\subset R\), its extension \(IS\) is finite because \(S\) is Noetherian. Express a finite generating list for \(IS\) using finitely many elements \(a_1,\ldots,a_r\) of \(I\), and let \(I_0=(a_1,\ldots,a_r)\) in \(R\). Then \(I_0S=IS\). Flatness identifies \(I\otimes_RS\) with \(IS\) and \(I_0\otimes_RS\) with \(I_0S\), by tensoring their inclusions into \(R\). Right exactness consequently gives \((I/I_0)\otimes_RS=0\). Faithfulness implies \(I=I_0\). Every ideal is finite, proving Noetherianity.

Fix \(\mathfrak p\subset R\). Faithful flatness supplies a prime \(\mathfrak q\subset S\) above it, by AG-CA-08, Theorem 2.1. Put \(A=R_{\mathfrak p}\), \(B=S_{\mathfrak q}\) and \(k=\kappa(\mathfrak p)\). The induced map \(A\to B\) is flat and local, hence faithfully flat by that same theorem. The ring \(B\) is regular local by the hypothesis.

Take a free resolution \(F_\bullet\to k\) over the Noetherian local ring \(A\). Tensoring with the flat algebra \(B\) gives a free resolution of \(k\otimes_AB\) over \(B\). The complex computing its self-Tor is \[(F_\bullet\otimes_AB)\otimes_B(k\otimes_AB)
\cong(F_\bullet\otimes_Ak)\otimes_AB.\] Exact tensor with \(B\) commutes with kernels and images, so the entire arbitrary-module resolution calculus AG-RG-S01, Lemma 1.A, gives \[\operatorname{Tor}_i^A(k,k)\otimes_AB
\cong\operatorname{Tor}_i^B(k\otimes_AB,k\otimes_AB).\] The regular-local global-dimension theorem AG-CA-14, Theorem 2.2, makes the right-hand groups zero for sufficiently large \(i\). Faithfulness makes the corresponding source groups zero.

The full minimal-resolution construction AG-CA-13, Theorem 2.2, gives a resolution of \(k\) by finite free \(A\)-modules whose differentials have entries in \(\mathfrak m_A\). Tensoring it with \(k\) makes every differential zero. Thus its degree-\(i\) free term modulo \(\mathfrak m_A\) is exactly \(\operatorname{Tor}_i^A(k,k)\). Eventual vanishing makes those finite free terms zero, and the resolution truncates. Therefore \(k\) has finite projective dimension. The reverse implication in AG-CA-14, Theorem 2.2, proves that \(A\) is regular local. This holds at every source prime, proving regularity of \(R\). ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-dimension-fibres-bounded-open-upstairs}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.39: dimension fibres bounded open upstairs}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.39-dimension-fibres-bounded-open-upstairs}

Reading source: \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/unofficial-stacks-project-ai-drafts/blob/565b10e987aba5969b21145a0833f42d69f96790/algebra.tex\#L32674-L32690}{AI Integrated Stacks, pinned Algebra, lines 32674--32690}.

For a finite-type ring map \(R\to S\) and \(\mathfrak q\subset S\) over \(\mathfrak p\subset R\), put \[n=\dim_{\bar{\mathfrak q}}\operatorname{Spec}
(S\otimes_R\kappa(\mathfrak p)),\] the dimension in a neighbourhood of its point in the fibre. Some principal open neighbourhood of \(\mathfrak q\) has fibre point-dimension at most \(n\) at every point. The base ring is arbitrary.

\textbf{Proof.} The fibre is a finite-type algebra over \(k=\kappa(\mathfrak p)\) and hence Noetherian. By the definition of point dimension and the complete field point-dimension theorem AG-CA-09, Theorem 6.1, choose a principal neighbourhood of \(\bar{\mathfrak q}\) in that fibre whose algebra has dimension exactly \(n\). Its defining element is a fraction \(b/a\) with \(b\in S\) and \(a\in R\setminus\mathfrak p\). Since \(a\) is a fibre unit, the same fibre open is defined by \(b\); also \(b\notin\mathfrak q\). Replace \(S\) temporarily by \(S_b\).

Apply the full Noether-normalization proof AG-CA-09, Lemma 2.1 and Corollary 3.2, to this fibre. It supplies \(n\) algebraically independent parameters and a finite map from their polynomial algebra to the fibre. These parameters lift to elements \(t_1,\ldots,t_n\in S_b\). Indeed that proof repeatedly replaces a generator by it minus an integer power of the last generator, so its chosen parameters are polynomials with integer coefficients in the original fibre generators. Dividing a relation by its nonzero leading coefficient proves integrality and does not change those parameter expressions.

The finite-type map \(R[T_1,\ldots,T_n]\to S_b\), \(T_i\mapsto t_i\), is quasi-finite at the chosen point. Its fibre there is a further fibre of the displayed finite \(k[T]\)-algebra, and is therefore finite-dimensional over the contracted polynomial prime's residue field. The entire open-locus proof \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/main/docs/courses/AG-RG/AG-RG-S04.md}{Zariski Main, Theorem C5.1}, using its algebraic Theorem C4.3 over arbitrary bases, gives a principal open around that point on which this polynomial map is quasi-finite everywhere. A defining fraction in \(S_b\) has numerator \(c\in S\); the resulting neighbourhood in the original spectrum is \(D(bc)\).

For any \(\mathfrak p'\subset R\), let \(U=S_{bc}\otimes_R\kappa(\mathfrak p')\). The map \(\kappa(\mathfrak p')[T]\to U\) is quasi-finite. This can be checked directly on its fibres: the polynomial base ring is a quotient and localization of \(R[T]\) along \(\mathfrak p'\), so a point and its residue field are those of the corresponding prime of \(R[T]\), and its fibre is the fibre of the quasi-finite polynomial map just constructed.

At a minimal prime \(\eta\) of a nonzero \(U\), its residue field is finite over the residue field of its contracted polynomial prime, by the full isolated-fibre criterion \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-isolated-point-fibre]{F.56}. The latter field has transcendence degree at most \(n\) over \(\kappa(\mathfrak p')\), since it is generated as a field by the images of \(n\) polynomial variables. Finite algebraic extension preserves this transcendence degree. AG-CA-09, Theorem 4.2, therefore gives \(\dim(U/\eta)\leq n\). Taking the maximum over its finitely many minimal primes gives \(\dim U\leq n\). Every neighbourhood dimension at a point of this fibre is at most its total dimension, proving the required bound on \(D(bc)\). Empty fibres have no point to check. The earlier conductor proof includes the polynomial-normality argument \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/main/docs/courses/AG-RG/AG-RG-S04.md}{Zariski Main over an arbitrary base, Corollary B1.2}; no Noetherian assumption on \(R\) or \(S\) has entered the argument. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-essentially-of-finite-type-into-artinian-local}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.40: essentially of finite type into artinian local}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.40-essentially-of-finite-type-into-artinian-local}

Reading source: \href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/07DT}{Stacks, Tag 07DT}.

Let \(R\to S\) be any ring map, with \(S\) Artinian local, maximal ideal \(\mathfrak m\), and residue field \(K=S/\mathfrak m\). Each of the following properties of \(S/R\) is equivalent to the same property of \(K/R\): finite, of finite type, and essentially of finite type.

\textbf{Proof.} The Artinian length theorem \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/d02d0a3669f42579db037cd44de1d113fdd770a1/docs/courses/AG-CA/src/noetherian-and-artinian-rings.md}{AG-CA-03, Theorem 4.2} gives a finite composition series of the \(S\)-module \(S\). Every simple factor is \(K\): a nonzero element of a simple module generates it, and its annihilator is the unique maximal ideal. If \(K\) is finite over \(R\), each factor is therefore a finite \(R\)-module. Finite generation passes through an extension directly: lift finitely many generators of the quotient and adjoin finitely many generators of the submodule. Induction on the composition series makes \(S\) finite over \(R\). The converse follows by taking the images of module generators in \(K\). This proves the finite assertion for an arbitrary source ring.

For finite type, a quotient keeps the images of any finite list of algebra generators. Conversely, lift finite \(R\)-algebra generators of \(K\) to \(s_1,\ldots,s_a\in S\). The polynomial map \(P=R[X_1,\ldots,X_a]\to S\), \(X_i\mapsto s_i\), is surjective on residues. Thus \(K\) is cyclic as a \(P\)-module. The finite assertion just proved makes \(S\) a finite \(P\)-module. Choose its module generators \(u_1,\ldots,u_b\). Every element is a sum of polynomials in the \(s_i\) times the \(u_j\), so \(s_i,u_j\) together generate \(S\) as an \(R\)-algebra.

Finally, a quotient of a localization of a finite-type algebra is the localization of its quotient, by the fraction formula. Hence essential finite type passes from \(S\) to \(K\). For the converse write \(K=T^{-1}C\), with \(C\) a finite-type \(R\)-algebra, and let \(C_0\) be the image of \(C\) in \(K\). The domain \(C_0\) has fraction field \(K\): every element of the displayed localization is a fraction of its elements, and the field \(K\) contains the inverse of every nonzero element of \(C_0\).

Lift a finite list of \(R\)-algebra generators of \(C_0\) to \(S\), and let \(A\subset S\) be the \(R\)-subalgebra they generate. Put \(\mathfrak p=A\cap\mathfrak m\). Then \(A/\mathfrak p=C_0\), so \(\kappa(\mathfrak p)=K\). Every element of \(A\setminus\mathfrak p\) maps to a unit in \(S\); thus the inclusion extends to \(A_{\mathfrak p}\to S\). Applying the finite assertion to this map makes \(S\) a finite \(A_{\mathfrak p}\)-module. Choose generators \(v_1,\ldots,v_c\) and set \(B=A[v_1,\ldots,v_c]\subset S\). This is a finite-type \(R\)-algebra. Localizing \(B\) at \(A\setminus\mathfrak p\) maps injectively into \(S\), because those denominators are units there, and surjectively because the \(v_j\) generate over \(A_{\mathfrak p}\). Therefore \(S\) is that localization of \(B\). This proves the last equivalence without a finiteness assumption on \(R\). ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-etale-standard-smooth}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.41: etale standard smooth}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.41-etale-standard-smooth}

Reading source: \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/unofficial-stacks-project-ai-drafts/blob/565b10e987aba5969b21145a0833f42d69f96790/algebra.tex\#L40737-L40760}{AI Integrated Stacks, pinned Algebra, lines 40737--40760}.

Every étale ring map \(R\to S\) has a standard smooth presentation with equally many variables and equations: \[S\cong R[X_1,\ldots,X_n]/(f_1,\ldots,f_n),\qquad
\det(\partial f_i/\partial X_j)\in S^\times.\]

\textbf{Proof.} If \(S=0\), take \(S=R[X]/(1)\). Its Jacobian determinant is zero, which is the unit element in the zero ring, so it has the required property.

Suppose \(S\ne0\) and choose a finite polynomial presentation \(P=R[X_1,\ldots,X_n]\twoheadrightarrow S\) with kernel \(I\). The complete formal/conormal comparison AG-CA-17, Theorem 3.1 and Section 4, says that the conormal differential of an étale presentation is an isomorphism: \[I/I^2\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\bigoplus_{i=1}^nS\,dX_i,\qquad
[f]\longmapsto\sum_i(\partial f/\partial X_i)dX_i.\] Specifically, formal smoothness gives a split injection and formal unramifiedness gives zero cokernel; étaleness supplies both. Thus \(I/I^2\) is finite free.

The entire global construction \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-huber]{F.55} replaces this presentation by \(S=R[Y_1,\ldots,Y_m]/J\) with \(J=(g_1,\ldots,g_c)\) and the classes of the \(g_j\) a basis of \(J/J^2\). Apply the same étale conormal comparison to this new presentation. In its actual equation and differential bases it is the Jacobian map \(S^c\xrightarrow{H}S^m\). It is an isomorphism. Choose any maximal ideal of the nonzero ring \(S\) and reduce this inverse pair modulo it. The resulting vector-space isomorphism forces \(c=m\).

The matrix \(H\) is now square and has an inverse over \(S\). The determinant product identity gives \(\det(H)\det(H^{-1})=1\), so its determinant is a unit. Relabeling these \(m\) variables and \(m\) equations produces the asserted presentation of the whole algebra. It proves global standard smoothness, with no Noetherian-base assumption or restriction to a neighbourhood. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-exact-sequence-NL}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.42: exact sequence NL}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.42-exact-sequence-nl}

Reading source: \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/unofficial-stacks-project-ai-drafts/blob/565b10e987aba5969b21145a0833f42d69f96790/algebra.tex\#L36838-L36913}{AI Integrated Stacks, pinned Algebra, lines 36838--36913}.

Let \(A\to B\to C\) be ring maps. Choose surjections \(P=A[x_s\mid s\in\mathcal S]\to B\) and \(Q=B[y_t\mid t\in\mathcal T]\to C\), with kernels \(I,J\). Put \(E=A[x_s,y_t]\) and \(K=\ker(E\to C)\). Variable sets may be infinite. Define \[N_A=(I/I^2)\otimes_BC,\quad N_B=K/K^2,\quad N_C=J/J^2,\] \[E_A=\bigoplus_sC\,dx_s,\quad
E_B=E_A\oplus\bigoplus_tC\,dy_t,\quad
E_C=\bigoplus_tC\,dy_t.\] Their conormal differentials give the commutative diagram with exact rows \[\begin{array}{ccccccccc}
0&\longrightarrow&E_A&\xrightarrow{i}&E_B&\xrightarrow{p}&E_C&\longrightarrow&0\\
&&\uparrow d_A&&\uparrow d_B&&\uparrow d_C\\
&&N_A&\xrightarrow{a}&N_B&\xrightarrow{b}&N_C&\longrightarrow&0.
\end{array}\] No injectivity of \(a\) is asserted. With the first cotangent homology \(H_1(L_{-/ -})\) computed by these presentation complexes, the resulting canonical exact sequence is \[\begin{gathered}
H_1(\operatorname{NL}_{B/A}\otimes_BC)\longrightarrow
H_1(L_{C/A})\longrightarrow H_1(L_{C/B})\\
\xrightarrow{\delta} C\otimes_B\Omega_{B/A}
\longrightarrow\Omega_{C/A}\longrightarrow\Omega_{C/B}\longrightarrow0.
\end{gathered}\] It extends the differential sequence \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/d02d0a3669f42579db037cd44de1d113fdd770a1/docs/courses/AG-CA/src/kahler-differentials.md}{AG-CA-15, Theorem 3.1}. If both \(\operatorname{Tor}_1^B(\Omega_{B/A},C)\) and \(\operatorname{Tor}_2^B(\Omega_{B/A},C)\) vanish, there is moreover a natural identification \[H_1(\operatorname{NL}_{B/A}\otimes_BC)
\cong H_1(L_{B/A})\otimes_BC.\]

\textbf{Proof.} The map \(i\) includes the \(dx_s\) coordinates, and \(p\) kills those coordinates and retains the \(dy_t\). Their row is split exact. Define \[a([f]\otimes c)=[\widetilde c f]\in K/K^2,\qquad
b([h])=[h\bmod IE]\in J/J^2,\] where \(\widetilde c\in E\) lifts \(c\). Changing this lift adds an element of \(K\) times \(f\in I\subset K\), hence an element of \(K^2\). Changing \(f\) by \(I^2\), or using a different polynomial lift of a coefficient in \(B\), also changes the result by \(K^2\). Multiplication of coefficient representatives proves the tensor-balancing relation, so \(a\) is well defined. The map \(E\to Q\) has kernel \(IE\), maps \(K\) onto \(J\), and maps \(K^2\) onto \(J^2\). Therefore the preimage of \(J^2\) in \(K\) is \(K^2+IE\): subtract a finite sum of products of lifts from \(K\) to leave an element of \(IE\). The image of \(a\) is exactly \((IE+K^2)/K^2\). This proves exactness at \(N_B\) and \(N_C\).

Differentiation gives \(d_B(\widetilde c f)=c\,df\), since \(f\) evaluates to zero in \(C\). Hence \(d_Ba=id_A\). Projecting a polynomial derivative to its \(dy_t\) part gives precisely its derivative in \(Q\) relative to \(B\), so \(pd_B=d_Cb\). These identities prove commutativity of the entire diagram.

We now give the connecting map and check every exactness assertion. For \(z\in\ker d_C\), choose \(y\in N_B\) with \(b(y)=z\). Then \(p(d_By)=d_Cz=0\), so the split exact upper row gives a unique \(v\in E_A\) with \(i(v)=d_By\). Set \(\delta(z)=[v]\in E_A/\operatorname{im}d_A\). If the lift \(y\) changes, its difference is \(a(x)\) for some \(x\in N_A\); the corresponding \(v\) changes by \(d_Ax\). Thus this class is well defined.

A cycle \(y\in\ker d_B\) mapping to zero under \(b\) is \(a(x)\), and \(0=d_Ba(x)=i(d_Ax)\) forces \(d_Ax=0\), since \(i\) is injective. This proves exactness at \(H_1(L_{C/A})\). At \(\ker d_C\), the class \(\delta(z)\) is zero precisely when the above \(v\) is \(d_Ax\) for some \(x\); then \(y-a(x)\) is a cycle lifting \(z\). Conversely a cycle lift has \(v=0\). This proves exactness at \(H_1(L_{C/B})\).

At \(E_A/\operatorname{im}d_A\), a class \([v]\) maps to zero in \(E_B/\operatorname{im}d_B\) precisely when \(i(v)=d_By\) for some \(y\). Its image \(b(y)\) is then a cycle in \(N_C\), and the construction gives \(\delta(b(y))=[v]\). At the next term, if \(p(w)=d_Cz\), choose \(y\) with \(b(y)=z\). Then \(p(w-d_By)=0\), so \(w-d_By=i(v)\) for a \(v\in E_A\). Thus \([w]\) comes from \([v]\). Conversely every image of \(i\) is killed by \(p\). Finally \(p\) is surjective, so its map on the cokernels is surjective as well. These calculations prove the complete displayed sequence.

The entire presentation comparison \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-NL-homotopy]{F.11} identifies the kernels and cokernels with the stated cotangent homology and differential modules. The sequence is canonical under those identifications. Indeed comparison maps are obtained by lifting each source polynomial variable to the new presentation. Make the lifts for \(B\) first, then lift the target variables for \(C\) and their coefficients; this gives comparison maps on \(P,Q,E\) respecting \(I,J,K\). Their relation-class and derivative maps commute with \(a,b,i,p\). Transporting a chosen lift \(y\) transports its derivative and the unique \(v\), so the connecting classes commute too. F.11 proves that alternative choices are homotopic and that the reverse comparisons induce inverse homology maps. Hence the induced sequence and its maps are independent of the chosen presentations.

For the final assertion write \(\operatorname{NL}_{B/A}=[F_1\xrightarrow{d}F_0]\), with \(F_0\) free, put \(N=\operatorname{im}d\), \(H=\ker d\) and \(\Omega=\operatorname{coker}d\). The short exact sequence \(0\to N\to F_0\to\Omega\to0\) and the first Tor hypothesis give \[0\longrightarrow N\otimes_BC\longrightarrow F_0\otimes_BC
\longrightarrow\Omega\otimes_BC\longrightarrow0.\] The long Tor sequence and freeness of \(F_0\) identify \(\operatorname{Tor}_1^B(N,C)\) with \(\operatorname{Tor}_2^B(\Omega,C)\), using the full resolution calculus of AG-RG-S01, Lemma 1.A. The second hypothesis therefore makes tensoring \(0\to H\to F_1\to N\to0\) give \[0\longrightarrow H\otimes_BC\longrightarrow F_1\otimes_BC
\longrightarrow N\otimes_BC\longrightarrow0.\] Since \(N\otimes_BC\) injects into \(F_0\otimes_BC\), these two sequences identify \(H\otimes_BC\) with the kernel of the tensor differential. This is the claimed natural first-homology identification. No flatness of \(F_1\) and no finite-variable assumption has been added. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-extension}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.43: extension}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.43-extension}

Reading source: \href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0519}{Stacks, Tag 0519}.

Let \(R\) be any ring and let \(0\to M_1\to M_2\to M_3\to0\) be exact. If the two end modules are finite, so is the middle module; a quotient of a finite module is finite. If both end modules are finitely presented, so is the middle module. A quotient of a finitely presented module by a finite submodule is finitely presented. Finally, if \(M_2\) is finite and \(M_3\) is finitely presented, then \(M_1\) is finite.

\textbf{Proof.} Identify \(M_1\) with its image in \(M_2\). To generate the middle module, take generators of \(M_1\) and lifts of generators of \(M_3\). Subtracting a combination of the latter from an arbitrary element leaves an element of \(M_1\). Images of any generating list generate a quotient. These observations prove the two assertions about finite modules.

We first establish the presentation calculation needed in the other assertions. Suppose \(q : G\twoheadrightarrow N\) is a finite free presentation with finitely generated kernel \(L\), and \(p : F\twoheadrightarrow N\) is any surjection from a finite free module. Choose maps \(u : F\to G\) and \(v : G\to F\) by lifting their finite bases, so that \(qu=p\) and \(pv=q\). For every \(z\in\ker p\), \[
z=v(uz)+(1-vu)z,
\qquad uz\in L.
\] Both \(v(L)\) and \((1-vu)F\) lie in \(\ker p\), since \(pv=q\) and \(pvu=qu=p\). Thus that kernel is generated by the images under \(v\) of a finite generating list of \(L\), together with the finitely many columns of \(1-vu\). In particular the kernel of every finite free surjection onto a finitely presented module is finite. The choices of lifts here use only the defining property of a free basis.

If \(M_2\) is finite, choose a finite free surjection \(F\to M_2\). When \(M_3\) is finitely presented, the kernel of the composite \(F\to M_3\) is finite by this calculation. Its image in \(M_2\) is exactly \(M_1\): an element mapping to zero in \(M_3\) has any chosen lift in that kernel. Hence \(M_1\) is finite.

Next write a finitely presented \(M_2\) as \(F/K\), with \(F\) finite free and \(K\) finite. If \(M_1\) is generated by \(a_1,\ldots,a_h\), choose lifts \(\widetilde a_i\in F\). The kernel of \(F\to M_3\) is \[
K+R\widetilde a_1+\cdots+R\widetilde a_h.
\] Indeed an element in that kernel maps to a combination of the \(a_i\) in \(M_2\); subtracting the corresponding lifted combination puts it in \(K\). This is a finite kernel and gives the asserted finite presentation of the quotient.

Finally choose finite free presentations \(p_i : F_i\twoheadrightarrow M_i\), with finite kernels \(K_i\), for \(i=1,3\). Lift the basis of \(F_3\) to obtain \(\ell : F_3\to M_2\), and use \[
F_1\oplus F_3\longrightarrow M_2,
\qquad (a,b)\longmapsto p_1(a)+\ell(b).
\] It is onto by the first generator argument. For each generator \(b_j\) of \(K_3\), the element \(\ell(b_j)\) lies in \(M_1\); choose \(a_j\in F_1\) with \(p_1(a_j)=-\ell(b_j)\). Its kernel is generated by \((K_1,0)\) and the finitely many pairs \((a_j,b_j)\). To see this, the second coordinate of any kernel element lies in \(K_3\). Subtract a combination of these pairs to make that coordinate zero; the first coordinate then lies in \(K_1\). We have constructed a finite generating list of relations, so \(M_2\) is finitely presented. Empty generating lists and zero modules satisfy the same formulas. No Noetherian assumption is used. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-finite-presentation-independent}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.44: finite presentation independent}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.44-finite-presentation-independent}

Reading source: \href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/00R2}{Stacks, Tag 00R2}.

If an \(R\)-algebra \(S\) is finitely presented, the kernel of every surjection \(\alpha : R[X_1,\ldots,X_n]\twoheadrightarrow S\) is a finitely generated ideal.

\textbf{Proof.} Fix one presentation \[
S=R[Y_1,\ldots,Y_m]/(f_1,\ldots,f_h).
\] Choose \(g_i(Y)\) representing \(\alpha(X_i)\), and, using the surjectivity of \(\alpha\), choose \(h_j(X)\) representing the class of \(Y_j\). In the polynomial ring \(P=R[X_1,\ldots,X_n]\), form the finite ideal \[
J=\bigl(f_1(h(X)),\ldots,f_h(h(X)),\;
X_i-g_i(h(X))\ (1\leq i\leq n)\bigr).
\] Each generator maps to zero under \(\alpha\), by the choices of representatives, so \(J\subset\ker\alpha\).

For the reverse inclusion, take \(F(X)\in\ker\alpha\). The polynomial \(F(g(Y))\) represents zero in the fixed presentation; hence there are polynomials \(c_l(Y)\) with \[
F(g(Y))=\sum_{l=1}^h c_l(Y)f_l(Y).
\] Substitute \(Y=h(X)\). This puts \(F(g(h(X)))\) in \(J\). Also \[
F(X)-F(g(h(X)))\in
\bigl(X_i-g_i(h(X)):1\leq i\leq n\bigr).
\] Here is the polynomial identity behind this last inclusion, valid over an arbitrary ring. Replace the variables one at a time and telescope the differences. At a single variable, every monomial difference is divisible by its coordinate difference, because \(U^a-V^a=(U-V)\sum_{b=0}^{a-1}U^{a-1-b}V^b\) for \(a>0\); the difference is zero for \(a=0\). Adding the monomials proves the inclusion without division by any coefficient. Thus \(F\in J\), proving \(\ker\alpha=J\). The argument includes either empty variable list, an empty relation list and the zero algebra. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-flat-fibre-smooth}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.45: flat fibre smooth}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.45-flat-fibre-smooth}

Reading source: \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/unofficial-stacks-project-ai-drafts/blob/565b10e987aba5969b21145a0833f42d69f96790/algebra.tex\#L39115-L39149}{AI Integrated Stacks, pinned Algebra, lines 39115--39149}.

Let \(R\to S\) be a ring map and let \(\mathfrak q\subset S\) lie over \(\mathfrak p\subset R\). Suppose that some \(s\in S\setminus\mathfrak q\) makes \(S_s\) finitely presented over \(R\), that \(R_{\mathfrak p}\to S_{\mathfrak q}\) is flat, and that \(S\otimes_R\kappa(\mathfrak p)\) is smooth at the point of this fibre induced by \(\mathfrak q\). Then \(R\to S\) is smooth at \(\mathfrak q\), over an arbitrary base ring.

\textbf{Proof.} Replace \(S\) by \(S_s\) and keep the same notation for the prime. Choose a finite presentation \(S=P/I\), where \(P=R[X_1,\ldots,X_n]\) and \(I=(a_1,\ldots,a_m)\). Let \(\mathfrak r\) be the inverse image of \(\mathfrak q\) in \(P\), and put \[A=R_{\mathfrak p},\quad k=\kappa(\mathfrak p),\quad
Q=P_{\mathfrak r},\quad B=S_{\mathfrak q}.\] Thus \(0\to I_{\mathfrak r}\to Q\to B\to0\) is exact over \(A\), and \(B\) is \(A\)-flat.

The full arbitrary-module Tor construction \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/main/docs/courses/AG-RG/AG-RG-S01.md\#1-the-algebra-of-localization}{AG-RG-S01, Lemmas 1.0 and 1.A} gives exactness after tensoring this sequence with \(k\). Indeed use a free resolution of \(k\) to compute \(\operatorname{Tor}_1^A(k,B)\); tensoring with flat \(B\) preserves the kernels and images of that exact resolution, so its positive homology is zero. The natural long exact Tor sequence therefore gives \[0\longrightarrow I_{\mathfrak r}/\mathfrak pI_{\mathfrak r}
\longrightarrow Q/\mathfrak pQ\longrightarrow B/\mathfrak pB\longrightarrow0.\] Set \(\bar Q=Q/\mathfrak pQ\), \(\bar B=B/\mathfrak pB\) and \(J=\ker(\bar Q\to\bar B)\). The injection identifies \(J\) with \(I_{\mathfrak r}/\mathfrak pI_{\mathfrak r}\). Quotient and localization commute by their fraction maps, giving \(\bar Q=k[X]_{\bar{\mathfrak r}}\) and \(\bar B=\bar Q/J\). These are local rings, \(J\) lies in the maximal ideal of \(\bar Q\), and \(J\) is generated by the finitely many images of the \(a_j\).

The smooth fibre has a smooth principal neighbourhood. Definition \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-definition-smooth]{F.6}, presentation comparison \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-NL-homotopy]{F.11}, and the full conormal criterion \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/d02d0a3669f42579db037cd44de1d113fdd770a1/docs/courses/AG-CA/src/formally-smooth-unramified-and-etale-ring-maps.md}{AG-CA-17, Theorem 3.1} make that neighbourhood formally smooth over \(k\): its injective conormal map has projective cokernel, so the sequence splits. The localization lifting proof in AG-CA-17, Theorem 1.2, gives formal smoothness of its local ring \(\bar B\). This argument does not assert that the local ring is finitely presented.

Apply formal smoothness to the square-zero surjection \(\bar Q/J^2\to\bar B\), lifting the identity of \(\bar B\) to a \(k\)-algebra section \(\sigma\). Then \[D(q)=q\bmod J^2-\sigma(q\bmod J)\in J/J^2\] is a \(k\)-derivation. Expanding \(q=\sigma(\bar q)+D(q)\) and \(q'=\sigma(\bar q')+D(q')\), the product of the two correction terms is zero, giving the Leibniz rule. For \(j\in J\), \(D(j)=[j]\). The universal differential construction thus supplies a left inverse of \[J/J^2\longrightarrow\Omega_{\bar Q/k}\otimes_{\bar Q}\bar B=\bar B^n.\] The differential basis and its localization are the complete \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/d02d0a3669f42579db037cd44de1d113fdd770a1/docs/courses/AG-CA/src/kahler-differentials.md}{AG-CA-15, Theorems 5.1 and 2.2}. In coordinates this conormal map sends \([j]\) to its partial derivatives. Consequently \(J/J^2\) is a finite projective direct summand of \(\bar B^n\).
