Choose from \(a_1,\ldots,a_m\) elements \(f_1,\ldots,f_c\) whose reduced conormal classes form a basis over the residue field \(\kappa(\mathfrak q)\). The finite Nakayama argument \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-NAK]{F.10} makes the map \(\bar B^c\to J/J^2\) surjective. Projectivity splits it. Its kernel is a finite direct summand of \(\bar B^c\), and its residue quotient is zero by the chosen residue basis; a second application of F.10 makes this kernel zero. Thus the chosen classes are a free basis.

Let \(H\) be their \(c\)-by-\(n\) equation-by-variable Jacobian over \(\bar B\). The conormal map has matrix \(H^{\mathsf T}\) and a left inverse, so its reduction modulo the maximal ideal is injective; hence \(c\leq n\). The full maximal-minor calculation \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-matrix-left-inverse]{F.70}, applied to this \(n\)-by-\(c\) matrix and its left inverse with scalar \(1\), makes its maximal minors generate one in \(\bar B\). Some minor is therefore a unit in this local ring. Transposing the selected minor preserves its determinant. Let \(\Delta\in P\) be the corresponding \(c\)-variable Jacobian determinant. Its residue in \(\kappa(\mathfrak q)\) is nonzero, so \(\Delta\notin\mathfrak r\). If \(c=0\), use the empty basis and \(\Delta=1\).

The chosen \(f_i\) generate the whole ideal after localizing at \(\mathfrak r\). First \(J=(\bar f_1,\ldots,\bar f_c)+J^2\). Its finite quotient by the displayed generators is equal to \(J\) times that quotient. Since \(J\) lies in the local maximal ideal, F.10 gives \(J=(\bar f_1,\ldots,\bar f_c)\). Now the finite \(Q\)-module \[M=I_{\mathfrak r}/(f_1,\ldots,f_c)Q\] has quotient \(M/\mathfrak pM=0\), by the exact tensor identification of \(J\). The ideal \(\mathfrak pQ\) lies in the maximal ideal of \(Q\), so F.10 gives \(M=0\). This is where the flat local quotient is used; neither ring has needed a chain condition.

For each original generator \(a_j\) of \(I\), write its image in \(Q\) as a finite combination of the \(f_i\). Clear all coefficient denominators, and also the multipliers outside \(\mathfrak r\) witnessing the resulting equalities in the localization. Their finite product \(v\notin\mathfrak r\) gives \[I_v=(f_1,\ldots,f_c)P_v,\qquad
S_{\bar v\bar\Delta}\cong R[X]_{v\Delta}/(f_1,\ldots,f_c).\] This uses the fraction equality criterion, including its annihilator factor, so no possible zero divisor has been cancelled.

Adjoin \(Z\) with equation \(v\Delta Z-1\). The selected Jacobian block for the \(c\) pivot variables and \(Z\) has zero \(Z\) entries in the first \(c\) rows; its determinant is \(\Delta(v\Delta)=v\Delta^2\), a unit in the quotient. The entire arbitrary-base standard-smooth proof \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-standard-smooth]{F.85} applies to this finite presentation and proves its smoothness. In terms of lifting, it inverts this square block, corrects the lifted pivot coordinates by the negative error vector, and the monomial expansion kills all terms containing two corrections in a square-zero ideal. Unit lifts then extend evaluation through the inverse-variable relation, exactly as proved in F.85.

Finally express the elements inverted in this neighbourhood of \(S_s\) as fractions with powers of \(s\) as denominators. Inverting \(s\) and their finitely many numerators gives one principal neighbourhood in the original \(\operatorname{Spec}S\) containing \(\mathfrak q\). Its smoothness proves the conclusion, including empty pivot lists. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-flat-over-regular}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.46: flat over regular}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.46-flat-over-regular}

Reading source: \href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/07DY}{Stacks, Tag 07DY}.

Let \(R\to S\) be a homomorphism of Noetherian local rings. Suppose \(R\) is regular and one regular system of parameters \(x_1,\ldots,x_d\) maps to an \(S\)-regular sequence. Then \(S\) is flat over \(R\). A regular sequence here has proper generated ideal.

\textbf{Proof.} The \(x_i\) generate the maximal ideal of \(R\). Their images belong to the maximal ideal of \(S\), because the ideal they generate is proper in that local ring. Thus the given map is local, even though this was not a separate assumption.

For \(0\leq i\leq d\), put \[
R_i=R/(x_1,\ldots,x_i),\qquad
S_i=S/(x_1,\ldots,x_i)S.
\] These are nonzero Noetherian local rings and their induced maps are local. The written regular-parameter theorem \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/d02d0a3669f42579db037cd44de1d113fdd770a1/docs/courses/AG-CA/src/regular-sequences-depth-and-cohen-macaulay-modules.md}{AG-CA-12, Theorem 6.1} makes the chosen list regular in \(R\). Therefore, for every \(i<d\), multiplication by \(x_{i+1}\) is injective on \(R_i\); the assumed regularity in \(S\) gives the same injection on \(S_i\).

At \(i=d\), the source \(R_d\) is the residue field of \(R\), so \(S_d\) is flat over it. Indeed a vector-space basis identifies tensoring with that space with a direct sum of copies of a module, which preserves injections.

We descend from \(i+1\) to \(i\). Since \(x_{i+1}\) is a nonzerodivisor of \(R_i\), \[
0\longrightarrow R_i\xrightarrow{x_{i+1}}R_i
\longrightarrow R_{i+1}\longrightarrow0
\] is a free resolution. Tensoring it with \(S_i\) computes \[
\operatorname{Tor}_1^{R_i}(R_{i+1},S_i)
=\ker(x_{i+1} : S_i\to S_i)=0.
\] The quotient \(S_i/x_{i+1}S_i=S_{i+1}\) is flat over \(R_{i+1}\) by the descending induction. Apply the complete ideal local criterion \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/d02d0a3669f42579db037cd44de1d113fdd770a1/docs/courses/AG-CA/src/faithful-flatness-and-the-local-criterion-for-flatness.md}{AG-CA-08, Corollary 4.4 and equation (6)} to \(R_i\to S_i\), the proper ideal \((x_{i+1})\subset R_i\), and the module \(S_i\). This module is finite over the target ring \(S_i\), being generated by \(1\); it need not be finite over the source. The Tor vanishing and quotient flatness prove that \(S_i\) is \(R_i\)-flat. The induction reaches \(S_0=S\) over \(R_0=R\). If \(d=0\), the initial field argument already proves the conclusion. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-flat-over-regular-with-regular-fibre}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.47: flat over regular with regular fibre}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.47-flat-over-regular-with-regular-fibre}

Reading source: \href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/031E}{Stacks, Tag 031E}.

Let \((R,\mathfrak m)\to(S,\mathfrak n)\) be a flat local map of Noetherian local rings. If \(R\) and the closed fibre \(F=S/\mathfrak mS\) are regular, then \(S\) is regular.

\textbf{Proof.} Put \(d=\dim R\) and \(e=\dim F\). Regularity supplies generators \(x_1,\ldots,x_d\) of \(\mathfrak m\) and generators \(\overline y_1,\ldots,\overline y_e\) of the maximal ideal \(\mathfrak n/\mathfrak mS\) of \(F\). Choose lifts \(y_j\in\mathfrak n\). Every \(z\in\mathfrak n\) reduces to a combination of the \(\overline y_j\); lifting the coefficients and subtracting that combination leaves an element of \(\mathfrak mS=(x_1,\ldots,x_d)S\). Consequently \[
\mathfrak n=(x_1,\ldots,x_d,y_1,\ldots,y_e)S.
\] Its cotangent space \(\mathfrak n/\mathfrak n^2\) is therefore spanned by at most \(d+e\) vectors over the residue field of \(S\).

The flat local dimension formula, with precisely the stated Noetherian and flatness hypotheses, is proved in \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/d02d0a3669f42579db037cd44de1d113fdd770a1/docs/courses/AG-CA/src/dimension-theory-of-noetherian-local-rings.md}{AG-CA-11, Theorem 5.1}; it gives \(\dim S=d+e\). Its Proposition 4.2 proves that the dimension of a Noetherian local ring is at most the dimension of its cotangent space: lifts of a cotangent basis generate the maximal ideal by finite Nakayama, and the parameter/height theorem bounds dimension by that generator count. Combining these inequalities gives \[
d+e=\dim S\leq
\dim_{\kappa(\mathfrak n)}\mathfrak n/\mathfrak n^2
\leq d+e.
\] Equality of dimension and embedding dimension is the definition of regularity, so \(S\) is regular. The empty source or fibre parameter lists when \(d=0\) or \(e=0\) obey the same calculation. No finite-type assumption on the ring map is needed. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-flatness-descends-more-general}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.48: flatness descends more general}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.48-flatness-descends-more-general}

Reading source: \href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0584}{Stacks, Tag 0584}.

Let \(S\to S'\) be a flat map of \(R\)-algebras, let \(M\) be any \(S\)-module, and put \(M'=S'\otimes_S M\). If \(M\) is flat over \(R\), so is \(M'\). If \(S\to S'\) is faithfully flat, the converse holds as well.

\textbf{Proof.} Test an arbitrary injection \(f:N\hookrightarrow N_1\) of \(R\)-modules. Write \[
Z=\ker\bigl(N\otimes_R M\xrightarrow{f\otimes1}N_1\otimes_R M\bigr).
\] Both tensor products, their map and \(Z\) are \(S\)-modules, using the action on \(M\). Flatness of \(S'\) over \(S\) preserves this kernel. The balancing relations give inverse isomorphisms \[
S'\otimes_S(N\otimes_R M)\ \longleftrightarrow\ N\otimes_R M',
\qquad s'\otimes(n\otimes m)\ \longleftrightarrow\ n\otimes(s'\otimes m),
\] and the same formula for \(N_1\). These maps commute with \(f\), so \[
S'\otimes_S Z\cong
\ker\bigl(N\otimes_R M'\longrightarrow N_1\otimes_R M'\bigr).
\] If \(M\) is \(R\)-flat, \(Z=0\), and the displayed kernel vanishes for every \(f\). If \(M'\) is \(R\)-flat, the right side is zero; faithful flatness then detects \(Z=0\). In either direction the injection characterization of flatness, proved for arbitrary modules in \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/d02d0a3669f42579db037cd44de1d113fdd770a1/docs/courses/AG-CA/src/tor-and-flat-modules.md}{AG-CA-07, Theorem 2.1}, gives the claimed flatness. No module in this calculation is required to be finite. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-formally-smooth-extensions-easy}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.49: formally smooth extensions easy}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.49-formally-smooth-extensions-easy}

Reading source: \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/unofficial-stacks-project-ai-drafts/blob/565b10e987aba5969b21145a0833f42d69f96790/algebra.tex\#L45971-L46012}{AI Integrated Stacks, pinned Algebra, lines 45971--46012}.

For a field extension \(K/k\), each of the following conditions implies formal smoothness of \(K\) over \(k\): it is purely transcendental; it is separable algebraic; or it is separable in the sense of \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-definition-separable-field-extension]{F.5}. Infinite generator sets and infinite algebraic extensions are allowed.

\textbf{Proof.} In the first case write \(K=k(x_j\mid j\in\mathcal J)\). Given a \(k\)-algebra \(D\), a square-zero ideal \(I\) and a \(k\)-map \(K\to D/I\), choose lifts \(a_j\in D\) of the variable images. Polynomial evaluation at these lifts is well defined because each polynomial involves finitely many variables. Every nonzero polynomial in the \(x_j\) is a unit in \(K\), so its evaluated image is a unit modulo \(I\). Units lift: if \(bc=1+r\) with \(r\in I\), then \(bc(1-r)=1\) since \(r^2=0\). Thus all the nonzero polynomials have unit evaluations in \(D\). The polynomial map extends uniquely, for these chosen variable lifts, through the fraction-field localization to a \(k\)-map \(K\to D\). Its reduction is the given map, proving the lifting property.

For a separable algebraic extension, a finite subset of \(K\) generates a finite separable subextension: successive degrees of its finitely many algebraic generators are finite and multiply along the tower. These subfields are directed under inclusion, since the union of two finite generator lists is finite, and their union is \(K\). The full separable-generator tower proof \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/d02d0a3669f42579db037cd44de1d113fdd770a1/docs/courses/AG-CA/src/formally-smooth-unramified-and-etale-ring-maps.md}{AG-CA-17, Proposition 6.3} gives a unique square-zero lift on every such finite field. The derivatives of its separable minimal polynomials are units, so its successive one-equation lifting steps apply. Consequently every finite subextension is formally étale. The entire compatible-lifts proof \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-colimit-formally-etale]{F.22} makes their colimit formally étale, and hence formally smooth.

In the third case use the directed family of finitely generated subfields \(K_i/k\). By F.5 each has a separating transcendence basis and is a finite separable extension of the resulting rational-function field. The first two cases give formal smoothness of both maps in that tower; the full composition lifting proof \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/d02d0a3669f42579db037cd44de1d113fdd770a1/docs/courses/AG-CA/src/formally-smooth-unramified-and-etale-ring-maps.md}{AG-CA-17, Theorem 1.2} gives formal smoothness of \(K_i/k\). The arbitrary-field criterion \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-characterize-formally-smooth-field-extension]{F.17} therefore gives \(H_1(L_{K_i/k})=0\).

Now \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-colimits-NL]{F.24} identifies the conormal complex of \(K/k\) with the filtered colimit of these complexes. Its representative proof of exactness of filtered module colimits also identifies their homology: a cycle is represented at a stage after its finite differential equality holds, and a boundary equality is witnessed at a common later stage. Thus \(H_1(L_{K/k})=\operatorname*{colim}_iH_1(L_{K_i/k})=0\). Applying F.17 again proves formal smoothness of \(K/k\). This uses the field criterion, rather than assuming a general permanence theorem for filtered colimits of formally smooth algebras. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-geometrically-regular}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.50: geometrically regular}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.50-geometrically-regular}

Reading source: \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/unofficial-stacks-project-ai-drafts/blob/565b10e987aba5969b21145a0833f42d69f96790/algebra.tex\#L48753-L48798}{AI Integrated Stacks, pinned Algebra, lines 48753--48798}.

Let \(A\) be a Noetherian \(k\)-algebra, where \(k\) is a field. Regularity of \(A\otimes_kK\) for every finitely generated field extension \(K/k\) is equivalent to regularity of \(A\otimes_kk'\) for every finite purely inseparable field extension \(k'/k\).

\textbf{Proof.} The forward implication includes the finite purely inseparable extensions among the finitely generated ones. For the converse, fix a finitely generated \(K/k\). The full separabilization construction \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-make-separably-generated]{F.69} gives finite purely inseparable extensions \(k'/k\) and \(K'/K\), inside a commuting field square, with \(K'/k'\) separably generated. This last extension is finitely generated: a finite field-generating list for \(K/k\) and finitely many generators for \(K'/K\) still generate \(K'\) after enlarging the coefficient field to \(k'\).

The entire forward smooth-domain construction \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-localization-smooth-separable]{F.64} supplies a smooth finite-type domain \(D\subset K'\) over \(k'\) with fraction field \(K'\). Its explicit separating-generator equations, denominator clearing and derivative localization have been proved there. They also give the smooth field model recognized by \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/d02d0a3669f42579db037cd44de1d113fdd770a1/docs/courses/AG-CA/src/smooth-algebras-over-a-field-and-the-jacobian-criterion.md}{AG-CA-18, Theorem 3.2}.

By assumption \(A'=A\otimes_kk'\) is regular. It is Noetherian by \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-Noetherian-field-extension]{F.12}. Form \(C=A'\otimes_{k'}D\). The coefficient-change polynomial presentation makes it finitely presented over \(A'\), and formal smoothness survives base change by \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/d02d0a3669f42579db037cd44de1d113fdd770a1/docs/courses/AG-CA/src/formally-smooth-unramified-and-etale-ring-maps.md}{AG-CA-17, Theorem 1.2}. Hence \(C/A'\) is smooth. It is also Noetherian, being finite type over the Noetherian ring \(A'\).

The complete smooth-flatness and regular-fibre results AG-CA-18, Theorems 6.1 and 2.1, make this map flat with regular residue-field fibres. At a prime of \(C\), the localized source is regular, and its closed fibre is the local ring of one of those regular fibres. The full ascent calculation \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-flat-over-regular-with-regular-fibre]{F.47} therefore makes the target local ring regular. This proves regularity of \(C\).

Localizing at all nonzero elements of \(D\) gives \[C\otimes_DK'=A'\otimes_{k'}K'\cong A\otimes_kK'.\] Every local ring of this localization is a local ring of the original regular ring, so it is regular. Finally choose a basis of the finite field extension \(K'/K\). As a module over \(B=A\otimes_kK\), the algebra \(A\otimes_kK'\) is the direct sum of \([K':K]\geq1\) copies of \(B\), by tensoring this basis. Tensoring an arbitrary \(B\)-module with that algebra therefore takes this positive finite number of copies; it preserves exactness and detects zero modules. Thus the map \(A\otimes_kK\to A\otimes_kK'\) is faithfully flat. The full arbitrary-source regularity descent proof \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-descent-regular]{F.38} makes \(A\otimes_kK\) regular. This holds for every chosen \(K\), proving the equivalence without a perfect-field assumption. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-geometrically-regular-descent}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.51: geometrically regular descent}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.51-geometrically-regular-descent}

Reading source: \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/unofficial-stacks-project-ai-drafts/blob/565b10e987aba5969b21145a0833f42d69f96790/algebra.tex\#L48815-L48834}{AI Integrated Stacks, pinned Algebra, lines 48815--48834}.

Let \(A\to B\) be a faithfully flat map of \(k\)-algebras. If \(B\) is geometrically regular over the field \(k\), then \(A\) is geometrically regular over \(k\). No separate Noetherianity hypothesis on \(A\) is needed.

\textbf{Proof.} The trivial extension \(k/k\) is among the field tests for geometric regularity, so \(B\) is regular. The full regularity descent proof \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-descent-regular]{F.38} makes \(A\) regular as well, deriving its Noetherianity by its finite-ideal argument.

For every finite purely inseparable extension \(k'/k\), set \(A'=A\otimes_kk'\) and \(B'=B\otimes_kk'\). Both are Noetherian by \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-Noetherian-field-extension]{F.12}. Tensor associativity identifies \(B'\) with \(A'\otimes_AB\), and for an arbitrary \(A'\)-module \(M\) it gives the inverse pure-tensor maps \[M\otimes_{A'}(A'\otimes_AB)\cong M\otimes_AB,\qquad
m\otimes(a'\otimes b)\longmapsto a'm\otimes b,\quad
m\otimes b\longmapsto m\otimes(1\otimes b).\] The balancing relations verify these maps and their inverse composites. Restriction from \(A'\)-modules to \(A\)-modules preserves exact sequences and detects the zero module. Since \(B\) is faithfully flat over \(A\), the displayed tensor identification proves that \(B'\) is faithfully flat over \(A'\).

Geometric regularity makes \(B'\) regular. Applying F.38 gives regularity of \(A'\) for every such \(k'\). The complete finite purely inseparable criterion \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-geometrically-regular]{F.50} now applies to the Noetherian algebra \(A\) and proves its geometric regularity over \(k\). ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-geometrically-regular-over-subfields}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.52: geometrically regular over subfields}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.52-geometrically-regular-over-subfields}

Reading source: \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/unofficial-stacks-project-ai-drafts/blob/565b10e987aba5969b21145a0833f42d69f96790/algebra.tex\#L48851-L48866}{AI Integrated Stacks, pinned Algebra, lines 48851--48866}.

Let \(A\) be a Noetherian algebra geometrically regular over the field \(k\).

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  For any field extension \(E/k\) such that \(C=A\otimes_kE\) is Noetherian, \(C\) is regular.
\item
  Under this same Noetherian tensor hypothesis, \(C\) is geometrically regular over \(E\).
\item
  If \(k\) is a directed union of subfields \(k_i\) and \(A\) is geometrically regular over every \(k_i\), then \(A\) is geometrically regular over \(k\).
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Proof.} For (1), write \(E\) as the union of its intermediate fields \(E_i\) generated by finite subsets over \(k\). They are directed, since the union of two finite generator sets is finite. Put \(C_i=A\otimes_kE_i\). An \(E_i\)-basis of \(E\) containing \(1\) gives \[C=C_i\otimes_{E_i}E\cong\bigoplus_{\beta\in\mathcal B_i}C_i.\] Here the structural inclusion \(C_i\to C\) is the coordinate belonging to \(1\). To obtain such a basis, take a maximal independent set containing \(1\); if it did not span, a vector outside its span could be adjoined, contradicting maximality. The tensor/direct-sum calculation is AG-RG-S01, Lemma 1.0. It proves both injectivity of this inclusion and flatness of \(C\) over \(C_i\), even when the basis is infinite. Every element of \(C\) uses finitely many field coefficients and so lies in one \(C_i\).

Suppose that \(C\) is Noetherian and fix \(\mathfrak q\subset C\). In the Noetherian local ring \(T=C_{\mathfrak q}\) choose a finite generating list \(x_1,\ldots,x_r\) for its maximal ideal \(\mathfrak m\). Write \(x_j=a_j/s_j\), with \(a_j\in\mathfrak q\) and \(s_j\notin\mathfrak q\). Put all their finitely many field coefficients into a common \(E_i\), so that every \(a_j,s_j\) lies in \(C_i\). Let \(\mathfrak q_i=\mathfrak q\cap C_i\) and \(B_i=(C_i)_{\mathfrak q_i}\). The fractions \(x_j\) now belong to \(B_i\), and their numerators lie in its maximal ideal.

The map \(B_i\to T\) is local and flat: it is obtained by localizing the free scalar-extension map above, and exact localization preserves its injection tests. Its extended maximal ideal is contained in \(\mathfrak m\) and contains every \(x_j\). Hence \[\mathfrak q_iT=\mathfrak m,\qquad
T\otimes_{B_i}\kappa(\mathfrak q_i)=T/\mathfrak m.\] The source \(B_i\) is Noetherian by \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-Noetherian-field-extension]{F.12}, and is regular because \(E_i/k\) is finitely generated and \(A\) is geometrically regular. The displayed closed fibre is a field, thus regular. The entire flat-local ascent proof \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-flat-over-regular-with-regular-fibre]{F.47} makes \(T\) regular. An empty generating list gives the same argument when \(\mathfrak m=0\). This proves regularity at every prime of \(C\); if \(C=0\), there are no primes to test.

For (2), let \(F/E\) be a finite purely inseparable extension. F.12 makes \(C\otimes_EF\) Noetherian. Tensor associativity identifies it with \(A\otimes_kF\), so (1), applied to the field extension \(F/k\), makes it regular. The complete finite purely inseparable criterion \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-geometrically-regular]{F.50} proves geometric regularity of \(C\) over \(E\).

For (3), we construct an actual finite purely inseparable field model. Let \(k'/k\) be finite purely inseparable. If it is trivial, use \(k_i'=k_i\) at any index. Otherwise the characteristic is \(p>0\). Choose a \(k\)-basis \(b_1=1,b_2,\ldots,b_d\) of \(k'\). A common exponent \(e\) satisfies \(b_j^{p^e}\in k\) for every \(j\), since the extension is purely inseparable and the list is finite. Write its finitely many multiplication constants \[b_jb_\ell=\sum_h c_{j\ell h}b_h,\qquad c_{j\ell h}\in k.\] Choose \(k_i\) containing all \(c_{j\ell h}\) and all \(b_j^{p^e}\). This is possible because the union is directed and the list is finite.

The subspace \(V=\bigoplus_j k_i b_j\subset k'\) contains \(1\) and is closed under multiplication by those identities. It is a finite-dimensional domain over \(k_i\). Multiplication by any nonzero \(v\in V\) is an injective endomorphism of that finite-dimensional vector space, hence surjective; a preimage of \(1\) gives its inverse. Therefore \(V\) is a field, denoted \(k_i'\). Moreover every \(v=\sum_j a_jb_j\) in it has \[v^{p^e}=\sum_j a_j^{p^e}b_j^{p^e}\in k_i.\] Thus \(k_i'/k_i\) is finite purely inseparable. This checks the exponent condition for every element of the field, beyond just its chosen generators.

The multiplication map \(k\otimes_{k_i}k_i'\to k'\), \(a\otimes v\mapsto av\), is an algebra isomorphism: its basis \(1\otimes b_j\) maps to the given \(k\)-basis \(b_j\), proving both bijectivity and compatibility with the prescribed products. Consequently \[A\otimes_kk'\cong A\otimes_{k_i}k_i'.\] The right side is regular by the hypothesis over \(k_i\). F.50 proves geometric regularity over \(k\). In characteristic zero all finite purely inseparable extensions are trivial, so the same conclusion follows from the trivial case. All three assertions are established. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-grothendieck-regular-sequence}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.53: grothendieck regular sequence}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.53-grothendieck-regular-sequence}

Reading source: \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/unofficial-stacks-project-ai-drafts/blob/565b10e987aba5969b21145a0833f42d69f96790/algebra.tex\#L24513-L24526}{AI Integrated Stacks, pinned Algebra, lines 24513--24526}.

Let \(R\to P\) be a flat local map of Noetherian local rings, and let \(\mathfrak m=\mathfrak m_R\). If the reductions of \(f_1,\ldots,f_c\in P\) form a regular sequence in \(P/\mathfrak mP\), then the list is regular in \(P\), and every \(P/(f_1,\ldots,f_i)\) is flat over \(R\).

\textbf{Proof.} Put \(P_i=P/(f_1,\ldots,f_i)\), including \(P_0=P\). The regular-sequence hypothesis includes a nonzero final fibre quotient. Consequently each \(\bar f_i\) belongs to the maximal ideal of the local closed fibre: a unit there would make the final quotient zero. Its lift \(f_i\) belongs to the maximal ideal of \(P\) as well. Every \(P_i\) is thus a nonzero Noetherian local quotient, and \(R\to P_i\) remains local. Its closed fibre is \[P_i/\mathfrak mP_i
\cong(P/\mathfrak mP)/(\bar f_1,\ldots,\bar f_i).\]

Induct on \(i\), keeping \(R\)-flatness of \(P_i\). The initial assertion is the assumed flatness of \(P\). On \(P_i\) consider multiplication by \(f_{i+1}\). Both its source and target are finite over this actual Noetherian local ring, and its target is \(R\)-flat by induction. The displayed fibre description and the original regular-list hypothesis make its reduction injective. The full lifting-injectivity proof \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/d02d0a3669f42579db037cd44de1d113fdd770a1/docs/courses/AG-CA/src/faithful-flatness-and-the-local-criterion-for-flatness.md}{AG-CA-08, Lemma 5.1} gives injectivity on \(P_i\) and \(R\)-flatness of its cokernel \(P_{i+1}\). This proves the induction.

Every multiplication in the list has now been proved injective on its preceding quotient, and the final quotient is nonzero, so the list is regular. The same induction has proved flatness of each successive quotient. If \(c=0\), the list is empty and the only quotient is the original flat ring \(P\), giving both assertions directly. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-henselian-cat-finite-etale}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.54: henselian cat finite etale}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.54-henselian-cat-finite-etale}

Reading source: \href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/04GK}{Stacks, Tag 04GK}.

For a henselian local ring \((R,\mathfrak m,k)\), reduction \(S\mapsto S/\mathfrak mS\) is an equivalence from finite étale \(R\)-algebras to finite products of finite separable extensions of \(k\). Ring maps are unital, and the zero algebra is the empty product.

\textbf{Proof.} The written idempotent and finite-algebra theorem \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/main/docs/courses/AG-CA/henselian-local-rings-and-henselization.html}{AG-CA-20, Theorem 2.2} decomposes a finite \(R\)-algebra into finitely many local factors. A factor of an étale algebra is étale, since it is localization at its component idempotent. For each such factor \(S_i\), reduction is an étale \(k\)-algebra and is local: every maximal ideal of a finite algebra contracts to \(\mathfrak m\), and \(S_i\) has only one. The field classification \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/d02d0a3669f42579db037cd44de1d113fdd770a1/docs/courses/AG-CA/src/formally-smooth-unramified-and-etale-ring-maps.md}{AG-CA-17, Theorem 7.2} makes this reduction a finite separable field. In particular \(\mathfrak mS_i\) is its maximal ideal. Every \(S_i\) is henselian by \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/main/docs/courses/AG-CA/henselian-local-rings-and-henselization.html}{AG-CA-20, Proposition 3.1}.

Construct a lift of a finite separable field extension \(L/k\) as follows. Choose finitely many field generators and use their successive fields \[
k=L_0\subset L_1\subset\cdots\subset L_a=L,
\qquad L_i=L_{i-1}(\alpha_i).
\] Each minimal polynomial is monic separable. Starting with \(T_0=R\), lift its coefficients to a monic \(h_i\in T_{i-1}[X]\) and define \(T_i=T_{i-1}[X]/(h_i)\). Its bounded powers of \(X\) are a free \(T_{i-1}\)-basis, by monic division. Reduction modulo \(\mathfrak m\) is \(L_i\). Every maximal ideal contracts to \(\mathfrak m\) by integrality, so the field reduction makes \(T_i\) local with maximal ideal \(\mathfrak mT_i\). The derivative \(h_i'\) has nonzero residue in that field and is consequently a unit. The one-equation Jacobian proof \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/d02d0a3669f42579db037cd44de1d113fdd770a1/docs/courses/AG-CA/src/formally-smooth-unramified-and-etale-ring-maps.md}{AG-CA-17, Theorem 4.1 and Section 6} makes \(T_i/T_{i-1}\) étale. Composition makes \(T_a/R\) finite étale, with free rank \([L:k]\) and reduction \(L\). Finite products of these lifts provide every desired residue algebra.

We next show explicitly that every local finite étale \(R\)-algebra \(S\), with residue \(L\), is isomorphic to this constructed \(T_a\). Given the residue identification, lift a map \(T_{i-1}\to S\) through the next step by choosing the root of \(h_i\) reducing to \(\alpha_i\). The simple-root Hensel statement, \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/main/docs/courses/AG-CA/henselian-local-rings-and-henselization.html}{AG-CA-20, Theorem 1.2}, gives exactly one such root in the henselian local ring \(S\), and hence exactly one map \(T_i\to S\) at each step. This constructs \(\phi:T_a\to S\) inducing the chosen isomorphism on residues.

By the complete arbitrary-base proof in \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/main/docs/courses/AG-RG/AG-RG-S04.md}{S04, Lemma E4.2}, a finite étale algebra is finite locally free. Its proof first obtains a finite module presentation from monic algebra equations, then applies Lemma A1.3 to a finitely presented flat module. Since \(R\) is local, \(S\) is finite free, of rank \(\dim_k(S/\mathfrak mS)=[L:k]\). Both modules in \(\phi\) therefore have this same finite rank. In chosen bases its matrix reduces to an invertible matrix over \(k\), so its determinant lies outside \(\mathfrak m\) and is a unit of \(R\). The adjugate matrix divided by this unit is its inverse. Thus \(\phi\) is an isomorphism of modules, and its bijective algebra map is an algebra isomorphism.

Now let \(S_1,S_2\) be local finite étale algebras and let \(L_1\to L_2\) be a \(k\)-field map between their residues. Replace \(S_1\) by its isomorphic tower \(T_a\). Starting with \(R\to S_2\), lift each successive generator to the unique simple root whose residue is its prescribed image in \(L_2\). The same Hensel calculation supplies a unique \(R\)-algebra map \(S_1\to S_2\) inducing the field map. Conversely, any algebra map has those generator values, so it is this unique lift. The map on residue fields is defined because \(\mathfrak mS_i\) is the maximal ideal.

For products, a map to a local target sends each source component idempotent to \(0\) or \(1\); orthogonality and their sum \(1\) force exactly one component to be chosen. The residue map chooses precisely that component, and the local result lifts its field map uniquely. Doing this independently for each target factor proves a bijection on all Hom sets. The empty-product cases follow from unital maps directly: there is one map to the zero ring and none from it to a nonzero ring. We have proved full faithfulness and essential surjectivity, hence the asserted equivalence, over every henselian local source. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-huber}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.55: huber}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.55-huber}

Reading source: \href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/07CF}{Stacks, Tag 07CF}.

Suppose a finitely presented \(R\)-algebra \(S\) has a finite polynomial presentation \(S=P/I\), where \(P=R[X_1,\ldots,X_n]\), and \(I/I^2\) is free over \(S\). Then \(S\) has another finite polynomial presentation whose defining equations themselves form a basis of its conormal module.

\textbf{Proof.} \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-finite-presentation-independent]{F.44} makes \(I\) finitely generated. Thus \(I/I^2\) has a finite basis: when \(S\ne0\), the supports of a finite generating list in any free basis have finite union, which must contain the entire basis; when \(S=0\), choose its empty conormal basis directly. Lift this basis to \(f_1,\ldots,f_c\in I\) and put \(K=(f_1,\ldots,f_c)\). The basis property gives \(I=K+I^2\). The finite \(P\)-module \(U=I/K\) consequently satisfies \(U=IU\).

Choose generators \(u_1,\ldots,u_t\) of \(U\) and coefficients \(b_{ij}\in I\) with \(u_i=\sum_j b_{ij}u_j\). The adjugate identity proved in \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-matrix-left-inverse]{F.70} applied to \(1_t-(b_{ij})\) shows that \[g=\det(1_t-(b_{ij})),\qquad gU=0,\qquad g\in1+I.\] For \(U=0\) take \(g=1\). Hence \(gI\subset K\) and \(I_g=K_g\). The image of \(g\) in \(S\) is exactly \(1\), so \(P_g/I_g=S\). It follows, with both inverse maps given by adjoining or evaluating \(g^{-1}\), that \[S=P[T]/(f_1,\ldots,f_c,gT-1).\]

Let \(L\) be the displayed equation ideal. After localization at \(g\), the classes of \(f_i\) form the given basis of \(I_g/I_g^2\). The explicit inverse-variable conormal calculation \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-principal-localization-NL]{F.72}, applied to \(P_g/I_g\) and this presentation, identifies \[L/L^2\cong S^c\oplus S.\] The first basis vectors are \([f_i]\) and the last is \([gT-1]\): the last equation has derivative \(g\), a unit, in its new variable, and the remaining classes are read by evaluation at \(T=g^{-1}\). These are exactly the claimed equation classes. No Noetherian hypothesis or cancellation of a free summand is used. Empty bases use the same determinant convention; if \(S=0\), all the displayed modules and bases are interpreted over the zero ring. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-isolated-point-fibre}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.56: isolated point fibre}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.56-isolated-point-fibre}

Reading source: \href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/00PK}{Stacks, Tag 00PK}.

Let \(R\to S\) be of finite type and let \(\mathfrak q\in\operatorname{Spec}S\) lie over \(\mathfrak p\). Put \(k=\kappa(\mathfrak p)\), \(T=S\otimes_R k\), and let \(x\in\operatorname{Spec}T\) be the corresponding point. The following conditions are equivalent: \(x\) is isolated; \(T_x=S_{\mathfrak q}/\mathfrak pS_{\mathfrak q}\) is finite-dimensional over \(k\); some \(g\in S\setminus\mathfrak q\) has \(x\) as the only point of its fibre neighbourhood; the fibre point-dimension at \(x\) is zero; \(x\) is closed and \(\dim T_x=0\); and \(\kappa(x)/k\) is finite and \(\dim T_x=0\).

\textbf{Proof.} All the geometry can be checked in the finite-type field algebra \(T\). Such an algebra and its principal localizations are Noetherian by \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/d02d0a3669f42579db037cd44de1d113fdd770a1/docs/courses/AG-CA/src/noetherian-and-artinian-rings.md}{AG-CA-03, Theorem 2.1}. We will use the following consequence of its Theorem 4.2. A zero-dimensional finite-type \(k\)-algebra \(B\) is Artinian, with finitely many local factors and nilpotent radical \(J\). Every residue field is finite over \(k\) by \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/d02d0a3669f42579db037cd44de1d113fdd770a1/docs/courses/AG-CA/src/the-nullstellensatz-and-jacobson-rings.md}{AG-CA-06, Theorem 2.1}. Each \(J^i/J^{i+1}\) is finite over the product \(B/J\) of those fields: \(B\) is Noetherian, so the ideals involved are finite. Its coordinate summands are consequently finite-dimensional over the residue fields, hence over \(k\). The finite filtration by powers of \(J\) proves that \(B\) is finite-dimensional over \(k\). The factor idempotents give a principal singleton neighbourhood of each of its points.

If \(x\) is isolated, choose \(h\in T\) with \(D(h)=\{x\}\). The algebra \(T_h\) has just one prime, so has dimension zero and is finite-dimensional by the preceding calculation. Every element outside its unique maximal ideal is a unit. Its localization at that ideal is therefore itself, and \(T_x=T_h\) is finite-dimensional.

Conversely, a finite-dimensional \(T_x\) is Artinian: chains of its ideals are chains of subspaces of a finite-dimensional \(k\)-space. Each of its prime quotients is a finite-dimensional domain, hence a field, because multiplication by a nonzero element is an injective, and thus surjective, linear map. Thus \(\dim T_x=0\), and its residue field is finite over \(k\). For a prime of a finite-type \(k\)-algebra, finiteness of the residue extension implies closedness: \(T/x\) embeds into the finite-dimensional field \(\kappa(x)\), so is a finite-dimensional domain and the same multiplication argument makes it a field. The converse follows from the cited weak Nullstellensatz.

Suppose now that \(x\) is closed and \(\dim T_x=0\). The prime corresponding to \(x\) is both maximal and minimal. There are finitely many other minimal primes, by AG-CA-03, Proposition 2.2. From each choose an element outside \(x\) and take their product \(h\); use \(h=1\) if there are none. A prime in \(D(h)\) contains none of those other minimal primes. Since every prime contains a minimal prime, it must contain \(x\) and therefore equal \(x\). Hence \(D(h)=\{x\}\) and \(x\) is isolated. This proves the equivalence of isolation, finite local fibre algebra, and the two residue-field/local-dimension conditions.

An isolated point has point-dimension zero, using its singleton open neighbourhood. Conversely, zero point-dimension supplies an open neighbourhood of dimension zero: the infimum defining that dimension is an attained nonnegative integer. Take a principal neighbourhood inside it. Its algebra has dimension zero, so the Artinian factor calculation above supplies a smaller principal singleton neighbourhood of \(x\). Thus zero point-dimension implies isolation as well.

Finally, every \(h\in T=S_{R\setminus\mathfrak p}/\mathfrak pS_{R\setminus\mathfrak p}\) is represented by \(g/s\) with \(g\in S\) and \(s\in R\setminus\mathfrak p\). The image of \(s\) is a fibre unit, so \(D(h)=D(\bar g)\), and \(h\notin x\) means \(g\notin\mathfrak q\). Conversely the fibre of \(D(g)\) is exactly \(D(\bar g)\). This proves the neighbourhood condition over the original ring, with no Noetherian assumption on \(R\). ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-lci}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.57: lci}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.57-lci}

Reading source: \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/unofficial-stacks-project-ai-drafts/blob/565b10e987aba5969b21145a0833f42d69f96790/algebra.tex\#L37341-L37441}{AI Integrated Stacks, pinned Algebra, lines 37341--37441}.

Let \(k\) be a field, \(S\) a finite-type \(k\)-algebra, and \(\mathfrak q\) a prime of \(S\). Fix any polynomial presentation \(S=P/I\), with \(P=k[X_1,\ldots,X_n]\), and let \(\mathfrak Q\subset P\) lie over \(\mathfrak q\). Put \[c=\operatorname{ht}\mathfrak Q-\operatorname{ht}\mathfrak q
=n-\dim_{\mathfrak q}\operatorname{Spec}S.\] The last equality is the point-codimension formula \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-codimension]{F.20}. The following are equivalent.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Some \(S_g\), with \(g\notin\mathfrak q\), is a global complete intersection over \(k\).
\item
  \(I_{\mathfrak Q}\) has a generating list of length \(c\).
\item
  \((I/I^2)_{\mathfrak q}\) has a generating list of length \(c\).
\item
  \((I/I^2)_{\mathfrak q}\) is free of rank \(c\) over \(S_{\mathfrak q}\).
\item
  \(I_{\mathfrak Q}\) is generated by a regular sequence in \(P_{\mathfrak Q}\).
\end{enumerate}

Whenever these hold, every list of \(c\) elements spanning \(I_{\mathfrak Q}/\mathfrak QI_{\mathfrak Q}\) is a regular sequence in \(P_{\mathfrak Q}\).

\textbf{Proof.} Write \(V=P_{\mathfrak Q}\) and \(J=I_{\mathfrak Q}\). The whole polynomial-local regularity proof \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/d02d0a3669f42579db037cd44de1d113fdd770a1/docs/courses/AG-CA/src/regular-local-rings.md}{AG-CA-14, Proposition 3.3}, starting with \(k\), makes \(V\) regular. The whole \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/d02d0a3669f42579db037cd44de1d113fdd770a1/docs/courses/AG-CA/src/regular-sequences-depth-and-cohen-macaulay-modules.md}{AG-CA-12, Theorem 6.1} makes it Cohen--Macaulay. Its dimension is \(\operatorname{ht}\mathfrak Q\), whereas \(V/J=S_{\mathfrak q}\) has dimension \(\operatorname{ht}\mathfrak q\). In particular \(J\) is proper and finite, and the dimension drop is \(c\).

Generators of \(J\) give generators of \(J/J^2=(I/I^2)_{\mathfrak q}\). Conversely lift \(c\) generators of this quotient to \(f_1,\ldots,f_c\in J\). Their quotient module \(N=J/(f_1,\ldots,f_c)V\) satisfies \(N=JN\). It is finite, and \(J\) lies in the maximal ideal of \(V\), so the determinant proof \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-NAK]{F.10} gives \(N=0\). Thus (2) and (3) are equivalent. The entire expected-dimension criterion AG-CA-12, Theorem 4.2, now says that any such generating list is regular: it lies in the maximal ideal and lowers the dimension of the Cohen--Macaulay ring by exactly its length. A list spanning \(J/\mathfrak QJ\) generates \(J\) by the same Nakayama argument, proving the final assertion too.

We spell out the conormal basis for a regular generating list. The regular-list cone proof \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-more-algebra-lemma-noetherian-finite-all-equivalent]{F.118} makes its first Koszul homology zero. If \(\sum_i a_if_i\in J^2\), write this sum as \(\sum_i b_if_i\) with every \(b_i\in J\). The vector \((a_i-b_i)\) is a first Koszul cycle, hence a boundary. Each coefficient of a degree-two Koszul boundary belongs to \(J\), because its differential has coefficients among the \(f_i\). Thus every \(a_i\in J\). This proves independence, as well as generation, of the classes of the \(f_i\) in \(J/J^2\). Consequently (3) implies (4); (4) plainly implies (3). The same criterion proves (2) implies (5). If (5) uses a regular list of length \(e\), successive regular quotients of a Cohen--Macaulay local ring lower dimension by one, by the complete depth and dimension proofs in AG-CA-12, Sections 2 and 4. Hence \[\operatorname{ht}\mathfrak q
=\dim(V/J)=\dim V-e=\operatorname{ht}\mathfrak Q-e,\] so \(e=c\), proving (5) implies (2).

Suppose (2) holds. Choose generators \(f_i=a_i/s_i\) with \(a_i\in I\) and \(s_i\notin\mathfrak Q\). Multiplication by these units shows that the \(a_i\) also generate \(J\) and form a regular list there. Since \(I\) is finite over the Noetherian polynomial ring, each generator of \(I/(a_1,\ldots,a_c)\) is killed by some element outside \(\mathfrak Q\). Their product \(h'\notin\mathfrak Q\) gives \(I_{h'}=(a_1,\ldots,a_c)_{h'}\).

Choose a principal neighbourhood \(D(h'')\) of \(\mathfrak q\) on which the dimension is its point dimension. Here is the finite-component construction from F.20: for every minimal prime \(\mathfrak p\) of \(S\) not contained in \(\mathfrak q\), choose an element in \(\mathfrak p\setminus\mathfrak q\) and multiply these finitely many elements. The product kills exactly the components not passing through the point; any surviving component has its original dimension, since a nonempty principal open in a finite-type domain over a field has the same transcendence degree and dimension. Thus the maximum surviving component dimension is the point dimension, by the whole AG-CA-09, Theorem 6.1, calculation. Lift this product to \(h''\in P\setminus\mathfrak Q\) and put \(h=h'h''\). Its image \(g\) is outside \(\mathfrak q\), and \[S_g\cong k[X_1,\ldots,X_n,Z]/
(a_1,\ldots,a_c,hZ-1),\qquad \dim S_g=n-c.\] This is the required global complete-intersection presentation: there are \(n+1\) variables, \(c+1\) equations and the prescribed dimension difference. This proves (1).

Conversely suppose (1), and choose a global complete-intersection presentation \(S_g=k[Y_1,\ldots,Y_m]/H\), with \(H=(b_1,\ldots,b_t)\) and \(\dim S_g=m-t\). Every minimal prime \(\mathfrak a\) over \(H\) has height at most \(t\) by the entire \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/d02d0a3669f42579db037cd44de1d113fdd770a1/docs/courses/AG-CA/src/dimension-theory-of-noetherian-local-rings.md}{AG-CA-11, Theorem 3.1}. Its component has dimension \(m-\operatorname{ht}\mathfrak a\) by the polynomial height formula in AG-CA-09, Theorem 4.3. Hence each component has dimension at least \(m-t\), while their maximum is the given dimension \(m-t\). All components therefore have dimension exactly \(m-t\). The point formula of AG-CA-09, Theorem 6.1, gives this same dimension at \(\mathfrak qS_g\).

At the polynomial prime \(\mathfrak Q''\) over that point, \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-codimension]{F.20} consequently gives \[t=\operatorname{ht}\mathfrak Q''-\operatorname{ht}\mathfrak q.\] The actual ambient polynomial local ring is regular and Cohen--Macaulay as above. The expected-dimension criterion makes its given \(b_1,\ldots,b_t\) regular. The conormal calculation already proved makes \((H/H^2)_{\mathfrak q}\) free of rank \(t\). The entire graph-presentation calculation \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-conormal-module-localize]{F.33}, localized at this point, supplies \[S_{\mathfrak q}^{\,t+n}
\cong (I/I^2)_{\mathfrak q}\oplus S_{\mathfrak q}^{\,m}.\] Thus the conormal module is a finite direct summand of a finite free module. Tensor injections restricted to this summand prove flatness; the finite complementary summand gives finite presentation. The full local finite-flat proof \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/main/docs/courses/AG-RG/AG-RG-S01.md}{AG-RG-S01, Lemma 1.2} makes it free. Reducing the displayed isomorphism to the residue field computes its rank as \[t+n-m=n-\dim_{\mathfrak q}\operatorname{Spec}S=c.\] This proves (4). Empty equation lists are included in the conormal and dimension calculations, so every implication and the last assertion also hold when \(c=0\). ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-lci-at-prime}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.58: lci at prime}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.58-lci-at-prime}

Reading source: \href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/00SG}{Stacks, Tag 00SG}.

For a finite-type \(k\)-algebra \(S\) and \(\mathfrak q\in\operatorname{Spec}S\), the following are equivalent: \(S_{\mathfrak q}\) is a complete intersection in the sense of \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-definition-lci-local-ring]{F.3}; it has a global complete-intersection principal neighbourhood; and the kernel of any finite polynomial presentation of \(S\) is generated by a regular sequence in the polynomial local ring above \(\mathfrak q\). Equivalently, there is a principal neighbourhood that is locally a complete intersection over \(k\).

\textbf{Proof.} Write \(C=S_{\mathfrak q}\) and \(P=k[X_1,\ldots,X_n]_{\mathfrak q'}\twoheadrightarrow C\). The field \(k\) is a regular ring: its only prime localization is itself, with dimension and maximal-ideal generating number both zero. Iterating the entire polynomial-regularity proof \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/d02d0a3669f42579db037cd44de1d113fdd770a1/docs/courses/AG-CA/src/regular-local-rings.md}{AG-CA-14, Proposition 3.3} makes \(k[X_1,\ldots,X_n]\) a regular ring. Its localization at the displayed prime is therefore regular local, by the definition of a regular ring. A regular generating list for its kernel therefore gives the ambient ring required by F.3. Conversely suppose F.3 gives \(C=Q/(a_1,\ldots,a_e)\), where \(Q\) is regular local and essentially of finite type over the same field \(k\), and this list is regular in its maximal ideal. We compare this local ambient with \(P\) explicitly.

Present \(Q\) as a quotient of a polynomial local ring \(V=k[Y_1,\ldots,Y_m]_{\mathfrak n}\). Both \(V\) and \(Q\) are regular local. AG-CA-14, Proposition 1.4, makes the kernel of \(V\to Q\) generated by part of a regular parameter system. Append lifts of the \(a_i\). The resulting list generates \(\ker(V\to C)\) and is regular: its first successive quotients are those by the parameter list, and its remaining multiplication injections are precisely those of the given regular list in \(Q\).

Let \(U=k[X,Y]_{\mathfrak r}\), where \(\mathfrak r\) is the preimage of the maximal ideal of \(C\) under the map using both sets of coordinates, and put \(L=\ker(U\to C)\). Lift the images of \(X_i\) to \(V\) and denote them by \(u_i(Y)\); these are fractions with denominators outside \(\mathfrak n\). Those denominators are units in \(U\). The quotient by \(X_i-u_i(Y)\) is \(V\), including its indicated localization: evaluating an element outside \(\mathfrak r\) gives an element outside \(\mathfrak n\), hence a unit, and every fraction defining \(V\) already occurs in \(U\). Translation of polynomial variables shows that the graph equations form a regular sequence. They remain regular after localization by exactness, and their quotient is nonzero. Appending the preceding regular list in \(V\) consequently gives a regular generating list for \(L\).

In the other direction lift the images of \(Y_j\) to fractions \(v_j(X)\) in \(P\). The identical graph calculation gives \[U/(Y_j-v_j(X))\cong P,\qquad L=(\ker(P\to C),Y_j-v_j(X))U.\] The constant and linear coefficient calculation of \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-conormal-module-localize]{F.33} works in this localized polynomial ring as well: first invert the finitely many denominators of the \(v_j\), translate \(Y_j\) by \(v_j\), and then localize at \(\mathfrak r\). Modulo \(L^2\) its constant terms are read modulo \(\ker(P\to C)^2\), its graph-linear coefficients modulo \(\ker(P\to C)\), and terms of graph-degree at least two vanish. The resulting mutually inverse maps give \[L/L^2\cong \ker(P\to C)/\ker(P\to C)^2\oplus C^m.\]

The regular list for \(L\) makes its conormal finite free by \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-regular-quasi-regular]{F.74}. Its rank is \(\dim U-\dim C\) by \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/d02d0a3669f42579db037cd44de1d113fdd770a1/docs/courses/AG-CA/src/regular-sequences-depth-and-cohen-macaulay-modules.md}{AG-CA-12, Corollary 6.2}. Hence the first summand in the display is finite projective, and is finite free over the local ring \(C\) by \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/main/docs/courses/AG-RG/AG-RG-S01.md}{S01, Lemma 1.2}. Reduction to its residue field computes its rank. The polynomial height formula \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/d02d0a3669f42579db037cd44de1d113fdd770a1/docs/courses/AG-CA/src/krull-dimension-and-noether-normalization.md}{AG-CA-09, Theorem 4.3} gives \(\dim U=\dim P+m\), since the two polynomial primes have the same residue field \(\kappa(\mathfrak q)\). The rank is thus \(\dim P-\dim C\). F.57 now supplies a regular generating list for \(\ker(P\to C)\) and a global complete-intersection principal neighbourhood of \(\mathfrak q\). This proves the assertion for every chosen polynomial presentation, including the local ambients in F.3.

Conversely a global complete-intersection neighbourhood has the regular local equation lists proved in F.57, so gives F.3 at \(\mathfrak q\). It is also locally a complete intersection: apply F.57 at each of its points. A locally complete-intersection principal neighbourhood contains a further global complete-intersection principal neighbourhood of the specified point by the defining local condition. If the further inverted element is \(b/g^r\) in \(S_g\), that neighbourhood is \(S_{gb}\), with \(gb\notin\mathfrak q\). This proves the last equivalence. All graph and rank calculations allow empty coordinate or equation lists. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-limit-essentially-finite-presentation}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.59: limit essentially finite presentation}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.59-limit-essentially-finite-presentation}

Reading source: \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/unofficial-stacks-project-ai-drafts/blob/565b10e987aba5969b21145a0833f42d69f96790/algebra.tex\#L33722-L33770}{AI Integrated Stacks, pinned Algebra, lines 33722--33770}.

Let \(R\to S\) be a local map of local rings, with \(S\) essentially finitely presented over \(R\). There are a directed set and local maps \(R_\lambda\to S_\lambda\) such that their colimit is \(R\to S\), each \(R_\lambda\) is essentially finite type over \(\mathbf Z\), each \(S_\lambda\) is essentially finite type over \(R_\lambda\), and, for \(\lambda\leq\mu\), \[S_\lambda\otimes_{R_\lambda}R_\mu\longrightarrow S_\mu\] is localization at a prime. All model rings are Noetherian, although \(R\) and \(S\) need not be.

\textbf{Proof.} Write \(S=(R[X_1,\ldots,X_n]/(f_1,\ldots,f_c))_{\mathfrak q}\). Such a prime localization represents the given local essentially finitely presented algebra: in any localization presentation, every element outside the inverse image of the local maximal ideal is a unit, so the two localization universal properties give the prime localization. Locality of \(R\to S\) makes \(\mathfrak q\cap R=\mathfrak m_R\).

Let \(\Lambda\) be the finite subsets of \(R\) containing all coefficients of the \(f_j\), ordered by inclusion. It is directed under finite union. Let \(A_\lambda\subset R\) be the subring generated by such a subset over the image of \(\mathbf Z\), put \(\mathfrak p_\lambda=A_\lambda\cap\mathfrak m_R\), and set \(R_\lambda=(A_\lambda)_{\mathfrak p_\lambda}\). Elements outside \(\mathfrak p_\lambda\) are units in \(R\), so this localization embeds in \(R\): a fraction becoming zero has zero numerator, since its denominator is a unit there and \(A_\lambda\) is a subring. The maps \(R_\lambda\to R_\mu\) are therefore inclusions and are local, with maximal ideals contracted from \(\mathfrak m_R\). Every element of \(R\) occurs in some finite subset, proving \(\operatorname*{colim}R_\lambda=R\).

Define \[C_\lambda=R_\lambda[X_1,\ldots,X_n]/(f_1,\ldots,f_c),\] where the fixed coefficient list lies in \(R_\lambda\). Let \(\mathfrak q_\lambda\) be the inverse image of the maximal ideal of \(S\) under \(C_\lambda\to S\), and set \(S_\lambda=(C_\lambda)_{\mathfrak q_\lambda}\). These are local rings, and \(R_\lambda\to S_\lambda\) is local because the maximal-ideal contractions agree. We verify the integer base and the permanence steps explicitly. A nonzero ideal of \(\mathbf Z\) has a least positive member \(d\). Repeated subtraction of \(d\) writes any nonnegative member as \(qd+r\) with \(0\le r<d\); the remainder is in the ideal and minimality forces \(r=0\). Negative members are handled by changing their sign. Thus every integer ideal is principal, including the zero ideal, so \(\mathbf Z\) is Noetherian.

Each \(A_\lambda\) is a quotient of a finite-variable polynomial ring over \(\mathbf Z\), and the Hilbert basis theorem AG-CA-03, Theorem 2.1, makes that polynomial ring Noetherian. An ideal of a quotient is the image of its inverse-image ideal, so is finitely generated. An ideal of a localization equals the localization of its contraction: if \(a/s\) is in the ideal, then \(a/1\) is too, and the converse follows by multiplying by \(1/s\). Its contracted ideal has finite generators, whose localized images generate the original ideal. These calculations prove quotient and localization permanence and make \(R_\lambda,C_\lambda,S_\lambda\) Noetherian. Their finite polynomial lists and prime localizations give the two essential finite-type assertions; composition of such maps was fully proved in \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-composition-essentially-of-finite-type]{F.31}.

Polynomial scalar extension gives \(C_\lambda\otimes_{R_\lambda}R_\mu\cong C_\mu\). The tensor with \(S_\lambda\) initially inverts the images of \(C_\lambda\setminus\mathfrak q_\lambda\). Those images avoid \(\mathfrak q_\mu\), by their definition as contractions from the same target. Thus \(\mathfrak q_\mu\) defines a prime of that tensor localization. Localizing at it inverts the remaining elements outside \(\mathfrak q_\mu\) and gives exactly \(S_\mu\). The fraction universal property proves both inverse maps, establishing the stipulated transition formula. The identical argument with the final base \(R\) gives \(S\) as a prime localization of \(S_\lambda\otimes_{R_\lambda}R\).

For the colimit of the target rings, every fraction in \(S\) uses finitely many coefficients in its numerator and denominator, so it has a representative in some \(S_\lambda\). If two representatives become equal in \(S\), their cross difference is killed in \(R[X]/(f)\) by a denominator outside \(\mathfrak q\). Lift that denominator to a polynomial and express the killed difference as a finite sum \(\sum_jh_jf_j\) in \(R[X]\). These polynomials and their equality use finitely many coefficients. Put them into one common later \(R_\mu\). The denominator still avoids \(\mathfrak q_\mu\), and the same ideal-membership equality holds there, so the representatives are already equal in \(S_\mu\). This proves injectivity as well as surjectivity of the colimit map. The structural maps from the base agree throughout, giving the entire claimed colimit of local ring maps. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-limit-module-essentially-finite-presentation}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.60: limit module essentially finite presentation}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.60-limit-module-essentially-finite-presentation}

Reading source: \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/unofficial-stacks-project-ai-drafts/blob/565b10e987aba5969b21145a0833f42d69f96790/algebra.tex\#L33804-L33859}{AI Integrated Stacks, pinned Algebra, lines 33804--33859}.

For a local essentially finitely presented map \(R\to S\) and a finitely presented \(S\)-module \(M\), the models in \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-limit-essentially-finite-presentation]{F.59} can be taken at sufficiently large stages with finitely presented \(S_\lambda\)-modules \(M_\lambda\) such that \[M_\lambda\otimes_{S_\lambda}S_\mu\cong M_\mu
\quad(\lambda\leq\mu),\qquad
\operatorname*{colim}_\lambda M_\lambda\cong M.\] In particular each module is finite over its model algebra, and all base/prime-localization assertions of F.59 remain valid.

\textbf{Proof.} Choose a finite presentation \[S^a\xrightarrow{H}S^b\longrightarrow M\longrightarrow0.\] The finitely many entries of \(H\) are elements of the colimit \(S\). The representative proof in F.59 puts them in a common \(S_{\lambda_0}\). Restrict to stages \(\lambda\geq\lambda_0\) and let \(H_\lambda\) be their images there. Define \[M_\lambda=\operatorname{coker}
\bigl(S_\lambda^a\xrightarrow{H_\lambda}S_\lambda^b\bigr).\] This is a finite presentation over \(S_\lambda\). Right exactness of tensor and the fixed free bases identify the tensor of this presentation with the presentation given by \(H_\mu\), proving the asserted transition isomorphism. The same calculation gives \(M_\lambda\otimes_{S_\lambda}S\cong M\).

We verify the colimit explicitly. Any element of \(M\) is represented by a vector in \(S^b\), whose finitely many coordinates occur at a common model stage, giving surjectivity from the module colimit. If \(x_\lambda\in S_\lambda^b\) represents a class that is zero in \(M\), its image is \(Hy\) for some finite vector \(y\in S^a\). Choose a later stage representing every coordinate of \(y\). The vector equality \(x=Hy\) is a finite list of ring equalities, so F.59 detects all of them at one common successor. There \(x_\mu=H_\mu y_\mu\), proving that the original class is zero in \(M_\mu\). This proves injectivity of the colimit map. The representative and transition calculations respect addition and the ring actions, so the isomorphism is an isomorphism of modules over \(\operatorname*{colim}S_\lambda=S\).

No ring models have been changed except for removing an initial segment of the directed set, which leaves all colimits unchanged: every earlier representative has an image at a common successor with \(\lambda_0\). Hence their local maps, essential finite-type properties and prime tensor-localizations are exactly those proved in F.59. The arguments include \(a=0\), \(b=0\) and the zero module. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-local-dimension-zero-henselian}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.61: local dimension zero henselian}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.61-local-dimension-zero-henselian}

Reading source: \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/unofficial-stacks-project-ai-drafts/blob/565b10e987aba5969b21145a0833f42d69f96790/algebra.tex\#L44097-L44121}{AI Integrated Stacks, pinned Algebra, lines 44097--44121}.

Every local ring \((R,\mathfrak m)\) of dimension zero is henselian. No Noetherian or nilpotent-maximal-ideal hypothesis is required.

\textbf{Proof.} The only prime of \(R\) is \(\mathfrak m\): any other prime is properly below the maximal ideal and would give a chain of length one. Every \(u\in\mathfrak m\) is nilpotent. Indeed, if no power of \(u\) were zero, \(R_u\) would be nonzero. A maximal proper ideal of this ring exists by the chain-union and Zorn argument, and its inverse image would be a prime of \(R\) avoiding \(u\). It cannot be the unique prime \(\mathfrak m\), a contradiction.

Use the simple-root definition of henselianity in \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/main/docs/courses/AG-CA/henselian-local-rings-and-henselization.html}{AG-CA-20, Section 1}. Let \(f\in R[T]\) be monic, and let \(\bar a\) be a root of its reduction with \(\bar f'(\bar a)\ne0\). Choose any lift \(a_0\in R\). The element \(f'(a_0)\) is a unit because its residue is nonzero, and \(\epsilon_0=f(a_0)\in\mathfrak m\) has some zero power \(\epsilon_0^N=0\).

Inductively set \[a_{j+1}=a_j-f'(a_j)^{-1}f(a_j).\] Every \(a_j\) has residue \(\bar a\), so each inverse in this formula exists. Expanding the polynomial by the binomial formula gives, for all \(a,h\), \[f(a+h)=f(a)+f'(a)h+h^2Q(a,h)\] for a polynomial \(Q\) over \(R\). Substitution of the correction therefore gives \[f(a_{j+1})\in(f(a_j)^2)
\subset(\epsilon_0^{\,2^{j+1}}).\] The correction remains in \(\mathfrak m\), as needed for the residue induction. Choose \(j\) with \(2^j\geq N\); then \(f(a_j)=0\). This supplies the required lifted root in finitely many steps, using only the nilpotence of the initial error.

For completeness it is unique with this residue. If \(a,b\) are two such roots, polynomial subtraction factors as \[0=f(b)-f(a)=(b-a)\bigl(f'(a)+(b-a)H(a,b)\bigr).\] The second factor has the nonzero residue \(\bar f'(\bar a)\) and is a unit, so \(b=a\). All simple residue roots have thus been lifted, proving henselianity. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-local-syntomic}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.62: local syntomic}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.62-local-syntomic}

Reading source: \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/unofficial-stacks-project-ai-drafts/blob/565b10e987aba5969b21145a0833f42d69f96790/algebra.tex\#L37927-L37941}{AI Integrated Stacks, pinned Algebra, lines 37927--37941}.

Let \(R\to S\) be any ring map. If finitely many principal opens \(D(g_i)\) cover \(\operatorname{Spec}S\) and every \(R\to S_{g_i}\) is syntomic, then \(R\to S\) is syntomic.

\textbf{Proof.} The assumed cover means the \(g_i\) generate the unit ideal. The whole finite-equation gluing proof \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-cover-upstairs]{F.35} gives finite presentation of \(S/R\) from the chart finite presentations.

To prove flatness, take an arbitrary injection \(M'\to M\) of \(R\)-modules and let \(K\) be the kernel of \(M'\otimes_RS\to M\otimes_RS\). Exactness of localization identifies \(K_{g_i}\) with the kernel after tensoring with \(S_{g_i}\); it is zero by chart flatness. If \(x\in K\), some power \(g_i^{e_i}\) kills \(x\) for each \(i\). These powers still generate the unit ideal: otherwise a maximal ideal containing all of them would contain all the \(g_i\). A linear combination equal to one then kills \(x\). Thus \(K=0\), proving flatness without a finiteness condition on these modules.

For every \(\mathfrak p\subset R\), put \(C=S\otimes_R\kappa(\mathfrak p)\). The images of the \(g_i\) still generate the unit ideal, and \[C_{g_i}\cong S_{g_i}\otimes_R\kappa(\mathfrak p)\] by the fraction universal property. Each is a local complete intersection over the field, by syntomicness of that chart. For a point of \(C\), choose a chart containing it and then a global complete-intersection principal neighbourhood there. If that second denominator is \(a/g_i^e\), its principal open in the chart is \(D(g_i)\cap D(a)=D(g_i a)\) in \(C\). Its coordinate algebra is exactly the same iterated localization. Thus these neighbourhoods give the required complete-intersection cover of the entire fibre, as in \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-definition-lci-field]{F.2}. Finite presentation, flatness and all fibre conditions are now proved. If the cover is empty, its spectrum is empty and \(S=0\); this algebra is finitely presented as \(R/(1)\), flat, and has empty fibres, so the conclusion holds as well. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-localization-colimit}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.63: localization colimit}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.63-localization-colimit}

Reading source: \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/unofficial-stacks-project-ai-drafts/blob/565b10e987aba5969b21145a0833f42d69f96790/algebra.tex\#L1260-L1278}{AI Integrated Stacks, pinned Algebra, lines 1260--1278}.

Let \(U\subset R\) be multiplicative and \(M\) an \(R\)-module. Then \(U^{-1}M\) is a filtered colimit of copies of \(M\) with transition maps given by multiplication by denominators. It is also the filtered colimit of the principal localizations \(M_s\) for \(s\in U\). In particular \(U^{-1}R\) is the corresponding filtered colimit of the rings \(R_s\).

\textbf{Proof.} We give a directed indexing set with specified transitions. Let \(\Lambda\) be the finitely supported functions \(\nu:U\to\mathbf N\), ordered coordinatewise, and put \(s_\nu=\prod_{u\in U}u^{\nu(u)}\). For \(\nu\leq\mu\), write \[s_\mu=s_\nu v_{\nu\mu},\qquad
v_{\nu\mu}=\prod_{u\in U}u^{\mu(u)-\nu(u)}.\] The maximum of two functions is a common successor. The displayed factor is specified even if the ring has zero divisors, and the factors multiply compatibly along three stages. Put one copy \(M^{(\nu)}=M\) at each stage, with transition \(m\mapsto v_{\nu\mu}m\).

The maps \(M^{(\nu)}\to U^{-1}M\), \(m\mapsto m/s_\nu\), commute with the transitions and are jointly surjective, since every denominator occurs as a one-element product. If \(m/s_\nu=n/s_\mu\), the fraction criterion gives \(u\in U\) with \[u(s_\mu m-s_\nu n)=0.\] At the successor \(\rho=\nu+\mu+\delta_u\), both representatives have become equal, their difference being the left side of this identity. Here \(\delta_u\) has value one at \(u\) and zero elsewhere. Conversely equality at any successor gives equality of the fractions. This proves bijectivity. To check addition, move two representatives to a common successor; addition there becomes the usual common-denominator addition. Scalar multiplication is preserved by every map, so the bijection is an \(R\)-module isomorphism.

For the principal-localization assertion use the same directed set, now with modules \(M_{s_\nu}\). If \(\nu\leq\mu\), \(s_\nu\) is a unit after inverting \(s_\mu=s_\nu v_{\nu\mu}\): its inverse is \(v_{\nu\mu}/s_\mu\). This gives the specified localization map. Each fraction in \(U^{-1}M\) is represented at a principal stage. If \(m/s_\nu^a\) and \(n/s_\mu^b\) become equal in the full localization, some \(u\in U\) kills their cross difference \[u(s_\mu^b m-s_\nu^a n)=0.\] At the principal successor \(s_\rho=s_\nu s_\mu u\), all three factors are units. The identity therefore makes the two fractions equal there. This proves both directions of the colimit isomorphism, including all module operations.

Taking \(M=R\), these transition maps are ring maps. The same fraction calculation preserves multiplication and one, proving the ring colimit. These diagrams represent the usual directed family of principal localizations: each product is itself in \(U\), and any finite family of its elements is inverted at their product. The argument includes \(0\in U\), in which case every representative vanishes at a successor containing that denominator. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-localization-smooth-separable}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.64: localization smooth separable}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.64-localization-smooth-separable}

Reading source: \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/unofficial-stacks-project-ai-drafts/blob/565b10e987aba5969b21145a0833f42d69f96790/algebra.tex\#L46075-L46088}{AI Integrated Stacks, pinned Algebra, lines 46075--46088}.

A finitely generated field extension \(K/k\) is separably generated if and only if it is the fraction field of a smooth finite-type \(k\)-domain.

\textbf{Proof.} For the forward direction choose a finite separating transcendence basis \(T_1,\ldots,T_d\), set \(F=k(T_1,\ldots,T_d)\), and write the remaining finite separable extension as a finite tower \[F=K_0\subset K_1\subset\cdots\subset K_r=K,\qquad K_i=K_{i-1}(y_i).\] A finite field-generating list gives such a tower; each step is separable. Let its monic minimal polynomial have degree \(e_i\). Successive monic division makes the products \(y_1^{a_1}\cdots y_{i-1}^{a_{i-1}}\), with \(0\leq a_j<e_j\), a basis of \(K_{i-1}\) over \(F\). Express every coefficient of the next minimal polynomial in this basis. There are only finitely many coefficients and basis vectors in the entire tower. One nonzero polynomial \(h\in k[T_1,\ldots,T_d]\) clears every rational-function denominator.

Put \(R_0=k[T_1,\ldots,T_d,1/h]\). The coefficient expressions give successive monic equations \(F_i\) in \(R_0[Y_1,\ldots,Y_i]\). Define \[C_i=R_0[Y_1,\ldots,Y_i]/(F_1,\ldots,F_i).\] Monic polynomial division, applied successively, makes the same standard monomials an \(R_0\)-basis of \(C_i\). Tensoring with \(F\) gives exactly \(K_i\). Since \(R_0\) is a domain and these modules are free, their maps to their tensors with \(F\) are injective. Thus each \(C_i\) is an actual subdomain of \(K_i\).

The derivative \(\delta_i=(\partial F_i/\partial Y_i)(y_1,\ldots,y_i)\) is nonzero in \(K_i\), by separability of its minimal polynomial. Form the successive rings \[D_0=R_0,\qquad
D_i=(D_{i-1}[Y_i]/(F_i))_{\delta_i}.\] Here the coefficient expressions are mapped from the preceding \(C_{i-1}\), and all previously inverted derivatives remain inverted. Inductively \(D_i\) is the corresponding localization of \(C_i\), so is a domain in \(K_i\). Each map \(D_{i-1}\to D_i\) is a standard étale one-equation map, with monic equation and inverted derivative. The entire \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/d02d0a3669f42579db037cd44de1d113fdd770a1/docs/courses/AG-CA/src/formally-smooth-unramified-and-etale-ring-maps.md}{AG-CA-17, Proposition 6.1} proves its unique square-zero lifts. The polynomial, localization and composition proofs in its Theorem 1.2 make \(D_r\) formally smooth over \(k\). All equations, variables and inverses are finite in number, so it is finitely presented, hence smooth. It contains every \(T_j\) and \(y_i\), and lies in \(K\), so its fraction field is exactly \(K\). Empty towers have no derivatives to invert and give the same construction.

Conversely let \(C\) be a smooth finite-type \(k\)-domain with fraction field \(K\). Choose a nonzero principal standard smooth chart \(D\) by the entire AG-CA-17, Theorem 5.1. Its fraction field remains \(K\). Reorder the variables of this finite polynomial presentation so the invertible square Jacobian minor uses the pivot variables, and call the remaining variables \(U_1,\ldots,U_t\). With \(B_0=k[U_1,\ldots,U_t]\), the identical chart is a finitely presented algebra over \(B_0\) with only the pivot variables and an invertible full square Jacobian. The explicit square-zero equation correction of AG-CA-17, Theorem 4.1, gives a unique lift: the square invertible matrix solves the error vector uniquely. Thus \(B_0\to D\) is étale. The whole arbitrary-base flatness proof \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/d02d0a3669f42579db037cd44de1d113fdd770a1/docs/courses/AG-CA/src/smooth-algebras-over-a-field-and-the-jacobian-criterion.md}{AG-CA-18, Corollary 6.2} makes it flat.

This structural map from \(B_0\) is injective. For \(0\ne b\in B_0\), multiplication by \(b\) is injective on the polynomial domain. Flat tensor with \(D\) preserves this injection. If \(b\) had zero structural image, that map on the nonzero ring \(D\) would be zero, a contradiction. Consequently the \(U_j\) are algebraically independent in \(K\).

Localize this base at its nonzero elements, obtaining \(F_0=k(U_1,\ldots,U_t)\). The domain \(D\otimes_{B_0}F_0\) is nonzero and étale over \(F_0\), by the full base-change proof of AG-CA-17, Theorem 1.2. Its entire Theorem 7.2 classifies it as a finite product of finite separable extensions of \(F_0\). A nonzero domain has no nontrivial orthogonal idempotents, so this product has exactly one factor. It is therefore a finite separable field. It contains \(D\) and lies in \(K\); every nonzero element of \(D\) is invertible in this field. Hence the field is precisely \(K\). Thus the independent \(U_j\) form a separating transcendence basis, proving the converse at every characteristic, without using F.91. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-localize-NL}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.65: localize NL}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.65-localize-nl}

Reading source: \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/unofficial-stacks-project-ai-drafts/blob/565b10e987aba5969b21145a0833f42d69f96790/algebra.tex\#L37118-L37133}{AI Integrated Stacks, pinned Algebra, lines 37118--37133}.

For any ring map \(A\to B\) and multiplicative subset \(U\subset B\), the canonical map \[\operatorname{NL}_{B/A}\otimes_B U^{-1}B
\longrightarrow \operatorname{NL}_{U^{-1}B/A}\] is a quasi-isomorphism.

\textbf{Proof.} Use the directed principal-localization diagram constructed in \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-localization-colimit]{F.63}, with stages \(B_{s_\nu}\) and colimit \(U^{-1}B\). At every stage the whole calculation \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-principal-localization-NL]{F.72} gives a homotopy equivalence \[\operatorname{NL}_{B/A}\otimes_B B_{s_\nu}
\longrightarrow\operatorname{NL}_{B_{s_\nu}/A}.\] These are the canonical maps induced by \(B\to B_{s_\nu}\); they are compatible with later localizations. Presentation comparisons and their explicit homotopies are proved in \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-NL-homotopy]{F.11}. No compatible choice of the individual contracting homotopies is needed for the induced homology maps.

Tensor commutes with this colimit term by term: a tensor is a finite sum of pure tensors, and each coefficient has a common-stage representative; its balancing relations and equalities hold at a later stage. The right side has colimit \(\operatorname{NL}_{U^{-1}B/A}\) by the complete canonical-presentation proof \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-colimits-NL]{F.24}.

Finally filtered colimits commute with homology here. A cycle in either colimit has a stage representative; its differential is zero at some later stage, giving a cycle there. If its homology class vanishes, it is the differential of a representative vector in the colimit. Put the two representatives and their equality at one common successor to obtain a boundary there. This proves both directions of the homology-colimit isomorphism. The stage maps induce isomorphisms in degrees one and zero, so their colimit does too. All other homology groups vanish since these complexes have only two terms. This proves the claimed quasi-isomorphism, without a Noetherian or finite-generation hypothesis on \(U\). The zero localization is included in the same diagrams. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-localize-relative-complete-intersection}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.66: localize relative complete intersection}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.66-localize-relative-complete-intersection}

Reading source: \href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/00ST}{Stacks, Tag 00ST}.

Let \(R\) be Noetherian and put \(S=R[X_1,\ldots,X_n]/(f_1,\ldots,f_c)\). In each situation below there are \(g\in S\) and a polynomial lift \(h\) of \(g\) for which \[S_g=R[X_1,\ldots,X_n,T]/(f_1,\ldots,f_c,hT-1)\] is a relative global complete intersection as defined in \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-definition-relative-global-complete-intersection]{F.4}.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  If every nonempty fibre over \(V(I)\), for an ideal \(I\subset R\), has dimension \(n-c\), one may require \(g\equiv1\pmod{IS}\).
\item
  If the fibre over \(\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Spec}R\) has dimension \(n-c\), one may require the image of \(g\) in that fibre to be a unit.
\item
  If a point \(\mathfrak q\) of the fibre over \(\mathfrak p\) has fibre point-dimension \(n-c\), one may require \(g\notin\mathfrak q\).
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Proof.} Set \(d=n-c\). The neighbourhood bound proved in \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-dimension-fibres-bounded-open-upstairs]{F.39} gives, around every point whose fibre point-dimension is at most \(d\), a principal neighbourhood on which every fibre point-dimension is at most \(d\). The union of these neighbourhoods is an open \(W\) with that same bound. Each of its nonempty fibres has dimension at most \(d\): a finite-type field fibre is Noetherian, and its component dimensions are its point-dimensions at the corresponding generic points, as in \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-codimension]{F.20}. Open subsets retain this bound.

In case (1) choose \(W\) containing \(V(IS)\); each point of those fibres has point-dimension at most their assumed dimension. Write the closed complement of \(W\) as \(V(J)\) in \(\operatorname{Spec}S\). The equality \(V(J+IS)=\varnothing\) implies \(J+IS=S\): a proper ideal would be contained in a maximal, hence prime, ideal. Write \(1=g+b\) with \(g\in J\) and \(b\in IS\). Then \(g\equiv1\pmod{IS}\), and \(D(g)\subset W\).

In case (2) take \(W\) containing the entire indicated fibre, and again write its complement as \(V(J)\). If \(k=\kappa(\mathfrak p)\), the image ideal \(J(S\otimes_R k)\) is the unit ideal.
