Choose a finite expression \(1=\sum_j\beta_j\bar g_j\), where \(g_j\in J\). Each \(\beta_j\) is represented in \(S_{R\setminus\mathfrak p}/\mathfrak pS_{R\setminus\mathfrak p}\). Clear their finitely many denominators to obtain \(b_j\in S\) and \(s\in R\setminus\mathfrak p\) with \(\beta_j=\bar b_j/\bar s\). Thus \(g=\sum_j b_jg_j\in J\) has fibre image \(\bar s\), a unit. Again \(D(g)\subset W\).

In case (3), one of the principal neighbourhoods supplied directly by F.39 is \(D(g)\) with \(g\notin\mathfrak q\) and the required upper bound. In all three cases select any polynomial lift \(h\) of \(g\). Adjoining the inverse of \(h\) gives the presentation in the statement, by the explicit substitution \(T\mapsto g^{-1}\) and its inverse. Every nonempty fibre of this presentation has dimension at least \[ (n+1)-(c+1)=d.\] Indeed, in its polynomial ring over the residue field a minimal prime over \(c+1\) equations has height at most \(c+1\), by \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/d02d0a3669f42579db037cd44de1d113fdd770a1/docs/courses/AG-CA/src/dimension-theory-of-noetherian-local-rings.md}{AG-CA-11, Theorem 3.1}; \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/d02d0a3669f42579db037cd44de1d113fdd770a1/docs/courses/AG-CA/src/krull-dimension-and-noether-normalization.md}{AG-CA-09, Theorem 4.3} gives that component dimension as \(n+1\) minus its height. The upper bound on \(D(g)\) makes the dimension exactly \(d\). This proves the relative global complete-intersection assertion, without presupposing flatness; its flatness is subsequently proved in F.77. Empty fibres impose no dimension test, and a zero localization is included. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-locally-smooth}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.67: locally smooth}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.67-locally-smooth}

Reading source: \href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/00TC}{Stacks, Tag 00TC}.

For any ring map \(R\to S\), smoothness is equivalent to the existence, around every prime of \(S\), of a principal localization that is smooth over \(R\).

\textbf{Proof.} Use the finite-presentation and cotangent-complex definition \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-definition-smooth]{F.6}. If \(S/R\) is smooth, then \(S_g\) is finitely presented by adjoining an inverse variable. The exact calculation \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-principal-localization-NL]{F.72}, together with the presentation comparison \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-NL-homotopy]{F.11}, identifies its conormal complex with the localized complex plus a contractible summand. Its first homology is zero and its differential module is the localization of a finite projective module. Localization keeps the splitting of a finite free module, so that module is still finite projective. Thus \(S_g/R\) is smooth.

For the converse, the elements defining the given neighbourhoods generate the unit ideal: otherwise a maximal ideal containing them would be an uncovered prime. A finite expression for \(1\) gives a cover by \(D(g_1),\ldots,D(g_r)\). The complete gluing proof \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-cover-upstairs]{F.35} makes \(S/R\) finitely presented. Fix \(S=R[X_1,\ldots,X_n]/I\) with \(I\) finite. For this presentation set \[K=\ker(I/I^2\xrightarrow{d}S^n),\qquad M=\operatorname{coker}(I/I^2\xrightarrow{d}S^n)=\Omega_{S/R}.\] The derivatives of a finite list generating \(I\) generate the image of \(d\), so \(M\) is finitely presented. Exact localization and F.72/F.11 identify \(K_{g_i}\) with the zero first homology of each smooth chart. The power-annihilator module calculation in F.35 therefore gives \(K=0\).

It remains to produce a global projective splitting for \(M\). Write \(\pi:S^n\twoheadrightarrow M\). On each chart \(M_{g_i}\) is finite projective. A section \(s_i\) of \(\pi_{g_i}\) exists: write that projective module as a summand of a finite free module, lift the free basis through \(\pi_{g_i}\), and restrict the resulting lift to the summand.

For a finitely presented module, localization of \(\operatorname{Hom}_S(M,S^n)\) is \(\operatorname{Hom}_{S_{g_i}}(M_{g_i},S_{g_i}^n)\). Indeed a finite presentation of \(M\) identifies both modules with the kernel of the same matrix between finite powers of \(S^n\), and localization is exact. Clear the denominator of \(s_i\) to obtain \(t_i:M\to S^n\) whose localized composite is \(g_i^{a_i}1_M\). The error \(\pi t_i-g_i^{a_i}1_M\) vanishes on a finite generating list after localization. A further common power of \(g_i\) kills those finitely many errors. After multiplying \(t_i\) by that power, we have an actual equality \[\pi t_i=g_i^{e_i}1_M.\] Increase \(e_i\) to a positive integer if needed. These powers generate \(1\): expand a finite unit expression in the \(g_i\) to exponent \(1+\sum_i(e_i-1)\); every monomial contains one of the required powers. Choose \(c_i\) with \(\sum_i c_ig_i^{e_i}=1\). Then \(t=\sum_i c_it_i\) satisfies \(\pi t=1_M\). Thus \(S^n=t(M)\oplus\ker\pi\), with both summands generated by projections of its finite basis. This proves finite projectivity of \(M\) directly.

We have proved finite presentation, zero first cotangent homology and finite projective differentials, exactly F.6. If \(S=0\), its finite presentation is \(R/(1)\) and both cotangent modules are zero, so the conclusion also holds for the empty spectrum. No Noetherian hypothesis is needed. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-make-etale-map-prescribed-residue-field}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.68: make etale map prescribed residue field}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.68-make-etale-map-prescribed-residue-field}

Reading source: \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/unofficial-stacks-project-ai-drafts/blob/565b10e987aba5969b21145a0833f42d69f96790/algebra.tex\#L41287-L41319}{AI Integrated Stacks, pinned Algebra, lines 41287--41319}.

Let \(\mathfrak p\) be a prime of a ring \(R\), and let \(L/\kappa(\mathfrak p)\) be finite separable. There are a finitely presented étale \(R\)-algebra \(R'\) and a prime \(\mathfrak p'\) over \(\mathfrak p\) with an isomorphism \(\kappa(\mathfrak p')\cong L\) respecting the given residue-field extension.

\textbf{Proof.} Choose a finite field-generating list \(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_r\) for \(L/\kappa(\mathfrak p)\), for example a vector-space basis. Put \(E_0=\kappa(\mathfrak p)\) and \(E_i=E_{i-1}(\alpha_i)\). Each step is finite separable: the minimal polynomial over \(E_{i-1}\) divides a separable polynomial over \(E_0\) and therefore has no repeated root.

Inductively construct a finitely presented étale \(R\)-algebra \(A_i\) with a prime \(\mathfrak q_i\) and a compatible identification \(\kappa(\mathfrak q_i)=E_i\). Start with \(A_0=R\) and \(\mathfrak q_0=\mathfrak p\). Suppose the preceding stage is constructed, and write \(A=A_{i-1}\), \(\mathfrak q=\mathfrak q_{i-1}\). Let \[\bar F_i(T)=T^{e_i}+\sum_{j<e_i}\bar a_jT^j\in E_{i-1}[T]\] be the monic minimal polynomial of \(\alpha_i\). The residue map \(A_{\mathfrak q}\to E_{i-1}\) is surjective, so lift each \(\bar a_j\) as a fraction \(a_j/s_j\) with \(s_j\notin\mathfrak q\). The product \(h=\prod_j s_j\) is outside \(\mathfrak q\), and all these lifts belong to the single principal localization \(A_h\). They give a monic polynomial \(F_i\in A_h[T]\). Set \[A_i=(A_h[T]/(F_i))_{F_i'}.\] Its defining equation has an invertible derivative. The full one-equation square-zero correction \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/d02d0a3669f42579db037cd44de1d113fdd770a1/docs/courses/AG-CA/src/formally-smooth-unramified-and-etale-ring-maps.md}{AG-CA-17, Proposition 6.1} makes this map étale. Principal localization is formally étale by its Theorem 1.2 and finitely presented by its inverse-variable equation. Finite composition, with the equation substitution proof \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-compose-finite-type]{F.28}, therefore makes \(A_i/R\) finitely presented and étale.

Evaluation at \(T=\alpha_i\) defines a ring map \(A_i\to E_i\): its derivative has nonzero value by separability, so its inverse can be evaluated. Let \(\mathfrak q_i\) be the kernel. It is prime, and its contraction to \(A\) is exactly \(\mathfrak q\), since the restriction is the given residue map and \(h\) has nonzero residue.

To compute its residue field, let \(D_i\) be the image of \(A_i\) in \(E_i\). It is a domain, and \(A_i/\mathfrak q_i=D_i\). The fraction field of the image of \(A_h\) is \(E_{i-1}\): this image is \((A/\mathfrak q)_h\), and localization does not change its fraction field \(\kappa(\mathfrak q)\). Thus \(\operatorname{Frac}D_i\) contains \(E_{i-1}\) as well as \(\alpha_i\), and so contains \(E_i=E_{i-1}(\alpha_i)\). It lies inside \(E_i\), giving equality. Localization at the kernel identifies \[\kappa(\mathfrak q_i)=\operatorname{Frac}(A_i/\mathfrak q_i)
=\operatorname{Frac}D_i=E_i.\] This uses the fraction field of the image; it does not require the evaluation map itself to be onto the field.

Continue through the finite tower. Taking \(R'=A_r\) and \(\mathfrak p'=\mathfrak q_r\) gives the required extension and prime, with all residue identifications commuting with the original map from \(R\). For the trivial extension the empty tower gives \(R'=R\) and \(\mathfrak p'=\mathfrak p\). ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-make-separably-generated}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.69: make separably generated}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.69-make-separably-generated}

Reading source: \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/unofficial-stacks-project-ai-drafts/blob/565b10e987aba5969b21145a0833f42d69f96790/algebra.tex\#L10182-L10253}{AI Integrated Stacks, pinned Algebra, lines 10182--10253}.

For any finitely generated field extension \(K/k\), there is a commutative square of inclusions \[
\begin{array}{ccc}
K&\longrightarrow&K'\\
\uparrow&&\uparrow\\
k&\longrightarrow&k'
\end{array}
\] in which \(k'/k\) and \(K'/K\) are finite purely inseparable and \(K'/k'\) is separably generated.

\textbf{Proof.} Choose a finite field-generating list and a maximal algebraically independent sublist \(T_1,\ldots,T_d\). Every remaining generator is algebraic over \(F=k(T_1,\ldots,T_d)\): a polynomial dependence using that generator has a nonzero coefficient after substituting the independent \(T_j\). A finite algebraic generator tower is finite. At each step, division by the monic minimal polynomial gives a power basis; multiplication of these bases gives a basis of the whole tower, since grouping a relation by the powers of the last generator proves independence inductively. Thus \(K/F\) is finite. In characteristic zero its irreducible polynomials have nonzero derivatives, so every tower step is separable. The entire separable-tower proof \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/d02d0a3669f42579db037cd44de1d113fdd770a1/docs/courses/AG-CA/src/formally-smooth-unramified-and-etale-ring-maps.md}{AG-CA-17, Lemma 7.1} gives the result with \(k'=k\) and \(K'=K\).

Assume now characteristic \(p>0\). We first prove the finite-extension facts used in the construction. For a finite extension \(E/F\), the elements separable over \(F\) form a subfield \(E_s\). Indeed if \(x,y\) are separable, the minimal polynomial of \(y\) over \(F(x)\) divides its separable polynomial over \(F\). The two separable steps and the same complete separable-tower proof make every element of \(F(x,y)\) separable over \(F\). This proves closure under sums, products and inverses. As a subspace of the finite-dimensional \(F\)-space \(E\), this field is finite over \(F\).

If \(x\in E\) has irreducible minimal polynomial \(f\), repeatedly remove zero derivatives to write \[f(X)=g(X^{p^e}),\qquad g'\ne0.\] This process terminates as degrees decrease; \(g\) is irreducible because a factorization would substitute to one of \(f\). Its derivative has smaller degree, so the Euclidean algorithm gives \(\gcd(g,g')=1\). Hence \(x^{p^e}\) is separable over \(F\) and lies in \(E_s\). A common exponent for a finite field-generating list makes every \(p^e\)th power from \(E\) belong to \(E_s\): apply Frobenius to its rational expressions. Thus \(E/E_s\) is purely inseparable.

We will use the degree calculation without an external \(p\)-basis result. If \(\beta^p\in H\) but \(\beta\notin H\), its minimal polynomial over \(H\) divides \(X^p-\beta^p=(X-\beta)^p\) in a field containing \(\beta\). A monic proper nonconstant factor of degree \(r<p\) has coefficient \(-r\beta\) at degree \(r-1\). Since \(r\) is nonzero in the field, a factor over \(H\) would force \(\beta\in H\), a contradiction. The minimal polynomial therefore has degree \(p\). By adjoining the powers of each purely inseparable generator in reverse order, starting from a power in the base, each nontrivial step has this degree. Multiplication of the power bases shows that every finite purely inseparable degree is a power of \(p\).

Apply these facts to \(K/F\), and call its separable subfield \(K_s\). Prove the desired assertion by strong induction on \(m=[K:K_s]\), for all finitely generated extensions with their chosen transcendence bases. If \(m=1\), the chosen \(T_j\) already separate \(K/k\). If \(m>1\), choose \(x\in K\setminus K_s\) and the least \(e\geq1\) with \(x^{p^e}\in K_s\). Put \[\beta=x^{p^{e-1}},\qquad \alpha=\beta^p\in K_s.\] Then \(\beta\notin K_s\). The degree calculation gives \([K_s(\beta):K_s]=p\) and \([K:K_s(\beta)]=m/p\).

Let \[P(X)=X^n+\sum_{i<n}a_iX^i\in F[X]\] be the separable minimal polynomial of \(\alpha\). Write all \(a_i\) as rational functions in \(T\), and list the finitely many coefficients of \(k\) occurring in their numerators and denominators. Adjoin their \(p\)th roots compatibly over \(K\), one at a time. Such a root exists in a field extension: take the quotient by an irreducible factor of \(X^p-c\). The quotient is a field by the Euclidean algorithm. A root is unique in any common extension, since \((u-v)^p=u^p-v^p\). All old fields therefore remain embedded in these successive root fields. Let \(k_1\) be the field generated by these roots over \(k\). It is finite purely inseparable, and \(k_1^p\subset k\), since taking the \(p\)th power of any rational expression puts all its coefficients and generators in \(k\).

In the same compatible extension adjoin \(U_j\) with \(U_j^p=T_j\). They are algebraically independent over \(k_1\): a nonzero polynomial relation would, after taking its \(p\)th power, be a nonzero relation among the \(T_j\) over \(k\). Its coefficients remain nonzero under Frobenius. Put \[F_1=k_1(U_1,\ldots,U_d),\qquad L=KF_1.\] This gives the actual commuting intermediate field square. The extension \(L/K\) is finite and purely inseparable; it adjoins finitely many roots with \(p\)th powers in \(K\). The \(p\)th power of any rational expression in them lies in \(K\).

Take coefficientwise \(p\)th roots of the chosen numerator and denominator for each \(a_i\), and substitute the \(U_j\). This gives \(b_i\in F_1\) with \(b_i^p=a_i\). The denominator is nonzero because its \(p\)th power is the original nonzero denominator. Define \[Q(X)=X^n+\sum_{i<n}b_iX^i,\qquad Q(X)^p=P(X^p).\] Then \(Q(\beta)^p=P(\alpha)=0\), so \(Q(\beta)=0\). The derivative calculation, using \(i^p=i\) in the prime field, gives \[Q'(\beta)^p=P'(\alpha)\ne0.\] Write \(Q=hq\) with \(h\) the minimal polynomial of \(\beta\) over \(F_1\). Evaluation of \(Q'=h'q+hq'\) at \(\beta\) implies \(h'(\beta)q(\beta)\ne0\). Thus \(h\) is separable, and \(\beta\) is separable over \(F_1\).

Every separable polynomial remains square-free after a field extension: its Euclidean identity with its derivative remains an identity equal to one after extending coefficients. The minimal polynomial of a generator after base change divides that polynomial and is therefore separable too. A finite generating tower for \(K_s/F\) consequently gives a separable tower for \(K_sF_1/F_1\). The minimal polynomial of the now separable \(\beta\) over this larger field divides its separable polynomial over \(F_1\), so this final step is separable as well. The separable-tower proof gives \[H=K_s(\beta)F_1\subset L_s,\] where \(L_s\) denotes the separable subfield of the finite extension \(L/F_1\).

To bound its remaining inseparable degree, take a basis of \(K\) over \(K_s(\beta)\) of size \(m/p\) and span it over \(H\) inside \(L\). This span contains \(K\) and \(H\), contains one, and is closed under multiplication, since the basis-product coefficients belong to \(K_s(\beta)\subset H\). It is a finite-dimensional domain over \(H\), hence a field: nonzero multiplication is injective, therefore surjective, and supplies an inverse. It contains \(F_1\) and \(K\), so equals \(L\). Consequently \[[L:L_s]\leq[L:H]\leq m/p<m.\] Also \(L/F_1\) is finite, by the same spanning argument starting with a basis of \(K/F\). The \(U_j\) are a transcendence basis for the finitely generated extension \(L/k_1\). Strong induction thus applies to this precise new data, giving finite purely inseparable \(k_2/k_1\) and \(L'/L\) with \(L'/k_2\) separably generated.

Finally finite purely inseparable extensions compose: for each element of \(L'\), a \(p\)-power lies in \(L\) and a further \(p\)-power lies in \(K\). The same argument applies to \(k_2/k\). Finiteness follows by multiplying their finite tower degrees. Taking \(K'=L'\) and \(k'=k_2\) gives the asserted square. Empty transcendence bases, trivial adjunctions and the base case are all included. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-matrix-left-inverse}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.70: matrix left inverse}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.70-matrix-left-inverse}

Reading source: \href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/07DQ}{Stacks, Tag 07DQ}.

Let \(A\) be an \(n\times m\) matrix over a commutative ring \(R\), where \(0\leq m\leq n\), and let \(J\) be the ideal of its maximal minors. Every \(f\in J\) has an \(m\times n\) matrix \(B\) with \(BA=f1_m\). Conversely, existence of such a \(B\) implies \(f^m\in J\).

\textbf{Proof.} For an increasing \(m\)-element subset \(I\) of \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), let \(E_I\) select those coordinates from \(R^n\), and put \(A_I=E_IA\). Its determinant is the corresponding minor. By the complete cofactor calculation in \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-charpoly]{F.19}, \[
\operatorname{adj}(A_I)E_IA=(\det A_I)1_m.
\] Thus, from an expression \(f=\sum_I c_I\det A_I\), the finite sum \[
B=\sum_I c_I\operatorname{adj}(A_I)E_I
\] constructs the required matrix.

For the converse, here is the determinant product calculation. Expand each column of \(BA\) as the linear combination of columns of \(B\) whose coefficients are entries of that column of \(A\). Multilinearity follows directly from the determinant permutation formula. A term choosing the same column twice is zero by the equal-column cancellation. For any fixed set \(I\) of distinct chosen columns, order those indices increasingly. Reordering them in all possible ways contributes their permutation signs; the signed sum of their coefficient products is exactly \(\det A_I\). The remaining column determinant is \(\det B^I\), where \(B^I\) uses the columns indexed by \(I\). Consequently \[
\det(BA)=\sum_{|I|=m}(\det B^I)(\det A_I)\in J.
\] When \(BA=f1_m\), its determinant is \(f^m\). This proves the converse over arbitrary rings, including rings with nilpotents. If \(m=0\), the sole minor is the empty determinant \(1\), so \(J=R\). The unique map to and from the zero module supplies the first assertion, and \(f^0=1\in J\) supplies the second. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-presentation-sym-exterior}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.71: presentation sym exterior}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.71-presentation-sym-exterior}

Reading source: \href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/00DO}{Stacks, Tag 00DO}. The quotient maps and both kernels are proved below.

For an exact sequence \(M_2\xrightarrow{u}M_1\xrightarrow{v}M\to0\) of modules over any commutative ring and every integer \(n\geq1\), there are exact sequences \[
M_2\otimes_R\operatorname{Sym}^{n-1}M_1
\longrightarrow\operatorname{Sym}^nM_1
\longrightarrow\operatorname{Sym}^nM\longrightarrow0,
\] \[
M_2\otimes_R\bigwedge^{n-1}M_1
\longrightarrow\bigwedge^nM_1
\longrightarrow\bigwedge^nM\longrightarrow0.
\] The first maps multiply, respectively wedge, with \(u(x)\); the second maps apply \(v\) to every factor. In degree zero both second maps are the identity of \(R\), so both kernels are zero.

\textbf{Proof.} Put \(N=\operatorname{im}u\), so exactness identifies \(M=M_1/N\). Construct the tensor algebra \(T(M_1)=\bigoplus_{d\geq0}M_1^{\otimes d}\) with multiplication by concatenation. Balancing in each tensor factor makes that product well defined. Its symmetric quotient imposes \(xy=yx\) for degree-one generators; its exterior quotient imposes \(x^2=0\) for every degree-one generator. In the latter quotient, expanding \((x+y)^2=0\) gives \(xy=-yx\) over every ring, including characteristic two.

In either algebra let \(L\) be the two-sided homogeneous ideal generated by the degree-one image of \(N\). The factorwise map to the corresponding algebra of \(M_1/N\) is onto: every pure tensor in the target lifts, and pure tensors generate each degree. It kills \(L\). Its inverse on the quotient is explicit. Send a class \(\bar x\in M_1/N\) to the class of any lift \(x\) in the source algebra modulo \(L\). Another lift differs by an element of \(N\), hence gives the same class. This map is linear, so its products extend to the tensor algebra by the tensor balancing relations. Those products obey commutation, respectively square-zero, relations in the indicated quotient; it therefore descends to the symmetric, respectively exterior, algebra. The two composites fix every degree-one generator and the scalar ring, hence every product and sum of generators. They are inverse graded algebra maps.

It remains to identify the degree-\(n\) part of \(L\). It is spanned by products having one selected factor in \(N\), since those generate the ideal and all factors have nonnegative degree. In the symmetric case move that factor to the front by commutation. In the exterior case move it to the front using \(xy=-yx\), retaining the resulting sign. Every remaining product has degree \(n-1\). Thus that part is exactly the image of \(N\otimes_R\operatorname{Sym}^{n-1}M_1\), respectively \(N\otimes_R\bigwedge^{n-1}M_1\), under multiplication. Each selected element of \(N\) lifts through \(u\), so these are also the images of the stated maps from \(M_2\). The inverse quotient maps just constructed prove that these images are exactly the kernels. The ideal has no degree-zero part, proving the separate degree-zero assertion. No module is assumed finite or free. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-principal-localization-NL}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.72: principal localization NL}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.72-principal-localization-nl}

Reading source: \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/unofficial-stacks-project-ai-drafts/blob/565b10e987aba5969b21145a0833f42d69f96790/algebra.tex\#L37031-L37116}{AI Integrated Stacks, pinned Algebra, lines 37031--37116}.

Let \(A\to B\) be a ring map, \(g\in B\), and \(P\twoheadrightarrow B\) a polynomial presentation over \(A\) with kernel \(I\). Choose \(f\in P\) mapping to \(g\). The map \(P[X]\to B_g\) extending the presentation and sending \(X\) to \(g^{-1}\) has kernel \(J=(I,fX-1)\), and:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \(J/J^2\cong(I/I^2)_g\oplus B_g[fX-1]\).
\item
  \(\Omega_{P[X]/A}\otimes_{P[X]}B_g\cong(\Omega_{P/A}\otimes_PB_g)\oplus B_g\,dX\).
\item
  The two-term conormal complex is isomorphic to \[\operatorname{NL}(P\to B)\otimes_BB_g
  \oplus(B_g\xrightarrow{g}B_g).\]
\end{enumerate}

Consequently the canonical map \(\operatorname{NL}_{B/A}\otimes_BB_g\to\operatorname{NL}_{B_g/A}\) is a homotopy equivalence.

\textbf{Proof.} The inverse-variable universal property gives \[P[X]/(I,fX-1)=B[X]/(gX-1)\cong B_g,\] including a nilpotent \(g\), when the last ring is zero. Put \(q=gX-1\in B[X]\). Multiplication by \(q\) is injective: if a polynomial has lowest nonzero coefficient at degree \(j\), the product's coefficient at that degree is its negative. Thus the map \[B[X]/(q)\longrightarrow(q)/(q^2),\quad [a]\longmapsto[aq]\] is an isomorphism. It is surjective by the definition of the principal ideal, and \(aq=bq^2\) implies \(a=bq\) by the proved multiplication injection. Therefore \((q)/(q^2)\) is free of rank one over \(B_g\), with the indicated generator, also when both modules are zero.

Reduction modulo \(I\) gives an exact sequence \[ (I/I^2)\otimes_BB_g\longrightarrow J/J^2
\longrightarrow(q)/(q^2)\longrightarrow0.\] For exactness in the middle, if an element of \(J\) becomes a multiple of \(q^2\), lift its coefficient to \(P[X]\) and subtract that coefficient times \((fX-1)^2\). The remainder lies in \(IP[X]\). Its class modulo \(J^2\) is a finite sum of classes of elements of \(I\), with coefficients evaluated in \(B_g\). This is exactly the image of the left map.

That map is injective and has a retraction. Define \[\pi:P[X]\longrightarrow(P/I^2)_f,\qquad X\longmapsto f^{-1}.\] It maps \(J\) into the square-zero ideal \(I_f/I_f^2\) and maps \(J^2\) to zero. The target ideal is naturally \((I/I^2)\otimes_BB_g\): the action factors through \(B_g\), and localization commutes with the quotient and square by its exact fraction identities. Hence \(\pi\) induces a \(B_g\)-linear map from \(J/J^2\) to this module. On the left map its composite is the identity, proving injectivity. It kills \([fX-1]\), whose image generates the right quotient. Lifting a right-quotient coefficient by \(a[fX-1]\), for \(a\in B_g\), gives the asserted direct sum and proves (1).

For (2), derivations out of \(P[X]\) are uniquely a derivation out of \(P\) together with the chosen value of \(X\). This proves the differential direct sum by the universal property, and tensoring yields the displayed formula.

Write \(E=\Omega_{P/A}\otimes_PB_g\). On the first summand the conormal differential is the original \([a]\mapsto da\). On the new generator it is \[d(fX-1)=g^{-1}df+g\,dX
=g\bigl(dX+g^{-2}df\bigr).\] Changing the new differential generator from \(dX\) to \(w=dX+g^{-2}df\) is invertible, with inverse \(dX=w-g^{-2}df\). It leaves \(E\) fixed. The two direct sums now identify the entire differential with the old conormal differential plus multiplication by \(g\), proving (3).

The new summand is contractible: multiplication by \(g^{-1}\) from degree zero to degree one has both composites with its differential equal to the identity. Inclusion of the old summand and projection onto it therefore have composite identity there, and their other composite differs from identity by this explicit homotopy. They are homotopy inverses. The inclusion is precisely the map induced by \(P\to P[X]\) and \(B\to B_g\). The full presentation comparison \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-NL-homotopy]{F.11} identifies it with the stated canonical map. The argument uses neither a nonnilpotence assumption on \(g\) nor a proper regular-sequence condition. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-product-local}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.73: product local}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.73-product-local}

Reading source: \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/unofficial-stacks-project-ai-drafts/blob/565b10e987aba5969b21145a0833f42d69f96790/algebra.tex\#L13035-L13062}{AI Integrated Stacks, pinned Algebra, lines 13035--13062}.

If a ring \(R\) has finitely many maximal ideals and locally nilpotent Jacobson radical, every prime is maximal and the natural map to the product of the corresponding localizations is an isomorphism.

\textbf{Proof.} Write the distinct maximal ideals as \(\mathfrak m_1,\ldots,\mathfrak m_r\), and put \(J=\bigcap_i\mathfrak m_i\). Each element of \(J\) is nilpotent. Any prime contains \(J\), hence contains \(\mathfrak m_1\cdots\mathfrak m_r\subset J\). If it contained none of the factors, choosing one element outside the prime from each factor would give a product outside the prime, a contradiction. It therefore equals one of the maximal ideals.

The maximal ideals are pairwise comaximal. For two comaximal ideals \(A,B\), choose \(a\in A,b\in B\) with \(a+b=1\); the element \(ub+va\) lifts prescribed residues \(u\) modulo \(A\) and \(v\) modulo \(B\). Also \(A\cap B=AB\), since \(x=x(a+b)\in AB\) when \(x\in A\cap B\). These identities inductively give the Chinese remainder isomorphism \[R/J\cong\prod_{i=1}^r R/\mathfrak m_i.\] For the induction, the intersection of preceding factors is comaximal with the next one: multiply elements in the preceding maximal ideals whose residues are one modulo the next ideal. Their product lies in the intersection and still has residue one.

We give the nil-ideal idempotent lift explicitly. If \(e_0^2-e_0=\epsilon\) is nilpotent, then \(u=2e_0-1\) is a unit, since \(u^2=1+4\epsilon\) has inverse given by a finite geometric series. Set \(e_1=e_0-u^{-1}\epsilon\). Direct expansion gives \[e_1^2-e_1=u^{-2}\epsilon^2.\] The correction lies in the nil ideal. Repeat; the error squares at each step, so a zero power of the initial error makes the process terminate at an idempotent with the prescribed residue. Uniqueness across a nil ideal follows as well: if \(e,f\) are two lifts, the idempotents \(e(1-f)\) and \(f(1-e)\) lie in that ideal. A nilpotent idempotent is zero, so \(e=ef=f\).

Lift the coordinate idempotents of \(R/J\) to \(e_i\in R\). Their products for distinct indices are idempotents in \(J\), hence zero. Their sum is then idempotent, so \(1-\sum_i e_i\) is an idempotent in \(J\) and is zero. Thus \[R\longrightarrow\prod_i e_iR,\quad r\longmapsto(e_ir)_i\] has inverse \((r_i)_i\mapsto\sum_i r_i\). Each factor, whose identity is \(e_i\), has exactly one prime, corresponding to \(\mathfrak m_i\), so it is local.

The factor is precisely \(R_{\mathfrak m_i}\). For \(s\notin\mathfrak m_i\), \(e_is\) avoids its unique maximal ideal and is a unit in \(e_iR\); this gives a map \(R_{\mathfrak m_i}\to e_iR\). Conversely \(e_i\) is an idempotent outside \(\mathfrak m_i\), hence becomes one in that localization, whereas the other \(e_j\) become zero. The map \(e_iR\to R_{\mathfrak m_i}\) is therefore unital, and the two fraction maps are inverse. This identifies the displayed product with the natural localization map. If there are no maximal ideals, the ring is zero by the maximal-proper-ideal Zorn argument, and the empty product is the zero ring. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-regular-quasi-regular}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.74: regular quasi regular}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.74-regular-quasi-regular}

Reading source: \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/unofficial-stacks-project-ai-drafts/blob/565b10e987aba5969b21145a0833f42d69f96790/algebra.tex\#L17680-L17766}{AI Integrated Stacks, pinned Algebra, lines 17680--17766}.

Let \(A\) be any ring, \(M\) any \(A\)-module, and \(f_1,\ldots,f_c\) an \(M\)-regular sequence. Put \(J=(f_1,\ldots,f_c)\). Then the natural graded map \[
(M/JM)[T_1,\ldots,T_c]\longrightarrow
\bigoplus_{n\geq0}J^nM/J^{n+1}M,\qquad
\bar mT^a\longmapsto[mf^a]
\] is an isomorphism. Thus a regular sequence is quasi-regular, both for rings and for arbitrary modules. In particular, for a regular sequence in \(A\), \(J/J^2\) is free over \(A/J\) on the classes of the \(f_i\).

\textbf{Proof.} Every degree is generated by products of the \(f_i\), so the map is surjective. Degree zero is the identity. We prove injectivity in every positive degree by induction on \(c\), without finiteness or Noetherian assumptions on \(M\).

For \(c=1\), a relation \(mf_1^n\in f_1^{n+1}M\) reads \(f_1^n(m-f_1v)=0\) for some \(v\). Multiplication by \(f_1\) is injective on \(M\), hence so is its \(n\)th power; thus \(m\in f_1M\). For \(c=0\), only degree zero is present.

Suppose now \(c>1\) and the assertion holds for the first \(c-1\) entries; write \(J'=(f_1,\ldots,f_{c-1})\) and \(f'= (f_1,\ldots,f_{c-1})\). A degree-\(n\) relation modulo \(J^{n+1}M\) can be made an exact zero relation by subtracting, from each coefficient, an element of \(JM\): every element of \(J^{n+1}M\) is a sum of degree-\(n\) products with coefficients in \(JM\). It suffices therefore to handle \[\sum_{e=0}^{\ell}\ \sum_{|a|=n-e}m_{a,e}(f')^a f_c^e=0
\quad(0\leq\ell\leq n).\] Induct on its largest exponent \(\ell\). If \(\ell=0\), the induction on \(c\) applied in degree \(n\) gives all coefficients in \(J'M\subset JM\). For \(\ell\geq1\), every lower-exponent term belongs to \(J'^{\,n-\ell+1}M\). Consequently \[\sum_{|a|=n-\ell}(f_c^\ell m_{a,\ell})(f')^a
\in J'^{\,n-\ell+1}M.\] The already proved degree-\(n-\ell\) assertion for the shorter list gives \(f_c^\ell m_{a,\ell}\in J'M\); in degree zero this is simply membership in \(J'M\). Since \(f_c\) is injective on \(M/J'M\), its powers are injective there, and hence \(m_{a,\ell}\in J'M\).

Write each such coefficient as \(\sum_{j<c}f_jb_{a,j}\). Replace its top term by \[m_{a,\ell}(f')^af_c^\ell
=\sum_{j<c}(f_cb_{a,j})(f')^{a+\delta_j}f_c^{\ell-1}.\] The new relation has largest exponent at most \(\ell-1\), and the only changed coefficients differ from the old ones by elements of \(f_cM\subset JM\). The induction on \(\ell\) puts all new coefficients in \(JM\). It therefore puts all old lower coefficients in \(JM\), and the old top coefficients were already in \(J'M\). This proves the homogeneous injectivity for every \(n\) and completes both inductions.

Taking \(M=A\) proves the ring assertion. Its degree-one isomorphism is exactly \((A/J)^c\to J/J^2\), with the stated basis. No permutation of the regular list, separatedness, or finite-module hypothesis has been used. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-regular-sequence-in-polynomial-ring}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.75: regular sequence in polynomial ring}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.75-regular-sequence-in-polynomial-ring}

Reading source: \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/unofficial-stacks-project-ai-drafts/blob/565b10e987aba5969b21145a0833f42d69f96790/algebra.tex\#L17576-L17624}{AI Integrated Stacks, pinned Algebra, lines 17576--17624}.

Let \(f_1,\ldots,f_r\in R\) generate a proper ideal in an arbitrary ring. These conditions are equivalent:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Every permutation of the list is regular.
\item
  Every subsequence in its original order is regular.
\item
  \(f_1X_1,\ldots,f_rX_r\) is regular in \(R[X_1,\ldots,X_r]\).
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Proof.} A subsequence can be placed first in a permutation, so (1) implies (2). To prove the converse we first check the interchange of two elements. If \(a,b\) is regular and \(b\) is also a nonzerodivisor, then \(b,a\) is regular. Indeed, if \(ax=by\), injectivity of \(b\) modulo \((a)\) gives \(y=az\). Injectivity of \(a\) then gives \(x=bz\), proving injectivity of \(a\) modulo \((b)\). The final ideal is the same proper ideal.

Induct on \(r\) to deduce (1) from (2). Any proper sublist inherits (2), so by induction all its permutations are regular. Given a permutation whose last entry is \(f_s\), the preceding entries are therefore regular, and it remains to check that \(f_s\) is injective modulo all the others. If \(s=r\), this is the last injection of the original list. If \(s<r\), put \[V=R/(f_1,\ldots,\widehat f_s,\ldots,f_{r-1}).\] Permuting the first \(r-1\) entries shows that \(f_s\) is a nonzerodivisor on \(V\). The original-order subsequence omitting \(f_s\) shows that \(f_r\) is one too. The pair \(f_s,f_r\) is regular in \(V\), since its second injection is the final injection of the original full list. The two-element interchange just proved makes \(f_r,f_s\) regular in \(V\), giving the required last injection. All quotient ideals are proper because they are contained in the original proper ideal.

For the polynomial condition, the coefficient of each monomial is independent of the coefficients of the others. After imposing the first \(i\) equations, this gives the exact \(R\)-module decomposition \[
R[X]/(f_1X_1,\ldots,f_iX_i)
\cong\bigoplus_{e\in\mathbf N^r}(R/J_e)\,X^e,\qquad
J_e=(f_j\mid j\leq i,\ e_j>0).
\] To verify it, a multiple of \(f_jX_j\) contributes to the coefficient of \(X^e\) precisely when \(e_j>0\), and then contributes a multiple of \(f_j\). Conversely any such coefficient is obtained by multiplying \(f_jX_j\) by that monomial with its \(j\)th exponent reduced by one. These two calculations identify the entire ideal coefficient by coefficient.

Multiplication by \(f_{i+1}X_{i+1}\) shifts each exponent to \(e+\delta_{i+1}\) and multiplies its coefficient by \(f_{i+1}\). The coefficient ideal \(J_e\) is unchanged by this shift, since only the first \(i\) indices occur in it. The multiplication is injective precisely when \(f_{i+1}\) is injective on every \(R/J_e\).

Under (2), the ordered list with indices \(\{j\leq i:e_j>0\}\) followed by \(i+1\) is a regular subsequence, giving every such injection. This proves (3). Conversely, for any subset \(U\subset\{1,\ldots,i\}\) choose \(e_j=1\) for \(j\in U\) and zero otherwise. The injection supplied by (3) says that \(f_{i+1}\) is injective on \(R/(f_j:j\in U)\). Apply it successively along any ordered subsequence to prove all of (2). The polynomial equation ideal is proper since evaluation at all \(X_j=0\) factors its quotient onto the nonzero ring \(R\). For the empty list all three conditions hold directly. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-relative-global-complete-intersection}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.76: relative global complete intersection}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.76-relative-global-complete-intersection}

Reading source: \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/unofficial-stacks-project-ai-drafts/blob/565b10e987aba5969b21145a0833f42d69f96790/algebra.tex\#L38280-L38292}{AI Integrated Stacks, pinned Algebra, lines 38280--38292}.

A relative global complete intersection over any commutative base ring is syntomic.

\textbf{Proof.} Write its presentation as \(S=R[X_1,\ldots,X_n]/(f_1,\ldots,f_c)\), with every nonempty residue-field fibre of dimension \(n-c\), as in the relative complete-intersection definition. The finite generator and equation lists give finite presentation. The entire arbitrary-base proof \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-relative-global-complete-intersection-conormal]{F.77} gives flatness of \(S\) over \(R\).

Each nonempty fibre has the displayed \(n\) polynomial variables, \(c\) equations and dimension \(n-c\), so is a global complete intersection over its field. It is consequently locally a complete intersection: the whole five-condition proof \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-lci]{F.57} applies at every fibre prime, or its global presentation itself is the required neighbourhood. Empty fibres have no point to check. These are the finite-presentation, flatness and fibre conditions for syntomicness. If \(S=0\), finite presentation is \(R/(1)\), flatness is immediate, and all fibres are empty, giving the same conclusion. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-relative-global-complete-intersection-conormal}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.77: relative global complete intersection conormal}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.77-relative-global-complete-intersection-conormal}

Reading source: \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/unofficial-stacks-project-ai-drafts/blob/565b10e987aba5969b21145a0833f42d69f96790/algebra.tex\#L38204-L38278}{AI Integrated Stacks, pinned Algebra, lines 38204--38278}.

Let \(R\) be any ring and \[S=R[X_1,\ldots,X_n]/(f_1,\ldots,f_c)\] a relative global complete intersection: every nonempty residue-field fibre has dimension \(n-c\). For a prime \(\mathfrak q\subset S\), let \(\mathfrak Q\subset R[X]\) be its inverse image. Then:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \(f_1,\ldots,f_c\) is regular in \(R[X]_{\mathfrak Q}\).
\item
  Every \(R[X]_{\mathfrak Q}/(f_1,\ldots,f_i)\), including \(i=0\), is flat over \(R\).
\item
  The global \(S\)-module \((f)/(f)^2\) is free on the classes of the \(f_i\).
\end{enumerate}

In particular \(S\) is flat over \(R\). These assertions include bases that are not Noetherian.

\textbf{Proof.} First take a Noetherian base. Fix \(\mathfrak Q\) and put \(\mathfrak p=\mathfrak Q\cap R\), \(k=\kappa(\mathfrak p)\). Its closed polynomial fibre is a localization of \(k[X]\) at the corresponding prime. In the nonempty quotient fibre, every minimal equation prime has height at most \(c\), by the whole AG-CA-11, Theorem 3.1. The polynomial height formula AG-CA-09, Theorem 4.3, makes each component dimension at least \(n-c\). Their maximum is the assumed dimension \(n-c\), so all have this dimension. The point formula of AG-CA-09, Theorem 6.1, gives dimension \(n-c\) at the chosen quotient point. Thus \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-codimension]{F.20} gives local dimension drop exactly \(c\) for this polynomial presentation. The full criterion \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-lci]{F.57} makes its actual \(c\)-element equation list regular in the ambient fibre local ring.

The map \(R_{\mathfrak p}\to R[X]_{\mathfrak Q}\) is flat and local: a polynomial ring is free, and localization preserves exact tensor injection tests. Both rings are Noetherian. Apply the complete successive-quotient lifting proof \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-grothendieck-regular-sequence]{F.53}. It proves both regularity in the polynomial local ring and flatness of every local successive quotient over \(R_{\mathfrak p}\), hence over \(R\).

For the general base we construct a finite Noetherian coefficient model. We first justify the field-dimension fact needed in this descent. For a nonzero finite-type \(k\)-algebra \(C\), the entire \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/d02d0a3669f42579db037cd44de1d113fdd770a1/docs/courses/AG-CA/src/krull-dimension-and-noether-normalization.md}{AG-CA-09, Corollary 3.2} gives an inclusion \(k[T_1,\ldots,T_d]\subset C\) with \(C\) finite over it, even when \(C\) is not reduced or a domain. For any field extension \(E/k\), a basis makes its tensor functor free and faithfully flat. Thus the inclusion remains an inclusion of \(E[T]\) into \(C\otimes_kE\), and finiteness remains true. The entire \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/d02d0a3669f42579db037cd44de1d113fdd770a1/docs/courses/AG-CA/src/integral-extensions-lying-over-going-up-and-going-down.md}{AG-CA-05, Theorem 5.1} and polynomial dimension AG-CA-09, Theorem 4.2, give \[\dim C=d=\dim(C\otimes_kE).\] The zero algebra stays zero. This proves precisely the field-extension dimension preservation used below.

Let \(R_a\subset R\) be generated over the image of \(\mathbf Z\) by all coefficients of the equations, and put \(S_a=R_a[X]/(f)\). These are finite-type Noetherian models, and \(S=R\otimes_{R_a}S_a\). At any actual \(\mathfrak q\subset S\), let \(\mathfrak p,\mathfrak q_a,\mathfrak p_a\) be its contractions. The residue fields give an inclusion \(\kappa(\mathfrak p_a)\subset\kappa(\mathfrak p)\), and the two corresponding fibres are related by that scalar tensor. The latter is nonempty, since the prime \(\mathfrak q\) lies over \(\mathfrak p\). Its dimension is \(n-c\). The proved field-dimension fact therefore gives that dimension for the model fibre as well.

The whole arbitrary-base neighbourhood proof \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-dimension-fibres-bounded-open-upstairs]{F.39} supplies \(g_{\mathfrak q}\in S_a\setminus\mathfrak q_a\) whose localized model fibres all have dimension at most \(n-c\). Indeed its bound is the dimension at the chosen fibre point, which is at most its total dimension \(n-c\); a bound at every point bounds the total dimension by testing the finitely many component generic points. The resulting opens pull back to a cover of \(\operatorname{Spec}S\). Choose finitely many, defined by \(g_1,\ldots,g_m\), by affine quasi-compactness: their images generate the unit ideal, because otherwise a maximal ideal would give an uncovered point.

Choose polynomial representatives \(G_j\in R_a[X]\). A unit-ideal relation in \(S\) has a finite polynomial witness \[1=\sum_j H_jG_j+\sum_i V_if_i\quad\text{in }R[X].\] Adjoin to \(R_a\) all coefficients of the finitely many \(H_j,V_i\), obtaining a finite-type integer subalgebra \(R_0\subset R\). Set \(S_0=R_0[X]/(f)\). The same identity now holds in \(R_0[X]\), so the images of the \(G_j\) cover \(\operatorname{Spec}S_0\).

For every base prime of \(R_0\), its residue field extends that of its contraction in \(R_a\). Each chart fibre is therefore the corresponding old chart fibre after a field extension. It retains dimension at most \(n-c\) by the proved dimension fact. A finite open cover has total dimension the maximum of the chart dimensions here: in a finite-type field algebra each component's generic point belongs to some chart, and that nonempty principal component open retains its dimension. Thus every nonempty fibre of \(S_0/R_0\) has dimension at most \(n-c\). The height bound for an ideal generated by \(c\) elements in a polynomial ring gives the reverse inequality at any minimal equation prime. Every nonempty model fibre consequently has dimension exactly \(n-c\). This constructs the required Noetherian relative global complete-intersection model, with the identical equation list and \[S=R\otimes_{R_0}S_0.\] If \(S=0\), a finite identity \(1=\sum_iV_if_i\) already gives a model with \(S_0=0\). The local claims are then vacuous and both conormal modules are zero; hence we may continue with a chosen actual prime.

Contract \(\mathfrak Q\) to \(\mathfrak Q_0\subset R_0[X]\) and \(\mathfrak p_0\subset R_0\). Put \[A_0=(R_0)_{\mathfrak p_0},\qquad
B_0=(R_0[X])_{\mathfrak Q_0},\qquad
B_i=B_0/(f_1,\ldots,f_i).\] The Noetherian case gives regularity and \(A_0\)-flatness of each \(B_i\), so for every \(i<c\) there is an exact sequence \[0\longrightarrow B_i\xrightarrow{f_{i+1}}B_i
\longrightarrow B_{i+1}\longrightarrow0.\] Tensor it with \(R_{\mathfrak p}\) over \(A_0\). It remains left exact because its quotient \(B_{i+1}\) is \(A_0\)-flat: the full Tor long exact sequence \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/main/docs/courses/AG-RG/AG-RG-S01.md}{AG-RG-S01, Lemma 1.A} gives zero for the possible first kernel. This is the exact reason regularity survives this possibly nonflat scalar change. Base change also makes each \(B_i\otimes_{A_0}R_{\mathfrak p}\) flat over \(R_{\mathfrak p}\), by the tensor associativity formula for injection tests.

The further prime localization of \(B_0\otimes_{A_0}R_{\mathfrak p}\) at the prime induced by \(\mathfrak Q\) is exactly \(R[X]_{\mathfrak Q}\). To check this, the tensor first inverts the images of \(R_0[X]\setminus\mathfrak Q_0\), all of which avoid the actual prime. The further localization inverts the remaining polynomials outside \(\mathfrak Q\). Every fraction in the full prime localization is then represented, and the two localization universal properties give inverse maps. Taking the same localizations of the quotient tensors gives exactly \(R[X]_{\mathfrak Q}/(f_1,\ldots,f_i)\). Exact localization preserves each displayed multiplication injection and its quotient. Its last quotient is \(S_{\mathfrak q}\ne0\), so the resulting list is regular. Localization preserves flatness of these target modules, and \(R_{\mathfrak p}\) is flat over \(R\). This proves (1) and (2) over the original arbitrary base.

Finally \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-regular-quasi-regular]{F.74} gives the conormal basis at every prime of \(S\). The global map \(S^c\to(f)/(f)^2\) is surjective by generation. Localization commutes with this ideal quotient; its kernel vanishes at every prime by the local bases. A nonzero module element would have a proper annihilator contained in a maximal ideal and would stay nonzero there, so the kernel is zero. This proves (3). For any injection of \(R\)-modules the tensor kernel with \(S\) likewise vanishes after localization at every \(\mathfrak q\), by (2) for its final quotient. The same module detection proves that kernel zero. Thus \(S\) is flat over \(R\), as asserted. Empty equation lists are included at every step. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-relative-global-complete-intersection-smooth}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.78: relative global complete intersection smooth}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.78-relative-global-complete-intersection-smooth}

Reading source: \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/unofficial-stacks-project-ai-drafts/blob/565b10e987aba5969b21145a0833f42d69f96790/algebra.tex\#L39071-L39113}{AI Integrated Stacks, pinned Algebra, lines 39071--39113}.

For a relative global complete-intersection presentation \(S=R[X_1,\ldots,X_n]/(f_1,\ldots,f_c)\) over any ring \(R\), smoothness at a prime \(\mathfrak q\subset S\) is equivalent to some \(c\times c\) Jacobian minor having image outside \(\mathfrak q\).

\textbf{Proof.} The whole unrestricted conormal proof \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-relative-global-complete-intersection-conormal]{F.77} identifies the conormal module with \(S^c\), on the actual equation classes. In the polynomial differential basis the conormal map is \[J:S^c\longrightarrow S^n,\qquad
e_j\longmapsto\sum_i\frac{\partial f_j}{\partial X_i}\,dX_i.\] Thus its maximal minors are precisely the stated polynomials.

If a selected minor \(\Delta\) has image \(g\notin\mathfrak q\), then \(S_g\) has the inverse-variable presentation \[S_g=R[X_1,\ldots,X_n,Z]/(f_1,\ldots,f_c,\Delta Z-1).\] Use the selected \(c\) variable columns together with \(Z\). Its square Jacobian block has the original selected block at the top, a zero top-right column, and \(\Delta\) at the bottom right. Its determinant is \(\Delta^2\), a unit in this algebra. The entire arbitrary-base standard smooth lifting proof \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/d02d0a3669f42579db037cd44de1d113fdd770a1/docs/courses/AG-CA/src/formally-smooth-unramified-and-etale-ring-maps.md}{AG-CA-17, Theorem 4.1} therefore makes this finitely presented algebra smooth. This proves the sufficient direction with an actual principal neighbourhood.

Conversely suppose some \(S_h\), with \(h\notin\mathfrak q\), is smooth. Its polynomial inverse-variable presentation has a split conormal map by the complete split-sequence proof AG-CA-17, Theorem 3.1. The entire \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-principal-localization-NL]{F.72} calculation identifies its conormal complex with the original localized complex \[S_h^c\xrightarrow{J_h}S_h^n\] plus a contractible rank-one complex, whose differential is multiplication by the unit \(h\). In these explicitly changed bases, restrict a left inverse of the full differential to the original degree-zero summand, and project its values to the original degree-one summand. The composite is a left inverse of \(J_h\). Reduction to \(\kappa(\mathfrak q)\) preserves this identity. Hence the resulting \(n\)-by-\(c\) matrix has rank \(c\), and the full minor calculation \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-matrix-left-inverse]{F.70} supplies a nonzero \(c\)-minor over that field. Its original image is outside \(\mathfrak q\), proving necessity.

For \(c=0\) the empty minor is one and the presentation is a polynomial algebra, smooth by arbitrary variable lifting. Thus this case obeys the same criterion. No Noetherian condition on the base or the target is used. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-section-smooth}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.79: section smooth}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.79-section-smooth}

Reading source: \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/unofficial-stacks-project-ai-drafts/blob/565b10e987aba5969b21145a0833f42d69f96790/algebra.tex\#L39859-L39914}{AI Integrated Stacks, pinned Algebra, lines 39859--39914}.

Let \(R\to S\) be smooth and let \(\sigma:S\to R\) be its section, with \(I=\ker\sigma\). Then \(I/I^2\) is finite projective over \(R\). If it is free of rank \(d\), the \(I\)-adic completion of \(S\) is isomorphic as an \(R\)-algebra to \(R[[T_1,\ldots,T_d]]\).

\textbf{Proof.} Define \[D:S\longrightarrow I/I^2,\qquad
D(s)=[s-\sigma(s)].\] Give the target its \(S\)-module action through \(\sigma\). Expanding a product and discarding the product of two elements of \(I\) proves the derivation identity. It is an \(R\)-derivation. The universal differential map therefore induces \(\Omega_{S/R}\otimes_{S,\sigma}R\to I/I^2\). Its inverse sends \([i]\) to \(di\otimes1\). This is well-defined since \(d(ij)\) vanishes after tensoring for \(i,j\in I\); on every \(ds\) its composite is \(d(s-\sigma(s))=ds\), and on every ideal class its other composite is the identity. Thus the two maps are inverse.

The entire \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/d02d0a3669f42579db037cd44de1d113fdd770a1/docs/courses/AG-CA/src/formally-smooth-unramified-and-etale-ring-maps.md}{AG-CA-17, Theorem 3.1} gives finite projectivity of the differential module of this finitely presented formally smooth algebra. Tensor of its finite free direct-summand description with \(R\) retains that description, proving the first assertion. The section ideal is finite as well: if \(x_1,\ldots,x_m\) are finite algebra generators, the polynomial difference identity makes the \(x_j-\sigma(x_j)\) generate its kernel.

Choose \(t_1,\ldots,t_d\in I\) representing a free conormal basis, and put \(P=R[[T_1,\ldots,T_d]]\), \(J=(T_1,\ldots,T_d)\). Continuous evaluation defines \[b:P\longrightarrow\widehat S=\varprojlim_n S/I^n,\qquad T_i\longmapsto t_i.\] This map is surjective. To see it, every element of \(I\) is an \(R\)-linear combination of the \(t_i\) modulo \(I^2\). Multiplying these expressions shows that the degree-\(n\) monomials in the \(t_i\) generate \(I^n/I^{n+1}\) over \(R\) for every \(n\). Start with the constant residue of a chosen element of \(\widehat S\), which is in \(S/I=R\). At step \(n\), the error in its coordinate modulo \(I^{n+1}\) lies in \(I^n/I^{n+1}\), so subtract a homogeneous degree-\(n\) polynomial in the \(t_i\) with coefficients in \(R\). The resulting sum of homogeneous corrections is a formal series in \(P\), with image the chosen compatible sequence. This proves surjectivity without a Noetherian completion theorem.

The square-zero section decomposition \(S/I^2=R\oplus I/I^2\) defines an \(R\)-map \(u_2:S\to P/J^2\), sending the chosen \(t_i\) to \(T_i\). Formal smoothness lifts it successively along \[P/J^{n+1}\longrightarrow P/J^n\quad(n\geq2),\] whose kernel \(J^n/J^{n+1}\) has square zero. Choose each lift to extend the preceding one. Their inverse limit is an \(R\)-map \(u:S\to P\) taking \(I\) into \(J\). Therefore the maps modulo \(J^n\) factor through \(S/I^n\) and give a continuous extension \(a:\widehat S\to P\).

The composite \(v=ab\) is an \(R\)-endomorphism of \(P\) with \[v(T_i)=T_i+\text{terms of degree at least two}.\] We prove that such a substitution is invertible. Having chosen inverse variable series through degree \(n-1\), compute the degree-\(n\) error after substitution. Adding its negative as the next homogeneous term removes it, since the identity linear part changes that degree by exactly the added term; all nonlinear changes have higher degree. This recursively constructs a right inverse. The substitution is injective: any nonzero series has a lowest nonzero homogeneous part, and the identity linear part leaves that part unchanged. If \(w\) is the right inverse, then \(v(wv)=v\); injectivity gives \(wv=1\), proving that it is also a left inverse. The coefficient calculations hold over arbitrary \(R\), including zero divisors.

Replace \(a\) by \(v^{-1}a\). Now \(ab=1\); hence \(b\) is injective, and it was already proved surjective. It is the desired \(R\)-algebra isomorphism. All maps are continuous for the displayed adic topologies. When \(d=0\), the homogeneous correction argument gives \(\widehat S=R\) directly, and the same assertion holds. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-silly}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.80: silly}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.80-silly}

Reading source: \href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/00DS}{Stacks, Tag 00DS}.

Let \(J,I_1,\ldots,I_r\) be ideals of any commutative ring. Suppose \(J\not\subset I_i\) for every \(i\), and at most two of the \(I_i\) are not prime. There is an element of \(J\) outside all the \(I_i\).

\textbf{Proof.} Remove repetitions and every listed ideal contained in another listed ideal. Avoiding the retained larger ideals also avoids the removed smaller ones. The remaining ideals are pairwise incomparable, and still at most two are not prime. We prove the assertion for this remaining list by induction on its length.

For the empty list choose \(0\in J\); there are no avoidance conditions. For one ideal the hypothesis supplies an element outside it. For two ideals choose \(a\in J\setminus I_1\) and \(b\in J\setminus I_2\). If either avoids both, it suffices. Otherwise \(a\in I_2\), \(b\in I_1\). Their sum belongs to neither: membership in \(I_1\) would force \(a=(a+b)-b\in I_1\), and membership in \(I_2\) would similarly force \(b\in I_2\).

For a list of length at least three, place a prime ideal last, calling it \(\mathfrak p=I_r\). Induction gives \(a\in J\) outside all earlier ideals. If \(a\notin\mathfrak p\), it already suffices. Otherwise choose \(b_0\in J\setminus\mathfrak p\) and, for each \(i<r\), choose \(b_i\in I_i\setminus\mathfrak p\); incomparability supplies the latter choices. The product \(b=b_0b_1\cdots b_{r-1}\) belongs to \(J\) and every earlier \(I_i\). It lies outside \(\mathfrak p\), because iterating the defining implication for a prime ideal shows that a product of elements outside it stays outside. Then \(a+b\in J\) still avoids every earlier ideal by subtraction of \(b\), and avoids \(\mathfrak p\) by subtraction of \(a\). This completes the induction without a Noetherian hypothesis. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-size-extension-pth-roots}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.81: size extension pth roots}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.81-size-extension-pth-roots}

Reading source: \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/unofficial-stacks-project-ai-drafts/blob/565b10e987aba5969b21145a0833f42d69f96790/algebra.tex\#L45787-L45812}{AI Integrated Stacks, pinned Algebra, lines 45787--45812}.

Let \(k\) have characteristic \(p>0\). If \(da_1,\ldots,da_n\) are linearly independent in \(\Omega_{k/\mathbf F_p}\), then \[[k(a_1^{1/p},\ldots,a_n^{1/p}):k]=p^n.\]

\textbf{Proof.} Roots can be adjoined successively by quotienting by an irreducible factor of \(X^p-a_i\). Such a factor exists by descent on degree, and its quotient is a field by the Euclidean algorithm. A \(p\)th root is unique in any field containing it: equal \(p\)th powers give \((x-y)^p=0\), hence \(x=y\). Thus these compatible adjunctions give the asserted root field.

We also prove the degree at a nontrivial step. If \(\beta^p=a\in H\) and \(\beta\notin H\), its minimal polynomial divides \(X^p-a=(X-\beta)^p\) in a field containing \(\beta\). A monic proper nonconstant factor has degree \(r\) with \(1\leq r<p\) and coefficient \(-r\beta\) at degree \(r-1\). If it were over \(H\), the nonzero scalar \(r\) would put \(\beta\) in \(H\), a contradiction. Thus the minimal polynomial has degree \(p\), and monic division gives the basis \(1,\beta,\ldots,\beta^{p-1}\).

Induct on the number of roots already adjoined. The zero-root extension is \(k\), of degree one. Suppose the first \(i-1\) roots have degree \(p^{i-1}\) and the standard monomials in them form a \(k\)-basis. If \(a_i\) were a \(p\)th power in that field, a root could be written in that basis. Raising it to the \(p\)th power would give \[a_i=\sum_{0\leq e_j<p}\lambda_e^p\prod_{j<i}a_j^{e_j},
\qquad \lambda_e\in k.\] Every \(p\)th power in \(k\) has zero differential, directly from the derivation product rule. Differentiating this finite equality therefore gives \[
da_i=\sum_e\ \sum_{\substack{j<i\\e_j>0}}
e_j\lambda_e^p\,a_j^{e_j-1}
\left(\prod_{\substack{\ell<i\\\ell\ne j}}a_\ell^{e_\ell}\right)da_j.
\] This is a linear dependence on the earlier differentials, contrary to the hypothesis. For \(i=1\) the right side is empty, giving the same contradiction. Hence the next root is not in the preceding field; the degree-\(p\) calculation applies. Its power basis multiplied by the old monomial basis gives the new monomial basis, proving both independence and generation. Degrees multiply along these finite vector-space towers, so the final degree is \(p^n\). This also covers \(n=0\), and uses no converse criterion for zero absolute differentials. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-smooth-over-field}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.82: smooth over field}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.82-smooth-over-field}

Reading source: \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/unofficial-stacks-project-ai-drafts/blob/565b10e987aba5969b21145a0833f42d69f96790/algebra.tex\#L38622-L38676}{AI Integrated Stacks, pinned Algebra, lines 38622--38676}.

Every smooth finite-type algebra over any field is locally a complete intersection.

\textbf{Proof.} Let \(S/k\) be smooth and choose a prime \(\mathfrak q\) of \(S\). The full principal-chart proof \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/d02d0a3669f42579db037cd44de1d113fdd770a1/docs/courses/AG-CA/src/formally-smooth-unramified-and-etale-ring-maps.md}{AG-CA-17, Theorem 5.1} supplies a standard smooth neighbourhood \(D=S_h\) containing it. Write its polynomial presentation as \[D=k[Y_1,\ldots,Y_N]/(F_1,\ldots,F_r),\] with an invertible \(r\)-column Jacobian minor. Let \(\mathfrak Q\) be the polynomial prime over the chosen point and put \(V=k[Y]_{\mathfrak Q}\), \(\mathfrak m=\mathfrak QV\).

The classes of the \(F_i\) in \(\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2\) are independent. Indeed the differential of a product of two elements of \(\mathfrak m\) is zero after tensoring with its residue field. A relation among these classes would consequently give the same residue-field relation among the vectors \(dF_i\); derivatives of its lifted coefficients multiply \(F_i\) and vanish in that residue field. The chosen nonzero Jacobian minor makes these vectors independent, proving the assertion. This does not assume that the entire cotangent-to-differential map is injective.

The entire polynomial-local regularity proof \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/d02d0a3669f42579db037cd44de1d113fdd770a1/docs/courses/AG-CA/src/regular-local-rings.md}{AG-CA-14, Proposition 3.3} makes \(V\) regular. Extend the independent classes to a basis of its finite-dimensional cotangent space and lift the added classes to \(\mathfrak m\). Nakayama makes this list a minimal generating list for \(\mathfrak m\). The whole \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/d02d0a3669f42579db037cd44de1d113fdd770a1/docs/courses/AG-CA/src/regular-sequences-depth-and-cohen-macaulay-modules.md}{AG-CA-12, Theorem 6.1} proves that every such list is regular in this order. Its initial list \(F_1,\ldots,F_r\) is therefore regular and generates the defining ideal in \(V\).

Condition (5) of the entire criterion \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-lci]{F.57} now gives a principal global complete-intersection neighbourhood of this point in \(D\). Its denominator is some \(a/h^e\) with \(a\in S\), so the same neighbourhood in \(\operatorname{Spec}S\) is \(D(ha)\), with the identical iterated localization as coordinate algebra. Every point thus has a global complete-intersection principal neighbourhood. This is precisely local complete-intersectionness over \(k\). The argument treats arbitrary primes and fields, including imperfect fields. For \(S=0\) its empty spectrum already has the required empty cover. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-smooth-syntomic}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.83: smooth syntomic}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.83-smooth-syntomic}

Reading source: \href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/00TA}{Stacks, Tag 00TA}.

A smooth map \(R\to S\) admits a cover of \(\operatorname{Spec}S\) by principal opens \(D(g)\) for which \(S_g\) is standard smooth over \(R\). When \(R\) is Noetherian, the map is also syntomic.

\textbf{Proof.} The case \(S=0\) has an empty cover. The zero algebra has the finite presentation \(R/(1)\), is flat as a zero module, and has no nonempty fibres, so it also satisfies the asserted syntomic condition. Hence consider a nonzero \(S\).

Fix a finite presentation \(P=R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\twoheadrightarrow S\) with kernel \(I=(f_1,\ldots,f_m)\), and put \(M=I/I^2\). The split conormal theorem \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/d02d0a3669f42579db037cd44de1d113fdd770a1/docs/courses/AG-CA/src/formally-smooth-unramified-and-etale-ring-maps.md}{AG-CA-17, Theorem 3.1} puts \(M\) inside \(S^n\) as a direct summand. Its complement is finite, because projections of the coordinate vectors generate it. The splitting therefore presents \(M\) finitely; it also proves flatness by restricting tensor injections for the free module. \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/main/docs/courses/AG-RG/AG-RG-S01.md}{S01, Lemma 1.2} makes \(M\) free over each local ring.

For a subset \(E\) of the equation indices, let \(U_E\) be the points where the classes indexed by \(E\) are a basis of \(M\). These loci are open and cover the spectrum. Here are the denominator details. At a prime \(\mathfrak q\), select a basis of the residue vector space from the spanning equation classes, with \(r\) selected members. Their map \(\varphi:S^r\to M\) is surjective over \(S_{\mathfrak q}\) by Nakayama. In a local free basis its matrix is square and invertible modulo the maximal ideal, hence invertible by the determinant and adjugate identities. The finite cokernel vanishes at \(\mathfrak q\); multiplying denominators which kill its generators gives \(a\notin\mathfrak q\) with \(\varphi_a\) surjective. Since \(M_a\) is projective, its kernel is a finite summand of \(S_a^r\). It vanishes at \(\mathfrak q\) too. Multiplying numerators of denominators which kill its generators gives \(b\notin\mathfrak q\) with \(\varphi_{ab}\) an isomorphism. Thus \(D(ab)\) lies in this basis locus. The same reasoning applies at every point of any fixed \(U_E\), proving openness. Selecting a basis from a spanning vector-space list proves covering. For rank zero the selected list is empty and empty denominator products are \(1\).

Choose principal opens inside these loci. On one such open \(D(g)\), adjoining a variable representing \(g^{-1}\) gives a finite polynomial presentation whose conormal module, by \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-principal-localization-NL]{F.72}, is \(M_g\oplus S_g\). It is free. \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-huber]{F.55} then supplies a polynomial presentation of \(S_g\) whose kernel is generated by a list which is itself a conormal basis. Denote this algebra temporarily by \(T\), and write its presentation as \[
R[y_1,\ldots,y_N]\twoheadrightarrow T,
\qquad K=(a_1,\ldots,a_c),\qquad K/K^2=T^c.
\]

The conormal differential has a left inverse. In these bases let its matrix be \(A:T^c\to T^N\), and let \(B:T^N\to T^c\) satisfy \(BA=1\). At a residue field this forces \(c\le N\). The determinant expansion \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-matrix-left-inverse]{F.70(2)} shows that its \(c\)-row minors \(\Delta_E\) generate \(1\). Each selected square map is invertible precisely on \(D(\Delta_E)\), by the adjugate formula, so these principal opens cover \(\operatorname{Spec}T\). The empty minor for \(c=0\) is \(1\).

On a selected minor open, order its \(c\) pivot variables first and let \(h\in R[y]\) represent the inverted element \(u=\Delta_E\in T\). Present \(T_u\) by \(a_1,\ldots,a_c,hz-1\). Its Jacobian on \(y_1,\ldots,y_c,z\) has diagonal blocks the selected Jacobian and \(u\), and upper right block zero. Its determinant is \(u\Delta_E\), a unit. This is a standard smooth presentation. Finally a principal open in \(S_g\) is principal in \(S\): write its defining fraction as \(s/g^k\), so its open corresponds to \(D(gs)\). The charts just constructed are consequently the required principal cover of the original spectrum.

If \(R\) is Noetherian, \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-standard-smooth]{F.85} makes each chart a relative global complete intersection. \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-relative-global-complete-intersection]{F.76} makes it syntomic, and \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-local-syntomic]{F.62} glues that condition on the target. This proves the last assertion. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-snake}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.84: snake}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.84-snake}

Reading source: \href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/07JW}{Stacks, Tag 07JW}.

Suppose the following diagram of abelian groups commutes and both rows are exact: \[
\begin{array}{ccccccccc}
&&X&\xrightarrow{a}&Y&\xrightarrow{b}&Z&\longrightarrow&0\\
&&\alpha\downarrow&&\beta\downarrow&&\gamma\downarrow\\
0&\longrightarrow&U&\xrightarrow{i}&V&\xrightarrow{j}&W.
\end{array}
\] There is a canonical exact sequence \[
\ker\alpha\xrightarrow{a}\ker\beta\xrightarrow{b}\ker\gamma
\xrightarrow{\partial}\operatorname{coker}\alpha
\xrightarrow{i}\operatorname{coker}\beta
\xrightarrow{j}\operatorname{coker}\gamma.
\] Its first map is injective if \(a\) is injective, and its last map is surjective if \(j\) is surjective.

\textbf{Proof.} For \(z\in\ker\gamma\), choose \(y\) with \(b(y)=z\). Commutativity gives \(j\beta(y)=0\), so exactness supplies \(u\) with \(i(u)=\beta(y)\). The injection \(i\) makes this \(u\) unique for the chosen \(y\). Define \(\partial z=[u]\) modulo \(\alpha(X)\). Replacing \(y\) by another lift changes it by \(a(x)\); commutativity and injectivity of \(i\) then change \(u\) by \(\alpha(x)\). Thus the class is independent of the lift. Adding lifts proves additivity. The other arrows are the restrictions or quotient maps induced by \(a,b,i,j\), which are well defined by the commutative squares.

For exactness at \(\ker\beta\), take \(y\) there with \(b(y)=0\). Write \(y=a(x)\). Since \(i\alpha(x)=\beta a(x)=0\) and \(i\) is injective, \(x\in\ker\alpha\). Conversely the image of such an \(x\) lies in that kernel and has zero \(b\)-image.

At \(\ker\gamma\), the condition \(\partial z=0\) says that the chosen \(u\) is \(\alpha(x)\) for some \(x\). Subtract \(a(x)\) from the chosen \(y\). This still maps to \(z\), and its \(\beta\)-image is zero. Conversely a lift already in \(\ker\beta\) allows \(u=0\), so has zero connecting class.

At \(\operatorname{coker}\alpha\), a class \([u]\) dies in \(\operatorname{coker}\beta\) exactly when \(i(u)=\beta(y)\) for some \(y\). Then \(z=b(y)\) satisfies \(\gamma(z)=j\beta(y)=ji(u)=0\), and the defining lift gives \(\partial z=[u]\). Every connecting class has zero image for this same reason.

At \(\operatorname{coker}\beta\), a class \([v]\) dies in \(\operatorname{coker}\gamma\) exactly when \(j(v)=\gamma(z)\) for some \(z\). Lift \(z\) to \(y\in Y\). The element \(v-\beta(y)\) has zero \(j\)-image, so is \(i(u)\) by bottom-row exactness. Hence \([v]\) comes from \([u]\). Conversely \(ji=0\) kills every such image. These checks prove exactness at every intermediate term. Restriction of an injective \(a\) remains injective. If \(j\) is onto, lift any representative in \(W\) to \(V\) to obtain surjectivity on the last cokernel. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-standard-smooth}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.85: standard smooth}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.85-standard-smooth}

Reading source: \href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/00T7}{Stacks, Tag 00T7}.

Let \(P=R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\), \(I=(f_1,\ldots,f_c)\), and \(S=P/I\) be standard smooth, with the first \(c\) variables chosen as pivots. Then:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \(R\to S\) is smooth.
\item
  \(\Omega_{S/R}\) has the free basis \(dx_{c+1},\ldots,dx_n\).
\item
  \(I/I^2\) has the free basis \([f_1],\ldots,[f_c]\).
\item
  Every principal localization \(S_g\) is standard smooth over \(R\).
\item
  For every base map \(R\to R'\), the algebra \(R'\otimes_R S\) is standard smooth over \(R'\).
\item
  If \(r\in R\) becomes a unit in \(S\), then \(S\) is standard smooth over \(R_r\).
\item
  This presentation makes \(S\) a relative global complete intersection over \(R\).
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Proof.} Let \(C=(\partial f_i/\partial x_j)_{1\le i,j\le c}\); its determinant is a unit in \(S\). The map \(S^c\to I/I^2\) taking the standard vectors to the equation classes is onto. Its composite with the conormal differential and projection onto the first \(c\) differential coordinates is an invertible matrix (the transpose of \(C\) under column-vector conventions). Thus this surjection is injective as well. The equation classes are a basis, and the conormal differential is split injective.

Write its image in \(S^n\) as the columns of \(\binom{C^{\mathsf t}}{D}\). An arbitrary vector \((v,w)\) differs from a unique conormal vector by \[
(v,w)-\binom{C^{\mathsf t}}{D}(C^{\mathsf t})^{-1}v
=(0,w-D(C^{\mathsf t})^{-1}v).
\] The conormal image meets the last coordinate summand only in zero. Its cokernel is therefore exactly that summand, with the asserted differential basis. Finite presentation and this split conormal sequence give smoothness by the complete criterion \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/d02d0a3669f42579db037cd44de1d113fdd770a1/docs/courses/AG-CA/src/formally-smooth-unramified-and-etale-ring-maps.md}{AG-CA-17, Theorem 3.1 and Section 4}. This proves (1)--(3), including \(c=0\).

To invert \(g\), choose a polynomial \(h\) representing it and use the equations \(f_1,\ldots,f_c,hz-1\). On pivot variables \(x_1,\ldots,x_c,z\), the Jacobian has blocks \[
\begin{pmatrix}C&0\\z(\partial h/\partial x_1,\ldots,\partial h/\partial x_c)&h\end{pmatrix}.
\] Its determinant \(h\det C\) is a unit in \(S_g\). This proves (4), even when the localization is zero. Under a base map, applying the map to every coefficient presents the tensor product; the same operation takes the determinant to its image, which remains invertible. This proves (5). For (6), the original equations over \(R_r\) present \(S_r=S\), since the image of \(r\) is already invertible; their determinant is unchanged.

For (7), it remains to compute every nonempty fibre's dimension. By (5) such a fibre is a nonzero standard smooth algebra \(B=k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/(\bar f_1,\ldots,\bar f_c)\) over its residue field \(k\). It is locally a complete intersection by \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-smooth-over-field]{F.82}. At any prime \(\mathfrak q\) of \(B\), let \(\mathfrak q'\) be its polynomial preimage. The conormal module is free of rank \(c\) by (3); reducing to the residue field determines that rank uniquely. \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-lci]{F.57} identifies it with \(\operatorname{height}(\mathfrak q')-\operatorname{height}(\mathfrak q)\). For a minimal prime \(\mathfrak q\) this gives \(\operatorname{height}(\mathfrak q')=c\). The polynomial height formula \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/d02d0a3669f42579db037cd44de1d113fdd770a1/docs/courses/AG-CA/src/krull-dimension-and-noether-normalization.md}{AG-CA-09, Theorem 4.3} therefore gives dimension \(n-c\) for every component.

The algebra \(B\) is Noetherian by \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/main/docs/courses/AG-RG/AG-RG-S01.md}{S01, Lemma 1.3}, so \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-topology-lemma-Noetherian]{F.136} and \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-topology-lemma-irreducible]{F.137} give a finite component cover. Dimension equals the largest component dimension: a finite chain of irreducible closed subsets lies in a component containing its largest member, and every chain inside a component is also a chain in the whole space. Thus \(\dim B=n-c\). This argument works over imperfect fields and for an empty equation list. Empty fibres require no dimension assertion, completing (7). ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-sum-two-terms}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.86: sum two terms}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.86-sum-two-terms}

Reading source: \href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/00S3}{Stacks, Tag 00S3}.

Let \(A_1\xrightarrow{d_A}A_0\) and \(B_1\xrightarrow{d_B}B_0\) be two-term complexes of modules over a ring. If they are homotopy equivalent, then \[
A_1\oplus B_0\cong B_1\oplus A_0.
\]

\textbf{Proof.} Choose chain maps \(\varphi:A_\bullet\to B_\bullet\) and \(\psi:B_\bullet\to A_\bullet\) and homotopies \(h:A_0\to A_1\), \(h':B_0\to B_1\) with \[
1-\psi_1\varphi_1=hd_A,\qquad 1-\psi_0\varphi_0=d_Ah,
\] \[
1-\varphi_1\psi_1=h'd_B,\qquad 1-\varphi_0\psi_0=d_Bh'.
\] Define \(U:B_1\oplus A_0\to A_1\oplus B_0\) and \(V\) in the reverse direction by \[
U=\begin{pmatrix}\psi_1&h\\-d_B&\varphi_0\end{pmatrix},\qquad
V=\begin{pmatrix}\varphi_1&-h'\\d_A&\psi_0\end{pmatrix}.
\] Multiplying the blocks and using the four homotopy identities and the two chain-map identities gives \[
UV=\begin{pmatrix}1&h\psi_0-\psi_1h'\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
VU=\begin{pmatrix}1&\varphi_1h-h'\varphi_0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.
\] Each off-diagonal matrix squares to zero, so negating that off-diagonal block gives the inverse product. Consequently \(L=(VU)^{-1}V\) is a left inverse of \(U\), and \(T=V(UV)^{-1}\) is a right inverse. The equality \(L=L(UT)=(LU)T=T\) makes them the same inverse. Hence \(U\) is an isomorphism, proving the claim without any finite-generation or freeness hypothesis. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-syntomic}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.87: syntomic}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.87-syntomic}

Reading source: \href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/00SY}{Stacks, Tag 00SY}.

Let \(R\) be Noetherian, and let \(\mathfrak q\in\operatorname{Spec}S\) lie over \(\mathfrak p\in\operatorname{Spec}R\). The following neighbourhood conditions are equivalent:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Some \(g\notin\mathfrak q\) makes \(R\to S_g\) syntomic.
\item
  Some \(g\notin\mathfrak q\) makes \(S_g\) a relative global complete intersection over \(R\).
\item
  Some \(g\notin\mathfrak q\) makes \(S_g\) finitely presented over \(R\), while \(R_{\mathfrak p}\to S_{\mathfrak q}\) is flat and \(S_{\mathfrak q}/\mathfrak pS_{\mathfrak q}\) is a complete-intersection local ring over \(k=\kappa(\mathfrak p)\) in the sense of \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-definition-lci-local-ring]{F.3}.
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Proof.} A syntomic neighbourhood is finitely presented and flat and has locally complete-intersection fibres; \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-lci-at-prime]{F.58} gives (3) from (1). \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-relative-global-complete-intersection]{F.76} gives (1) from (2). We prove the remaining implication with all rings localized explicitly.

Under (3), first replace \(S\) by the indicated finitely presented neighbourhood, retaining the prime. Write \(P=R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\twoheadrightarrow S\) with kernel \(I\) and polynomial preimage \(\mathfrak q'\). In the fibre \(\bar P=k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\), write \(\bar I\) for the image ideal and \(\bar{\mathfrak q}'\) for the induced prime. By \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-lci-at-prime]{F.58} and \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-lci]{F.57}, the ideal \(\bar I_{\bar{\mathfrak q}'}\) has a regular generating list of length \(c\), its minimal number of generators. Choose \(f_1,\ldots,f_c\in I\) whose images give a basis of \(\bar I_{\bar{\mathfrak q}'}/\bar{\mathfrak q}'\bar I_{\bar{\mathfrak q}'}\). This is possible by selecting a basis from the images of a finite generating list of \(I\). Nakayama gives generation in the fibre local ring, and the last assertion of F.57 makes this very list regular there.
