Set \(T=P/(f_1,\ldots,f_c)\) and \(J=\ker(T\to S)\). The polynomial ring is Noetherian by \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/main/docs/courses/AG-RG/AG-RG-S01.md}{S01, Lemma 1.3}, so \(J\) is finite. Localize the short exact sequence at \(\mathfrak q'\) as \(P\)-modules: \[
0\longrightarrow J_{\mathfrak q'}\longrightarrow T_{\mathfrak q'}\longrightarrow S_{\mathfrak q}\longrightarrow0.
\] These are \(R_{\mathfrak p}\)-modules. Flatness of the last module makes tensoring with \(k\) injective on the first arrow, by the tensor-kernel calculation \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/main/docs/courses/AG-RG/AG-RG-S01.md}{S01, Lemma 1.2 and Lemma 1.A}. The last arrow becomes an isomorphism after tensoring, because the chosen fibre equations generate the localized fibre ideal. Hence \[
J_{\mathfrak q'}/\mathfrak pJ_{\mathfrak q'}=0.
\] Over the local polynomial ring \(P_{\mathfrak q'}\), the ideal \(\mathfrak pP_{\mathfrak q'}\) is contained in its maximal ideal. Applying \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-NAK]{F.10} to the finite module \(J_{\mathfrak q'}\) gives zero. Clear annihilating denominators for a finite generating list of \(J\): some \(u\in P\setminus\mathfrak q'\) gives \(J_u=0\), and thus \(T_u=S_u\).

The fibre of \(T\) at the induced prime has the same local quotient by the chosen regular list. F.57 gives its point dimension \(n-c\). Applying \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-localize-relative-complete-intersection]{F.66(3)} to this \(c\)-equation presentation produces a relative global complete-intersection principal neighbourhood of that point. Apply this to \(T_u\), using its presentation with the additional equation \(uz-1\); the fibre point dimension remains \(n-c\), and the variable and equation counts both increase by one. The resulting neighbourhood is therefore a principal localization of \(S_u\) with a relative global complete-intersection presentation. Writing its inverted element as a fraction in \(S_u\) makes the composite neighbourhood \(S_g\) for some \(g\notin\mathfrak q\). This is (2). Empty regular lists use the same argument with \(c=0\). ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-syntomic-presentation-ideal-mod-squares}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.88: syntomic presentation ideal mod squares}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.88-syntomic-presentation-ideal-mod-squares}

Reading source: \href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/07BT}{Stacks, Tag 07BT}.

Let \(R\) be Noetherian, let \(S=R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/I\) with \(I\) finitely generated, and suppose \(S_g\) is syntomic over \(R\). Then \((I/I^2)_g\) is finite projective over \(S_g\).

\textbf{Proof.} Put \(A=S_g\) and \(M=(I/I^2)_g\). If \(A=0\), then \(M=0\) and the assertion follows. Otherwise \(A\) is Noetherian by \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/main/docs/courses/AG-RG/AG-RG-S01.md}{S01, Lemma 1.3} and localization, so the finite module \(M\) is finitely presented.

At every prime of \(A\), \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-syntomic]{F.87} supplies a principal relative global complete-intersection neighbourhood. \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-relative-global-complete-intersection-conormal]{F.77} makes the conormal of its displayed equations finite free. The presentation comparison \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-conormal-module-localize]{F.33} identifies \(M\) there, up to finite free summands, with that conormal. Therefore \(M\) is finite projective there: the comparison realizes it as a summand of a finite free module. Choose finitely many of these neighbourhoods \(D(a_i)\) covering \(\operatorname{Spec}A\). The finite choice follows from the principal-open cover criterion: the ideal of all covering elements is not contained in any prime, hence contains \(1\), which is a finite sum.

Here is the global splitting argument. Choose a finite free surjection \(\pi:A^N\to M\). Its localization on \(D(a_i)\) has a right inverse \(s_i\), because \(M_{a_i}\) is projective. A finite presentation \(A^r\to A^s\to M\to0\) realizes \(\operatorname{Hom}_A(M,A^N)\) as the kernel of a map between finite matrix modules. Localization is exact and commutes with these finite modules, so \[
\operatorname{Hom}_A(M,A^N)_{a_i}
=\operatorname{Hom}_{A_{a_i}}(M_{a_i},A_{a_i}^N).
\] Consequently some global \(t_i:M\to A^N\) represents \(a_i^{k_i}s_i\). The map \(\pi t_i-a_i^{k_i}1_M\) becomes zero after inverting \(a_i\). Multiplying by another power of \(a_i\) kills its values on all members of a finite generating list of \(M\). Replacing \(t_i\) by that multiple gives \[
\pi t_i=a_i^{e_i}1_M.
\] The powers \(a_i^{e_i}\) still generate \(1\): if a proper ideal contained them, a containing prime would contain all the corresponding \(a_i\), contradicting the cover. Choose \(b_i\) with \(\sum_i b_i a_i^{e_i}=1\). Then \(\sum_i b_i t_i\) is a global right inverse of \(\pi\). Thus \(M\) is a direct summand of \(A^N\), which proves finite projectivity. All denominator and zero-module cases are included. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-total-ring-fractions-no-embedded-points}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.89: total ring fractions no embedded points}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.89-total-ring-fractions-no-embedded-points}

Reading source: \href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/02LX}{Stacks, Tag 02LX}.

Suppose a ring \(R\) has finitely many minimal primes \(\mathfrak q_1,\ldots,\mathfrak q_t\), and its zerodivisors are exactly their union. Its total ring of fractions has the canonical decomposition \[
Q(R)\cong\prod_{i=1}^t R_{\mathfrak q_i}.
\]

\textbf{Proof.} If \(t=0\), the assumed zerodivisor set is empty. A nonzero ring would make \(0\) a zerodivisor, since it annihilates \(1\ne0\), so \(R=0\). Both its localization and the empty ring product are zero. Now assume \(t>0\). Let \(D\) be the multiplicative set of nonzerodivisors and put \(A=D^{-1}R\). Every element of \(D\) avoids every \(\mathfrak q_i\), so each map \(R\to R_{\mathfrak q_i}\) extends to \(A\). The prime correspondence for localization identifies the primes of \(A\) with primes of \(R\) disjoint from \(D\). Such a prime is contained in \(\bigcup_i\mathfrak q_i\). By \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-silly]{F.80} it is contained in one \(\mathfrak q_i\), and minimality forces equality. Thus the primes of \(A\) are precisely the extensions \(\mathfrak m_i=D^{-1}\mathfrak q_i\). They are distinct and incomparable, hence all maximal.

We construct the product decomposition, including possible nilpotents. For each \(i\) and \(j\ne i\), choose an element in \(\mathfrak m_j\setminus\mathfrak m_i\), and multiply these choices to obtain \(a_i\). Then \(a_i\) avoids \(\mathfrak m_i\) and belongs to every other prime. For \(t=1\) use the empty product \(a_1=1\). Each product \(a_i a_j\) for \(i\ne j\) belongs to every prime, and hence is nilpotent by \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/d02d0a3669f42579db037cd44de1d113fdd770a1/docs/courses/AG-CA/src/spectra-of-rings.md}{AG-CA-01, Theorem 1.2}. Choose a common positive integer \(N\) with \(a_i^N a_j^N=0\) for every pair. The elements \(a_i^N\) generate the unit ideal, since no prime contains all of them. Write \(1=\sum_i b_i a_i^N\) and set \(e_i=b_i a_i^N\). The \(e_i\) are orthogonal and sum to \(1\); multiplying this sum by \(e_i\) gives \(e_i^2=e_i\). Modulo \(\mathfrak m_i\), only the \(i\)th summand survives, so \(e_i\) is \(1\) there and is zero at every other prime.

The maps \(a\mapsto(e_i a)_i\) and \((u_i)_i\mapsto\sum_i u_i\) are inverse ring maps between \(A\) and \(\prod_i e_iA\). Each factor has only the prime induced by \(\mathfrak m_i\), and is therefore local: a nonunit lies in a maximal ideal, which must be that prime. The projection \(A\to e_iA\) consequently inverts every element outside \(\mathfrak m_i\). Conversely, in \(A_{\mathfrak m_i}\) the idempotent \(e_i\) is a unit and hence equals \(1\), so the complementary factor vanishes. These universal properties give \(e_iA\cong A_{\mathfrak m_i}\cong R_{\mathfrak q_i}\). The isomorphism is the canonical map stated above. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-when-colimit}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.90: when colimit}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.90-when-colimit}

Reading source: \href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/07C3}{Stacks, Tag 07C3}.

For an arbitrary ring map \(R\to\Lambda\), the following are equivalent: \(\Lambda\) is a filtered colimit of smooth \(R\)-algebras; every \(R\)-algebra map from a finitely presented algebra \(A\) to \(\Lambda\) factors through a smooth \(R\)-algebra.

\textbf{Proof.} First suppose such a filtered presentation of \(\Lambda\) is given. Write \(A\) with finitely many polynomial generators and finitely many defining equations. The images of its generators have representatives at a common stage. Each defining equation becomes zero at a later stage, by the equality criterion in a filtered colimit. A common successor of those finitely many stages therefore satisfies every equation. The generator images define the required map to that smooth stage.

For the converse, form the category whose objects are smooth \(R\)-algebras \(B\) with a map \(B\to\Lambda\), and whose arrows commute with those maps. Smooth algebras are finitely presented. This category can be taken small: finite polynomial presentations form a set, and a map from each one to \(\Lambda\) is specified by a finite tuple of elements of \(\Lambda\); use these presentations as representatives. The object \(R\to\Lambda\) makes it nonempty.

Given two objects \(B_1,B_2\), the tensor product \(B_1\otimes_R B_2\) is finitely presented: combine their finite generator lists and equations. Factor its induced map to \(\Lambda\) through a smooth algebra. The two structure maps into that algebra give a common successor in the category. For parallel arrows \(u,v\colon B\rightrightarrows C\), choose finite algebra generators \(b_1,\ldots,b_r\) of \(B\). The quotient \[
C/(u(b_1)-v(b_1),\ldots,u(b_r)-v(b_r))
\] is finitely presented by adding these finitely many equations to a presentation of \(C\). Its map to \(\Lambda\) factors through a smooth algebra by the hypothesis. The resulting arrow from \(C\) equalizes \(u\) and \(v\), because equality on the generators gives equality on every polynomial in them. These two constructions prove filteredness.

Let \(L\) be this category's colimit and \(L\to\Lambda\) its induced map. It is surjective: for any \(\lambda\in\Lambda\), apply the factoring hypothesis to \(R[T]\to\Lambda\) with \(T\mapsto\lambda\); the intermediate object supplies a representative of \(\lambda\) in \(L\). For injectivity, a representative \(b\in B\) with zero image in \(\Lambda\) gives a map \(B/(b)\to\Lambda\). This quotient is finitely presented, so its factorization through a smooth object yields a successor at which \(b=0\). Hence its colimit class is zero. Two representatives can be moved to a common stage and this argument applied to their difference, proving equality detection as well. Thus \(L\to\Lambda\) is an isomorphism of \(R\)-algebras, establishing the filtered presentation without any Noetherian hypothesis. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-algebra-proposition-characterize-separable-field-extensions}

\subsubsection{Proposition F.91: characterize separable field extensions}\label{AG-RG-S05-proposition-f.91-characterize-separable-field-extensions}

Reading source: \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/unofficial-stacks-project-ai-drafts/blob/565b10e987aba5969b21145a0833f42d69f96790/algebra.tex\#L46037-L46069}{AI Integrated Stacks, pinned Algebra, lines 46037--46069}.

For every field extension \(K/k\), the following are equivalent: separability in \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-definition-separable-field-extension]{F.5}; geometric reducedness over \(k\); algebraic formal smoothness over \(k\); \(H_1(L_{K/k})=0\); and injectivity of \[\iota:K\otimes_k\Omega_{k/P}\longrightarrow\Omega_{K/P},\] where \(P\) is the prime field. In characteristic \(p>0\) they are also equivalent to the condition that an absolute \(p\)-basis of \(k\) remains \(p\)-independent over \(K^p\). In characteristic zero all the conditions hold. For finitely generated extensions they agree with the existence of a separating transcendence basis.

\textbf{Proof.} We give the comparisons in an order that does not assume the last finitely generated assertion.

First, every field is formally smooth over its prime field. In characteristic zero, choose a transcendence basis over \(\mathbf Q\); the remaining algebraic extension is separable, because a nonconstant irreducible polynomial has nonzero derivative of smaller degree and hence is relatively prime to it. The two entire lifting constructions in \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-formally-smooth-extensions-easy]{F.49}, together with the composition lifting proof AG-CA-17, Theorem 1.2, give formal smoothness, for arbitrary bases and algebraic extensions.

In characteristic \(p\), take an absolute \(p\)-basis \(B\) of a field \(H\) by the whole \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-more-algebra-lemma-p-basis]{F.119}. Given a prime-field map \(\psi:H\to D/J\), \(J^2=0\), define a lift on \(H^p\) by \[\theta(a^p)=\widetilde{\psi(a)}^{\,p}.\] The root \(a\) is unique in \(H\), and changing its chosen lift by \(j\in J\) does not change this power, since \(j^p=0\). Frobenius of sums and products proves that \(\theta\) is a unital ring map. Choose arbitrary lifts of the \(\psi(b)\) for \(b\in B\). Their \(p\)th powers are \(\theta(b^p)\); the exact presentation \[H=H^p[T_b:b\in B]/(T_b^p-b^p)\] proved in F.119 therefore extends them to a lift on \(H\). This establishes prime-field formal smoothness in both characteristics.

Suppose \(\iota\) is injective. In a square-zero lifting problem for \(K/k\), obtain a \(P\)-lift \(u:K\to D\) by the preceding argument. Write \(v:k\to D\) for the prescribed structural map. The difference \(u|_k-v\) takes values in \(J\) and is a \(P\)-derivation for the common action modulo \(J\), by expanding a product and using \(J^2=0\). The given map \(K\to D/J\) makes \(J\) a \(K\)-vector space. Its derivation corresponds to a linear map from \(K\otimes_k\Omega_{k/P}\) to \(J\); extend it along the injection \(\iota\) to \(\Omega_{K/P}\) by extending a vector-space basis. The resulting derivation \(\delta:K\to J\) gives the corrected lift \(u-\delta\). Indeed \[
(u(x)-\delta(x))(u(y)-\delta(y))
=u(xy)-u(x)\delta(y)-u(y)\delta(x)
=u(xy)-\delta(xy).
\] It preserves one and agrees with \(v\) on \(k\), proving formal smoothness.

Conversely, any \(P\)-derivation \(d:k\to V\), for a \(K\)-vector space \(V\), makes \(K\oplus V\) a \(k\)-algebra by \(a\mapsto(a,d(a))\); its multiplication is \((x,v)(y,w)=(xy,xw+yv)\). Formal smoothness lifts the identity through the square-zero quotient to \(K\). The second component of that lift is a derivation extending \(d\). Thus every linear functional on the domain of \(\iota\) extends to its codomain. If a nonzero vector lay in its kernel, extend that vector to a basis and take a functional equal to one on it; such a functional could not extend. Hence \(\iota\) is injective. The whole \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-characterize-formally-smooth-field-extension]{F.17} proves precisely the equivalence with the displayed first cotangent homology condition, in arbitrary field scope.

In characteristic \(p\), F.119 identifies the differentials of an absolute \(p\)-basis \(B\) of \(k\) with a basis of \(\Omega_{k/P}\). Applied over \(P\) to \(K\), its other equivalence says their images are independent exactly when the standard monomials in \(B\) are independent over \(K^p\). This proves the equivalence with \(\iota\)'s injectivity.

We next compare this condition with reducedness. A finite root algebra \[K\otimes_k k(b^{1/p}:b\in B_0)
=K[T_b:b\in B_0]/(T_b^p-b),\qquad B_0\subset B\ {\rm finite},\] is free on the standard monomials. The corresponding root-field monomials are independent over \(K\) exactly when the monomials in \(B_0\) are independent over \(K^p\): raise a proposed relation to its \(p\)th power, and take roots of its coefficients for the converse. If independent, the algebra maps isomorphically to the root field. If dependent, that map has a nonzero kernel. Every element of the root algebra has \(p\)th power in \(K\); a kernel element therefore has \(p\)th power zero in the algebra itself. It is a nonzero nilpotent. The full algebra \(K\otimes_k k^{1/p}\) is the union of these algebras with injective transitions, since a full \(p\)-basis expansion expresses every root using finitely many basis roots. Reducedness of this union is equivalent to reducedness of every finite stage. Thus geometric reducedness implies the \(p\)-basis condition.

For the converse we must test all field extensions. The independence persists through all root heights. More explicitly, a relation \[\sum_a c_a^{p^r}B^a=0,\qquad 0\leq a_b<p^r,\] can be grouped by \(a=pu+v\), \(0\leq v_b<p\). The coefficient of \(B^v\) is \[\left(\sum_u c_{pu+v}^{p^{r-1}}B^u\right)^p.\] Independence over \(K^p\) makes each coefficient zero. Frobenius is injective in a field; induction on \(r\) then kills every \(c_a\). Iterating the unique finite \(p\)-basis expansions in \(k\) shows that the monomials with exponents below \(p^r\) are a basis of \(k\) over \(k^{p^r}\). Taking roots gives the standard presentation and basis of every finite subset root extension of height \(r\). The preceding relation calculation makes all its base changes to \(K\) fields; their directed union \(K\otimes_k k^{1/p^r}\) is a field too.

Every finite purely inseparable extension \(k'/k\) embeds over \(k\) in some \(k^{1/p^r}\): choose finitely many generators and a common root height. Tensoring its inclusion with the vector space \(K\) is injective. Hence \(K\otimes_k k'\) is a finite-dimensional domain over \(K\), and is a field by the multiplication-inverse argument.

Now take a finitely generated field extension \(E/k\). In characteristic \(p\), the entire \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-make-separably-generated]{F.69} supplies finite purely inseparable \(k'/k\), an extension \(E'/E\) containing \(k'\), and a separating transcendence basis for \(E'/k'\). Put \(H=K\otimes_k k'\), a field as just proved. In characteristic zero use \(k'=k\), \(H=K\) and \(E'=E\): a maximal algebraically independent subset of finite field generators leaves a finite algebraic, necessarily separable, extension.

In either case, for a separating basis \(T\), the ring \[C=H\otimes_{k'}k'(T)=\bigl(k'[T]\setminus\{0\}\bigr)^{-1}H[T]\] is a domain. The algebra \(C\otimes_{k'(T)}E'\) is finite free over \(C\), by a vector-space basis of the finite separable field extension \(E'/k'(T)\). It therefore injects into its localization over \(\operatorname{Frac}(C)\). That generic algebra is reduced: express the finite separable extension by a finite tower of simple generators. At each step a monic minimal polynomial is relatively prime to its derivative, and its Bézout identity remains valid after any field extension. Its irreducible factors are consequently distinct. The two-factor Bézout Chinese remainder formula and its finite induction, proved in \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-product-local]{F.73}, identify its quotient with a product of fields. Repeat on every field factor at the next step of the tower. The final tensor algebra is a finite product of fields, hence reduced. Its subalgebra \(C\otimes E'=H\otimes_{k'}E'=K\otimes_kE'\) is reduced as well.

The inclusion \(E\subset E'\) remains injective after tensoring over \(k\) with \(K\), since field-vector-space inclusions split by extending bases. Thus \(K\otimes_kE\) is reduced. An arbitrary field extension of \(k\) is the directed union of its finitely generated subfields, with injective tensor transitions. A nilpotent and its finite power relation occur at one stage, so the union is reduced. This proves geometric reducedness from the \(p\)-basis condition; it also proves it for all extensions in characteristic zero.

It remains to connect formal smoothness with the definition of separability. For a finitely generated formally smooth field \(L/k\), choose a finite-type domain \(B=k[a_1,\ldots,a_n]\subset L\) with fraction field \(L\), and a polynomial presentation \(Q=k[X_1,\ldots,X_n]\to B\) with prime kernel \(I\). Hilbert's basis theorem AG-CA-03, Theorem 2.1, makes \(I\) finite. The entire localization comparison \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-localize-NL]{F.65}, together with F.17 for \(L/k\), makes \[
(I/I^2)\otimes_B L\longrightarrow L^n
\] injective: exact field-of-fractions localization identifies this map's kernel with the localized first cotangent homology. Choose \(f_1,\ldots,f_c\in I\) whose conormal classes form a basis of this finite-dimensional space. Their differentials are independent, giving a \(c\)-column Jacobian determinant \(\Delta\notin I\).

The local ring \(Q_I\) has maximal ideal \(IQ_I\) and residue field \(L\). Its cotangent space is exactly the conormal space just used. The whole \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-NAK]{F.10} makes the \(f_i\) generate \(IQ_I\). The finite module \(I/(f_1,\ldots,f_c)\) then vanishes there. Kill its finite generator list by a product \(h_0\notin I\) of annihilating denominators. For \(h=h_0\Delta\) and its image \(g\in B\) this gives \[B_g=k[X_1,\ldots,X_n,Z]/(f_1,\ldots,f_c,hZ-1).\] The square Jacobian block using the selected columns and \(Z\) has determinant \(h\Delta\), a unit. The full AG-CA-17, Theorem 4.1, makes this a standard smooth domain. Its fraction field is \(L\), and the entire domain calculation \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-localization-smooth-separable]{F.64} gives a separating transcendence basis. This includes \(c=0\), with empty minor one. Conversely such a basis gives a purely transcendental extension followed by a finite separable one; F.49 and the full formal composition proof make \(L/k\) formally smooth.

If \(K/k\) is separable by F.5, the whole F.49(3) gives formal smoothness, hence the conditions already compared. Conversely, in characteristic \(p\) the \(p\)-basis condition descends to every finitely generated intermediate \(L\): coefficients in \(L^p\) are also in \(K^p\). The differential and lifting comparisons make \(L/k\) formally smooth, and the preceding finite construction makes it separably generated. This is exactly F.5's definition for \(K/k\). In characteristic zero the finite transcendence-basis argument above gives that definition for every intermediate field. Finally F.49 gives formal smoothness there, hence differential injectivity and the homology condition. All comparisons and the finite-generation assertion are now proved. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-more-algebra-definition-G-ring}

\subsubsection{Definition F.92: G ring}\label{AG-RG-S05-definition-f.92-g-ring}

Reading source: \href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/07GH}{Stacks, Tag 07GH}.

The term \emph{G-ring} imposes two requirements on \(R\): it is Noetherian, and at every prime \(\mathfrak p\) its localization-to-completion map is regular. The map in this second requirement is \[
R_{\mathfrak p}\longrightarrow\widehat{R_{\mathfrak p}},
\qquad
\widehat{R_{\mathfrak p}}
=\varprojlim_{n\ge1}R_{\mathfrak p}/(\mathfrak pR_{\mathfrak p})^n.
\] Thus the completion used in the definition is taken at the maximal ideal of the local ring, separately for each prime.

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-more-algebra-definition-excellent}

\subsubsection{Definition F.93: excellent}\label{AG-RG-S05-definition-f.93-excellent}

Reading source: \href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/07QT}{Stacks, Tag 07QT}.

For a Noetherian ring \(R\), \emph{quasi-excellence} means that \(R\) satisfies the G-ring condition of \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-more-algebra-definition-G-ring]{F.92} and the J-2 condition. Here J-2 requires the regular locus \[
\{\mathfrak q\in\operatorname{Spec}B:B_{\mathfrak q}\text{ is regular}\}
\] to be open for each finite-type \(R\)-algebra \(B\); this is the terminology of \href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/07P7}{Stacks, Tag 07P7}.

An \emph{excellent} ring has these properties and is universally catenary. To specify that last condition, a ring is catenary when, between each fixed pair of comparable primes, the lengths of finite strict chains have a common finite bound and the chains into which no further prime can be inserted all have equal length. A Noetherian ring is universally catenary when every finite-type algebra over it has this property. These two definitions are \href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/00NI}{Stacks, Tag 00NI} and \href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/00NL}{Tag 00NL}.

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-more-algebra-definition-local-complete-intersection}

\subsubsection{Definition F.94: local complete intersection}\label{AG-RG-S05-definition-f.94-local-complete-intersection}

Reading source: \href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/07D0}{Stacks, Tag 07D0}.

For a map \(A\to B\) of finite type, choose a surjection \[
P=A[T_1,\ldots,T_n]\twoheadrightarrow B,
\qquad I=\ker(P\to B).
\] The map is a \emph{local complete intersection} when \(I\) is a Koszul-regular ideal, with that ideal condition understood exactly as in \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-more-algebra-definition-regular-ideal]{F.95}. Checking one such presentation suffices: the full arbitrary-ring proof \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-more-algebra-lemma-lci-presentation-independent]{F.94.A} below shows that every other finite polynomial presentation then has a Koszul-regular kernel. Neither this definition nor that comparison assumes \(A\) Noetherian.

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-more-algebra-lemma-lci-presentation-independent}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.94.A: arbitrary-ring presentation independence}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.94.a-arbitrary-ring-presentation-independence}

Reading source: \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/unofficial-stacks-project-ai-drafts/blob/565b10e987aba5969b21145a0833f42d69f96790/more-algebra.tex\#L8869-L8942}{AI Integrated Stacks, pinned More Algebra, lines 8869--8942}; \href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/07CZ}{Stacks, Tag 07CZ}.

Let \(A\) be an arbitrary ring and suppose an algebra \(C\) has finite polynomial presentations \[P=A[T_1,\ldots,T_n]\twoheadrightarrow C=P/I,\qquad
Q=A[X_1,\ldots,X_m]\twoheadrightarrow C=Q/J.\] If \(I\) is a Koszul-regular ideal as defined in \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-more-algebra-definition-regular-ideal]{F.95}, then \(J\) is also Koszul-regular. Moreover \(C\) is finitely presented. This proves the presentation-independence assertion in F.94 without Noetherian hypotheses.

\textbf{Proof.} We first supply the elementary complex calculations used to compare the two presentations.

For a list \(f=(f_1,\ldots,f_c)\) over a ring \(V\), take a free module with basis \(e_1,\ldots,e_c\) and form \[K_j(f;V)=\bigwedge^jV^c,\qquad
d(e_{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge e_{i_j})
=\sum_{a=1}^j(-1)^{a-1}f_{i_a}
e_{i_1}\wedge\cdots\widehat{e_{i_a}}\cdots\wedge e_{i_j}.\] Deleting a pair of indices in the two orders gives opposite signs, so \(d^2=0\). Its degree-zero homology is \(V/(f)\). Appending \(u\) identifies the new degree-\(j\) term with \(K_j(f)\oplus K_{j-1}(f)\), with differential \[d(a,b)=(d_fa+ub,-d_fb);\] the sign identification multiplies the wedge ending in the added basis vector by \((-1)^{j-1}\).

If \(K(f)\) has zero positive homology and \(u\) acts injectively on \(V/(f)\), this cone has zero positive homology too. Indeed a degree-\(j\) cycle satisfies \(d_fb=0\) and \(d_fa=-ub\). For \(j>1\), write \(b=d_fc\) using the old acyclicity. For \(j=1\), the last equation makes \(u[b]=0\) in \(H_0(K(f))\); injectivity likewise gives \(b=d_fc\). Subtract the boundary of \((0,-c)\) to obtain \((a+uc,0)\), an old positive-degree cycle. Its old bounding chain makes this remaining vector a boundary in the cone. Degree zero is the additional quotient by \(u\). This proves the appending assertion, including empty initial lists.

A second calculation will detect conormal ranks. If \(H_1(K(f))=0\), the classes of the \(f_i\) give a basis of \((f)/(f)^2\) over \(V/(f)\). They generate by definition. Given \(\sum_i b_if_i\in(f)^2\), write the right side as \(\sum_{i,j}a_{ij}f_if_j\) and replace \(b_i\) by \(b_i-\sum_j a_{ij}f_j\). Their scalar product is now exactly zero, so the resulting vector is a degree-one cycle. A degree-two Koszul boundary has every coordinate in \((f)\). Vanishing of \(H_1\) therefore puts all the corrected coefficients, and hence every \(b_i\), in \((f)\). This proves independence.

We next prove that the kernels are finite. The principal charts in the Koszul-regularity condition cover \(V(I)\). If their denominators are \(a_\lambda\in P\), then \(I+(a_\lambda)=P\): a proper ideal is contained in a maximal ideal, which would give an uncovered prime containing \(I\). Thus finitely many denominators and an element \(b\in I\) satisfy \[1=b+\sum_{\ell=1}^s c_\ell a_\ell.\] Choose numerators in \(I\) of every finite local generator list for \(I_{a_\ell}\), and let \(I_0\) be generated by those numerators and \(b\). At a prime where some \(a_\ell\) is invertible, \(I_0\) and \(I\) have the same localization. At any other prime, the identity makes \(b\) a unit, so both localize to the unit ideal. Therefore \((I/I_0)\) vanishes at every prime, and is zero. Here is local detection for this possibly infinite module: a nonzero element has a proper annihilator contained in a maximal ideal; if it became zero there, an element outside that ideal would annihilate it, a contradiction. Hence \(I=I_0\) is finite. This makes \(C\) finitely presented, and the entire \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-finite-presentation-independent]{F.44} then makes \(J\) finite. If \(C=0\), both kernels are unit ideals and their required prime tests are empty. We now assume \(C\ne0\) and fix \(\mathfrak q\in\operatorname{Spec}C\).

Choose \(p_j(T)\in P\) representing each image of \(X_j\) and \(q_i(X)\in Q\) representing each image of \(T_i\). In \(W=A[T,X]\) the kernel \(L\) of the common map to \(C\) has two exact descriptions: \[L=(I,u_1,\ldots,u_m)=(J,s_1,\ldots,s_n),\qquad
u_j=X_j-p_j(T),\quad s_i=T_i-q_i(X).\] Quotienting by the added equations eliminates those variables and recovers the specified maps to \(C\), which proves both descriptions. Let \(\mathfrak r\subset W\) be the inverse image of \(\mathfrak q\), and \(\mathfrak p_P,\mathfrak p_Q\) its contractions. Translation is a polynomial-ring isomorphism \(W=Q[s_1,\ldots,s_n]\). Constant and linear coefficients in these variables give an exact decomposition \[L/L^2=(J/J^2)\oplus C^n.\] The constant part is taken modulo \(J^2\), the linear coefficients modulo \(J\), and all terms with at least two \(s\) factors disappear. Sending these data to their constant-plus-linear representatives and reading them back gives inverse maps, so the decomposition is valid over arbitrary rings.

Pick \(a\in P\setminus\mathfrak p_P\) and a Koszul-regular list \(f\) generating \(I_a\). Polynomial extension is free and localization is flat, by the entire tensor/localization proofs AG-RG-S01, Lemmas 1.0--1.1; exact flat tensor preserves each cycle and boundary quotient of this complex. Hence \(f\) remains Koszul-regular over \(W_a\). In the quotient by \(f\), the \(u_j\) are successive polynomial variables after translation. Multiplication by each is injective by comparison of coefficients, and remains so after localization. Applying the cone calculation one entry at a time proves that \((f,u)\) is Koszul-regular over \(W_a\). Its conormal classes consequently form a basis of \(L/L^2\) at \(\mathfrak r\).

The decomposition above now makes \((J/J^2)_{\mathfrak q}\) a finite direct summand of a finite free \(C_{\mathfrak q}\)-module. Such a summand is flat by restricting the free tensor injection test. It is finitely presented: the projection onto its complementary summand sends a finite free basis to finitely many generators of the kernel of the projection onto the original summand. The whole AG-RG-S01, Lemma 1.2, therefore makes it finite free over this local ring.

From a finite generating list of \(J\) choose \(g_1,\ldots,g_d\) whose conormal residue classes form a basis. Relative to a basis of the finite free conormal module, their square coefficient matrix is invertible modulo the maximal ideal, hence has unit determinant and is invertible by the cofactor formula. They thus form a basis over \(C_{\mathfrak q}\). In \(Q_{\mathfrak p_Q}\) this says \(J=(g)+J^2\). The finite module \(J/(g)\) equals \(J\) times itself; \(J\) lies in the maximal ideal. The entire Nakayama proof in AG-RG-S01, Lemma 1.2, gives \(J_{\mathfrak p_Q}=(g)\). Since \(J\) is finite, kill the finitely many quotient generators by denominators outside \(\mathfrak p_Q\). Their product \(v_0\notin\mathfrak p_Q\) gives \(J_{v_0}=(g)\) on an actual principal chart.

In \(W_{\mathfrak r}\) both \((f,u)\) and \((g,s)\) generate \(L_{\mathfrak r}\) and their conormal classes are bases. Their lengths agree by reduction to the residue field. Expressing the second list in the first gives a square matrix \(M\) whose reduction modulo \(\mathfrak r\) is invertible: \(L^2\subset\mathfrak rL\), so these are precisely the two bases of \(L/\mathfrak rL\). The determinant is therefore a unit. The exterior powers of the map on free generator modules give an isomorphism of the Koszul complexes. Indeed that map preserves their degree-one scalar-product functional, so the alternating deletion formula checks commutation with \(d\) on every wedge; the exterior powers of the inverse matrix give the inverse complex map. Permuting \((g,s)\) to \((s,g)\) is the same calculation with a permutation matrix.

All of this can be realized on a principal neighbourhood. Include \(a\) and \(v_0\) in a denominator product. Include representatives outside \(\mathfrak r\) of every denominator in the finite matrix and both finite generator comparisons, and the numerator of its determinant. For each asserted equality in the stalk, also include a denominator outside \(\mathfrak r\) that kills its cross-difference. Their product \(h\notin\mathfrak r\) gives the actual generator equalities over \(W_h\) and an invertible comparison matrix there. This clearing uses annihilating denominators and never cancels a zero divisor. The complex on \((s,g)\) over \(W_h\) is consequently isomorphic to the acyclic-positive complex on \((f,u)\).

Evaluate \(h\) by \(T_i=q_i(X)\), and call the resulting element of \(Q\) \(v\). Its image in \(C\) agrees with that of \(h\), so \(v\notin\mathfrak p_Q\). Elimination and localization give \[W_h/(s)=Q_v,\qquad J_v=(g).\] The second equality holds because \(v_0\) was a factor of \(h\), and hence of \(v\).

Finally \(K(s;W_h)\) is a free resolution of \(Q_v\). Before localization this follows by appending the successive polynomial variables \(s_i\) with the cone calculation above; exact localization preserves it. Form its double complex with the finite free complex \(K(g;W_h)\). The total complex is \(K(s,g;W_h)\), with differential \(d_s+(-1)^i d_g\) at \(s\)-degree \(i\). Augmentation maps it to \(K(g;Q_v)\) and induces an isomorphism on homology. To verify this without a spectral sequence, augment each vertical column by its quotient in degree \(-1\). Every such column is exact because the fixed \(g\) term is free. For a total cycle, its component of greatest \(g\) degree is a vertical cycle: no component of greater \(g\) degree contributes to its differential. Lift it in that exact column and subtract the resulting total boundary. This removes that component and changes only smaller \(g\) degrees. The procedure terminates, because there are only finitely many \(g\) degrees. It proves the augmented total complex acyclic, equivalently both surjectivity and injectivity of the augmentation on homology by lifting cycles and boundaries.

The source total complex has zero positive homology. Thus \(K(g;Q_v)\) does too, and its entries generate \(J_v\). We have produced the required Koszul-regular principal neighbourhood of the specified prime of \(C\). Repeating for every prime proves the claim for \(J\). The equations, complexes and finite eliminations include all empty variable and generator lists. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-more-algebra-definition-regular-ideal}

\subsubsection{Definition F.95: regular ideal}\label{AG-RG-S05-definition-f.95-regular-ideal}

Reading sources: \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/unofficial-stacks-project-ai-drafts/blob/565b10e987aba5969b21145a0833f42d69f96790/more-algebra.tex\#L8710-L8731}{AI Integrated Stacks, pinned More Algebra, lines 8710--8731}; \href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/061P}{Stacks, Tag 061P}.

Let \(R\) be any ring. For a finite list \(f=(f_1,\ldots,f_c)\) put \(J=(f_1,\ldots,f_c)\).

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  The list is \textbf{regular} when \(J\ne R\) and multiplication by \(f_i\) is injective on \(R/(f_1,\ldots,f_{i-1})\) for every \(i\).
\item
  It is \textbf{Koszul-regular} when every positive-degree homology module of the exterior-power Koszul complex \(K(f;R)\) is zero.
\item
  It is \textbf{\(H_1\)-regular} when \(H_1(K(f;R))=0\).
\item
  It is \textbf{quasi-regular} when the graded \(R/J\)-algebra map \[
  (R/J)[Z_1,\ldots,Z_c]\longrightarrow
  \operatorname{gr}_J(R)=\bigoplus_{d\ge0}J^d/J^{d+1},
  \quad
  Z_1^{e_1}\cdots Z_c^{e_c}\longmapsto
  f_1^{e_1}\cdots f_c^{e_c}\bmod J^{1+\sum_i e_i}
  \] is an isomorphism.
\end{enumerate}

For an ideal \(I\subset R\), each of these four conditions defines the corresponding \textbf{regular}, \textbf{Koszul-regular}, \textbf{\(H_1\)-regular}, or \textbf{quasi-regular ideal} by the following local requirement: for every prime \(\mathfrak p\) containing \(I\), there are \(g\in R\setminus\mathfrak p\) and a finite list in \(R_g\) generating \(I_g\) and satisfying that list condition. The denominator and list may depend on the prime. This specifies all four ideal definitions over arbitrary rings.

\textbf{Verification of the formulas.} The complex in (2) and (3) has term \(\bigwedge^dR^c\) and differential \[
d(e_{i_1}\wedge\cdots\wedge e_{i_d})
=\sum_{a=1}^d(-1)^{a-1}f_{i_a}
e_{i_1}\wedge\cdots\widehat{e_{i_a}}\cdots\wedge e_{i_d}.
\] Each pair of deleted indices contributes twice to \(d^2\), with opposite signs, so this is a complex in every characteristic. Its degree-zero homology is \(R/J\), since the degree-one differential has image \(J\). The whole complex calculations in \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-more-algebra-lemma-lci-presentation-independent]{F.94.A} also apply to the empty list.

The map in (4) is well defined on coefficients modulo \(J\): changing a coefficient by an element of \(J\) changes a degree-\(d\) value by an element of \(J^{d+1}\). Multiplication of representatives respects the displayed graded products, so it is a graded algebra map. It is surjective in every degree because \(J^d\) is generated by the degree-\(d\) products of the \(f_i\). If it is an isomorphism, degree one gives precisely \[
(R/J)^c\overset{\sim}{\longrightarrow}J/J^2,
\qquad (a_i)\longmapsto\sum_i a_if_i\bmod J^2.
\] Thus quasi-regularity includes the conormal basis used later.

For the empty list \(J=0\), the complex consists only of \(R\) in degree zero and the graded map is the identity of \(R\) in degree zero. It supplies all four local tests for the zero ideal at its primes. For \(I=R\), no prime contains it and the ideal conditions are vacuous. These conventions handle both the zero ring and empty charts without a Noetherian hypothesis. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-more-algebra-lemma-G-ring-goes-up-quasi-finite}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.96: G ring goes up quasi finite}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.96-g-ring-goes-up-quasi-finite}

Reading source: \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/unofficial-stacks-project-ai-drafts/blob/565b10e987aba5969b21145a0833f42d69f96790/more-algebra.tex\#L12823-L12870}{AI Integrated Stacks, pinned More Algebra, lines 12823--12870}.

Let \(R\to R'\) be finite type between Noetherian rings. Let \(\mathfrak q'\subset\mathfrak p'\) be primes of \(R'\) contracting to \(\mathfrak q\subset\mathfrak p\) in \(R\), and assume the map is quasi-finite at \(\mathfrak p'\).

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  If \(\widehat{R_{\mathfrak p}}\otimes_R\kappa(\mathfrak q)\) is geometrically regular over \(\kappa(\mathfrak q)\), then \(\widehat{R'_{\mathfrak p'}}\otimes_{R'}\kappa(\mathfrak q')\) is geometrically regular over \(\kappa(\mathfrak q')\).
\item
  If all formal fibres of \(R_{\mathfrak p}\) are geometrically regular, the same holds for \(R'_{\mathfrak p'}\).
\item
  A quasi-finite algebra over a Noetherian G-ring is a G-ring.
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Proof.} Put \(A=\widehat{R_{\mathfrak p}}\), \(B=\widehat{R'_{\mathfrak p'}}\), \(k=\kappa(\mathfrak q)\) and \(E=\kappa(\mathfrak q')\). The injection \(R/\mathfrak q\to R'/\mathfrak q'\) gives a field map \(k\to E\): nonzero elements remain nonzero, so invert in the target fraction field. The specified completion-factor construction \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-completion-at-quasi-finite-prime]{F.26} supplies an isomorphism of \(R'\)-algebras \[T=A\otimes_RR'\cong B\times D,\] whose projection onto \(B\) is the natural completed-local map. No finiteness assertion about the unneeded second factor is required.

The ring \(A\) is Noetherian by \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/d02d0a3669f42579db037cd44de1d113fdd770a1/docs/courses/AG-CA/src/completion.md}{AG-CA-19, Theorem 3.3}, and \(T\) is a finite-type \(A\)-algebra, hence Noetherian by the earlier Hilbert basis theorem. Tensor associativity identifies \[T\otimes_{R'}E\cong(A\otimes_Rk)\otimes_kE.\] The left ring is Noetherian: writing \(U=R'\setminus\mathfrak q'\), it equals \(U^{-1}(T/\mathfrak q'T)\). The hypothesis makes \(A\otimes_Rk\) geometrically regular, so the field-extension assertion \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-geometrically-regular-over-subfields]{F.52}, with this target Noetherianness checked, makes the displayed ring geometrically regular over \(E\).

The product splitting gives \[T\otimes_{R'}E\cong(B\otimes_{R'}E)\times(D\otimes_{R'}E).\] For any finite purely inseparable extension \(E'/E\), the tensor of this product with \(E'\) is regular. Its first factor is localization at the idempotent \((1,0)\): inverting that idempotent kills exactly the second factor. Its prime local rings are therefore prime local rings of the regular product, so it is regular. That first factor is also Noetherian, as a quotient of the Noetherian product. The same quotient argument makes \(B\otimes_{R'}E\) Noetherian. The finite purely inseparable criterion \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-geometrically-regular]{F.50} proves (1), including zero factors, which have no prime local rings.

For (2), every prime of \(R'_{\mathfrak p'}\) comes from a \(\mathfrak q'\subset\mathfrak p'\) and contracts to a \(\mathfrak q\subset\mathfrak p\). Its fibre is exactly the ring in (1), by localization and tensor associativity. Thus (1) proves all the required geometric-regularity assertions. The completion map is flat by AG-CA-19, Theorem 3.2, so these fibres make it regular. For (3), quasi-finiteness applies at every \(\mathfrak p'\), and the G-ring hypothesis gives the assumption of (2) at its contracted \(\mathfrak p\). Definition \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-more-algebra-definition-G-ring]{F.92} then gives a regular completion map at every prime of \(R'\), exactly the G-ring condition. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-more-algebra-lemma-another-helper-G-ring}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.97: another helper G ring}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.97-another-helper-g-ring}

Reading source: \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/unofficial-stacks-project-ai-drafts/blob/565b10e987aba5969b21145a0833f42d69f96790/more-algebra.tex\#L13103-L13159}{AI Integrated Stacks, pinned More Algebra, lines 13103--13159}.

Let \(R\) be a complete Noetherian local domain with fraction field \(K\). For every prime \(\mathfrak q\subset R[X]\), the ring \(\widehat{R[X]_{\mathfrak q}}\otimes_RK\) is regular. Moreover, if \(\mathfrak q\) lies over the maximal ideal of \(R\) and \(0\ne\mathfrak r\subset\mathfrak q\) contracts to zero in \(R\), then \[\widehat{R[X]_{\mathfrak q}}\otimes_{R[X]}\kappa(\mathfrak r)\] is geometrically regular over \(\kappa(\mathfrak r)\). The second assertion includes the maximal-ideal, positive-characteristic case of the reading source.

\textbf{Proof.} Choose the finite regular complete local subring \(A_0\subset R\) from \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-complete-local-Noetherian-domain-finite-over-regular]{F.25}, and put \(F=\operatorname{Frac}(A_0)\). A finite-dimensional domain over \(F\) is a field: multiplication by a nonzero element is an injective endomorphism of a finite-dimensional vector space, hence surjective and has an inverse element. Therefore \(R\otimes_{A_0}F\) is a field containing \(R\) and equals \(K\). In particular \(K/F\) is finite.

Contract \(\mathfrak q\) to \(\mathfrak q_0\subset A_0[X]\). Applying \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-completion-finite-extension]{F.27} to the finite map \(A_0[X]\to R[X]\) gives \[\widehat{A_0[X]_{\mathfrak q_0}}\otimes_{A_0[X]}R[X]
\cong\prod_i\widehat{R[X]_{\mathfrak q_i}},\] where the finitely many \(\mathfrak q_i\) are all primes above \(\mathfrak q_0\), including \(\mathfrak q\). Tensoring over \(R\) with \(K\) identifies the left side with \[\bigl(\widehat{A_0[X]_{\mathfrak q_0}}\otimes_{A_0}F\bigr)\otimes_FK.\] The ring in parentheses is geometrically regular by the first assertion of \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-more-algebra-lemma-helper-G-ring]{F.110}. Its tensor with \(K\) is Noetherian, since \(K/F\) is finite, and is regular by \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-geometrically-regular-over-subfields]{F.52}. On the right it is the product of the rings \(\widehat{R[X]_{\mathfrak q_i}}\otimes_RK\). Each factor is localization of that product at its factor idempotent, so its local rings are regular and it is Noetherian. This proves the first assertion for every prime, without a formal-smoothness criterion for regularity.

For the second assertion set \(E=\kappa(\mathfrak r)\). The prime \(\mathfrak r\) remains nonzero in \(K[X]\): choose a nonzero polynomial in it, and localization is injective because \(R[X]\) is a domain. Its extension is a proper prime, by the localization correspondence, and hence is generated by an irreducible polynomial of positive degree in the Euclidean ring \(K[X]\). Thus \(E=K[X]/\mathfrak rK[X]\) is finite over \(K\). The equality with the residue field follows because this quotient is already a field containing the image of \(R[X]/\mathfrak r\) and all its fractions.

Fix a finite purely inseparable extension \(L/E\). It is finite over \(K\). Choose finitely many algebraic field generators of \(L/K\) and multiply each by a nonzero element of \(R\) so that its monic equation has coefficients in \(R\): for a degree-\(d\) equation, the coefficient of degree \(j\) is multiplied by the \((d-j)\)th power of that scalar. The resulting integral generators define a finite domain \(B\subset L\), \(R\subset B\), with fraction field \(L\). The ring \(B\) is complete local, as follows directly from \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-completion-finite-extension]{F.27} applied to the complete ring \(R\) at its maximal ideal. Its left side is \(B\), so \[B\cong\prod_j\widehat{B_{\mathfrak n_j}}.\] Integral maximal-ideal correspondence makes the \(\mathfrak n_j\) exactly its maximal ideals. Each factor is nonzero, since its residue-field quotient is nonzero. A domain has only the idempotents zero and one: \(e(1-e)=0\) proves this. Hence there is exactly one factor. The resulting unique maximal ideal makes \(B=B_{\mathfrak n}\), and the natural isomorphism identifies it with its maximal-adic completion. Finiteness over Noetherian \(R\) also makes \(B\) Noetherian.

Let \(a\in L\) be the image of \(X\) through \(R[X]\to E\to L\), and let \(\mathfrak r'=\ker(B[X]\to L)\) for the map evaluating \(X\) at \(a\). The quotient image is a domain containing \(B\), so its fraction field contains \(\operatorname{Frac}(B)=L\) and equals \(L\). Thus \(\kappa(\mathfrak r')=L\), and \(\mathfrak r'\) contracts to \(\mathfrak r\) in \(R[X]\). Its extension to \(L[X]\) is exactly \((X-a)\).

Put \(H=\widehat{R[X]_{\mathfrak q}}\). The finite map \(R[X]\to B[X]\) and F.27 identify the tested extension with \[\begin{aligned}
\bigl(H\otimes_{R[X]}E\bigr)\otimes_EL
&=H\otimes_{R[X]}L\\
&\cong\prod_i\bigl(\widehat{B[X]_{\mathfrak q_i}}\otimes_{B[X]}L\bigr),
\end{aligned}\] where \(\mathfrak q_i\) run over the primes above \(\mathfrak q\). In each factor tensor first with \(L=\operatorname{Frac}(B)\) over \(B\) and then impose the evaluation relation in \(L[X]\). Its ring is precisely \[\bigl(\widehat{B[X]_{\mathfrak q_i}}\otimes_BL\bigr)/(X-a).\] The parent ring is Noetherian regular by the already proved first assertion, applied to the complete local domain \(B\) and the prime \(\mathfrak q_i\); no maximality assumption on this prime is needed. Polynomial differentiation \(\partial/\partial X\) kills \(B\). The three successive extensions through prime localization, completion and localization by \(B\setminus\{0\}\) are furnished by \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-more-algebra-lemma-derivation-extends]{F.104}. Its fraction formula shows that it kills \(L\) as well, and it sends \(X-a\) to one. The full hypersurface argument \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-more-algebra-lemma-quotient-regular]{F.122} therefore makes this quotient regular. A zero quotient is included. A finite product of regular Noetherian rings is regular: each prime contains all but one factor idempotent and its local ring is the corresponding factor local ring. The tested fibre is consequently regular for every \(L/E\). It is Noetherian as a localized quotient of \(H\) before the finite field extension. Criterion \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-geometrically-regular]{F.50} proves the claimed geometric regularity. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-more-algebra-lemma-cartier-equality}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.98: cartier equality}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.98-cartier-equality}

Reading source: \href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/07E1}{Stacks, Tag 07E1}.

For a finitely generated field extension \(K/k\), the spaces of differentials and first conormal homology are finite-dimensional, and \[
\dim_K\Omega_{K/k}-\dim_K H_1(L_{K/k})
=\operatorname{trdeg}_k K.
\]

\textbf{Proof.} Put \(d=\operatorname{trdeg}_k K\). Apply the explicit monic-tower construction in \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-colimit-syntomic]{F.23} to a finite field-generating list for \(K/k\). It gives a domain \(C\subset K\) containing that list and having fraction field \(K\). In that construction there are \(d\) transcendence variables, \(r\) algebraic tower variables and one inverse variable. Consequently its polynomial presentation has \[
N=d+r+1\quad\text{variables},\qquad c=r+1\quad\text{equations}.
\] The first equation is \(hZ-1\) for the chosen nonzero denominator polynomial \(h\). The remaining equations, after imposing this first equation, are the successive monic minimal polynomials in the tower. Multiplication by \(hZ-1\) is injective: the lowest nonzero coefficient of a polynomial in its product with \(hZ-1\) is the negative of that coefficient. Each subsequent monic equation is injective on its polynomial ring by its highest-coefficient calculation. Thus this ordered list is regular, exactly as in the construction of F.23.

Write \(C=k[X_1,\ldots,X_N]/I\). \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-regular-quasi-regular]{F.74} identifies \(I/I^2\) with \(C^c\) on the equation classes. Polynomial differentials identify the other term with \(C^N\) on \(dX_i\). Presentation comparison \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-NL-homotopy]{F.11} and localization \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-localize-NL]{F.65}, applied at all nonzero elements of the domain \(C\), therefore identify the first conormal homology and the differential module of \(K/k\) with the kernel and cokernel of a linear map \[
D:K^c\longrightarrow K^N.
\] Localization is exact by \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/main/docs/courses/AG-RG/AG-RG-S01.md}{S01, Lemma 1.1}, so it preserves the kernel and cokernel used in this comparison.

If \(\rho\) is the rank of \(D\), choosing bases for its image and extending them to bases gives \[
\dim_K\ker D=c-\rho,\qquad
\dim_K\operatorname{coker}D=N-\rho.
\] Their difference is \(N-c=d\), and both numbers are finite. This proves the asserted equality without a separability hypothesis. Equivalently the parameter count is \(\dim C=d=\operatorname{trdeg}_k K\), as proved for finite-type domains in \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/d02d0a3669f42579db037cd44de1d113fdd770a1/docs/courses/AG-CA/src/krull-dimension-and-noether-normalization.md}{AG-CA-09, Theorem 4.2}. Empty transcendence or tower lists obey the same count, including \(K=k\). ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-more-algebra-lemma-check-G-ring-easy}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.99: check G ring easy}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.99-check-g-ring-easy}

Reading source: \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/unofficial-stacks-project-ai-drafts/blob/565b10e987aba5969b21145a0833f42d69f96790/more-algebra.tex\#L12803-L12821}{AI Integrated Stacks, pinned More Algebra, lines 12803--12821}.

A Noetherian ring \(R\) is a G-ring exactly when, for every pair of primes \(\mathfrak q\subset\mathfrak p\), the algebra \[
\widehat{(R/\mathfrak q)_{\mathfrak p}}\otimes_{R/\mathfrak q}\kappa(\mathfrak q)
\] is geometrically regular over \(\kappa(\mathfrak q)\). The completion is at the maximal ideal of the displayed local quotient.

\textbf{Proof.} Fix \(\mathfrak p\) and put \(A=R_{\mathfrak p}\), \(\mathfrak m=\mathfrak pA\). Primes of \(A\) correspond exactly to primes \(\mathfrak q\subset\mathfrak p\) of \(R\), by extension and contraction in localization. Their residue fields are the same \(\kappa(\mathfrak q)=\operatorname{Frac}(R/\mathfrak q)\): tensoring with that field already inverts every denominator outside \(\mathfrak p\).

Since \(A\) is Noetherian, both \(\mathfrak qA\) and \(A/\mathfrak qA\) are finite \(A\)-modules. The whole completion exactness and tensor theorem \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/d02d0a3669f42579db037cd44de1d113fdd770a1/docs/courses/AG-CA/src/completion.md}{AG-CA-19, Theorem 3.1} applied to \[0\longrightarrow\mathfrak qA\longrightarrow A\longrightarrow A/\mathfrak qA\longrightarrow0\] gives the natural ring identification \[
\widehat A/\mathfrak q\widehat A
\ \cong\ \widehat{A/\mathfrak qA}
=\widehat{(R/\mathfrak q)_{\mathfrak p}}.
\] The completion topology on the quotient is the correct maximal-ideal topology: its degree-\(r\) quotient is \(A/(\mathfrak m^r+\mathfrak qA)\). The kernel image is \(\mathfrak q\widehat A\), since the tensor map from the finite ideal sends its generators and coefficients to their products in \(\widehat A\).

Because \(\mathfrak q\) annihilates \(\kappa(\mathfrak q)\), the defining balanced tensor relations now give \[
\widehat A\otimes_A\kappa(\mathfrak q)
\cong \widehat A\otimes_R\kappa(\mathfrak q)
\cong(\widehat A/\mathfrak q\widehat A)\otimes_{R/\mathfrak q}\kappa(\mathfrak q).
\] Explicitly the last map sends \(\widehat a\otimes\lambda\) to \((\widehat a\bmod\mathfrak q\widehat A)\otimes\lambda\). Its inverse chooses a representative; changing the representative adds products by elements of \(\mathfrak q\), whose tensors vanish. The first identity holds because the inverted denominators act invertibly in both factors. These maps preserve the specified residue-field algebra structures.

The entire AG-CA-19, Theorem 3.2, makes \(A\to\widehat A\) flat. Thus it is regular precisely when all its residue-field fibres are geometrically regular, by the regular-map definition. The identities above identify those fibres with exactly the algebras in the assertion. By \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-more-algebra-definition-G-ring]{F.92}, being a G-ring means that this regularity holds at every \(\mathfrak p\). Applying the equivalence at each prime proves both directions. If \(R=0\), there are no primes and the two conditions are vacuous. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-completion-flat-local-map}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.99A: completion of a flat local map}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.99a-completion-of-a-flat-local-map}

Reading sources: \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/d02d0a3669f42579db037cd44de1d113fdd770a1/docs/courses/AG-CA/src/completion.md}{AG-CA-19, Proposition 2.2 and Theorems 3.2--3.3}; \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/d02d0a3669f42579db037cd44de1d113fdd770a1/docs/courses/AG-CA/src/faithful-flatness-and-the-local-criterion-for-flatness.md}{AG-CA-08, Theorems 4.2 and 2.1}.

If \((A,\mathfrak m)\to(B,\mathfrak n)\) is a flat local map of Noetherian local rings, its induced map on maximal-ideal completions \(\widehat A\to\widehat B\) is faithfully flat. The residue fields may differ.

\textbf{Proof.} Since \(\mathfrak m^r\) maps into \(\mathfrak n^r\), the finite-quotient maps \(A/\mathfrak m^r\to B/\mathfrak n^r\) commute with their transitions. Their inverse limit defines the asserted map.

The entire completion proofs AG-CA-19, Proposition 2.2 and Theorem 3.3, make the completions Noetherian and complete, with \[\widehat A/\mathfrak m\widehat A=A/\mathfrak m=\kappa,
\qquad \widehat B/\mathfrak n\widehat B=B/\mathfrak n.\] These are local rings with the indicated extended maximal ideals. Explicitly, an element whose residue is nonzero has an inverse modulo the extended ideal. Its product with a chosen inverse is \(1-j\); the series \(\sum_{r\geq0}j^r\) converges in the complete ring and inverts this product. Thus every element outside the extended maximal ideal is a unit. The completion map sends \(\mathfrak m\widehat A\) into \(\mathfrak n\widehat B\), so it is local.

Choose a free \(A\)-resolution \(F_\bullet\to\kappa\) by the whole construction \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/main/docs/courses/AG-RG/AG-RG-S01.md}{AG-RG-S01, Lemma 1.A}. The full AG-CA-19, Theorem 3.2, proves \(A\to\widehat A\) flat, so \(F_\bullet\otimes_A\widehat A\) is an exact free \(\widehat A\)-resolution of \(\kappa\otimes_A\widehat A=\kappa\). The same theorem makes \(\widehat B\) flat over \(B\), and the given flatness of \(B/A\) then makes it flat over \(A\) by tensor associativity. Consequently tensoring the original resolution with \(\widehat B\) is exact in positive degrees, and \[
\operatorname{Tor}^{\widehat A}_1(\kappa,\widehat B)
=H_1\bigl((F_\bullet\otimes_A\widehat A)
\otimes_{\widehat A}\widehat B\bigr)
=H_1(F_\bullet\otimes_A\widehat B)=0.
\]

Apply the complete local criterion AG-CA-08, Theorem 4.2, to the actual local map of Noetherian rings \(\widehat A\to\widehat B\) and the module \(\widehat B\). This module is finite over the stipulated target \(\widehat B\), which is the required finiteness condition; no finiteness over \(\widehat A\) is being assumed. The vanishing just proved gives flatness.

Its closed fibre is nonzero: \(\mathfrak m\widehat B\subset\mathfrak n\widehat B\), so \(\widehat B/\mathfrak m\widehat B\) surjects onto the nonzero field \(B/\mathfrak n\). The entire local faithful-flatness proof AG-CA-08, Theorem 2.1, therefore makes the map faithfully flat. This proves the full assertion without identifying the two residue fields. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-more-algebra-lemma-check-G-ring-maximal-ideals}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.100: check G ring maximal ideals}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.100-check-g-ring-maximal-ideals}

Reading source: \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/unofficial-stacks-project-ai-drafts/blob/565b10e987aba5969b21145a0833f42d69f96790/more-algebra.tex\#L13001-L13037}{AI Integrated Stacks, pinned More Algebra, lines 13001--13037}.

A Noetherian ring \(R\) is a G-ring if and only if \(R_{\mathfrak m}\) has geometrically regular formal fibres for every maximal ideal \(\mathfrak m\).

\textbf{Proof.} If \(R\) is a G-ring, definition \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-more-algebra-definition-G-ring]{F.92} gives the stated property at every maximal ideal. Conversely assume those properties, and fix any prime \(\mathfrak p\subset R\). Choose a maximal ideal \(\mathfrak m\supset\mathfrak p\). Put \(C=\widehat{R_{\mathfrak m}}\). The local completion map \(R_{\mathfrak m}\to C\) is faithfully flat by \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/d02d0a3669f42579db037cd44de1d113fdd770a1/docs/courses/AG-CA/src/completion.md}{AG-CA-19, Theorem 3.2}. Hence its fibre at \(\mathfrak pR_{\mathfrak m}\) is nonzero. Choose a prime of that fibre and take its preimage \(\mathfrak p'\subset C\); the residue-field map is injective, so its contraction is exactly \(\mathfrak pR_{\mathfrak m}\). This is the prime lifting supplied by faithful flatness.

Set \(B=C_{\mathfrak p'}\) and \(\widehat B=\widehat{C_{\mathfrak p'}}\). The map \(R_{\mathfrak p}\to B\) is local and flat: it is induced by the localized completion map, and its closed prime contraction is \(\mathfrak pR_{\mathfrak p}\). A local map sends every power of the source maximal ideal into the corresponding power of the target maximal ideal. Taking inverse limits therefore constructs the map \(\widehat{R_{\mathfrak p}}\to\widehat B\). Naturality of reduction makes both squares in the actual diagram commute: \[\begin{array}{ccccc}
C&\longrightarrow&B&\longrightarrow&\widehat B\\
\uparrow&&\uparrow&&\uparrow\\
R_{\mathfrak m}&\longrightarrow&R_{\mathfrak p}&\longrightarrow&\widehat{R_{\mathfrak p}}.
\end{array}\]

All rings here are Noetherian. By assumption and completion flatness, the first vertical map \(R_{\mathfrak m}\to C\) is regular. The map \(C\to B\) is regular: localization is flat; at a prime of \(C\) its fibre is its residue field if the multiplicative set avoids that prime, and the zero ring otherwise. Every extension of that residue field leaves a field, hence a regular ring. Also \(C\) is complete Noetherian local, so \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-more-algebra-proposition-Noetherian-complete-G-ring]{F.132} makes it a G-ring and gives regularity of \(B\to\widehat B\). Applying \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-more-algebra-lemma-regular-composition]{F.124} twice proves \(R_{\mathfrak m}\to\widehat B\) regular.

This composite factors through \(R_{\mathfrak p}\). It makes \(\widehat B\) flat over \(R_{\mathfrak p}\): tensoring any injection of \(R_{\mathfrak p}\)-modules with \(\widehat B\) is the same as tensoring the underlying \(R_{\mathfrak m}\)-modules, by the localization universal property. Its fibres at primes of \(R_{\mathfrak p}\) are the corresponding fibres over \(R_{\mathfrak m}\), since their residue fields are identical. Thus \(R_{\mathfrak p}\to\widehat B\) is regular as well.

The proved flat local map \(R_{\mathfrak p}\to B\) satisfies precisely the hypotheses of \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-completion-flat-local-map]{F.99A}, which makes the induced map \(\widehat{R_{\mathfrak p}}\to\widehat B\) faithfully flat. The factorization in the right square and \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-more-algebra-lemma-regular-permanence]{F.125} therefore descend regularity of \(R_{\mathfrak p}\to\widehat B\) to regularity of \(R_{\mathfrak p}\to\widehat{R_{\mathfrak p}}\). As \(\mathfrak p\) was arbitrary, F.92 says \(R\) is a G-ring. For the zero ring both sets of tests are empty, so the equivalence still holds. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-more-algebra-lemma-conormal-sequence-H1-regular-ideal}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.101: conormal sequence H1 regular ideal}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.101-conormal-sequence-h1-regular-ideal}

Reading source: \href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/07CX}{Stacks, Tag 07CX}.

For ideals \(I\subset J\) of an arbitrary ring \(A\), suppose the ideal \(J/I\) of \(A/I\) is \(H_1\)-regular. Then \[
I\cap J^2=IJ.
\]

\textbf{Proof.} The inclusion \(IJ\subset I\cap J^2\) follows from \(I\subset J\). We prove the other inclusion at each prime of \(A\). Exact localization commutes with the intersection, the product and the quotient in this assertion; the fraction proof and the detection of a zero module are \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/main/docs/courses/AG-RG/AG-RG-S01.md}{S01, Lemma 1.1}. These facts will turn the local equalities into the global one.

At a prime outside \(V(J)\), the ideal \(J\) becomes the unit ideal, and both sides become \(I\). At a prime containing \(J\), localize \(A\) there. The defining neighbourhood in \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-more-algebra-definition-regular-ideal]{F.95} supplies a finite list \(g_1,\ldots,g_s\in J\) whose images generate \(J/I\) and have zero first Koszul homology over \(A/I\). Indeed we can lift the list from its quotient neighbourhood and localize further at the prime; exact localization preserves cycles, boundaries and their homology. In this local ring \(J=I+(g_1,\ldots,g_s)\).

Take \(x\in I\cap J^2\). Expanding a finite expression for \(x\) as a sum of products of members of \(J\) gives \[
x=u+\sum_{i=1}^s g_i b_i,
\qquad u\in IJ,\quad b_i\in J.
\] Terms having a factor in \(I\) were absorbed in \(u\); all other terms have two factors from the displayed list. Reducing modulo \(I\) makes \((\bar b_i)\) a degree-one Koszul cycle because its scalar product with \((\bar g_i)\) is zero. The zero first homology says this cycle is a boundary. With the convention \[
\partial(e_i\wedge e_j)=\bar g_i e_j-\bar g_j e_i,
\] it is a finite sum of these displayed vectors with coefficients in \(A/I\).

Lift those coefficients to \(A\) and subtract the corresponding vectors \(g_i e_j-g_j e_i\) from \((b_i)\). Their scalar products with \((g_i)\) are exactly zero in \(A\), so this subtraction leaves \(\sum_i g_i b_i\) unchanged. Its new coefficients reduce to zero modulo \(I\), hence belong to \(I\). The sum is therefore in \(IJ\), as is \(u\), proving \(x\in IJ\). An empty list gives the same calculation with sum zero. No finite generation of \(I\) and no Noetherian condition were used. Applying local detection to \((I\cap J^2)/IJ\) completes the proof. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-more-algebra-lemma-cotangent-complex-symmetric-algebra}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.102: cotangent complex symmetric algebra}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.102-cotangent-complex-symmetric-algebra}

Reading source: \href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/07EV}{Stacks, Tag 07EV}.

Let \(A\) be any ring and let \[
0\longrightarrow K\longrightarrow A^m\xrightarrow{q}M\longrightarrow0
\] be exact, where \(M\) is finite projective. Set \(C=\operatorname{Sym}_A(M)\) and let \(\alpha:A[y_1,\ldots,y_m]\twoheadrightarrow C\) be the presentation induced by \(q\), with kernel \(J\). The natural map \[
K\otimes_A C\longrightarrow J/J^2,
\qquad (k_1,\ldots,k_m)\otimes c
\longmapsto c\sum_i k_i y_i\bmod J^2
\] is an isomorphism. With this identification the conormal complex and its cokernel are \[
\operatorname{NL}(\alpha)=[K\otimes_A C\longrightarrow C^m],
\qquad \Omega_{C/A}=M\otimes_A C,
\] where the differential is obtained from \(K\hookrightarrow A^m\) by tensoring with \(C\).

\textbf{Proof.} Choose a section \(s:M\to A^m\) using projectivity. The map \((k,m)\mapsto k+s(m)\) identifies \(K\oplus M\) with \(A^m\): its inverse sends \(a\) to \((a-sq(a),q(a))\). We compute the presentation using this decomposition, keeping track of its specified natural map.

For a module \(V\), the symmetric algebra is the tensor algebra modulo the relations that interchange two adjacent factors. A linear map \(V\to D\) into a commutative \(A\)-algebra extends on a pure tensor by multiplying its images; the interchange relations vanish, and these products determine the extension uniquely. This proves the symmetric-algebra universal property from the tensor construction \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/main/docs/courses/AG-RG/AG-RG-S01.md}{S01, Lemma 1.0}. It also gives its grading by tensor degree, with degree zero \(A\) and degree one \(V\).

That property and the algebra tensor universal property give inverse maps \[
\operatorname{Sym}_A(K\oplus M)
\ \cong\ \operatorname{Sym}_A(K)\otimes_A C.
\] In one direction send \(k\) to \(k\otimes1\) and \(m\) to \(1\otimes m\). In the other direction use the inclusions of \(K\) and \(M\) into \(K\oplus M\) on the two tensor factors. Both composites fix the algebra generators, hence are identities. Likewise the symmetric algebra of \(A^m\) is the polynomial ring on its coordinate basis. Under these identifications \(\alpha\) is the augmentation on the \(K\) factor and the identity on \(C\).

Grade the tensor product by \(K\) degree. The direct-sum tensor formula of S01, Lemma 1.0 gives \[
J=\bigoplus_{d\ge1}\operatorname{Sym}_A^d(K)\otimes_A C,
\qquad
J^2=\bigoplus_{d\ge2}\operatorname{Sym}_A^d(K)\otimes_A C.
\] For the second equality, a product of positive degrees has degree at least two. Conversely each degree-\(d\) term is generated by products \(k_1\cdots k_d\otimes c\); when \(d\ge2\) separate its first factor from the rest to express it as a product of two elements of \(J\). Quotienting thus leaves precisely \(K\otimes_A C\). Its generator \(k\otimes c\) corresponds in the original coordinates to \(c\sum_i k_i y_i\), proving exactly the natural isomorphism in the statement, independently of the auxiliary section.

Relative differentiation sends this linear polynomial to \(\sum_i k_i\,dy_i\). The polynomial differentials are free on these \(m\) symbols, so the displayed complex has exactly the claimed differential. Tensoring the split sequence with \(C\) remains split exact, and its cokernel is \(M\otimes_A C\). This proves the assertion about \(\Omega_{C/A}\) as well, including zero modules and the empty coordinate basis.

The projectivity hypothesis prevents additional conormal relations. For example let \(A=k[\varepsilon]/(\varepsilon^2)\), let \(M=k^2\) via \(\varepsilon M=0\), and let \(q:A^2\to M\) be reduction. Then \(K=\varepsilon A^2\), \(C=A[y_1,y_2]/(\varepsilon y_1,\varepsilon y_2)\), and \(J=(\varepsilon y_1,\varepsilon y_2)\) has square zero. The source \(K\otimes_A C\) is \(k[y_1,y_2]^2\), whereas the vector \((y_2,-y_1)\) maps to \(\varepsilon y_1y_2-\varepsilon y_2y_1=0\) in \(J/J^2\) and is nonzero in that source. Thus the same conormal identity need not hold after dropping the hypothesis. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-more-algebra-lemma-degree-p-extension-regular}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.103: degree p extension regular}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.103-degree-p-extension-regular}

Reading source: \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/unofficial-stacks-project-ai-drafts/blob/565b10e987aba5969b21145a0833f42d69f96790/more-algebra.tex\#L12453-L12467}{AI Integrated Stacks, pinned More Algebra, lines 12453--12467}.

Let \(R\) be a Noetherian regular ring and let \(D:R\to R\) be a derivation such that \(D(f)\) is a unit. For every integer-coefficient polynomial \(P(Z)\), the ring \(R[Z]/(P(Z)-f)\) is regular. In particular this holds for \(P(Z)=Z^n\), \(n\ge1\), including degree-\(p\) adjunctions in characteristic \(p\).

\textbf{Proof.} The whole polynomial-regularity argument \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/d02d0a3669f42579db037cd44de1d113fdd770a1/docs/courses/AG-CA/src/regular-local-rings.md}{AG-CA-14, Proposition 3.3} makes \(V=R[Z]\) regular; Hilbert's basis theorem also makes it Noetherian. Extend the derivation by the explicit formula \[D_V\!\left(\sum_i a_iZ^i\right)=\sum_i D(a_i)Z^i.\] Coefficient convolution and the product rule in \(R\) prove the product rule for \(D_V\), and additivity is coefficientwise. The identity \(D(1)=2D(1)\) gives \(D(1)=0\); additivity and additive inverses then give \(D(n)=0\) for every integer scalar \(n\). Hence \(D_V(P)=0\) and \[D_V(P-f)=-D(f).\] This is a unit already in \(V\), and remains a unit in its quotient. The entire hypersurface result \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-more-algebra-lemma-quotient-regular]{F.122}, with its localized-derivation and parameter-quotient proofs, applies to \(V\) and \(P-f\). It makes the quotient regular, for every specified \(P\). Constant polynomials, units and the zero quotient obey the same calculation. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-more-algebra-lemma-derivation-extends}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.104: derivation extends}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.104-derivation-extends}

Reading source: \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/unofficial-stacks-project-ai-drafts/blob/565b10e987aba5969b21145a0833f42d69f96790/more-algebra.tex\#L12363-L12405}{AI Integrated Stacks, pinned More Algebra, lines 12363--12405}.

Let \(D:R\to R\) be a derivation of an arbitrary ring.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  It extends uniquely to every localization \(U^{-1}R\).
\item
  For every ideal \(I\), it has a canonical continuous extension to \(\widehat R=\varprojlim_n R/I^n\), with its inverse-limit topology. This extension is unique among continuous extensions.
\item
  If \(R\subset R'\) is finite type, \(g\in R\) is a nonzerodivisor in \(R'\), and the inclusions identify \(R_g=R'_g\), then some \(g^ND\) extends to a derivation \(R'\to R'\).
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Proof.} For (1), the map \(r\mapsto r+\epsilon D(r)\) into \((U^{-1}R)[\epsilon]/(\epsilon^2)\) is a ring map. Each \(s\in U\) has image with inverse \[s^{-1}-\epsilon s^{-2}D(s).\] Localization's universal property therefore extends the map. Its constant component is the structural map on the localized ring, so its second component is a derivation, with formula \[D_U(r/s)=D(r)/s-rD(s)/s^2.\] This constructs a well-defined derivation even with zero divisors. Any extension must have that formula by differentiating \(s\,s^{-1}=1\), proving uniqueness.

For (2), a product of \(n+1\) ideal elements differentiates into \(I^n\); finite sums and coefficient derivatives give \[D(I^{n+1})\subset I^n\qquad(n\ge1).\] For a compatible family \(a=(a_n)\in\widehat R\), choose \(r\in R\) representing \(a_{n+1}\) and define its derivative's \(n\)th coordinate as \(D(r)\bmod I^n\). Replacing \(r\) changes its derivative by an element of \(I^n\), so this is well defined. Comparing representatives of \(a_{n+2}\) and \(a_{n+1}\) gives compatibility of these derivative coordinates. They therefore define \(\widehat D(a)\in\widehat R\).

Represent \(a,b\) modulo \(I^{n+1}\) by \(r,s\). Their sum and product are represented by \(r+s,rs\). The identities in \(R\), reduced modulo \(I^n\), give \[
\widehat D(a+b)_n=\widehat D(a)_n+\widehat D(b)_n,\qquad
\widehat D(ab)_n=a_n\widehat D(b)_n+b_n\widehat D(a)_n.
\] Thus the inverse-limit map is a derivation and extends \(D\) through the canonical map \(R\to\widehat R\).

Write \(K_n=\ker(\widehat R\to R/I^n)\). The formula gives \(\widehat D(K_{n+1})\subset K_n\), proving continuity. Canonical images of \(R\) are dense: any coordinate modulo \(I^m\) has a representative in \(R\), matching all lower coordinates too. If another continuous extension were given, their difference would be a continuous additive map vanishing on this dense image. For a prescribed output coordinate choose a sufficiently deep input kernel mapped into its kernel by continuity, and choose an \(R\)-representative matching that input coordinate. The difference has zero prescribed output coordinate. This holds for every coordinate, and the inverse limit is separated, so the difference is zero. The construction uses the inverse-limit kernels, without assuming an infinitely generated ideal's extended powers agree with those kernels.

For (3), \(R'\) embeds in \(R'_g\): if \(x/1=0\), some \(g^j x=0\), and injectivity of multiplication by \(g\) repeatedly gives \(x=0\). Choose algebra generators \(x_1,\ldots,x_s\) of \(R'/R\). The localized equality writes each as a fraction from \(R\) with denominator a power of \(g\); the embedding just proved makes those cleared equalities hold in \(R'\). Thus a common \(n\ge0\) satisfies \(g^nx_i\in R\) for every \(i\).

Inside the common localization apply (1). The product rule, including \(D(g^n)=ng^{n-1}D(g)\) when \(n>0\), gives \[g^{n+1}D_U(x_i)=gD(g^nx_i)-n(g^nx_i)D(g)\in R.\] For \(n=0\) the second term is zero and the same identity holds directly. Multiplying a derivation by the scalar \(g^{n+1}\) still gives a derivation. It sends \(R\) into \(R\) and each generator into \(R\), so repeated product and sum rules send every polynomial expression in the generators into \(R'\). Since this is the restriction of an actual derivation on the localization, all relations in \(R'\) are respected. Restriction therefore gives the required extension with \(N=n+1\). Empty generator lists and the zero ring cause no exception. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-more-algebra-lemma-find-D}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.105: find D}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.105-find-d}

Reading source: \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/unofficial-stacks-project-ai-drafts/blob/565b10e987aba5969b21145a0833f42d69f96790/more-algebra.tex\#L12469-L12520}{AI Integrated Stacks, pinned More Algebra, lines 12469--12520}.

Let \(p\) be prime, let \(B\) be a domain of characteristic \(p\), and let \(f\in B\) be outside \(\operatorname{Frac}(B)^p\). If \(B\) is finite type over a complete Noetherian local ring, there is a derivation \(D:B\to B\) with \(D(f)\ne0\).

\textbf{Proof.} Let \(R_1\to B\) be such a finite-type map. Its kernel is prime. Exact completion on finite modules \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/d02d0a3669f42579db037cd44de1d113fdd770a1/docs/courses/AG-CA/src/completion.md}{AG-CA-19, Theorem 3.1} identifies the quotient \(R_1/\ker(R_1\to B)\) with its maximal-adic completion: tensor the finite quotient with \(\widehat{R_1}=R_1\). Thus its image is again a complete Noetherian local domain, of characteristic \(p\). By \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-complete-local-Noetherian-domain-finite-over-regular]{F.25} it is finite over an embedded power-series ring \(R=k[[X_1,\ldots,X_n]]\). A finite module generating list for the image ring, together with the finite algebra generating list for \(B\) over that image, makes \(B\) finite type over \(R\). In particular \(R\subset B\) is injective.

Put \(K_0=\operatorname{Frac}(R)\). Noether normalization \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/d02d0a3669f42579db037cd44de1d113fdd770a1/docs/courses/AG-CA/src/krull-dimension-and-noether-normalization.md}{AG-CA-09, Corollary 3.2} supplies algebraically independent parameters in \(B\otimes_RK_0\) over which that algebra is finite. Multiply each parameter by a nonzero scalar of \(R\) to put it in \(B\); independence and the parameter algebra over \(K_0\) are unchanged. Write the resulting parameters as \(y_1,\ldots,y_d\), and put \(A=R[y_1,\ldots,y_d]\). Choose finite \(A\)-algebra generators \(b_i\) of \(B\). Each satisfies a monic equation over \(K_0[y]\). There is a common nonzero \(g\in R\) for which every coefficient belongs to \(A_g\).

Write such an equation as \(b_i^{e_i}+\sum_{j<e_i}c_{ij}b_i^j=0\). Choose \(N\) such that \(g^{N(e_i-j)}c_{ij}\in A\) for every \(i,j\). Multiplying by \(g^{Ne_i}\) gives a monic equation over \(A\) for \(g^Nb_i\). Consequently \[B'=A[g^Nb_1,\ldots,g^Nb_t]\subset B\] is finite over \(A\): reduce powers of each generator using its monic equation, obtaining a finite spanning list of bounded monomials. Moreover \(B'_g=B_g\), since all \(b_i\) belong to \(B'_g\). A sufficiently large \(r\geq0\) therefore puts \(f'=g^{pr}f\) in \(B'\).
