The fraction fields of \(B'\) and \(B\) agree; call this field \(L\). Since \(g^{pr}=(g^r)^p\), membership of \(f'\) in \(L^p\) would imply membership of \(f\) in \(L^p\). Thus \(f'\notin L^p\). Finiteness over \(A\) makes \(L\) finite over \(K=\operatorname{Frac}(A)\): the localization \(B'\otimes_AK\) is a finite-dimensional domain, hence a field, and contains all fractions of \(B'\).

The complete power-series calculation \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-more-algebra-lemma-power-series-ring-subfields]{F.120} supplies a nonempty downward-directed family of coefficient subrings \[A_J=k_J[[X_1^p,\ldots,X_n^p]][y_1^p,\ldots,y_d^p]\subset A,\] with \(A\) finite free over \(A_J\) and fraction fields \(K_J\) containing \(K^p\), whose intersection is \(K^p\). Here \(J\) runs over finite subsets of an absolute \(p\)-basis of \(k\), and \(k_J\) is generated over \(k^p\) by the basis elements outside \(J\); no perfection hypothesis is imposed. The finite-extension assertion of \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-more-algebra-lemma-intersection-subfields]{F.112} gives \(\bigcap_JL^pK_J=L^p\). Since \(f'\notin L^p\), choose \(J\) with \(f'\notin L^pK_J\).

The relative \(p\)-basis theorem \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-more-algebra-lemma-p-basis]{F.119} extends \(\{f'\}\) to a \(p\)-basis of \(L/K_J\). Indeed its first degree is \(p\): a proper monic factor of \(T^p-(f')^p=(T-f')^p\) has coefficient \(-ef'\), \(1\leq e<p\), and would put \(f'\) in \(L^pK_J\). The coordinate derivation from the full presentation in F.119 consequently gives \(\delta:L\to L\) killing \(K_J\) with \(\delta(f')=1\).

The ring \(B'\) is finite over \(A_J\), by the two finite module spanning lists. Choose \(A_J\)-module generators \(v_1,\ldots,v_s\). Write each \(\delta(v_i)\) as a fraction of \(B'\) and let \(h\in B'\setminus\{0\}\) be the product of their nonzero denominators. Then \(D'=h\delta\) sends every \(v_i\) into \(B'\) and kills \(A_J\). Differentiating an arbitrary expression \(\sum_i a_iv_i\), \(a_i\in A_J\), proves \(D'(B')\subset B'\). Its value on \(f'\) is \(h\ne0\).

Finally \(B\) is finite type over \(B'\), \(g\) is a nonzerodivisor in both domains, and \(B'_g=B_g\). The third assertion of \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-more-algebra-lemma-derivation-extends]{F.104} therefore gives \(s\geq0\) for which \(g^sD'\) restricts to a derivation \(D:B\to B\). In the common fraction field, the fraction formula and \(D'(g^{pr})=prg^{pr-1}D'(g)=0\) yield \[D(f)=g^sD'(g^{-pr}f')=g^{s-pr}h\ne0.\] Its membership in \(B\) follows from the restriction just proved; the displayed expression proves its nonvanishing. Empty parameter lists or a coefficient field as base require no changes. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-more-algebra-lemma-formally-smooth}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.106: formally smooth}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.106-formally-smooth}

Reading source: \href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/07EC}{Stacks, Tag 07EC}.

Let \(\varphi:R\to S\) be continuous. If the underlying algebra map is formally smooth, it is formally smooth when \(R\) has any linear topology and \(S\) has a pre-adic topology. Moreover, if the topologies on \(R\) and \(S\) are given by the powers of ideals \(\mathfrak m\) and \(\mathfrak n\), formal smoothness is unchanged when the topology on \(R\) is replaced by the discrete topology.

\textbf{Proof.} We specify the topological test. Give a ring \(D\) and its quotient \(D/J\) the discrete topology, where \(J^2=0\). Fix continuous maps \(a:R\to D\) and \(b:S\to D/J\) such that \(b\varphi\) is the reduction of \(a\). A solution is a continuous \(R\)-algebra map \(c:S\to D\) reducing to \(b\). Topological formal smoothness requires a solution for every such test; algebraic formal smoothness uses the same tests without continuity conditions. The latter definition is \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/d02d0a3669f42579db037cd44de1d113fdd770a1/docs/courses/AG-CA/src/formally-smooth-unramified-and-etale-ring-maps.md}{AG-CA-17, Section 1}.

For a pre-adic topology on \(S\), choose \(\mathfrak n\) whose powers form a neighbourhood basis at zero. A ring map from \(S\) to a discrete ring is continuous precisely when its kernel contains some \(\mathfrak n^r\): continuity at zero gives this condition, and translation gives continuity at every point. Algebraic formal smoothness supplies a lift \(c\) in the test. Continuity of \(b\) gives \(b(\mathfrak n^r)=0\) for some \(r\ge1\). Thus \(c(\mathfrak n^r)\subset J\), and multiplication of two such ideal powers gives \[
c(\mathfrak n^{2r})\subset J^2=0.
\] The lift is therefore continuous. The linear topology on \(R\) needs no further restriction beyond continuity of the stipulated maps.

Now assume both topologies are given by the stated ideal powers. If formal smoothness holds with discrete \(R\), any test with continuous \(a\) is among its tests, so the same property holds with the original topology on \(R\). In the other direction, start with a test having discrete \(R\); the map \(a\) is initially allowed to be arbitrary. Continuity of \(\varphi\) gives an integer \(s\ge1\) with \(\varphi(\mathfrak m^s)\subset\mathfrak n\). For the integer \(r\) supplied by \(b\) as above, compatibility implies \[
a(\mathfrak m^{sr})\subset J,
\qquad a(\mathfrak m^{2sr})=0.
\] Hence \(a\) was continuous for the \(\mathfrak m\)-power topology as well. Formal smoothness for that topology now gives the desired continuous lift. This proves both directions, with no finite-generation or Noetherian assumption. Neither completeness nor separatedness of \(S\) was required. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-more-algebra-lemma-formally-smooth-completion}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.107: formally smooth completion}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.107-formally-smooth-completion}

Reading source: \href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/07ED}{Stacks, Tag 07ED}.

Let \(R\to S\) be a continuous map of Noetherian rings with topologies defined by finitely generated ideals \(\mathfrak m\subset R\) and \(\mathfrak n\subset S\). Write \(\widehat R\) and \(\widehat S\) for the corresponding completions. The following three properties are equivalent: \(R\to S\) is formally smooth for the \(\mathfrak n\)-power topology; \(R\to\widehat S\) is formally smooth for the \(\mathfrak n\widehat S\)-power topology; and \(\widehat R\to\widehat S\) is formally smooth for that target topology.

\textbf{Proof.} The continuous map induces the last completion map by applying it to compatible finite-order coordinates. \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/d02d0a3669f42579db037cd44de1d113fdd770a1/docs/courses/AG-CA/src/completion.md}{AG-CA-19, Proposition 2.2} proves the exact quotient identities \[
\widehat R/\mathfrak m^q\widehat R=R/\mathfrak m^q,
\qquad
\widehat S/\mathfrak n^q\widehat S=S/\mathfrak n^q
\quad(q\ge1).
\] These identities use the canonical maps and commute with all transition maps. That proposition also proves completeness for the extended-ideal topologies.

A continuous homomorphism \(u:S\to D\) to a discrete ring kills some \(\mathfrak n^q\). Its factorization through \(S/\mathfrak n^q\) and the second displayed identity define a homomorphism \(\widehat u:\widehat S\to D\) killing \(\mathfrak n^q\widehat S\). It extends \(u\). It is the only continuous extension: any other extension kills a possibly different ideal power; pass to an exponent at least as large as both, where its map is determined by the same surjective finite quotient. Restriction and extension are inverse, and they commute with maps between discrete target rings. The identical argument applies to \(R\) and \(\widehat R\).

Use the tests defined in \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-more-algebra-lemma-formally-smooth]{F.106}, with \(D\to D/J\) square-zero. First compare \(R\to S\) with \(R\to\widehat S\). Keep the structural map from \(R\) fixed. The just-proved correspondence identifies every continuous map to \(D/J\), every continuous lift to \(D\), and their compatibility with \(R\). Thus one test has a solution exactly when its counterpart does.

Next compare \(R\to\widehat S\) with \(\widehat R\to\widehat S\). With the original topology on the base, extension and restriction identify the structural maps to both discrete test rings. Compatibility after restriction implies compatibility after extension: the two continuous maps from \(\widehat R\) agree by uniqueness of extension. The test diagrams and their dotted lifts therefore correspond in both directions. Finally F.106 identifies each of these topological-base tests with the tests using discrete base. In particular a structural map allowed in a discrete-base test is automatically continuous when it is compatible with the continuous target map modulo \(J\); that is precisely the ideal-power calculation in F.106. This proves the three equivalences in the stipulated Noetherian scope. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-more-algebra-lemma-gamma-commutative-diagram}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.108: gamma commutative diagram}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.108-gamma-commutative-diagram}

Reading source: \href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/07E3}{Stacks, Tag 07E3}.

Consider a commutative square of fields with arrows \(k\to k'\), \(k\to K\), \(k'\to K'\) and \(K\to K'\). Assume \(k'/k\) and \(K'/K\) are finitely generated. For the natural maps \[
\alpha:\Omega_{K/k}\otimes_KK'\longrightarrow\Omega_{K'/k'},
\qquad
\beta:H_1(L_{K/k})\otimes_KK'\longrightarrow H_1(L_{K'/k'}),
\] all four kernels and cokernels are finite-dimensional, and \[
\dim\ker\alpha-\dim\operatorname{coker}\alpha
-\dim\ker\beta+\dim\operatorname{coker}\beta
=\operatorname{trdeg}_k k'-\operatorname{trdeg}_K K'.
\]

\textbf{Proof.} All vector spaces below are over \(K'\), and all omitted scalar extensions are to \(K'\). Apply the full field-transitivity proof \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-more-algebra-lemma-transitivity-gamma]{F.131} to \(k\subset k'\subset K'\) and \(k\subset K\subset K'\). Let \[
V=H_1(L_{K'/k}),\qquad U=\Omega_{K'/k}.
\] For the first row put \(P_1=H_1(L_{k'/k})\otimes_{k'}K'\), \(W_1=H_1(L_{K'/k'})\), \(Q_1=\Omega_{k'/k}\otimes_{k'}K'\) and \(Z_1=\Omega_{K'/k'}\). For the second put \(P_2=H_1(L_{K/k})\otimes_KK'\), \(W_2=H_1(L_{K'/K})\), \(Q_2=\Omega_{K/k}\otimes_KK'\) and \(Z_2=\Omega_{K'/K}\). The two exact rows are \[
0\longrightarrow P_i\longrightarrow V\longrightarrow W_i
\longrightarrow Q_i\longrightarrow U\longrightarrow Z_i\longrightarrow0
\qquad(i=1,2).
\] Their first injections identify \(P_1,P_2\) with subspaces of \(V\). Naturality of the representative and derivative maps in \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-exact-sequence-NL]{F.42} identifies \(\beta\) with \(P_2\to V\to W_1\) and \(\alpha\) with \(Q_2\to U\to Z_1\).

We calculate only finite defects, so no subtraction of infinite dimensions is involved. Set \[
T=P_1\cap P_2,\quad Y=V/(P_1+P_2),\quad
A_i=\ker(Q_i\to U),\quad B_i=\operatorname{im}(Q_i\to U).
\] Write \(i_0=\dim T\), \(r=\dim(P_1/T)\), \(y=\dim Y\), \(a_i=\dim A_i\), \(j=\dim(B_1\cap B_2)\), \(s=\dim(B_1/(B_1\cap B_2))\) and \(z=\dim(U/(B_1+B_2))\). These are finite. Indeed \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-more-algebra-lemma-cartier-equality]{F.98} makes \(P_1,Q_1,W_2,Z_2\) finite. The space \(Y\) is a quotient of \(V/P_2\), which embeds in \(W_2\); \(A_2\) is a quotient of \(W_2\); and the space measured by \(z\) is a quotient of \(Z_2\). All other spaces on the list are subspaces or quotients of \(P_1\) or \(Q_1\).

The kernel of \(\beta\) is \(T\). Exactness of the first row gives an injection \(V/P_1\to W_1\) with quotient \(A_1\). Dividing its image by the image of \(P_2\) therefore yields \[
0\longrightarrow Y\longrightarrow\operatorname{coker}\beta
\longrightarrow A_1\longrightarrow0.
\] For \(\alpha\), its kernel consists of the elements of \(Q_2\) whose image in \(U\) lies in \(B_1\). Mapping them into \(U\) gives a surjection onto \(B_1\cap B_2\) with kernel \(A_2\). Its cokernel is \(U/(B_1+B_2)\). Hence \[
\dim\ker\beta=i_0,\quad \dim\operatorname{coker}\beta=y+a_1,
\qquad \dim\ker\alpha=a_2+j,\quad \dim\operatorname{coker}\alpha=z.
\] The second row identifies \(V/P_2\) with the kernel of \(W_2\to Q_2\). Inside \(V/P_2\), the image of \(P_1\) is \(P_1/T\) and has quotient \(Y\). Similarly \(U/B_2\) contains the image \(B_1/(B_1\cap B_2)\) with quotient \(U/(B_1+B_2)\). The resulting finite exact sequences give \[
\dim P_1=i_0+r,\quad \dim W_2=r+y+a_2,
\qquad \dim Q_1=a_1+j+s,\quad \dim Z_2=s+z.
\] Subtracting these finite numbers shows that the expression in the statement equals \[
(a_2+j)-z-i_0+(y+a_1)
=\dim Q_1-\dim P_1-\dim Z_2+\dim W_2.
\] F.98 applied to \(k'/k\) and \(K'/K\) gives the required transcendence-degree difference. This also proves finiteness of every defect without requiring \(K/k\) or \(K'/k'\) to be finitely generated. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-more-algebra-lemma-geometrically-regular-over-field}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.109: geometrically regular over field}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.109-geometrically-regular-over-field}

Reading source: \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/unofficial-stacks-project-ai-drafts/blob/565b10e987aba5969b21145a0833f42d69f96790/more-algebra.tex\#L9460-L9501}{AI Integrated Stacks, pinned More Algebra, lines 9460--9501}.

Let \(k\) have characteristic \(p>0\), and let \((A,\mathfrak m,K)\) be a geometrically regular Noetherian local \(k\)-algebra. Let \(k\subset F\subset K\) be finitely generated over \(k\). Suppose a map \(\varphi:k[y_1,\ldots,y_m]\to A\) has residue images \(\overline y_i\in F\), with \(d\overline y_1,\ldots,d\overline y_m\) a basis of \(\Omega_{F/k}\). Put \(\mathfrak p=\varphi^{-1}(\mathfrak m)\). Then \[k[y_1,\ldots,y_m]_{\mathfrak p}\longrightarrow A\] is flat, and \(A/\mathfrak pA\) is regular.

\textbf{Proof.} Write \(R_0=k[y_1,\ldots,y_m]_{\mathfrak p}\), \(\mathfrak m_0=\mathfrak pR_0\), and \(K_0=R_0/\mathfrak m_0\). The residue map embeds \(K_0\) into \(F\), and \[K_0=k(\overline y_1,\ldots,\overline y_m).\] Indeed it is the fraction field of the domain image of \(k[y]\) in \(K\); localizing at the kernel inverts every nonzero image. The polynomial and fraction differential formulas in \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/d02d0a3669f42579db037cd44de1d113fdd770a1/docs/courses/AG-CA/src/kahler-differentials.md}{AG-CA-15, Sections 1--2 and Theorem 5.1} make \(\Omega_{R_0/k}\) free on \(dy_i\), and make their images span \(\Omega_{K_0/k}\). They are independent in that last space: a \(K_0\)-linear relation maps to an \(F\)-linear relation between the assumed basis of \(\Omega_{F/k}\), so every coefficient vanishes in \(F\), and hence in \(K_0\). Thus \[\Omega_{R_0/k}\otimes_{R_0}K_0\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\Omega_{K_0/k}.\]

The ring \(R_0\) is regular local by iterating \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/d02d0a3669f42579db037cd44de1d113fdd770a1/docs/courses/AG-CA/src/regular-local-rings.md}{AG-CA-14, Proposition 3.3} from the field and using the definition of a regular ring at its prime localizations. For a finite purely inseparable \(k'/k\), its tensor is the localization of \(k'[y]\) at the images of \(k[y]\setminus\mathfrak p\), and is Noetherian regular. Criterion \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-geometrically-regular]{F.50} therefore makes \(R_0\) geometrically regular over \(k\). The geometric-regularity characterization \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-more-algebra-proposition-characterization-geometrically-regular]{F.133} gives injectivity of the connecting map \[\gamma_0:H_1(L_{K_0/k})\longrightarrow\mathfrak m_0/\mathfrak m_0^2.\] The full quotient sequence \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-exact-sequence-NL]{F.42} gives \[H_1(L_{K_0/k})\longrightarrow\mathfrak m_0/\mathfrak m_0^2
\longrightarrow\Omega_{R_0/k}\otimes_{R_0}K_0
\longrightarrow\Omega_{K_0/k}\longrightarrow0.\] The last nonzero arrow is the displayed isomorphism, so exactness also makes \(\gamma_0\) surjective. Hence it is an isomorphism.

All arrows in the following square are the connecting and scalar-extension maps of the same quotient presentations: \[\begin{array}{ccc}
H_1(L_{K_0/k})\otimes_{K_0}K&\xrightarrow{\gamma_0\otimes1}&
(\mathfrak m_0/\mathfrak m_0^2)\otimes_{K_0}K\\
\downarrow&&\downarrow\\
H_1(L_{K/k})&\xrightarrow{\gamma}&\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2.
\end{array}\] It commutes: a lifted polynomial relation has the same differentiated representative whether mapped first to \(A\) or first to its residue field, as in F.42. The left arrow is injective by the first injection of the field-tower sequence \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-more-algebra-lemma-transitivity-gamma]{F.131} for \(k\subset K_0\subset K\). The bottom arrow is injective by F.133 applied to the assumed geometrically regular \(A\). The top arrow is an isomorphism, since tensor over a field is exact. If a vector in its upper-right space maps to zero below, take its preimage in the upper-left space. Commutativity and the two injections force that preimage, and then the vector, to be zero. This proves injectivity of the right arrow.

Choose a regular system of parameters \(x_1,\ldots,x_d\) of \(R_0\). Their classes are a \(K_0\)-basis of \(\mathfrak m_0/\mathfrak m_0^2\); after scalar extension they remain a \(K\)-basis. The right injection says their images have independent classes in \(\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2\). The ring \(A\) is regular, by F.133. Extend those classes to a basis of this finite-dimensional \(K\)-space and lift the additional basis vectors to \(\mathfrak m\). Nakayama's lemma \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-NAK]{F.10} makes the resulting list a minimal generating list for \(\mathfrak m\). The complete parameter theorem \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/d02d0a3669f42579db037cd44de1d113fdd770a1/docs/courses/AG-CA/src/regular-sequences-depth-and-cohen-macaulay-modules.md}{AG-CA-12, Theorem 6.1} makes it a regular sequence. In particular its prefix, the images of \(x_1,\ldots,x_d\), is regular in \(A\), with proper generated ideal.

The map \(R_0\to A\) is local by the definition of \(\mathfrak p\). Therefore \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-flat-over-regular]{F.46} applies to these images and proves flatness. The full successive parameter-quotient result \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/d02d0a3669f42579db037cd44de1d113fdd770a1/docs/courses/AG-CA/src/regular-local-rings.md}{AG-CA-14, Theorem 1.1 and Corollary 1.2} makes \(A/(x_1,\ldots,x_d)A\) regular local. Since the parameters generate \(\mathfrak m_0\), their image ideal is exactly \(\mathfrak pA\). This is the asserted regular quotient. If \(d=0\), \(R_0\) is a field, its flatness assertion is the vector-space argument, and the quotient is \(A\) itself; the proof also covers \(m=0\). ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-more-algebra-lemma-helper-G-ring}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.110: helper G ring}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.110-helper-g-ring}

Reading source: \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/unofficial-stacks-project-ai-drafts/blob/565b10e987aba5969b21145a0833f42d69f96790/more-algebra.tex\#L12915-L12963}{AI Integrated Stacks, pinned More Algebra, lines 12915--12963}.

Let \(A_0\) be a regular complete Noetherian local domain, put \(P=A_0[Y_1,\ldots,Y_m]\), and let \(\mathfrak q\subset P\) be any prime. Both \[\widehat{P_{\mathfrak q}}\otimes_{A_0}\operatorname{Frac}(A_0)
\quad\hbox{and}\quad
\widehat{P_{\mathfrak q}}\otimes_P\operatorname{Frac}(P)\] are geometrically regular over their displayed fields. The second assertion contains the power-series helper; the first is the additional form used in F.97.

\textbf{Proof.} Polynomial regularity and localization are \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/d02d0a3669f42579db037cd44de1d113fdd770a1/docs/courses/AG-CA/src/regular-local-rings.md}{AG-CA-14, Proposition 3.3 and Theorem 3.2}. Thus \(P_{\mathfrak q}\) is regular local. Its completion \(H=\widehat{P_{\mathfrak q}}\) is Noetherian regular local by \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/d02d0a3669f42579db037cd44de1d113fdd770a1/docs/courses/AG-CA/src/completion.md}{AG-CA-19, Theorem 4.1}. Each displayed ring is a localization of \(H\), so is Noetherian and regular. If the indicated field has characteristic zero, its only finite purely inseparable extension is itself, and \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-geometrically-regular]{F.50} proves geometric regularity.

Suppose the characteristic is \(p>0\). In this case \(A_0\cong k[[X_1,\ldots,X_n]]\), with no assumption that \(k\) is perfect. To check this specialization, \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/d02d0a3669f42579db037cd44de1d113fdd770a1/docs/courses/AG-CA/src/coefficient-rings-and-cohen-structure.md}{AG-CA-19S, Theorem 6.1} evaluates the variables at a minimal list of generators of the maximal ideal of \(A_0\), giving a surjection from \(k[[X_1,\ldots,X_n]]\). Regularity makes \(n=\dim A_0\). The source is regular local of dimension \(n\), by the polynomial completion calculation and AG-CA-19, Theorem 4.1. If the kernel contained a nonzero element, the one-equation dimension theorem \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/d02d0a3669f42579db037cd44de1d113fdd770a1/docs/courses/AG-CA/src/dimension-theory-of-noetherian-local-rings.md}{AG-CA-11, Theorem 3.2} would make the quotient dimension at most \(n-1\), a contradiction. The evaluation kernel is therefore zero.

Treat the two assertions together by taking \(Q=A_0\), \(F=\operatorname{Frac}(A_0)\) in the first case, and \(Q=P\), \(F=\operatorname{Frac}(P)\) in the second. We prove that \(H\otimes_Q L\) is regular for every finite purely inseparable extension \(L/F\), by induction on its degree. The base case is the localization already proved regular. Such an extension has a tower of degree-\(p\) steps: take finite field generators, with successive \(p\)-powers in \(F\), and adjoin their roots one at a time; at a nontrivial step the proper-factor argument in \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-more-algebra-lemma-p-basis]{F.119} gives degree \(p\). Thus at the final step write \(F\subset M\subset L=M(z)\), \(z^p=f\in M\setminus M^p\), and assume \(E=H\otimes_QM\) regular.

There is a finite domain \(B\), \(Q\subset B\subset M\), with fraction field \(M\) and, after rescaling \(z\), with \(f\in B\). Here are the denominator details. Choose finitely many algebraic generators \(u_i\) of \(M/F\). For a monic equation \(u_i^{d_i}+\sum_{j<d_i}c_{ij}u_i^j=0\), multiplication by a suitable nonzero \(a_i\in Q\) makes every \(a_i^{d_i-j}c_{ij}\) lie in \(Q\). Hence \(a_iu_i\) is integral over \(Q\). The algebra generated by these elements is finite by bounded monic reductions, and its fraction field is \(M\). Write \(f=b/d\) in that algebra. A monic integral equation for \(d\ne0\) can be shortened, by cancelling powers of \(d\) in this domain, until its constant coefficient \(a\in Q\) is nonzero. The equation expresses \(a/d\) in \(B\). Replace \(z\) by \(az\). Its new \(p\)th power is \(a^pf=b a^{p-1}(a/d)\in B\), and remains outside \(M^p\), since \(a^p\) is a nonzero \(p\)th power. Relabel this generator and its power as \(z,f\). The monic irreducible equation makes \(C=B[Z]/(Z^p-f)\) a finite domain with fraction field \(L\); injectivity in \(L\) follows from the degree-\(p\) minimal polynomial.

The base \(Q\) is a normal domain. In the first case this is regular local normality; in the second it is polynomial regularity followed by \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/d02d0a3669f42579db037cd44de1d113fdd770a1/docs/courses/AG-CA/src/discrete-valuation-rings-normal-rings-and-serres-criterion.md}{AG-CA-15, Corollary 4.5}. Every element of \(B\) or \(C\) has some \(p\)-power in \(F\), since its fraction field is finite purely inseparable over \(F\). That power is integral over \(Q\), because the element is integral. Normality therefore puts the power in \(Q\).

Set \(T=B[Y_1,\ldots,Y_m]\) in the first case, and \(T=B\) in the second. Then \(P\subset T\) is finite, and every element of \(T\) has a sufficiently high \(p\)-power in \(P\). For a polynomial in the first case, take a common exponent for its finitely many coefficients and apply Frobenius to the sum. Lying over gives a prime \(\mathfrak r\) above \(\mathfrak q\), and it is unique: for \(t^{p^e}\in P\), membership of \(t\) in a prime above \(\mathfrak q\) is equivalent to membership of \(t^{p^e}\) in \(\mathfrak q\). The full finite-completion product theorem \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-completion-finite-extension]{F.27} thus has one factor and gives \[H\otimes_PT\cong\widehat{T_{\mathfrak r}}.\] Tensoring with \(M=\operatorname{Frac}(B)\) over \(B\), and using \(P\otimes_{A_0}B=T\) in the first case, gives the actual identity \[E=H\otimes_QM\cong\widehat{T_{\mathfrak r}}\otimes_BM.\] In particular \(E\) is a localization of a Noetherian completed local ring. These are the maximal-ideal completions specified in F.27, not a replacement by an unrelated topology.

The domain \(B\) is finite type over the complete local ring \(A_0\), in either case. Since \(f\notin M^p\), \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-more-algebra-lemma-find-D]{F.105} produces a derivation \(D:B\to B\) with \(D(f)\ne0\). Extend it coefficientwise to \(T\) in the first case, assigning zero to the \(Y_i\); coefficient convolution proves the product rule. In the second case it is already a derivation of \(T\). By \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-more-algebra-lemma-derivation-extends]{F.104} it extends successively to \(T_{\mathfrak r}\), its maximal-adic completion, and the localization by \(B\setminus\{0\}\). The resulting derivation of \(E\) sends \(f\) to the original nonzero element \(D(f)\in M\). This is a unit in every nonzero \(M\)-algebra \(E\); if \(E=0\), the next test ring is also zero and already regular.

Finally tensor associativity and \(L=M[Z]/(Z^p-f)\) give \[H\otimes_QL\cong E\otimes_ML\cong E[Z]/(Z^p-f).\] The polynomial quotient identity follows by reducing each polynomial to its degree-less-than-\(p\) remainder, or directly from its finite monic presentation. \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-more-algebra-lemma-degree-p-extension-regular]{F.103} applies: \(E\) is Noetherian regular and its derivation has unit value on \(f\). It proves this next ring regular. The induction covers every finite purely inseparable extension. Criterion F.50 now gives both assertions. Empty lists of \(X_i\) or \(Y_i\) are included throughout. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-more-algebra-lemma-helper-integral}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.111: helper integral}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.111-helper-integral}

Reading source: \href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09XG}{Stacks, Tag 09XG}.

Let \(A\to B\) be an integral ring map, \(I\subset A\) an ideal, and \(y\in B\) have idempotent image in \(B/IB\). There are an integer \(d\geq1\) and a monic polynomial \(f(T)\in A[T]\) such that \[
f(y)=0,\qquad f(T)\bmod I=T^d(T-1)^d.
\]

\textbf{Proof.} Write \(z=y^2-y=\sum_{i=1}^h a_ib_i\) with \(a_i\in I\) and \(b_i\in B\). This is a finite sum by the definition of the extended ideal. The subalgebra \(C=A[y,b_1,\ldots,b_h]\subset B\) is a finite \(A\)-module: each of its finitely many generators satisfies a monic equation over \(A\), and successive substitution reduces every monomial to one whose exponent in each generator is below that equation's degree. Those finitely many bounded monomials generate \(C\). This argument uses the image of \(A\); injectivity of \(A\to B\) is unnecessary.

Choose a finite module generating list \(c_1,\ldots,c_d\) for \(C\), including \(1\), so \(d\geq1\). Since \(zC\subset IC\), express each \(zc_i\) as \(\sum_j m_{ij}c_j\) with all \(m_{ij}\in I\). For the column \(c=(c_i)\) these equations say \((z1_d-M)c=0\), where \(M=(m_{ij})\). Multiplying by the adjugate, whose identity was proved completely in \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-charpoly]{F.19}, gives \[
g(z)c_i=0\quad\hbox{for all }i,
\qquad g(U)=\det(U1_d-M)\in A[U].
\] The included generator \(1\) makes \(g(z)=0\) in \(C\), hence in \(B\). The determinant expansion makes \(g\) monic of degree \(d\); reducing the entries of \(M\) modulo \(I\) gives \(g(U)\bmod I=U^d\). Set \(f(T)=g(T^2-T)\). Its leading coefficient is \(1\), it annihilates \(y\), and its reduction is \((T^2-T)^d=T^d(T-1)^d\). The same construction permits an empty sum for \(z\), the zero target algebra, and \(I=A\). ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-more-algebra-lemma-intersection-subfields}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.112: intersection subfields}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.112-intersection-subfields}

Reading source: \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/unofficial-stacks-project-ai-drafts/blob/565b10e987aba5969b21145a0833f42d69f96790/more-algebra.tex\#L12067-L12128}{AI Integrated Stacks, pinned More Algebra, lines 12067--12128}.

Let \(K\) have characteristic \(p>0\). Let \((F_\lambda)\) be a nonempty downward-directed family of subfields of \(K\) containing \(K^p\), with intersection \(K^p\). Then \[
\bigcap_\lambda\ker\bigl(\Omega_{K/\mathbf F_p}\to\Omega_{K/F_\lambda}\bigr)=0.
\] For every finite field extension \(L/K\), the composita in \(L\) also satisfy \[\bigcap_\lambda L^pF_\lambda=L^p.\]

\textbf{Proof.} Take an absolute \(p\)-basis of \(K\) by the entire \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-more-algebra-lemma-p-basis]{F.119}. If a nonzero absolute differential \(\omega\) vanished in every indicated relative module, write it in that differential basis using a finite nonempty subset \(b_1,\ldots,b_c\) and coefficients not all zero. At every \(\lambda\) those relative differentials would be dependent. F.119's full equivalence makes their \(p\)-monomials dependent over \(F_\lambda K^p=F_\lambda\).

Index those finitely many monomials by \(e\), \(0\le e_i<p\), and form the actual \(K\)-subspace \[V=\{(a_e)\in K^{p^c}:\ \sum_e a_e b^e=0\}.\] Its intersection with \(F_\lambda^{p^c}\) is nonzero at every index. The entire newly proved \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-more-algebra-lemma-intersection-subfields-subspace]{F.113} gives a nonzero intersection with \((K^p)^{p^c}\), contradicting independence of the absolute \(p\)-basis monomials. Hence no such \(\omega\) exists, proving the first assertion.

We prove the second assertion through finite simple steps. Here is the reduction for an arbitrary finite extension. Choose finitely many field generators \(\alpha_i\). For each monic irreducible polynomial over \(K\), remove a common factor \(p\) from its positive exponents repeatedly until writing it as \(G_i(T^{p^{e_i}})\) with \(G_i'\ne0\). This terminates because its degree decreases. The polynomial \(G_i\) is irreducible, since a factorization would give one of the original polynomial, and its nonzero derivative is relatively prime to it. Thus \(\beta_i=\alpha_i^{p^{e_i}}\) is separable over \(K\).

The field \(M=K(\beta_i)\) is finite separable: at each successive adjunction its minimal polynomial divides the original squarefree polynomial over the larger coefficient field, and remains separable. The full separable-tower transitivity proof \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/d02d0a3669f42579db037cd44de1d113fdd770a1/docs/courses/AG-CA/src/formally-smooth-unramified-and-etale-ring-maps.md}{AG-CA-17, Lemma 7.1} proves that this tower is separable over \(K\). From \(M\), adjoin each successive \(p\)th root needed to recover the \(\alpha_i\). Each step has degree one or \(p\): if the root is absent, the proper-factor coefficient calculation in F.119 proves its degree-\(p\) polynomial irreducible. This gives a tower of separable simple steps followed by degree-\(p\) purely inseparable steps.

If the desired intersection identity has been proved up to an intermediate field \(M\), the fields \(E_\lambda=M^pF_\lambda\subset M\) are downward directed, contain \(M^p\), and have intersection \(M^p\). For the next field \(N\), one has \(N^pE_\lambda=N^pF_\lambda\), since \(M^p\subset N^p\). Thus the same statement for that next simple step proves it for the composite. It remains to prove the two types of simple steps.

For a separable simple extension \(L=K(\alpha)\), put \(\theta=\alpha^p\). The minimal polynomial over \(K(\alpha^p)\) divides both the original squarefree polynomial and \(T^p-\alpha^p=(T-\alpha)^p\). It must therefore have degree one, so \(K(\theta)=L\) and \(\theta\in L^p\). Write \(d=[L:K]\). Frobenius transports the \(K\)-basis \(1,\alpha,\ldots,\alpha^{d-1}\) to the \(K^p\)-basis \(1,\theta,\ldots,\theta^{d-1}\) of \(L^p\): raising expansions to the \(p\)th power proves spanning, and unique roots of coefficients prove independence. The same powers are a \(K\)-basis of \(L\), because \(K(\theta)=L\).

Consequently they are independent over every \(F_\lambda\subset K\). Their monic relation over \(K^p\) gives spanning over \(F_\lambda\), so the algebra \(F_\lambda[\theta]\) is a finite-dimensional domain and therefore a field, by multiplication and inversion. It is exactly \(L^pF_\lambda\), with the displayed basis. An element in every compositum has a unique expansion in the \(K\)-basis of \(L\); its coefficients must belong to every \(F_\lambda\), hence to \(K^p\). It therefore lies in \(L^p\), proving the identity for this step.

For a nontrivial degree-\(p\) purely inseparable step, write \(L=K(\theta)\) with \(\theta^p=t\in K\setminus K^p\). Frobenius of its power basis gives \[L^p=K^p(t),\qquad 1,t,\ldots,t^{p-1}\ \text{a }K^p\text{-basis}.\] Choose \(\lambda_0\) with \(t\notin F_{\lambda_0}\), possible from the intersection assumption. Restrict to members contained in \(F_{\lambda_0}\). This family is cofinal under refinement: downward directedness refines any given member together with \(\lambda_0\). Its intersection is still \(K^p\), by the same refinement argument in F.113, and taking the intersection of the composita over it does not change the full intersection.

For every such member, \(t^p\in K^p\subset F_\lambda\) while \(t\notin F_\lambda\). The proper-factor calculation gives degree \(p\), so \(L^pF_\lambda=F_\lambda(t)\) has basis \(1,t,\ldots,t^{p-1}\). Use the unique expansion over the fixed coarse field \(F_{\lambda_0}\); every refined-field expansion must have those same coefficients. They belong to all refined fields and hence to \(K^p\). The element is therefore in \(K^p(t)=L^p\). The reverse inclusion is automatic. This cofinal argument includes indices where \(t\) was initially already in the field, without presuming a degree-\(p\) basis there.

Both step types are proved. Applying the tower reduction establishes the identity for every finite extension, including the trivial one. Both assertions and all directed-family hypotheses have now been checked. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-more-algebra-lemma-intersection-subfields-subspace}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.113: intersection subfields subspace}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.113-intersection-subfields-subspace}

Reading source: \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/unofficial-stacks-project-ai-drafts/blob/565b10e987aba5969b21145a0833f42d69f96790/more-algebra.tex\#L12027-L12065}{AI Integrated Stacks, pinned More Algebra, lines 12027--12065}.

Let \((F_\lambda)\) be a nonempty downward-directed family of subfields of a field \(K\), and put \(F=\bigcap_\lambda F_\lambda\). For every \(K\)-linear subspace \(V\subset K^n\), \[
V\cap F^n\ne0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
V\cap F_\lambda^n\ne0\ \text{for every }\lambda.
\]

\textbf{Proof.} A nonzero vector in the intersection over \(F\) belongs to every larger field's intersection. For the other implication induct on \(n\). At \(n=0\) both nonzero-intersection assertions are false, since the family is nonempty. At \(n=1\), a \(K\)-subspace of \(K\) is zero or all of \(K\); the hypothesis excludes zero, and the vector one lies in \(F\).

For \(n>1\), let \(V_0\) be the subspace of vectors of \(V\) with first coordinate zero, viewed in \(K^{n-1}\). If \(V_0\cap F^{n-1}\) is nonzero, adjoining the zero first coordinate finishes the proof. Otherwise the induction hypothesis gives an index \(\lambda_0\) with \(V_0\cap F_{\lambda_0}^{n-1}=0\). Choose a nonzero vector of \(V\cap F_{\lambda_0}^n\). Its first coordinate cannot vanish; divide by it to get a vector \(v\) with first coordinate one.

For any other vector \(w\) in this intersection, subtract \(w_1v\). The difference is in \(V_0\cap F_{\lambda_0}^{n-1}\) and hence zero. Thus its normalized vector is uniquely \(v\). In particular, for every member \(F_\mu\subset F_{\lambda_0}\), the hypothesized nonzero intersection contains a vector whose first coordinate is nonzero, and normalization gives this same \(v\). All coordinates of \(v\) consequently belong to the intersection of these refined fields.

That intersection is \(F\). One inclusion follows because \(F\) lies in every member. For the other, given any index \(\lambda\), downward directedness supplies a member contained in both \(F_{\lambda_0}\) and \(F_\lambda\); membership in every refinement then implies membership in \(F_\lambda\). Thus \(v\in F^n\), and it is nonzero because its first coordinate is one. This proves the induction and the full equivalence. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-more-algebra-lemma-lci-local}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.114: lci local}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.114-lci-local}

Reading source: \href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/07D1}{Stacks, Tag 07D1}.

Let \(R\) be Noetherian and let \(S\) be a finitely presented \(R\)-algebra. A kernel of a finite polynomial presentation of \(S\) is a regular ideal if and only if this property holds for polynomial presentations on a finite principal cover of \(\operatorname{Spec}S\). The condition does not depend on the chosen presentations.

\textbf{Proof.} The arbitrary-ring comparison \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-more-algebra-lemma-lci-presentation-independent]{F.94.A} proves presentation independence for Koszul-regular kernels. The finite polynomial rings and their localizations are Noetherian by \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/d02d0a3669f42579db037cd44de1d113fdd770a1/docs/courses/AG-CA/src/noetherian-and-artinian-rings.md}{AG-CA-03, Theorem 2.1}; its Theorem 1.1 and Proposition 1.2 make their finite-module submodules finite. In these rings, \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-more-algebra-lemma-noetherian-finite-all-equivalent]{F.118} converts a Koszul-regular generating list in a local maximal ideal into a regular list. To obtain the neighbourhood condition in \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-more-algebra-definition-regular-ideal]{F.95}, we will explicitly spread the successive injections, rather than infer global regularity merely from Koszul acyclicity.

Fix \(P=R[X_1,\ldots,X_n]\twoheadrightarrow S\) with kernel \(I\), and a prime \(\mathfrak q\supset I\) of \(P\). Suppose a chart \(S_g\) containing its image has a regular presentation. Choose \(u\in P\) lifting \(g\), so \(u\notin\mathfrak q\). A presentation of that chart is \[
Q=P[Z]\twoheadrightarrow S_g,\qquad H=(I,t),\quad t=uZ-1.
\] The prime \(\mathfrak q'\) of \(Q\) given by \(\mathfrak q\) and \(Z=1/u\) satisfies \[
Q_{\mathfrak q'}/(t)=P_{\mathfrak q}.
\] Indeed quotienting first gives \(P_u\), and then localization at the prime over \(\mathfrak q\) gives \(P_{\mathfrak q}\). Presentation comparison and F.118 give a regular generating list for \(H_{\mathfrak q'}\). Its conormal classes are a basis by \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-regular-quasi-regular]{F.74}. Meanwhile \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-principal-localization-NL]{F.72} gives, at this point, \[
(H/H^2)_{\mathfrak q'}
\cong (I/I^2)_{\mathfrak q}\oplus S_{\mathfrak q/I}\,t.
\] The first summand is a finite direct summand of a finite free module. It is flat and finitely presented, hence free over the local quotient by \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/main/docs/courses/AG-RG/AG-RG-S01.md}{S01, Lemma 1.2}. Choose \(f_1,\ldots,f_c\in I\) whose classes are a basis there; denominators may be cleared since their values outside \(\mathfrak q\) are units. The list \(t,f_1,\ldots,f_c\) is a conormal basis. Nakayama applied to \(H_{\mathfrak q'}/(t,f_1,\ldots,f_c)\) makes it a generator list for \(H_{\mathfrak q'}\).

Compare it with the regular generator list just obtained. Both have the same length, equal to the conormal rank. Express the new list in the old one. Modulo the maximal ideal the coefficient matrix takes one basis of the conormal fibre to the other, so its determinant is a unit in \(Q_{\mathfrak q'}\). Its exterior powers identify the Koszul complexes: the differential on a wedge deletes one entry with its alternating sign, and this formula commutes with the change of basis. Thus \(t,f_1,\ldots,f_c\) has zero first homology. F.118 makes this very order regular, with \(t\) first. Quotienting by \(t\) proves that \(f_1,\ldots,f_c\) is a regular list generating \(I_{\mathfrak q}\).

Here is the required principal neighbourhood. The module \(I/(f_1,\ldots,f_c)\) is finite and vanishes at \(\mathfrak q\). For each \(i\), the kernel of multiplication by \(f_i\) on \(P/(f_1,\ldots,f_{i-1})\) is also finite, because \(P\) is Noetherian; it vanishes at \(\mathfrak q\) by the just-proved regularity. Exact localization and the finite-generator fraction-zero argument \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/main/docs/courses/AG-RG/AG-RG-S01.md}{S01, Lemma 1.1} give one element \(h\notin\mathfrak q\) annihilating all these finitely many modules. In \(P_h\) the list therefore generates \(I_h\) and every successive multiplication is injective. Its final quotient is nonzero because the prime \(\mathfrak qP_h\) still contains \(I_h\). The list is regular on this actual neighbourhood, as required by F.95.

The argument applies at every point lying in one of the stipulated charts, hence at every prime above \(I\). Conversely, localization preserves the successive injections of a regular list. For a chart where a given neighbourhood also inverts \(u\), present the localization by adjoining \(Z\) and put \(uZ-1\) first. Multiplication by this polynomial is injective by its lowest-coefficient calculation, and its quotient is \(P_u\); the remaining localized list is regular wherever the quotient is nonzero. Charts with zero quotient have no primes to check. Thus the kernel condition restricts to every principal chart. The local neighbourhoods cover the target, and a finite subcover exists by the finite unit-ideal calculation \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/d02d0a3669f42579db037cd44de1d113fdd770a1/docs/courses/AG-CA/src/spectra-of-rings.md}{AG-CA-01, Proposition 2.3}. Applying the same comparison to a second initial presentation proves the claimed independence. If \(S=0\), all these prime conditions are vacuous, including the empty-cover case. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-more-algebra-lemma-lift-factorization-monic}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.115: lift factorization monic}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.115-lift-factorization-monic}

Reading source: \href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0ALH}{Stacks, Tag 0ALH}.

Let \(I\subset A\) be any ideal. Suppose the reduction of a monic \(f\in A[T]\) has a factorization \(\bar f=\bar G\bar H\) into coprime monic polynomials over \(A/I\). There is a finitely presented étale map \(A\to A'\) such that its canonical map \(A/I\to A'/IA'\) is an isomorphism and \(f=G'H'\) in \(A'[T]\), with monic factors reducing to the prescribed ones.

\textbf{Proof.} If \(I=A\), take \(A'=0\), the principal localization at zero; its closed fibre and the prescribed factors are zero, so all requirements hold. Assume \(A/I\ne0\). Put \(d=\deg\bar G\) and \(e=\deg\bar H\). Introduce \(d+e\) variables for the lower coefficients of monic polynomials \(G\) and \(H\) of those degrees. The \(d+e\) lower coefficients of \(GH-f\) are equations in these variables. Write \(C_0\) for their quotient algebra and \(\Delta\) for the determinant of their square Jacobian matrix.

Over \(D=A/I\), the derivative of multiplication at the given factors is \[
D[T]_{<d}\oplus D[T]_{<e}\longrightarrow D[T]_{<d+e},
\qquad (v,w)\longmapsto\bar H v+\bar G w.
\] Here \(D[T]_{<r}\) is the free module on \(1,T,\ldots,T^{r-1}\). Monic division works over this arbitrary ring: for a monic polynomial \(p\) of degree \(r\), subtract the current leading coefficient times \(T^k p\) until the remainder has degree below \(r\). For a nonzero polynomial \(q\), the product \(qp\) has degree \(\deg q+r\), with the same nonzero leading coefficient as \(q\). Hence no nonzero multiple of \(p\) has degree below \(r\), and the quotient and remainder are unique. For \(r=0\), the monic polynomial is \(1\) and the remainder is zero. Choose a Bezout identity \(a\bar G+b\bar H=1\). For a polynomial \(q\) in the right module, let \(v\) be the remainder of \(bq\) on monic division by \(\bar G\). Then \(q-\bar H v\) is divisible by \(\bar G\); its quotient \(w\) has degree below \(e\). This constructs a preimage of \(q\). If the image of \((v,w)\) is zero, reduction modulo \(\bar G\) and invertibility of \(\bar H\) there give \(v=0\), by its degree bound, and monic multiplication then gives \(w=0\). Thus this is an isomorphism even when \(D\) has zero divisors. Degree-zero factors are covered by empty polynomial modules.

Consequently \(\Delta\) has a unit value at the prescribed coefficient tuple. Set \(C=(C_0)_\Delta\). The square Jacobian calculation \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/d02d0a3669f42579db037cd44de1d113fdd770a1/docs/courses/AG-CA/src/formally-smooth-unramified-and-etale-ring-maps.md}{AG-CA-17, Theorem 4.1} gives formal smoothness, and there are no remaining differential coordinates. Theorem 2.2 of that lesson therefore gives formal unramifiedness. The finite equations and principal localization give finite presentation, so \(C/A\) is étale. The coefficient tuple defines a \(D\)-algebra retraction \(\sigma:E=C/IC\to D\) of its structural map.

We select exactly this section in the closed fibre. Let \(L=\ker\sigma\). Finite algebra generators \(x_i\) of \(E/D\) give finite ideal generators \(x_i-\sigma(x_i)\) for \(L\): replace each variable by its constant value in a polynomial and telescope the difference one variable at a time. The map \[
\delta:E\longrightarrow L/L^2,\qquad
x\longmapsto x-\sigma(x)\pmod {L^2}
\] is a \(D\)-derivation, with \(E\) acting on \(L/L^2\) through \(\sigma\). To check products, expand \(x=\sigma(x)+\ell\) and \(y=\sigma(y)+m\) and discard \(\ell m\in L^2\). Since \(E/D\) is étale by base change, its differentials vanish by the same Theorem 2.2. The universal differential property makes \(\delta=0\). Its restriction to \(L\) is the quotient map, so \(L=L^2\).

Choose finite ideal generators \(\ell_i\) and write \(\ell_i=\sum_j m_{ij}\ell_j\) with \(m_{ij}\in L\). The adjugate identity of \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/main/docs/courses/AG-RG/AG-RG-S01.md}{S01, Lemma 1.2} shows that \(a=\det(1-M)\) annihilates \(L\), while \(a\equiv1\pmod L\). Put \(p=1-a\in L\). Then \(p\ell=\ell\) for every \(\ell\in L\), so \(p^2=p\) and \(L=pE\). Inverting \(1-p\) kills precisely \(L\) and induces \(E_{1-p}\cong E/L=D\), compatibly with its structural map. Lift \(1-p\) to \(h\in C\) and put \(A'=C_h\). Its closed fibre is this very copy of \(D\), and principal localization preserves finite presentation and étaleness by AG-CA-17, Theorem 1.2 and Section 4. The universal polynomials in \(A'[T]\) supply \(G',H'\). If both degrees are zero, one can directly take \(A'=A\) and both factors equal to one. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-more-algebra-lemma-lift-idempotent-upstairs}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.116: lift idempotent upstairs}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.116-lift-idempotent-upstairs}

Reading source: \href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/07M4}{Stacks, Tag 07M4}.

Suppose \(A\to B\) is integral and \(I\subset A\) is an ideal. Every idempotent \(\bar e\in B/IB\) lifts to an idempotent of \(B\otimes_A A'\) after a finitely presented étale map \(A\to A'\) for which \(A/I\to A'/IA'\) is an isomorphism.

\textbf{Proof.} Choose \(y\in B\) reducing to \(\bar e\). The determinant proof \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-more-algebra-lemma-helper-integral]{F.111} gives an integer \(d\ge1\) and a monic \(f\in A[T]\) with \[
f(y)=0,\qquad \bar f=T^d(T-1)^d.
\] The two factors generate the unit ideal: in the expansion of \((T+(1-T))^{2d-1}=1\), every term contains either \(T^d\) or \((1-T)^d\). Apply \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-more-algebra-lemma-lift-factorization-monic]{F.115}. Over its étale algebra \(A_1\) we have \(f=GH\) with reductions \(T^d\) and \((T-1)^d\). Put \(B_1=B\otimes_AA_1\), write \(y_1\) for the image of \(y\), and set \(b_1=G(y_1)\), \(b_2=H(y_1)\). Then \[
b_1b_2=0,\qquad
\bar b_1=\bar e,\quad \bar b_2=(-1)^d(1-\bar e).
\] Thus \(b_1,b_2\) generate the unit ideal modulo \(IB_1\).

The map \(A_1\to B_1\) remains integral. Indeed each tensor element uses finitely many elements of \(B\); their monic equations generate a finite module algebra after base change, and its elements are integral by the determinant test \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/d02d0a3669f42579db037cd44de1d113fdd770a1/docs/courses/AG-CA/src/integral-extensions-lying-over-going-up-and-going-down.md}{AG-CA-05, Theorems 1.1--1.2}. Let \(K\) be the inverse image in \(A_1\) of the ideal \((b_1,b_2)B_1\). The closed-image and lying-over proof in Theorem 3.4 of that lesson gives \[
\operatorname{image}V_{B_1}(b_1,b_2)=V_{A_1}(K).
\] No prime in this image can contain \(IA_1\), since its prime upstairs would contain \(IB_1\) as well as \(b_1,b_2\). Hence \(V(K+IA_1)\) is empty and \(K+IA_1=A_1\), by the prime-separation proof \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/d02d0a3669f42579db037cd44de1d113fdd770a1/docs/courses/AG-CA/src/spectra-of-rings.md}{AG-CA-01, Lemma 1.1}. Choose \(a\in K\) with \(a\equiv1\pmod {IA_1}\) and set \(A'=(A_1)_a\).

In \(B'=B_1\otimes_{A_1}A'\), the image of \(a\) is a unit belonging to \((b_1,b_2)\). Choose \(u,v\in B'\) with \(ub_1+vb_2=1\) and put \(e'=ub_1\). The equations give \[
e'(1-e')=uvb_1b_2=0,
\] so \(e'\) is idempotent. Reducing \(ub_1+vb_2=1\) and multiplying by \(\bar e\) gives \(\bar u\bar e=\bar e\), proving that \(e'\) reduces to the specified idempotent. Finally \(a\) reduces to one, so the last localization leaves the quotient \(A_1/IA_1=A/I\) unchanged. Its composition with \(A\to A_1\) is finitely presented étale by the proved stability in AG-CA-17, Theorem 1.2 and Section 4. This supplies every stated property, including the zero closed fibre. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-more-algebra-lemma-lift-projective-module}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.117: lift projective module}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.117-lift-projective-module}

Reading source: \href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/07M5}{Stacks, Tag 07M5}.

For an ideal \(I\) of any ring \(A\) and a finite projective \(A/I\)-module \(\bar P\), there is a finitely presented étale map \(A\to A'\) inducing \(A/I\cong A'/IA'\), and a finite projective \(A'\)-module \(P'\) with \(P'/IP'\cong\bar P\) under that identification.

\textbf{Proof.} Realize \(\bar P\) as a direct summand of \((A/I)^n\) and let \(\bar p\) be its projector. Such a realization follows from projectivity by splitting a finite free surjection, as in \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/main/docs/courses/AG-RG/AG-RG-S01.md}{S01, Lemma 1.0}. Lift the finitely many entries of \(\bar p\) to a matrix \(\varphi\) over \(A\). Its characteristic polynomial \(f(T)=\det(T1-\varphi)\) is monic. The full coefficient proof of Cayley--Hamilton \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-charpoly]{F.19} gives an algebra map \[
B=A[T]/(f)\longrightarrow\operatorname{End}_A(A^n),
\qquad x\longmapsto\varphi,
\] where \(x\) is the class of \(T\). For \(n>0\), subtracting the leading coefficient times the appropriate power of \(T\) times the monic polynomial \(f\) reduces any polynomial to degree below \(n\). Conversely, for nonzero \(q\), the leading coefficient of \(qf\) equals that of \(q\) and its degree is \(\deg q+n\); thus no nonzero multiple of \(f\) has degree below \(n\). These two calculations show that \(1,x,\ldots,x^{n-1}\) are a free \(A\)-basis of \(B\), even when \(A\) has zero divisors. The proved finite-algebra determinant criterion \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/d02d0a3669f42579db037cd44de1d113fdd770a1/docs/courses/AG-CA/src/integral-extensions-lying-over-going-up-and-going-down.md}{AG-CA-05, Theorem 1.2} now makes \(A\to B\) integral. The case \(n=0\) is handled directly below.

In each residue field of \(A/I\), an idempotent linear operator decomposes the vector space into its image and kernel: \(v=\bar p v+(1-\bar p)v\), and applying \(\bar p\) proves the intersection zero. Choose bases of the two summands. Its characteristic polynomial there is \(T^{n-r}(T-1)^r\) for the dimension \(r\) of its image. Consequently at every prime of \(B/IB\) the image of \(x\) is zero or one: pass to the field of that prime and use this factorization. The nilradical calculation \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/d02d0a3669f42579db037cd44de1d113fdd770a1/docs/courses/AG-CA/src/spectra-of-rings.md}{AG-CA-01, Theorem 1.2} then gives an integer \(N\ge1\) such that \[
x^N(1-x)^N=0\quad\text{in }E=B/IB.
\] This uses a single nilpotent element, with no Noetherian condition.

Set \(a=x^N\), \(b=(1-x)^N\) in \(E\). They generate the unit ideal: expand \((x+(1-x))^{2N-1}\), whose every term is divisible by \(a\) or \(b\). Also \(ab=0\). Choose \(u,v\) with \(ua+vb=1\). Then \((a+b)(u^2a+v^2b)=u^2a^2+v^2b^2=(ua+vb)^2=1\). Thus \(a+b\) is a unit, and \[
\epsilon=\frac{a}{a+b},\qquad
\epsilon(1-\epsilon)=\frac{ab}{(a+b)^2}=0
\] is an idempotent. Under the reduction of the displayed endomorphism map, \(a\) goes to \(\bar p^N=\bar p\), \(b\) to \((1-\bar p)^N=1-\bar p\), and their sum to the identity. Hence \(\epsilon\) maps to exactly \(\bar p\).

Apply \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-more-algebra-lemma-lift-idempotent-upstairs]{F.116} to the integral algebra \(B/A\) and this idempotent of \(B/IB\). It supplies the required étale \(A'\) and an idempotent of \(B\otimes_AA'\) lifting \(\epsilon\). Its image in \(\operatorname{End}_{A'}((A')^n)\) is a projector \(p'\) reducing to \(\bar p\). Put \(P'=\operatorname{im}p'\). The decomposition \[
(A')^n=\operatorname{im}p'\oplus\operatorname{im}(1-p')
\] follows by writing each vector as the sum of its two projections; applying \(p'\) makes their intersection zero. The projections of the finite coordinate basis generate each summand, so \(P'\) is finite projective. Reduction preserves this split decomposition and identifies its first summand with \(\operatorname{im}\bar p=\bar P\). If \(n=0\), take \(A'=A\) and \(P'=0\) directly. This also handles \(A/I=0\) by choosing its zero module with \(n=0\). ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-more-algebra-lemma-noetherian-finite-all-equivalent}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.118: noetherian finite all equivalent}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.118-noetherian-finite-all-equivalent}

Reading source: \href{https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/09CC}{Stacks, Tag 09CC}, together with the regular-sequence and Koszul arguments cited there. The proof below is independently written for finite modules.

For a nonzero finite module over a Noetherian local ring and a list in its maximal ideal, regularity, vanishing of all positive Koszul homology, vanishing of first Koszul homology, and the polynomial associated-graded condition are equivalent.

\textbf{Proof.} Write \((A,\mathfrak m)\) for the ring, \(M\) for the module, and \(J=(f_1,\ldots,f_r)\). The fourth assertion means that the natural graded map \[\theta:(M/JM)[T_1,\ldots,T_r]\longrightarrow\bigoplus_{n\geq0}J^nM/J^{n+1}M,\qquad \bar mT^a\longmapsto[mf^a],\] is an isomorphism. It is always surjective. If \(r=0\), the Koszul complex has only \(M\) in degree zero, \(J=0\), and \(\theta\) is the identity in degree zero. The empty list is regular because \(M\ne0\). Thus all four assertions hold in that case; assume \(r>0\).

Use the exterior complex on the symbols \(e_1,\ldots,e_r\), with coefficients in \(M\), differential \(d(e_i)=f_i\), and the signed product rule. Separating wedges which contain \(e_r\) identifies it with the cone of multiplication by \(f_r\) on the complex for the first \(r-1\) entries. Its homology sequence contains \[H_1(K_{r-1})\xrightarrow{f_r}H_1(K_{r-1})\longrightarrow H_1(K_r)\longrightarrow H_0(K_{r-1})\xrightarrow{f_r}H_0(K_{r-1}).\] For the two consequences needed here, exactness can also be checked directly. A degree-one cycle of \(K_{r-1}\) becomes a boundary in \(K_r\) when \(H_1(K_r)=0\). Writing that boundary as the sum of a wedge without \(e_r\) and a wedge containing \(e_r\) shows that its class in \(H_1(K_{r-1})\) is \(f_r\) times a class represented by a cycle. This gives surjectivity of the first arrow. If \(f_rm\in(f_1,\ldots,f_{r-1})M\), choose coefficients for this equality to obtain a degree-one cycle in \(K_r\) with last coefficient \(m\). A degree-two boundary has last coefficient in \((f_1,\ldots,f_{r-1})M\), so \([m]=0\) in \(H_0(K_{r-1})\). This gives injectivity of the last arrow.

If \(H_1(K_r)=0\), the preceding \(H_1\) is a finite \(A\)-module, since its complex consists of finite modules over a Noetherian ring. Nakayama, with \(f_r\in\mathfrak m\), makes it zero by the surjectivity just proved. Induction therefore gives all successive multiplication injections, including the final one displayed above. Their last quotient is nonzero by Nakayama applied to \(M/JM\). This proves regularity. Conversely, assume the list regular and the preceding complex acyclic in positive degrees. A cycle in \(K_r\) of degree \(k\) has a component \(v\) multiplying \(e_r\), and \(v\) is a cycle of degree \(k-1\) in \(K_{r-1}\). For \(k\geq2\), preceding acyclicity makes \(v\) a boundary. For \(k=1\), the cycle identity says \(f_r[v]=0\) in \(H_0(K_{r-1})\); regularity again makes \(v\) a boundary. Subtract the differential of a suitable wedge containing \(e_r\) to remove \(v\). What remains is a degree-\(k\) cycle in \(K_{r-1}\) and is a boundary by preceding acyclicity. This proves acyclicity in every positive degree by induction. In particular it implies vanishing of \(H_1\).

We next prove that a regular list makes \(\theta\) injective. In degree zero this is the defining quotient \(M/JM\). In degree one, suppose \(\sum_i f_im_i\in J^2M\). Express this element as \(\sum_i f_iu_i\) with \(u_i\in JM\), and subtract. The vector \((m_i-u_i)\) is a degree-one Koszul cycle. By the preceding acyclicity it is a boundary, whose coefficients all belong to \(JM\), since the degree-two differential has coefficients \(f_i\). Consequently every \(m_i\in JM\). This proves directly the module version of the conormal calculation in \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-algebra-lemma-regular-quasi-regular]{F.74}.

Here is a coefficient calculation for any degree \(n\geq1\). In a relation \[\sum_{|a|=n}m_af^a\in J^{n+1}M,\] collect every term involving one of \(f_1,\ldots,f_{r-1}\) into their generated submodule. The only remaining term on the left is \(m_{(0,\ldots,0,n)}f_r^n\); the only remaining type on the right is \(u f_r^{n+1}\). Thus \[\bigl(m_{(0,\ldots,0,n)}-uf_r\bigr)f_r^n+\sum_{i<r}f_iv_i=0\] for suitable \(u,v_i\in M\). The list \(f_1,\ldots,f_{r-1},f_r^n\) is regular by AG-CA-12, Proposition 1.3, whose power argument applies to modules. Its first Koszul homology is zero by the cone argument. Hence the last coefficient of this relation belongs to \((f_1,\ldots,f_{r-1})M\), so \(m_{(0,\ldots,0,n)}\in JM\).

To recover the coefficients of all monomials, put \(B=A[U_1,\ldots,U_r,U_r^{-1}]\), \(N=M\otimes_AB\), and \[g_i=f_i-(U_i/U_r)f_r\quad(i<r),\qquad g_r=f_r/U_r.\] The ring \(B\) is free and faithfully flat over \(A\), with its Laurent monomials as a basis. Tensoring preserves Koszul acyclicity. The displayed change of generators is invertible, so its exterior powers identify the two Koszul complexes and give \(H_1(K(g;N))=0\).

Fix a prime \(\mathfrak p\) of \(B\). If \(N_{\mathfrak p}=0\), every term of every Koszul complex with these coefficients is zero. If \(N_{\mathfrak p}\ne0\) and \(JB\subset\mathfrak p\), the local criterion already proved makes \(g_1,\ldots,g_r\) regular on the nonzero finite \(B_{\mathfrak p}\)-module \(N_{\mathfrak p}\). Its power list \(g_1,\ldots,g_{r-1},g_r^n\) is regular and has zero \(H_1\). Finally, if \(JB\not\subset\mathfrak p\), at least one \(g_i\) is a unit in \(B_{\mathfrak p}\). The power list still contains a unit, so choose \(a_i\) with \(\sum_{i<r}a_ig_i+a_rg_r^n=1\). Wedge multiplication by \(\sum_i a_ie_i\) satisfies \(dh+hd=1\) by the signed product rule, and contracts its Koszul complex. These three cases show that the power list has zero first homology at every prime. Localization commutes with the complex and its homology; a module whose localizations at all primes vanish is zero. The global \(H_1\) therefore vanishes as well.

The preceding pure-last-coefficient calculation now applies to \(g\) on \(N\). Substituting \(f_i=g_i+U_ig_r\) for \(i<r\) and \(f_r=U_rg_r\) makes the coefficient of \(g_r^n\) equal to \(\sum_{|a|=n}m_aU^a\). Thus this element belongs to \(JN\). Since \(N/JN=(M/JM)\otimes_AB\) is the direct sum of its Laurent monomial copies of \(M/JM\), each coefficient \(m_a\) belongs to \(JM\). This proves injectivity of \(\theta\) in every degree.

For the converse, suppose \(\theta\) is an isomorphism. Krull intersection, AG-CA-03, Theorem 6.1, gives \(\bigcap_{n\geq0}J^nM=0\). Every nonzero \(m\in M\) therefore has a finite order \(v\), characterized by \(m\in J^vM\setminus J^{v+1}M\). Its initial class is nonzero; multiplication by \(T_1\) is injective on \((M/JM)[T_1,\ldots,T_r]\), so \(f_1m\) is nonzero and has order \(v+1\). In particular \(f_1\) acts injectively on \(M\). The same calculation gives \[f_1M\cap J^nM=f_1J^{n-1}M\qquad(n\geq1):\] if \(f_1m\in J^nM\) and \(m\ne0\), its order forces \(m\in J^{n-1}M\); the reverse inclusion follows from \(f_1\in J\).

Set \(M'=M/f_1M\) and let \(J'\) be the ideal induced by \(J\). In degree \(n\geq1\), the last equality identifies the kernel of \(J^nM/J^{n+1}M\to J'^nM'/J'^{n+1}M'\) with multiplication by \(T_1\) from degree \(n-1\). Indeed an element in that kernel is \(y+f_1m\), with \(y\in J^{n+1}M\); then \(f_1m\in J^nM\), so \(m\in J^{n-1}M\). Degree zero is unchanged. It follows that \[\operatorname{gr}_{J'}M'\simeq(M/JM)[T_2,\ldots,T_r].\] Repeat the order and quotient argument for the remaining entries. Nakayama ensures that each finite intermediate module and the final quotient are nonzero. This proves regularity and hence all four equivalences. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-more-algebra-lemma-p-basis}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.119: p basis}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.119-p-basis}

Reading source: \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/unofficial-stacks-project-ai-drafts/blob/565b10e987aba5969b21145a0833f42d69f96790/more-algebra.tex\#L11972-L12025}{AI Integrated Stacks, pinned More Algebra, lines 11972--12025}.

Let \(L/F\) be a field extension of characteristic \(p>0\) and put \(E=FL^p\). A subset \(C\subset L\) is \emph{\(p\)-independent over \(F\)} when its monomials, with finite support and exponents between \(0\) and \(p-1\), are linearly independent over \(E\). It is a \emph{\(p\)-basis} when those monomials are a basis of \(L\) over \(E\). Independence holds exactly when the differentials \(dc\) are linearly independent over \(L\) in \(\Omega_{L/F}\). Every such subset extends to a \(p\)-basis. Moreover \(C\) is a \(p\)-basis exactly when its differentials form an \(L\)-basis of \(\Omega_{L/F}\).

\textbf{Proof.} All derivations over \(F\) annihilate \(E\): they kill \(F\), the product rule kills \(p\)th powers, and the inverse rule kills the field generated by these elements. We first construct the coordinate system for a maximal \(p\)-independent set.

Order the \(p\)-independent supersets of the prescribed set by inclusion. A chain has an independent union, since any proposed relation involves finitely many elements contained together in one member of the chain. Zorn's lemma gives a maximal set \(B\). For each finite \(B_0\subset B\), the algebra \(E[B_0]\) is spanned by its standard monomials, because \(b^p\in E\). It is a finite-dimensional domain and therefore a field: multiplication by any nonzero element is an injective linear endomorphism, hence surjective, and its inverse image of one supplies an inverse. The union \(E[B]\) is consequently a field as well.

Suppose \(x\in L\setminus E[B]\). Its minimal polynomial over that field divides \(T^p-x^p\). In \(L[T]\) this polynomial is \((T-x)^p\), and unique Euclidean factorization shows that any monic divisor is \((T-x)^r\). If \(0<r<p\) and this divisor were defined over \(E[B]\), its next coefficient \(-rx\) would put \(x\) there, a contradiction. Thus the minimal polynomial has degree \(p\). The power basis of this degree-\(p\) extension, together with independence of the old monomials, proves that \(B\cup\{x\}\) remains \(p\)-independent. Maximality rules this out, so \(E[B]=L\).

There is now an exact presentation \[
L=E[T_b:b\in B]/(T_b^p-b^p:b\in B).
\] Surjectivity follows from \(E[B]=L\). For injectivity, reduce a polynomial, which involves only finitely many variables, by the displayed monic relations. Its reduced standard-monomial expression can vanish only when every coefficient is zero, by \(p\)-independence. This proves the presentation for infinite sets too.

Differentiate polynomials in a single variable \(T_b\), killing \(E\) and all other variables. Each defining relation has derivative zero, so this operation descends through the exact presentation to an \(F\)-derivation \(\partial_b:L\to L\). It sends \(b\) to one and every other member of \(B\) to zero. These derivations prove that the \(db\) are independent. The finite monomial expansion of each element, differentiated by the product rule, proves they span \(\Omega_{L/F}\). This establishes the differential-basis assertion for \(B\), and shows that every \(p\)-independent subset has independent differentials.

Conversely, let \(dc_1,\ldots,dc_r\) be independent. Each coordinate functional on their span extends to all of \(\Omega_{L/F}\). For completeness, order the extensions to larger subspaces by extension; chain unions give compatible upper bounds. A maximal extension must have the whole space as domain, since otherwise one can adjoin a vector outside its domain and assign it value zero. This is another application of Zorn's lemma. The universal differential property turns these extended functionals into \(F\)-derivations \(D_i\) with \(D_i(c_j)=\delta_{ij}\), all killing \(E\).

If these elements had a nonzero standard-monomial relation over \(E\), choose its polynomial \(P\) with least total degree. This degree is positive. Some partial derivative of \(P\) is nonzero: a nonconstant monomial has a positive exponent strictly below \(p\), and distinct monomials containing that variable have distinct differentiated monomials. Applying the corresponding \(D_i\) gives the smaller-degree relation \((\partial P/\partial T_i)(c)=0\), a contradiction. Thus the finite set is \(p\)-independent. Since every relation on any subset is finite, this proves the equivalence in general.

Finally, if the \(dc\) form a basis, the equivalence makes \(C\) \(p\)-independent. Extend it to \(B\) by the construction above. An additional \(b\in B\setminus C\) would have a differential independent of all the \(dc\), contradicting their spanning property. Hence \(B=C\) and \(C\) is a \(p\)-basis. The converse has already been proved by the presentation. Empty bases and arbitrary infinite transcendence degree are included. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-more-algebra-lemma-power-series-ring-subfields}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.120: power series ring subfields}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.120-power-series-ring-subfields}

Reading source: \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/unofficial-stacks-project-ai-drafts/blob/565b10e987aba5969b21145a0833f42d69f96790/more-algebra.tex\#L12130-L12171}{AI Integrated Stacks, pinned More Algebra, lines 12130--12171}.

Let \(k\) have characteristic \(p>0\) and let \(B\) be a \(p\)-basis of \(k\) over \(\mathbf F_p\). Set \[A=k[[X_1,\ldots,X_n]][Y_1,\ldots,Y_m],\qquad K=\operatorname{Frac}(A).\] For each finite \(J\subset B\), define \[
k_J=k^p(B\setminus J),\quad
A_J=k_J[[X_1^p,\ldots,X_n^p]][Y_1^p,\ldots,Y_m^p],
\quad K_J=\operatorname{Frac}(A_J).
\] Then \(A\) is finite free over \(A_J\). The subfields \(K_J\) contain \(K^p\), are downward directed, and have intersection \(K^p\).

\textbf{Proof.} The whole \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-more-algebra-lemma-p-basis]{F.119} gives the standard monomial basis of \(k\) over \(k^p\). In particular the subalgebra generated by any subset of \(B\) is a field: each element lies in a finite-dimensional domain generated by finitely many of those elements, and multiplication by a nonzero element gives its inverse there. Thus \(k_J=k^p[B\setminus J]\).

The \(p^{|J|}\) monomials in \(J\) form a basis of \(k\) over \(k_J\). They span by grouping each finite standard-monomial expansion according to its exponents in \(J\). For independence, expand any finitely many coefficients from \(k_J\) in the monomials of \(B\setminus J\). A relation then becomes a relation between distinct monomials in the full \(p\)-basis, so all coefficients vanish. The same uniqueness shows \[\bigcap_{J\subset B,\ J\ {\rm finite}}k_J=k^p:\] if an element's unique finite expansion has a monomial involving \(b\in B\), it cannot belong to \(k_{\{b\}}\).

The algebra \(A\) is a domain. For two nonzero power series, the product of their first nonzero total-degree homogeneous polynomials is nonzero: polynomial domains follow by taking a leading monomial. This product is the first nonzero homogeneous part of their product. Adjoining the polynomial variables preserves the domain property by the same leading-monomial test.

A basis of \(A\) as an \(A_J\)-module is the finite list \[
\left\{\prod_{b\in J}b^{e_b}\prod_iX_i^{r_i}\prod_jY_j^{s_j}:
0\leq e_b,r_i,s_j<p\right\}.
\] Indeed expand each coefficient in the finite \(k_J\)-basis just proved, and group the \(X\) and \(Y\) exponents by their residues modulo \(p\). The grouped coefficients are power series in \(X^p\) and polynomials in \(Y^p\) over \(k_J\). There are finitely many \(Y\) terms initially, so these expressions remain polynomials. Coefficient comparison and uniqueness of the field basis prove linear independence. The rank is \(p^{|J|+n+m}\), including empty variable lists.

The characteristic-\(p\) identity for a series is computed in each finite degree, where only finitely many terms contribute. It gives \(a^p\in A_J\) for every \(a\in A\), hence \(K^p\subset K_J\). Also \(k_{J\cup J'}\subset k_J\cap k_{J'}\), so \(K_{J\cup J'}\subset K_J\cap K_{J'}\). This proves downward directedness.

It remains to identify the intersection; fractions cannot be compared by their coefficients directly. Write a candidate as \(u=f/g^p\) with \(f,g\in A\) and \(g\ne0\), by multiplying an arbitrary numerator and denominator by the \((p-1)\)st power of its denominator. Fix finite \(J\) and suppose \(u\in K_J\). Writing it as \(a/h\) with \(a,h\in A_J\), \(h\ne0\), gives \[u=(ah^{p-1})/h^p.\] Rename this numerator \(a\) and put \(b=h\). Cross multiplication yields \(b^pf=ag^p\in A_J\).

Any \(A_J\)-derivation \(D:A\to A\) consequently gives \(b^pD(f)=0\), because the derivatives of \(p\)th powers vanish. The domain property makes \(D(f)=0\). The formal partial derivatives in every \(X_i\) and \(Y_j\) are such derivations. Their product rules hold coefficient by coefficient, since each convolution coefficient is a finite sum. Distinct monomials containing a given variable have distinct derivative monomials; their scalar exponents are nonzero precisely when not divisible by \(p\). Therefore only exponents divisible by \(p\) can occur in \(f\).

For \(b\in J\), the coordinate derivation of \(k/k_J\) differentiates its unique \(J\)-monomial expansion. It kills \(k_J\) and exists by the exact presentation in F.119, or by restricting its \(b\)-coordinate derivation. Its extension to \(A\) applies it to each coefficient and kills \(X,Y\); the finite convolution formula again proves the product rule. The common kernel of these derivations on \(k\) is exactly \(k_J\): differentiation of the finite \(J\)-basis expansion kills precisely the coefficient terms with a positive exponent in an excluded variable. Thus every coefficient of \(f\) belongs to \(k_J\).

If \(u\) belongs to every \(K_J\), all these conclusions hold for every finite \(J\). Its coefficients then lie in \(k^p\) by the field intersection above, and all its variable exponents are multiples of \(p\). Choose the unique \(p\)th root of each coefficient and divide each exponent by \(p\); this defines an element \(v\in A\) with \(v^p=f\). The polynomial variables still have bounded degree. It follows that \(u=(v/g)^p\in K^p\). Together with the first inclusion this proves the claimed intersection, even with an infinite coefficient \(p\)-basis. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-more-algebra-lemma-quasi-regular-ideal-finite-projective}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.121: quasi regular ideal finite projective}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.121-quasi-regular-ideal-finite-projective}

Reading source: \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/unofficial-stacks-project-ai-drafts/blob/565b10e987aba5969b21145a0833f42d69f96790/more-algebra.tex\#L8769-L8778}{AI Integrated Stacks, pinned More Algebra, lines 8769--8778}.

For an arbitrary ring \(R\) and quasi-regular ideal \(I\), the module \(I/I^2\) is finite projective over \(R/I\).

\textbf{Proof.} Put \(S=R/I\) and \(M=I/I^2\). If \(S=0\), then \(I=R\) and \(M=0\), so the assertion holds. Otherwise the explicit quasi-regularity definition \hyperref[AG-RG-S05-more-algebra-definition-regular-ideal]{F.95} gives principal neighbourhoods of all primes of \(S\) on which the ideal is generated by a finite quasi-regular list. The degree-one graded isomorphism identifies its conormal module with the free module on that list. Exact localization gives the same identification for \(M_g\) over \(S_g\).

The chart denominators generate \(S\): if their ideal were proper, a maximal ideal containing it would lie outside every chart. A finite list \(g_1,\ldots,g_s\) therefore already generates the unit ideal and supplies finite free localizations of \(M\). We record the detection argument needed without any finiteness assumption on a module \(N\). If \(N_{g_i}=0\) for every \(i\), each \(x\in N\) satisfies \(g_i^{e_i}x=0\) for positive integers \(e_i\). These powers generate the unit ideal too, since a maximal ideal containing all of them would contain all the \(g_i\). Multiply an expression \(1=\sum_i a_i g_i^{e_i}\) by \(x\) to obtain \(x=0\). Hence \(N=0\).

For every local basis, represent its finitely many elements by fractions from \(M\) and take their numerators. Multiplication by the corresponding powers of the unit \(g_i\) still gives a basis locally. The finite submodule generated by all these numerators has quotient zero on every chart; the detection argument makes that quotient zero globally. Thus \(M\) is finite. Choose a finite free surjection \(S^t\to M\) with kernel \(H\).

Localizing on a chart gives a surjection onto a finite free module, so it splits by lifting a basis. The complementary projection of the \(t\) standard vectors then generates \(H_{g_i}\). Exact localization identifies this kernel with the localization of \(H\); clear the finitely many denominators of its displayed generators and collect their numerators from \(H\). They generate a finite submodule \(H_0\) with \((H/H_0)_{g_i}=0\) everywhere. Detection again gives \(H=H_0\), so \(M\) is finitely presented.

Every stalk of \(M\) is free, because a chart contains that prime. The entire \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/d02d0a3669f42579db037cd44de1d113fdd770a1/docs/courses/AG-CA/src/tor-and-flat-modules.md}{AG-CA-07, Theorem 3.3} gives flatness over \(S\). The full proof of \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/d02d0a3669f42579db037cd44de1d113fdd770a1/docs/courses/AG-CA/src/tor-and-flat-modules.md}{AG-CA-07, Theorem 5.3} then splits a finite presentation of this flat module, making it a direct summand of a finite free module. This is finite projectivity. The argument supplies the missing global finite presentation and applies without Noetherianity or finite generation of \(I\) in \(R\). ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-more-algebra-lemma-quotient-regular}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.122: quotient regular}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.122-quotient-regular}

Reading source: \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/unofficial-stacks-project-ai-drafts/blob/565b10e987aba5969b21145a0833f42d69f96790/more-algebra.tex\#L12407-L12424}{AI Integrated Stacks, pinned More Algebra, lines 12407--12424}.

Let \(R\) be a Noetherian regular ring. If a derivation \(D:R\to R\) satisfies that \(D(f)\) is a unit in \(R/(f)\), then \(R/(f)\) is regular.

\textbf{Proof.} Fix a prime \(\mathfrak p\) containing \(f\) and set \(V=R_{\mathfrak p}\), \(\mathfrak m=\mathfrak pV\). We first extend the derivation without a finiteness or continuity assumption. The map \[r\longmapsto r+\epsilon D(r),\qquad \epsilon^2=0,\] is a ring homomorphism to \(V[\epsilon]/(\epsilon^2)\) by the product rule. For \(s\notin\mathfrak p\) its image has the explicit inverse \(s^{-1}-\epsilon s^{-2}D(s)\). The universal property of localization extends this map to \(V\). Its constant component is the identity, so its \(\epsilon\) component is a derivation \(D_V:V\to V\) extending \(D\), with \[D_V(a/s)=D(a)/s-aD(s)/s^2.\] This construction proves well-definedness and the product rule for the fraction formula.

The hypothesis gives \(uD(f)+vf=1\) for some \(u,v\in R\). At \(\mathfrak p\), this makes \(D_V(f)\) a unit modulo \(\mathfrak m\), and in particular outside \(\mathfrak m\). If \(f\) belonged to \(\mathfrak m^2\), express it as a finite sum \(\sum_j a_jb_j\) with \(a_j,b_j\in\mathfrak m\). The product rule would give \[D_V(f)=\sum_j\bigl(a_jD_V(b_j)+b_jD_V(a_j)\bigr)\in\mathfrak m,\] a contradiction. Thus \(f\in\mathfrak m\setminus\mathfrak m^2\).

Regularity of \(R\) makes \(V\) regular local. The entire \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/d02d0a3669f42579db037cd44de1d113fdd770a1/docs/courses/AG-CA/src/regular-local-rings.md}{AG-CA-14, Corollary 1.2} proves \(V/fV\) regular: extend the nonzero class of \(f\) to a cotangent basis, lift it, and apply the proved successive parameter-quotient theorem. These quotients are exactly the local rings of \(R/(f)\) at its corresponding primes. The quotient is Noetherian, so this proves regularity. If no prime contains \(f\), the quotient is zero and has no local rings to test. ∎

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-S05-more-algebra-lemma-regular-base-change}

\subsubsection{Lemma F.123: regular base change}\label{AG-RG-S05-lemma-f.123-regular-base-change}

Reading source: \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/unofficial-stacks-project-ai-drafts/blob/565b10e987aba5969b21145a0833f42d69f96790/more-algebra.tex\#L11022-L11047}{AI Integrated Stacks, pinned More Algebra, lines 11022--11047}.

For a regular map \(R\to\Lambda\) of Noetherian rings and any finite-type \(R\)-algebra \(R'\), the map \[R'\longrightarrow T=\Lambda\otimes_RR'\] is regular.

\textbf{Proof.} Both \(R'\) and \(T\) are Noetherian: a finite algebra-generating list for \(R'\) makes it a quotient of a polynomial ring over \(R\), and makes \(T\) a quotient of the corresponding polynomial ring over \(\Lambda\). The entire Hilbert basis theorem AG-CA-03, Theorem 2.1, applies to each.
