Indeed a matrix which commutes with every matrix unit is scalar over any \(k\)-algebra: the diagonal units kill its off-diagonal entries, and the other matrix units make all diagonal entries equal. An invertible scalar matrix has a unit scalar. Such a matrix fixes the line \(kv\), so its preimage in \(C\) belongs to the schematic stabilizer \(M\). Conversely the scalar action just proved makes every \(M\)-point lie in the kernel. This avoids any assumption that a projective linear image is already the desired quotient.

Let \(H\) be the schematic image of \(\rho\). It is an affine finite-type group: its coordinate algebra is the finitely generated Hopf subalgebra \[
 B=\operatorname{im}\bigl(k[\operatorname{GL}(\operatorname{End}W)]\longrightarrow k[C]\bigr),
\] and the kernel of the coordinate map is a Hopf ideal. To check the full Hopf structure, write the ambient coordinate algebra as \(P\) and its kernel as \(J\). The identity \(\ker(P\otimes_k P\to B\otimes_k B)=J\otimes_k P+P\otimes_k J\) follows by taking vector-space complements to \(J\). The injection \(B\otimes_k B\hookrightarrow k[C]\otimes_k k[C]\) and the group homomorphism identity make comultiplication preserve that kernel; the identity and inverse maps give the counit and antipode identities. Thus all Hopf operations descend. For every field extension \(L/k\), the injection \(B\hookrightarrow k[C]\) remains injective after tensoring. Since \(C_{\bar k}\) is smooth connected and therefore integral by Lemma 2.L, \(H_{\bar k}\) is integral as well. The reduced-target image proof in AG-GS, \emph{Quotients and torsors}, Lemma 11.1c applies over \(\bar k\) and makes \(C_{\bar k}\to H_{\bar k}\) faithfully flat of finite presentation. Its full kernel is \(M_{\bar k}\). The integral algebraic group \(H_{\bar k}\) is smooth by the reduction argument of Lemma 2.L. Faithfully flat descent, S04 Lemmas A1.3 and A1.3a, consequently makes \(C\to H\) faithfully flat of finite presentation and \(H\) smooth over \(k\). Its geometric fibre is connected, because it is the surjective image of \(C_{\bar k}\).

For every test scheme, two \(C\)-points have the same image in \(H\) exactly when their quotient lies in \(M\). Multiplication and quotient give inverse maps \[
 C\times M\xrightarrow{\sim}C\times_H C,
 \qquad(c,m)\longmapsto(c,cm),\qquad
 (c,d)\longmapsto(c,c^{-1}d).
\] The faithfully flat map \(C\to H\) therefore is an \(M\)-torsor and identifies \(H\) with the fppf quotient \(C/M\). Applying the full orbit-dimension calculation of S08 Lemma G.4.D over \(\bar k\) gives \[
 \dim H=\dim C-\dim M<\dim G.
\] Dimension is unchanged by field extension by that same lemma. The induction hypothesis now supplies a geometrically maximal \(k\)-torus \(Q\subset H\).

Put \(E=C\times_H Q\), an affine closed subgroup of \(C\). Its map to \(Q\) is the base change of the \(M\)-torsor. Every geometric fibre is a nonempty finite-type \(M\)-torsor over an algebraically closed field. The weak Nullstellensatz gives a rational point; translating by that point identifies the full fibre scheme with the split torus \(M\) over that field. The map is flat of finite presentation; the fibre criterion of AG-FSE, \emph{Smooth morphisms}, Theorem 3.1 makes \(E\to Q\) smooth. Hence \(E\) is smooth over \(k\). It is geometrically connected. To check this over \(\bar k\), its smooth components are disjoint open and closed by Lemma 2.L. Their images in \(Q_{\bar k}\) are open by S08 Lemma G.4.F. A connected fibre cannot meet two such components, so those images are disjoint; surjectivity makes them cover the connected \(Q_{\bar k}\). There is only one component.

The quotient \(Q\) is commutative and the kernel \(M\) is central, so the commutator of \(E\) takes values in \(M\), and the next commutator is trivial. Thus \(E_{\bar k}\) is a smooth connected solvable group. Theorem 2.K writes it as its smooth connected unitriangular radical semidirect a torus. Every character of that radical is trivial by Lemma 2.A, so its map to \(Q_{\bar k}\) is trivial and it lies in \(M_{\bar k}\). Lemma 2.A also makes its intersection with this diagonalizable group trivial, with full scheme structure. The radical is therefore the identity, and \(E_{\bar k}\) is a torus. The complete field splitting proof in \href{AG-RG-S08.html\#finite-separable-splitting}{AG-RG-S08, Lemma G.0.T} gives a finite separable extension over which \(E\) is the split torus with its free geometric character group. Thus \(E\) is a \(k\)-torus.

Finally suppose a \(\bar k\)-torus \(A\subset G_{\bar k}\) contains \(E_{\bar k}\). It contains \(M_{\bar k}\), hence centralizes it; its connected image lies in the identity component \(C_{\bar k}\), with full scheme factorization from S08 Lemma G.0.1. Lemma 4.S represents the fppf quotient \(A/M_{\bar k}\) as a split torus: its character group is the kernel of the surjection \(X^*(A)\to X^*(M_{\bar k})\), a finite free subgroup of \(X^*(A)\). The full torsor relation for \(C\to H\) makes the map \(A\to H_{\bar k}\) constant on the \(M\)-fibres, so S04 Lemma A1.5 descends it to this quotient.

Its induced map \(A/M_{\bar k}\to H_{\bar k}\) has trivial schematic kernel. On any test scheme, lift a kernel point fppf-locally to \(A\). Its image in \(H\) is the identity, so that lift lies in the full kernel \(M\) of \(C\to H\); its quotient point is therefore the identity. Faithful descent of this equality proves triviality before the cover, including nilpotent test schemes. The closed-embedding assertion of Lemma 4.S now makes its image a closed torus in \(H_{\bar k}\). It contains \(Q_{\bar k}\), because \(E\subset A\) and \(E\to Q\) is fppf-surjective. Geometric maximality of \(Q\) makes that image \(Q_{\bar k}\). Consequently the map of \(A\) factors through \(C_{\bar k}\times_{H_{\bar k}}Q_{\bar k}=E_{\bar k}\). Since the opposite inclusion was assumed, \(A=E_{\bar k}\) as closed subgroup schemes. Thus \(E\) is geometrically maximal in \(G\), proving the lemma. \(\square\)

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-01-central-affine-quotient}

\textbf{Lemma 4.Q (the central affine quotients used in the induction).} Let \(G\) be a smooth geometrically connected affine group over a field \(k\), and let \(D\subset G\) be any closed central subgroup. Its fppf quotient is represented by a smooth geometrically connected affine \(k\)-group \(H\). The map \(G\to H\) is faithfully flat of finite presentation with full kernel \(D\), and is a \(D\)-torsor. If \(D\) is finite, this map is finite locally free of rank \(\dim_k k[D]\).

\textbf{Proof.} Smoothness makes \(G\) locally of finite type, and S08 Lemma G.0.3 makes its connected identity component quasi-compact; thus \(G\) is of finite type. The complete detecting-line construction of Section 2 gives a finite-dimensional representation \(V\) and a nonzero vector \(v\) whose line has full schematic stabilizer \(D\). Let \(W\) be the cyclic subrepresentation generated by \(v\). Concretely write its coaction as \(\sum_i w_i\otimes a_i\) with independent \(a_i\in k[G]\). The counit puts \(v\) in their span; coassociativity and coefficient functionals make that span a subrepresentation. The character \(\chi\) of \(D\) on \(kv\) acts by the same scalar on \(W\): on the universal \(G\times D\) point, centrality gives \(d(gv)=g(dv)=\chi(d)gv\), and independence of the \(a_i\) compares every coefficient. This is an equality on every test algebra, including nilpotent ones.

Let \(\rho:G\to\operatorname{GL}(\operatorname{End}_k W)\) be conjugation through the representation on \(W\). Its kernel is \(D\). A matrix commuting with all matrix units is scalar over any algebra: the diagonal units force every off-diagonal entry to vanish and the other units make all diagonal entries equal. Its invertibility makes that scalar a unit. Such an element fixes \(kv\) in \(V\), hence belongs to \(D\); conversely the scalar action of \(D\) just proved makes it lie in the kernel.

Put \(B=\operatorname{im}(k[\operatorname{GL}(\operatorname{End}W)]\to k[G])\) and \(H=\operatorname{Spec}B\). This is a finite-type Hopf algebra and defines an affine group. To check the Hopf ideal explicitly, the injection \(B\hookrightarrow k[G]\) remains injective on tensor squares over the field. Write \(P=k[\operatorname{GL}(\operatorname{End}W)]\) and \(J\) for the kernel. Exact field tensor gives \(\ker(P\otimes P\to B\otimes B)=J\otimes P+P\otimes J\). Comultiplication of \(u\in J\) maps to zero in \(k[G]\otimes k[G]\), hence in its injected \(B\otimes B\); therefore \(\Delta(u)\in J\otimes P+P\otimes J\). Compatibility of the counit and antipode gives \(\epsilon(J)=0\) and \(S(J)\subset J\). The group operations therefore descend to \(B\). Exact field tensor also makes \(B_{\bar k}\) the image algebra after extension. Since \(G_{\bar k}\) is smooth connected, its algebra is a domain by Lemma 2.L; hence \(B_{\bar k}\) is a domain.

The complete integral-target image argument of AG-GS, \emph{Quotients and torsors}, Lemma 11.1c applies to \(G_{\bar k}\to H_{\bar k}\), whose coordinate map is injective. It is faithfully flat of finite presentation. S04 Lemma A1.3 descends flatness, and Lemma A1.3a descends finite presentation along \(B\to B\otimes_k\bar k\). Faithfulness also descends: if tensoring a \(B\)-module with \(k[G]\) gives zero, extending to \(\bar k\) and using the faithful map upstairs makes its extended module zero, and faithful field tensor then makes the original module zero. Thus \(G\to H\) is faithfully flat of finite presentation. The integral group \(H_{\bar k}\) is smooth by Lemma 2.L and connected as the surjective image of \(G_{\bar k}\). The full field smoothness-descent proof of S08 Lemma G.2.1 makes \(H\) smooth over \(k\); the same geometric image argument proves geometric connectedness.

The kernel calculation gives the full torsor relation \[
 G\times D\xrightarrow{\sim}G\times_H G,
 \qquad(g,d)\longmapsto(g,gd),
 \qquad(g,h)\longmapsto(g,g^{-1}h).
\] Both are scheme morphisms and are inverse on every test scheme, because equality of the two images is exactly membership of their quotient in \(D\). The fppf cover \(G\to H\), with this relation, identifies its sheaf quotient by \(D\) with \(H\): every \(H\)-point lifts fppf-locally, and two lifts differ uniquely by \(D\).

If \(D\) is finite, pull back the quotient map along its own faithfully flat cover \(G\to H\). Its coordinate module becomes \(k[G]\otimes_k k[D]\), free of rank \(\dim_k k[D]\) over \(k[G]\). The finite generation, finite presentation and flatness descent in S04 Lemma A1.3 makes the original \(B\)-module \(k[G]\) finite locally free. The rank can be read after the same cover, and is that constant dimension. Thus the quotient map is finite locally free of precisely that rank. \(\square\)

\textbf{Lemma 4.A (a commutative finite extension of multiplicative-type groups).} A finite commutative \(k\)-group \(E\) in an fppf exact sequence \[
 1\longrightarrow N\longrightarrow E\longrightarrow Q\longrightarrow1
\] with \(N\) and \(Q\) of multiplicative type is of multiplicative type.

\textbf{Proof.} Work first over an algebraic closure. Both end groups are diagonalizable, and their invariant functors are exact by the complete weight decomposition in AG-GS, \emph{Diagonalizable groups}, Theorem 3.1. For a finite-dimensional \(E\)-representation \(W\), the space \(W^N\) is \(E\)-stable, since \(N\) is normal. Its action factors through \(Q\) on all test schemes. Indeed the kernel identity gives the full torsor relation \(E\times N\simeq E\times_Q E\), with inverse \((a,b)\mapsto(a,a^{-1}b)\). The fppf-surjective quotient becomes \(N\) times its base after an fppf lift. The finite \(Q\) has a finite discrete spectrum by Artinian decomposition. Choose finitely many affine pieces of such lifts covering those points and combine them into one affine faithfully flat cover. The trivial projection is flat; flat descent from AG-CA, \emph{Faithful flatness and the local criterion for flatness}, Corollary 3.2 makes the quotient flat, and its surjectivity makes it faithfully flat. Each matrix coefficient of the action on \(W^N\) has equal pullbacks along that relation, because \(N\) acts trivially. The faithfully flat equalizer proved in AG-RG-S04, Lemma A1.0 descends these coefficients to \(Q\); its algebra and group identities descend by the same faithful comparison. Hence \[
 W^E=(W^N)^Q,
\] and \(E\)-invariants are exact.

For a subrepresentation \(V\subset W\), the map \[
 \operatorname{Hom}(W/V,W)\longrightarrow\operatorname{Hom}(W/V,W/V)
\] is a surjective equivariant linear map: lift the images of a vector-space basis to prove surjectivity, and use the representation \((g\cdot f)(v)=g f(g^{-1}v)\) on each Hom space for equivariance. Exactness of invariants lifts its invariant identity to an equivariant section. A nonzero finite-dimensional representation has a simple subrepresentation by choosing a nonzero subrepresentation of smallest dimension. The section splits it off, and induction on dimension decomposes every finite-dimensional representation into simples.

Put \(C=k[E]\) and \(H=C^\vee\). Choose a basis \(c_j\) of \(C\) with dual basis \(h_j\) of \(H\). A coaction \(\lambda\) defines \(h w=(1\otimes h)\lambda(w)\), and an \(H\)-action defines \(\lambda(w)=\sum_j(h_j w)\otimes c_j\). These formulas are inverse by the dual-basis identity. Pairing both tensor factors with that basis identifies coassociativity with associativity of the action, and the counit identity with its unit identity. Thus \(C\)-comodules and \(H\)-modules are exactly the same representations. Since \(E\) is commutative, its comultiplication on \(C\) is cocommutative, so the finite-dimensional algebra \(H\) is commutative. Its regular module is semisimple by the preceding paragraph. Decompose it into simple ideals \(H=\bigoplus_i L_i\), and project one to \(e_i\in L_i\). For \(x\in L_i\), the products \(xe_j\) lie in \(L_i\cap L_j\), hence vanish for \(j\ne i\), while \(x=\sum_j xe_j=xe_i\). Thus \(e_i\) is the identity of \(L_i\), the \(e_i\) are orthogonal idempotents and each commutative \(L_i\) has no proper nonzero ideal. Every nonzero element is invertible, so each \(L_i\) is a field. It is a finite extension of the algebraically closed base, and therefore equals that base. Hence \(H=k^M\) for a finite set \(M\).

The Hopf maps of \(H\) give a group structure on this finite set: a map between finite products of the field sends a standard idempotent to a sum of standard idempotents, and hence specifies a map between their indexing sets. The Hopf identities give associativity, identity and inverse. Commutativity of \(C\) makes the dual comultiplication cocommutative, so \(M\) is abelian. Dualizing its idempotent basis gives the group-algebra Hopf algebra \(C=k[M]\): basis products encode the multiplication of \(M\), and each basis element has comultiplication \(e^m\otimes e^m\) and counit one. Thus \(E\) is diagonalizable over the algebraic closure. The full finite-separable splitting proof of AG-RG-S08, Lemma G.0.T now proves the assertion over the original \(k\), including imperfect fields. \(\square\)

\textbf{Lemma 4.B (composite kernels stay central).} Suppose \(G\) is smooth geometrically connected, \(N\) is a finite connected central multiplicative-type subgroup, and \(Q\) is a finite connected central multiplicative-type subgroup of \(G/N\). Its inverse image \(E\) in \(G\) is finite connected central and of multiplicative type.

\textbf{Proof.} The kernel identity gives \(E\times N\simeq E\times_Q E\), and fppf-local lifts identify \(E\to Q\) with the projection from \(N\) times the base. The finite \(Q\) has a finite discrete spectrum by Artinian decomposition, so finitely many affine pieces of these lifts give a single affine faithfully flat cover. Effective affine descent in S04 Lemma A1.2, with comparison morphisms from Lemma A1.5, represents this torsor by an affine scheme. Its coordinate module becomes free of rank \(\dim_k k[N]\) after that cover. S04 Lemma A1.3 descends finite local freeness, and the local lifts give surjectivity. Thus \(E\to Q\) is finite faithfully flat and \(E\) is finite over \(k\). After algebraic closure, Lemma G.0.2 of S08 makes the finite connected \(N\) and \(Q\) connected; each has one underlying point and has its identity as a rational point. The single geometric fibre of \(E\to Q\) is a nonempty finite-type \(N\)-torsor. A rational point supplied by the weak Nullstellensatz identifies its full scheme with \(N\). Thus \(E\) is geometrically connected, hence connected.

Since \(Q\) is commutative and \(N\) is central, the commutators in \(E\) take values in \(N\). Replacing either lift by its product with an element of \(N\) leaves that commutator unchanged. The fppf comparison proof in S04 Lemma A1.5 therefore descends the commutator to \(b:Q\times Q\to N\). The identities \([aa',c]=[a,c][a',c]\) and \([a,cc']=[a,c][a,c']\), when the commutators are central, make \(b\) a homomorphism in each variable. They follow by inserting \(a'^{-1}a^{-1}\) and the other inverse products into the commutator formula and commuting only the central commutators.

Over the algebraic closure write \(Q=D(M_Q)\), \(N=D(M_N)\), and put \(R=k[Q]\). As a family of homomorphisms in the second variable, \(b\) is a Hopf map \(R[M_N]\to R[M_Q]\). The coefficient calculation in S08 Lemma G.0.T makes the image of each character a sum of basis characters with orthogonal idempotent coefficients summing to one. A connected ring spectrum has only idempotents zero and one: \(D(c)\) and \(D(1-c)\) are disjoint clopen subsets covering it, and a nonzero idempotent is not nilpotent, so has a nonempty principal open by S04 Lemma P0.1. Consequently the image is one basis character, independent of the first variable even along nilpotent test directions. Evaluation at that variable's identity gives the trivial homomorphism. Thus every character maps to one and \(b\) is trivial as a scheme map. Faithful scalar extension proves that \(E\) is commutative over the original field. Lemma 4.A makes \(E\) of multiplicative type.

Conjugation preserves \(E\), as the preimage of the normal \(Q\). Over the algebraic closure write \(E=D(M_E)\). On any nonempty affine open of \(G\), conjugation is a family of group homomorphisms of this diagonalizable group. That open is irreducible by S08 Lemma G.0.3, hence connected. The same coefficient argument makes every character image a fixed basis character throughout the open, including its nilpotents. Any two such opens meet and their families agree there, so their basis characters agree; for example evaluate at a rational point of the nonempty intersection. The open containing the identity gives the identity homomorphism. Thus conjugation is the identity family on all of \(G\). Faithful field descent proves centrality schematically over \(k\).

In the affine case used in Theorem 4.2, the full central-quotient proof of Lemma 4.Q applies to the now-central \(E\). It represents \(G/E\) as a smooth geometrically connected affine group and makes \(G\to G/E\) finite locally free of rank \(\dim_k k[E]\). This additional affineness assertion uses the affine hypothesis; the central-kernel statement above retains its stated generality. \(\square\)

\textbf{Lemma 4.C (descending the torus in a central affine group).} Let \(Z\) be an affine commutative algebraic \(k\)-group. The torus factor of \((Z_{\bar k}^0)_{\mathrm{red}}\) is defined over \(k\). In particular, a nontrivial such torus descends even if \(k\) is imperfect.

\textbf{Proof.} Let \(n\) range over the positive integers invertible in \(k\), and let \(I_n\subset A=k[Z]\) define \(Z[n]\). Its coordinate algebra is finite and is a product of finite separable field extensions. Here is the full calculation. The differential of multiplication at the identity is addition: its restrictions to either tangent summand are the identity, so its linear map is their sum. Iterating gives \(d[n]=n\), whose kernel is zero. Thus \(Z[n]\) has zero tangent space at the identity and, by translation, at every rational point over an algebraic closure. On each of its Noetherian local rings at such a point, \(\mathfrak m/\mathfrak m^2=0\); Nakayama gives \(\mathfrak m=0\). Every prime lies under a maximal ideal, and the local field there has no smaller prime, so every prime is maximal. The zero-dimensional Noetherian and Artinian decomposition proofs of AG-CA, \emph{Noetherian and Artinian rings}, Theorems 3.3 and 4.2 make the geometric coordinate algebra a finite product of copies of \(\bar k\), using the weak Nullstellensatz for their residue fields. The finite-algebra argument in S08 Lemma G.0.T now applies: independence of vectors proves finite dimensionality before extension; injectivity proves reducedness; and an inseparable element in a field factor would give a nonzero nilpotent after extension. Thus all its finite field factors are separable. In particular every \(Z[n]\) is geometrically reduced.

Define the ideal and closed subscheme directly over the original field by \[
 I=\bigcap_{\substack{n\in\mathbf Z_{>0}\\ n\cdot1_k\ne0}} I_n,
 \qquad Y=\operatorname{Spec}(A/I).
\] Here the indexing condition means that the integer \(n\) is invertible in \(k\). This intersection commutes with every field extension \(L/k\). Write an element of \(A\otimes_kL\) as \(\sum_i f_i\otimes a_i\), with the finitely many \(a_i\) linearly independent over \(k\). Its image in \((A/I_n)\otimes_k L\) is zero precisely when each \(f_i\) lies in \(I_n\), by applying linear functionals selecting these coefficients. Membership in every extended ideal is therefore precisely membership in \(I\otimes_kL\). Consequently \((A/I)\otimes_kL\) embeds in the product of the reduced algebras \((A/I_n)\otimes_kL\). It is reduced. Thus \(Y\) is geometrically reduced, and the closure construction commutes with all field extensions without a perfectness assumption.

Over \(\bar k\), put \(H=\bigcup_n Z[n](\bar k)\). These finite schemes are reduced, so their rational-point evaluations detect their functions; the preceding intersection equality says exactly that \(Y_{\bar k}\) is the reduced schematic closure of \(H\). The set \(H\) is a subgroup, since \(Z\) is commutative and the product of elements killed by \(n\) and \(m\) is killed by \(nm\). It is schematically dense in \(Y_{\bar k}\), and \(H\times H\) is schematically dense in its product. For the latter assertion write a tensor as \(\sum_i b_i\otimes c_i\) with the \(c_i\) independent. If its values on \(H\times H\) vanish, evaluation at each first-coordinate point gives an element vanishing on all second-coordinate points, hence zero. Independence makes each \(b_i\) vanish on \(H\), hence zero. Multiplication, inverse and identity therefore restrict to \(Y_{\bar k}\): the equations of \(Y\) pull back to zero on those dense sets. The same equations hold before extension by faithful field tensor. Thus \(Y\) is a \(k\)-subgroup of \(Z\), with its full scheme structure.

Over \(\bar k\), put \(R=(Z_{\bar k}^0)_{\mathrm{red}}\). Reduction is a subgroup here: products of reduced finite-type schemes are reduced by S08 Lemma G.4.1, so the group operations factor through it. This connected commutative group is smooth by Lemma 2.L. The complete solvable structure theorem 2.K gives \(R=T_Z\times U_Z\), since commutativity makes the semidirect action trivial. The unitriangular factor has no nontrivial torsion of order invertible in the field. In characteristic \(p\), a matrix \(1+N\), with \(N\) nilpotent, has \(p\)-power order by \((1+N)^{p^r}=1+N^{p^r}\). In characteristic zero, if \((1+N)^n=1\), its binomial expansion is \(N(nI+N B)=0\) for a polynomial \(B\) in \(N\); the second factor is invertible by a finite geometric sum, so \(N=0\). Hence \(H\cap R\) consists exactly of the invertible-order torsion points of \(T_Z\).

These points are schematically dense in \(T_Z\). For a nonzero Laurent polynomial choose an invertible integer \(n\) larger than every absolute coordinate difference between its finitely many exponent vectors. Those vectors are distinct modulo \(n\mathbf Z^r\), so their monomials stay independent in the coordinate algebra of \(T_Z[n]\). Its restriction is nonzero, and that finite reduced scheme has a rational point where it is nonzero. The identity component of \(Z_{\bar k}\) is open and closed by S08 Lemma G.0.3, so closure in that component is closure of the intersection with it. Its rational points factor through \(R\). It follows that the intersection of \(Y_{\bar k}\) with that component has exactly the underlying space of \(T_Z\). Both are reduced closed schemes there, hence equal as schemes; equivalently both defining ideals are the radical ideal of that same closed subset, by S04 Lemma P0.1. This intersection is connected, so \(Y_{\bar k}^0=T_Z\).

Finally put \(W=Y^0\), with the canonical component structure of S08 Lemma G.0.3. It is an open and closed \(k\)-subgroup, and that lemma's full field-base-change assertion gives \(W_{\bar k}=T_Z\) as schemes. It is affine and of finite type, being closed in the affine finite-type \(Y\). The complete finite-separable splitting proof of S08 Lemma G.0.T makes \(W\) a \(k\)-torus with that geometric fibre. This is the required descent. \(\square\)

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-01-central-kernel-order-and-finite-field-tori}

\textbf{Lemma 4.O (one order bound for a torus-free reduced centre).} Let \(Z\) be a connected commutative affine algebraic group over an algebraically closed field \(K\), retaining its possible nilpotents. If its reduction \(R\) has no nontrivial torus, there is one integer \(B\) bounding the order of every finite multiplicative-type closed subgroup \(E\subset Z\).

\textbf{Proof.} Put \(A=K[Z]\) and let \(J\) be its nilradical. S01 Lemmas 1.0 and 1.3 make \(A\) Noetherian, so \(J\) is generated by finitely many nilpotent elements \(u_i\). If \(u_i^{n_i}=0\), every monomial of degree \(1+\sum_i(n_i-1)\) contains one of these zero powers. Consequently choose \(N\ge1\) with \(J^N=0\). Let \(d\) generators generate the augmentation maximal ideal \(\mathfrak m\) of \(A\).

The reduction is a connected commutative subgroup: S08 Lemma G.4.1 makes \(R\times R\) reduced, so the multiplication and inverse maps kill the nilradical and factor through \(R\). Its underlying space is the connected space of \(Z\). Lemma 2.L makes this reduced group smooth. The full solvable structure of Theorem 2.K and the hypothesis make \(R\) unitriangular. Over \(K\), the subgroup \(E\) is diagonalizable by the definition of multiplicative type and S08 Lemma G.0.T. Its full intersection \(E\cap R\) is diagonalizable by Lemma 4.S. Lemma 2.A says that a diagonalizable subgroup of a unitriangular group is the trivial scheme, including when that subgroup is finite and nonreduced.

Write \(C=K[E]\). The intersection just computed has coordinate ring \(C/JC=K\), and the identity map shows that \(JC\) is the augmentation maximal ideal \(\mathfrak n\) of \(C\). It is generated by the images of the \(d\) generators of \(\mathfrak m\), since \(A\twoheadrightarrow C\). Moreover \(\mathfrak n^N=0\). For \(0\le j<N\), every class in \(\mathfrak n^j/\mathfrak n^{j+1}\) is a \(K\)-linear combination of the at most \(d^j\) words of length \(j\) in those generators: a coefficient in \(C\) can be reduced modulo \(\mathfrak n\), and its remainder raises the degree. For \(j=0\) the empty word gives the one-dimensional quotient. The finite filtration therefore gives the uniform bound \[
 |E|=\dim_K C\ \le\ B:=\sum_{j=0}^{N-1}d^j.
\] Take \(d^0=1\), including when \(d=0\). Both \(d\) and \(N\) depend only on \(Z\), proving the assertion. \(\square\)

\textbf{Lemma 4.G (finite-field Borel and maximal-torus descent).} A smooth connected affine group over \(\mathbf F_q\) has a Borel subgroup and a geometrically maximal torus defined over \(\mathbf F_q\).

\textbf{Proof.} Over \(\overline{\mathbf F}_q\), choose a torus \(T\) of largest dimension, starting with the trivial torus. Dimensions are bounded by \(\dim G\), and a proper inclusion of tori strictly increases dimension by the earlier domain dimension theorem; thus \(T\) is maximal. Choose a smooth connected solvable subgroup \(B\) of largest dimension containing \(T\), exactly as in the proof of Theorem 2.2; it is a Borel. Borel--torus pairs are conjugate: Lemma 2.1 first conjugates their Borels, and Lemma 2.N conjugates the two maximal tori within the common Borel.

Let \(\sigma(a)=a^q\) on the algebraic closure, and let \(\sigma(B,T)\) denote the full pair obtained by this coefficient transport. Since \(G\) is defined over \(\mathbf F_q\), it is again such a pair. Choose \(g\in G(\overline{\mathbf F}_q)\) with \(\sigma(B,T)=g(B,T)g^{-1}\). On rational points this coefficient transport is the Frobenius \(F\). Lemma 4.L gives \(h\) with \(h^{-1}F(h)=g^{-1}\). Consequently \(F(h)g=h\), and the full transported pair \((B',T')=h(B,T)h^{-1}\) satisfies \(\sigma(B',T')=(B',T')\), as closed subgroup schemes.

We give the finite descent details. The ambient coordinate algebra is finitely presented, and the two ideals have finite generating lists by S01 Lemmas 1.0 and 1.3. Their finitely many coefficients lie in a finite extension \(L/\mathbf F_q\), since every element of the algebraic closure is algebraic. Include the finitely many coefficients of their Hopf identities and finite algebra presentations as well, so they define closed subgroup schemes over \(L\). If \([L:\mathbf F_q]=n\), then \(|L|=q^n\). Multiplication by any nonzero \(a\in L\) permutes the nonzero elements. Comparing their nonzero products gives \(a^{q^n-1}=1\). Therefore all elements are the \(q^n\) distinct roots of \(X^{q^n}-X\); its derivative is \(-1\). All minimal polynomials over \(\mathbf F_q\) divide this split separable polynomial, so \(L\) is normal and separable. Its Frobenius has order exactly \(n\): its \(n\)-th power is the identity, whereas for \(0<r<n\), being the identity would give \(q^n\) roots to \(X^{q^r}-X\), whose degree is \(q^r\). The embedding count and fixed-field proof following S08 Lemma G.5.2 show that its Galois group has order \(n\); it is consequently generated by this Frobenius.

Both ideals over \(L\) are Frobenius-stable. Indeed their scalar extensions to the algebraic closure have that stability, and extension of field scalars is injective and detects equality of subspaces. The whole finite Galois group therefore preserves them. Apply the complete invariant-space proof of S08 Lemma G.5.2 to each ideal and to \(L\otimes_{\mathbf F_q}\mathbf F_q[G]\). It identifies each ideal with the scalar extension of its invariant ideal in \(\mathbf F_q[G]\). Multiplication and all Hopf maps descend by that lemma; their ideal identities are detected after faithful field extension. This gives closed subgroup schemes \(B_0,T_0\) over \(\mathbf F_q\) with the prescribed geometric fibres. S08 Lemma G.2.1 descends smoothness, and Lemma G.0.T makes \(T_0\) a torus. Its geometric maximality and the Borel property of \(B_0\) are exactly the properties of those fibres. This proves the lemma. \(\square\)

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-01-rational-semisimple-directions-and-torus-preimages}

\textbf{Lemma 4.R (rational semisimple directions in positive characteristic).} Let \(k\) be infinite of characteristic \(p>0\), and let \(G/k\) be a smooth affine algebraic group. If \(G_{\bar k}\) has a nontrivial torus, then \(\operatorname{Lie}G(k)\) contains a nonzero matrix-semisimple vector in any faithful linear representation.

\textbf{Proof.} Choose a closed \(\mathbf G_m\) in that split geometric torus. In a weight basis of the faithful representation its integer weights generate \(\mathbf Z\), by the full trivial-kernel calculation of Lemma 4.S. Thus at least one weight is not divisible by \(p\). The Lie generator is a nonzero diagonal matrix, so its characteristic polynomial is not a pure power of its variable. At least one coefficient of the characteristic polynomial of the universal matrix in \(\operatorname{Lie}G\) is therefore a nonzero polynomial over \(k\).

A nonzero polynomial over an infinite field has a rational point where it is nonzero. Induct on the number of variables: retain a nonzero coefficient polynomial in the last variable, choose values of the preceding variables by induction, and then choose the last value outside the finitely many roots of the resulting nonzero one-variable polynomial. The degree root bound follows by the repeated linear-factor division in S02 Lemma 4.A. Choose the resulting \(Y\in\operatorname{Lie}G(k)\). Its characteristic polynomial is not \(T^n\), so \(Y\) is not nilpotent.

We give the exact matrix-power argument. Over \(\bar k\), the characteristic polynomial splits. Cayley--Hamilton, S06 Section 1, and the polynomial Bézout/Chinese remainder proofs decompose the space into the generalized eigenspaces: the pairwise coprime powers \((T-\lambda)^n\) give polynomial orthogonal projectors summing to one. On a projector's image \(Y=\lambda I+N_\lambda\), with \(N_\lambda^n=0\). For \(p^r\ge n\), the characteristic-\(p\) binomial identity gives \[
 Y^{p^r}=\lambda^{p^r}I
\] on that entire summand. Thus \(Y^{p^r}\) is semisimple and nonzero, because some eigenvalue is nonzero. The matrix \(Y^{p^r}\) is rational over \(k\) simply because \(Y\) is, and Lemma 4.H puts every iterated \(p\)-power in \(\operatorname{Lie}G\). This is the required vector; no descent of the semisimple component itself is used. \(\square\)

\textbf{Lemma 4.P (a torus in a finite infinitesimal central extension).} Suppose \(P\) is an affine algebraic \(k\)-group and \(q:P\to Q\) is a faithfully flat map of finite presentation to a nontrivial \(k\)-torus. Suppose its full kernel \(E\) is finite connected central and of multiplicative type. Then \(P\) contains a nontrivial \(k\)-torus. Smoothness of \(P\) and perfection of \(k\) are not assumed.

\textbf{Proof.} The full kernel relation gives \(P\times E\simeq P\times_QP\). Pulling \(q\) back along its own fppf cover therefore gives the finite free coordinate module \(k[P]\otimes_k k[E]\), of rank \(\dim_k k[E]\). S04 Lemma A1.3 descends this property, so \(q\) is finite locally free. The commutator of \(P\) takes values in \(E\), since \(Q\) is commutative. Changing either input by a central \(E\)-point leaves it unchanged. S04 Lemma A1.5, applied to the full torsor relation in both inputs, descends it to \(Q\times Q\to E\).

Over \(\bar k\), Lemmas G.0.2 and G.0.T of S08 make \(E\) a connected finite diagonalizable scheme with one underlying point, its identity, and reduced algebra \(\bar k\). The split \(Q\times Q\) is reduced. Its map to \(E\) kills the nilradical and hence factors through that identity. The commutator is therefore zero after scalar extension, and faithful field extension detects this equality of affine coordinate maps before extension. Thus \(P\) is commutative.

Every geometric fibre of the finite surjection \(q\) is an \(E\)-torsor. The weak Nullstellensatz supplies a rational point on that nonempty finite fibre, and translation identifies its full scheme with \(E\). Its underlying space has one point. This remains true after every base change. A finite map is universally closed by the integral closed-map proof in S04 Lemma P0.4; hence \(q\) is a universal homeomorphism. In particular \(P_{\bar k}\) is connected and its connected reduction \(R\) still maps onto the underlying space of \(Q_{\bar k}\).

The reduction \(R\) is a subgroup, because products of reduced affine groups over the algebraically closed field are reduced by S08 Lemma G.4.1. Lemma 2.L makes \(R\) smooth, and the full commutative solvable structure of Theorem 2.K writes it as a torus times a smooth connected unitriangular group \(U\). Its map \(U\to Q_{\bar k}\) is trivial by Lemma 2.A, so \(U\) lies in the finite full kernel \(E_{\bar k}\). Therefore \(U\) is finite. Its coordinate algebra is a finite-dimensional domain by Lemma 2.L; it is a field, and algebraic closedness makes that field \(\bar k\). Thus \(U=1\) as a scheme. It follows that \(R\) is a torus, and it is nontrivial since its underlying image is the nontrivial \(Q_{\bar k}\). Finally apply Lemma 4.C to the commutative affine group \(P\): it descends precisely this torus factor of its geometric reduced identity group to \(k\). The descended torus is nontrivial and is a closed subgroup of \(P\). \(\square\)

\textbf{Theorem 4.2 (Grothendieck).} Every smooth connected affine group over a field \(k\) has a geometrically maximal torus defined over \(k\).

\textbf{Proof.} Induct on the finite dimension of \(G\), for all fields at once. S08 Lemma G.0.3 shows that a connected field-group is geometrically irreducible and that its identity component commutes with field extension. A smooth connected affine group of dimension zero is trivial: over an algebraic closure, Lemma 2.L makes its coordinate ring a finite-type domain; the dimension/transcendence-degree theorem, AG-CA, \emph{Noether normalization and dimension}, Theorem 4.2, gives transcendence degree zero. Its generators are algebraic over the algebraically closed field, so the ring is a finite field extension and equals that field. Faithful field extension descends the trivial group. Its trivial torus is maximal. For the induction step all smaller-dimensional smooth connected affine groups, over any field, have the asserted torus.

If \(G_{\bar k}\) has a central maximal torus, it is unique, since all maximal tori are conjugate. Put \(Z=Z(G)\), with its scheme-theoretic structure. The torus factor of \((Z_{\bar k}^0)_{\mathrm{red}}\) is that maximal torus: it contains every central torus, and maximality leaves no larger torus. Lemma 4.C descends this factor to a \(k\)-torus. Its geometric fibre is the chosen maximal torus. This proves the theorem in the central-maximal-torus case, including the trivial-torus case; the same lemma will later descend a merely nontrivial central torus.

Suppose \(k\) is infinite and \(G_{\bar k}\) has a noncentral torus. We will find a nontrivial \(k\)-torus and then use Lemma 4.1, whose smaller-dimension hypothesis is supplied by this induction. Choose a faithful representation by Section 2 and regard \(\mathfrak g=\operatorname{Lie}(G)\) inside its matrix algebra. Lemma 4.K proves the entire additive Jordan assertions used here: geometric Lie membership, perfect-field rationality and functoriality for all algebraic-group homomorphisms, in particular the adjoint representation.

First assume that \(\mathfrak g(k)\) contains a semisimple element \(X\) with \(\operatorname{ad}(X)\ne0\). In characteristic zero its full stabilizer \(C_G(X)\), defined by the matrix equations \(\operatorname{Ad}(g)X=X\), is a finite-type closed subgroup and is smooth by S08 Theorem G.3.4. Its Lie algebra is \(\ker\operatorname{ad}(X)\): substitute \(g=I+\varepsilon Y\) in the conjugation equation to obtain \(X+\varepsilon[Y,X]=X\). Thus the stabilizer is proper. Its smoothness makes its defining ideal radical; over \(\bar k\), the integral coordinate ring of \(G\) and the strict-specialization/dimension proofs in AG-CA, \emph{Noether normalization and dimension}, Lemma 4.1 and Theorem 4.2, make its dimension strictly smaller than \(\dim G\). Its identity component is smooth geometrically connected by S08 Lemma G.0.3, and contains the tangent vector \(X\), since that component is open at the identity. After algebraic closure it is not unipotent: Lemma 2.A makes the Lie action in a faithful representation strictly upper triangular for a unipotent group, which excludes a nonzero semisimple \(X\). Dimension induction supplies a geometrically maximal \(k\)-torus in this smaller-dimensional centralizer component. Lemma 2.D makes its geometric fibre positive-dimensional, so it is nontrivial.

In characteristic \(p>0\), a version of the same argument avoids smoothness questions for a Lie-element stabilizer. Put

\[
\mathfrak h=\operatorname{span}_k\{X,X^{[p]},X^{[p^2]},\ldots\}.
\]

This is a commutative restricted Lie subalgebra: in a diagonalization of \(X\), its powers and their linear combinations remain diagonal, and the \(p\)-operation preserves their span. Over \(\bar k\) this operation has zero kernel, since a diagonal matrix with zero \(p\)-th power is zero. Its image is a vector subspace because every scalar has a \(p\)-th root in \(\bar k\); in finite dimension injectivity therefore gives an invertible semilinear operation. The full subgroup correspondence and multiplicative-type assertion of Lemma 4.H give a closed \(H\subset G[F]\) with \(H_{\bar k}\simeq\mu_p^d\), \(d=\dim\mathfrak h>0\).

The centralizer \(C_G(H)\) is smooth by the complete fixed-subgroup theorem in AG-GS, \emph{Diagonalizable groups}, Theorem 3.4, whose coefficient and invariant-cohomology proof includes nonreduced multiplicative-type acting groups. Its Lie algebra is the centralizer of \(\mathfrak h\), by Lemma 4.H, so \(\operatorname{ad}(X)\ne0\) makes it proper. Its identity component contains the connected \(H\), with the full factorization of S08 Lemmas G.0.1 and G.0.3. After algebraic closure that component cannot be unitriangular: Lemma 2.A excludes its nontrivial diagonalizable closed subgroup \(H_{\bar k}\). Dimension induction therefore supplies a geometrically maximal torus in this smaller-dimensional smooth geometrically connected centralizer, and the no-torus criterion of Lemma 2.D makes it nontrivial.

It remains to find a usable semisimple direction or to remove the central directions obstructing this method. Over \(\bar k\), split the given noncentral torus into its coordinate copies of \(\mathbf G_m\). At least one is noncentral, since if each coordinate subgroup centralized \(G\), their product would do so on every test algebra. Its adjoint action on \(\mathfrak g_{\bar k}\) has a nonzero integer weight. Indeed, if all weights were zero, the weight decomposition of AG-GS, \emph{Diagonalizable groups}, Theorem 3.1 and the centralizer Lie formula proved in Lemma 3.1 would make its smooth centralizer have the full Lie algebra and dimension of \(G\). The integral-group dimension argument just used, followed by radicality of the smooth centralizer ideal, would make that entire centralizer equal to \(G\), contradicting noncentrality. In characteristic zero a nonzero integer weight has nonzero differential, so the Lie generator has a nonzero adjoint eigenvalue. Therefore at least one nonconstant coefficient of the characteristic polynomial of \(\operatorname{ad}(Y)\) is a nonzero polynomial on the \(k\)-vector space \(\mathfrak g\). A nonzero polynomial over an infinite field has a rational point where it is nonzero: induct on the number of variables, specialize a nonzero coefficient polynomial in the preceding variables, and then choose the last variable outside the finitely many roots, using S02 Lemma 4.A. Choose such a rational \(Y\). Its adjoint matrix is not nilpotent. The characteristic-zero field is perfect, so Lemma 4.K makes \(Y_s\) rational and identifies \(\operatorname{ad}(Y_s)\) as the semisimple part of \(\operatorname{ad}(Y)\); it is nonzero. This supplies the case already treated.

In characteristic \(p\), the Lie generator of a noncentral torus can be central: the adjoint weights may have zero differential. If a semisimple rational vector has nonzero adjoint action, the preceding case applies. Otherwise all semisimple rational vectors are central in \(\mathfrak g\). Lemma 4.R nevertheless supplies a nonzero such vector by a rational \(p\)-power of a nonnilpotent matrix. That proof establishes rationality directly, including over imperfect fields.

Choose a nonzero semisimple rational \(X\). It is central in \(\mathfrak g\), and so are its restricted powers, since the matrix commutator formula gives \(\operatorname{ad}(X^{[p]})=(\operatorname{ad}X)^p\). Their span \(\mathfrak h\) is commutative with geometrically injective, hence invertible, semilinear operation. Lemma 4.H gives its nontrivial height-one multiplicative-type subgroup \(M\). Its full centralizer is smooth by AG-GS, \emph{Diagonalizable groups}, Theorem 3.4, and Lemma 4.H gives its whole Lie algebra as \(\mathfrak g\). Over \(\bar k\), its dimension is consequently \(\dim G\). The smooth connected \(G_{\bar k}\) is integral by Lemma 2.L; the earlier domain dimension theorem excludes a proper closed subset of that dimension. The centralizer's defining ideal is radical, since it is smooth, and vanishes on the entire underlying space, so it is zero in the reduced coordinate ring of \(G_{\bar k}\). Faithful field extension descends this equality. Thus \(C_G(M)=G\) as schemes, and \(M\) is central. No descent of the span of all semisimple vectors is needed.

Pass to \(G/M\) and repeat if all its rational semisimple vectors are central. Lemma 4.B makes every composite kernel \(E_i\) finite connected central and of multiplicative type and the quotient smooth geometrically connected affine. The geometric torus needed to continue persists. Indeed its intersection with a finite \(E_i\) is a finite diagonalizable subgroup by Lemma 4.S; the quotient torus is represented there and has the same positive rank, since its character kernel has finite index in a nonzero free lattice. Its induced map into \((G/E_i)_{\bar k}\) has trivial full kernel by fppf lifting, so Lemma 4.S makes it a closed torus. If a geometric maximal torus of the new group is central, the first case gives a nontrivial \(k\)-torus there, because its geometric group still contains the positive-rank torus just constructed; otherwise Lemma 4.R again supplies a nonzero rational semisimple direction. Whenever a quotient torus is found, Lemma 4.P recovers a nontrivial torus in \(G\), and Lemma 4.1 completes the induction. If no quotient torus is found, each next height-one kernel is nontrivial and its order increases as follows.

If the iteration continues indefinitely, its composite kernels \(E_i\) are finite connected central and of multiplicative type by Lemma 4.B. Their orders strictly increase: the exact finite locally free rank assertion in that lemma gives \(|E_{i+1}|=|E_i|\,|H_i|\), and the new nontrivial height-one kernel has order \(|H_i|=p^{\dim\mathfrak h_i}>1\). After algebraic closure these connected kernels lie in \(Z=Z(G_{\bar k})^0\), with full factorization through that identity component from S08 Lemmas G.0.1 and G.0.3. If its connected reduction \(R\) had no nontrivial torus, the single bound of Lemma 4.O would bound every \(|E_i|\), a contradiction. Thus \(R\) has a nontrivial torus; Theorem 2.K gives its torus factor, and Lemma 4.C descends that factor to a nontrivial \(k\)-torus. Lemma 4.1 finishes this branch of the dimension induction.

If the iteration stops at a nontrivial \(k\)-torus \(Q\subset G/E_i\), its inverse image \(P\) has the full finite connected central multiplicative-type kernel \(E_i\) and is its fppf torsor over \(Q\). Lemma 4.P supplies a nontrivial \(k\)-torus in \(P\subset G\), with the full commutator descent, universal-homeomorphism and geometric-reduction arguments proved there. Lemma 4.1 makes it geometrically maximal in \(G\). This finishes the infinite-field induction.

Finally let \(k=\mathbf F_q\). Lemma 4.G gives a Borel and a geometrically maximal torus over \(k\), with the Lang equation, full finite-field Galois calculation and descent of the defining Hopf ideals already proved. This closes the induction in every characteristic and over every field. \(\square\)

The infinitesimal step is needed because a noncentral group torus may have a central Lie algebra. In \(\operatorname{SL}_2\) in characteristic two, the Lie algebra of the diagonal torus consists of scalar matrices. The torus itself still acts nontrivially on the upper and lower root groups.

\section{5. The finite symmetry left after centralizing}\label{AG-RG-01-the-finite-symmetry-left-after-centralizing}

For a maximal torus in a reductive group scheme, define the fppf quotient

\[
W_G(T)=N_G(T)/T.
\]

The quotient is a sheaf of groups: the definition of the normalizer makes \(T\) normal in it, so multiplying local coset representatives gives a well-defined local coset, compatible with their overlaps. A representative \(n\) acts on \(T\) by conjugation. Replacing it by \(nt\) for \(t\in T\) gives the same automorphism, since \(T\) is commutative. Thus the action descends through the fppf sheaf quotient, and composition/inverse on characters and cocharacters gives its actions on both sheaves. Representability and finiteness are not assumed in this definition.

The general finite étale Weyl-scheme theorem is taught with its complete proof in \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/main/docs/courses/AG-RG/AG-RG-04.md\#4-borel-subgroups-are-positive-systems}{Root data, Weyl chambers and the Bruhat decomposition, Theorem 4.2}, after the centralizer and reflection arguments it consumes. The matrix examples below have their own direct proofs here.

\textbf{Example 5.2.} Let \(A\) normalize the diagonal torus of \(\mathrm{GL}_n\) over a test algebra \(R\), including its nilpotents. Its induced torus automorphism is, by Lemma D.1, locally a fixed invertible integer map \(f\) on the character lattice. On each part where \(f\) is fixed, the intertwining equation for the standard representation is \[
 (z^{e_i}-z^{f(e_j)})a_{ij}=0\quad\text{in }R[z_1^{\pm1},\ldots,z_n^{\pm1}].
\] If the two characters differ, their distinct coefficients force \(a_{ij}=0\). If some \(f(e_j)\) were not among the \(e_i\), the whole \(j\)th column would vanish, contradicting invertibility. The distinct \(f(e_j)\) thus permute the \(n\) distinct \(e_i\). Only the corresponding one entry per column survives; the determinant is a signed product of these entries and is a unit, so each entry is a unit. Thus \(A\) is a permutation matrix times an invertible diagonal matrix on this part. Conversely multiplication by such matrices induces the stated character permutation and normalizes the torus on every test algebra. The local permutation is unique, and therefore glues as a section of the constant finite scheme \(\mathfrak S_n\). This proves the entire functor identity

\[
N_{\operatorname{GL}_n}(D)=D\rtimes(\mathfrak S_n)_S,\qquad
W_{\operatorname{GL}_n}(D)=(\mathfrak S_n)_S.
\]

The permutation is locally constant; over a disconnected algebra it need not be a single global permutation.

\section{6. Exercises}\label{AG-RG-01-exercises}

\textbf{Exercise 6.1 (first steps).} Over an arbitrary scheme, compute the centralizer and normalizer of the diagonal torus of \(\operatorname{GL}_3\). Explain how the answer changes when the test algebra is disconnected.

\textbf{Exercise 6.2 (descent).} Show that the two real tori in Example 1.2 are conjugate over \(\mathbb C\) but not over \(\mathbb R\). Show also that the multiplication torus \(\operatorname{Res}_{\mathbb C/\mathbb R}\mathbf G_m\) in \(\operatorname{GL}_{2,\mathbb R}\) is maximal and nonsplit.

\textbf{Exercise 6.3 (finite fields).} For a smooth connected affine group over \(\mathbb F_q\), construct a Borel--torus pair over \(\mathbb F_q\) from one over \(\overline{\mathbb F}_q\). The only cohomological input permitted is Lang's theorem.

\textbf{Exercise 6.4 (a family).} Over \(\mathbb Z\), let \(D\) be the diagonal torus in \(\operatorname{SL}_2\). Show that its nontrivial Weyl element is represented by \(\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\) even in characteristic two, and explain why the quotient is étale there.

\section{Solutions}\label{AG-RG-01-solutions}

\subsection{Solution 6.1}\label{AG-RG-01-solution-6.1}

The universal Laurent-polynomial computation in Example 1.1 makes the centralizer diagonal. A normalizer induces a permutation of the three rank-one character summands in the standard representation. After a decomposition by idempotents, the permutation is fixed on each piece. The normalizer is therefore \(D\rtimes(\mathfrak S_3)_S\), with quotient the constant finite étale group \(\mathfrak S_3\). Disconnected test algebras allow different permutations on different open and closed pieces, exactly as sections of a constant étale scheme do.

\subsection{Solution 6.2}\label{AG-RG-01-solution-6.2}

The eigenvectors \((1,-i)\) and \((1,i)\) diagonalize the rotation matrix, with eigenvalues \(a+bi\) and \(a-bi\). On the norm-one subgroup these are inverse, so the eigenbasis carries it to the diagonal torus of \(\operatorname{SL}_2\). Rescale a column to obtain a determinant-one change of basis. Conjugation on its character lattice is \(m\mapsto-m\), whereas the diagonal real torus has trivial action, which rules out a real conjugation. For the multiplication torus, the two eigenvalues vary independently after complex base change; it becomes the full diagonal torus of \(\operatorname{GL}_2\). It is therefore maximal. Its two character generators are exchanged by conjugation, so it is nonsplit over \(\mathbb R\).

\subsection{Solution 6.3}\label{AG-RG-01-solution-6.3}

Lemma 2.1 conjugates the two Borels, and Lemma 2.N conjugates their maximal tori inside the common Borel. Hence choose \(g\) with \(F(B,T)=g(B,T)g^{-1}\). Lemma 4.L gives \(h^{-1}F(h)=g^{-1}\). Direct substitution then makes both \(hBh^{-1}\) and \(hTh^{-1}\) Frobenius-stable. For the descent, their finitely generated defining ideals have coefficients in some finite extension \(L/\mathbb F_q\), because every coefficient in the algebraic closure is algebraic. Frobenius-stability after faithful field extension detects stability of those ideals over \(L\), so the whole cyclic Galois group preserves them. S08 Lemma G.5.2 supplies the full invariant-space proof identifying each ideal with the scalar extension of its invariant ideal; it also descends the Hopf identities. Smoothness descends by S08 Lemma G.2.1, and Lemma G.0.T identifies the descended geometric torus as a torus. Its maximality and the Borel property are those of the unchanged geometric fibres. This is precisely the explicit descent construction of Lemma 4.G. Connectedness of \(G\) is a hypothesis of the proved Lang equation.

\subsection{Solution 6.4}\label{AG-RG-01-solution-6.4}

Conjugation by the displayed matrix sends \(\operatorname{diag}(t,t^{-1})\) to \(\operatorname{diag}(t^{-1},t)\). A normalizer permutes the two universal weight lines, giving two components, each a coset of \(D\). Its quotient is the constant scheme with two points over \(\mathbb Z\), not \(\mu_2\). In characteristic two \(\mu_2\) is nonreduced, whereas a constant two-point scheme is still the disjoint union of two copies of the field and remains étale. The representative squares to \(-I\in D\); it need not itself have order two before taking the quotient.

\section{Exact supporting prerequisites and proof order}\label{AG-RG-01-exact-supporting-prerequisites-and-proof-order}

The classical triangularization, fixed-point, stabilizer, solvable structure and conjugacy arguments are in Section 2. Section 3 proves formal multiplicative-type homomorphism effectivity and the closed-immersion criterion. Section 4 proves Lang's theorem and supplies the Jordan and restricted-Lie arguments used in the field existence theorem. Their historical sources remain credited below.

The supporting geometric proofs are \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/main/docs/courses/AG-GS/AG-GS-03.html}{Group schemes over a field}, for orbits and the closed-orbit lemma; \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/main/docs/courses/AG-GS/AG-GS-04.html}{Quotients and torsors}, for finite free-action quotients; \href{prerequisites.html\#prerequisite-ag-dfg-02}{Faithfully flat descent}, for affine schemes, representations and character descent; \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/d02d0a3669f42579db037cd44de1d113fdd770a1/docs/courses/AG-GS/src/diagonalizable-groups.md}{Diagonalizable groups and groups of multiplicative type}, for the field character classification; \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/main/docs/courses/AG-MO/AG-MO-03.html}{Limits of schemes and Noetherian approximation}, for finite-presentation spreading; the complete \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/main/docs/courses/AG-RG/AG-RG-S05.md}{Artin approximation proof and application}, Sections 1--5, used in Section 3; and \emph{Dualizing sheaves and Serre duality for projective schemes}, for duality of curves. The prerequisite guide records their full statements and proof locations. The tori and reductive-group theorems assigned to this lesson are proved here.

The general cocharacter construction is proved here. The relative maximal-torus application is proved in the second lesson after the centralizer equality, and the finite Weyl-scheme theorem is proved in the fourth lesson after its reflection calculation. Their obligations are retained at those proof locations.

The \href{prerequisites.html}{course prerequisite guide} records the exact supporting statements, their full proof routes, and the hypotheses needed in their applications.

\setcounter{chapter}{1}
\chapter{Regular elements and centralizers}\label{AG-RG-02-regular-elements-and-centralizers}

\emph{Written by GPT-6.1 Sol (OpenAI) in Codex, Ultra setting, October 2026. Self-checked by the writing AI, GPT-6.1 Sol (OpenAI). Public domain (CC0).}

A maximal torus describes a reductive group by diagonal symmetries. A regular semisimple element describes the same torus by one element: the torus is the identity component of its centralizer. This observation is useful in families, where the centralizer of a section is easier to specify than a choice of eigenvectors.

We use the torus deformation and conjugacy arguments of \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/main/docs/courses/AG-RG/AG-RG-01.md}{Tori, maximal tori and their conjugacy}. The classical geometric input concerning Borel subgroups is used below to prove the centralizer theorem, rather than importing that theorem from a reference. All centralizers are scheme-theoretic. Over a field, a geometric assertion means an assertion after algebraic closure.

\section{1. The geometry behind the centralizer theorem}\label{AG-RG-02-the-geometry-behind-the-centralizer-theorem}

We first work over an algebraically closed field \(k\). A Borel subgroup of a smooth connected affine group \(H\) is a maximal smooth connected solvable subgroup. Write \(B=U\rtimes T\) for a Borel subgroup and one of its maximal tori. The solvable-group construction in the preceding lesson identifies \(U\) with the unipotent radical of \(B\).

We shall need several consequences of that construction. Every smooth connected solvable subgroup lies in a Borel: among those containing it choose one of largest dimension, bounded by \(\dim H\). A proper inclusion would strictly increase dimension, since both groups are reduced connected and hence integral by RG01 Lemma 2.L, and the earlier domain dimension theorem excludes a proper closed subset of the same dimension. Thus the chosen subgroup is maximal. RG01 Lemma 2.1 proves that \(H/B\) is projective and that all Borel subgroups are conjugate. The scheme-theoretic normalizer theorem is proved below, after the centralizer and Borel-intersection arguments needed for its induction.

\textbf{Lemma 1.A (unipotent radicals).} A smooth connected affine \(H/k\) has a unique largest smooth connected normal unipotent subgroup \(R_u(H)\). It is preserved by every automorphism. Every smooth connected normal unipotent subgroup lies in every Borel. If \(K\) is a smooth connected normal solvable subgroup of \(H\), then \(R_u(K)\) is normal in \(H\).

\textbf{Proof.} We first prove the precise affine image assertion used here. If \(f:E\to H\) is a homomorphism with \(E\) smooth connected affine of finite type, then \(k[E]\) is a domain: Lemma 1.0 below gives irreducibility, and smooth local rings are regular and therefore domains by AG-CA, \emph{Smooth algebras over a field and the Jacobian criterion}, Theorem 2.1, and the regular-parameter theorem. Let \(C\) be the image of \(k[H]\to k[E]\). This is a finitely generated domain. Comultiplication, inversion and counit restrict to it, because they commute with \(f\) and tensoring vector-space inclusions over \(k\) is injective. Their identities therefore restrict as well. Thus \(J=\operatorname{Spec}C\) is a closed subgroup of \(H\), and \(E\to J\) is schematically dominant. The complete monic-division and translation argument of AG-GS, \emph{Quotients and torsors}, Lemma 11.1c makes it faithfully flat and of finite presentation, in precisely its integral-target case.

The group \(J\) is smooth and connected. Put \(r=\operatorname{trdeg}_k\operatorname{Frac}C\). Noether normalization, proved in AG-CA, \emph{Krull dimension and Noether normalization}, Corollary 3.2, makes this field finite over a rational function field with \(r\) parameters. S02 Lemma 3.F gives its differential dimension \(r\), since \(k\) is perfect. At the generic point the local dimension is zero and the residue transcendence degree is \(r\), so the earlier Jacobian Theorem 2.1 makes that point smooth. Its Corollary 2.2 gives a nonempty smooth open. This open contains a \(k\)-point by the weak Nullstellensatz. Translation by the rational points of \(J\) makes every rational point smooth; a nonempty closed complement of the smooth locus would again have a rational point. Hence \(J\) is smooth everywhere. Its coordinate domain makes it irreducible and connected. This proves the entire finite-type affine image assertion needed here, without consuming an image theorem for arbitrary group schemes.

For smooth connected normal unipotent \(N_1,N_2\), the semidirect product \(N_1\rtimes N_2\) has underlying scheme \(N_1\times N_2\). It is smooth and integral by Lemma 1.0, the regular-local-domain calculation above and S08 Lemma G.4.1, so is connected. Apply the preceding image proof to multiplication into \(H\); denote its closed image by \(N_1N_2\). It contains both factors. Normality holds schematically: conjugation by any \(H\)-point preserves both factors, hence their multiplication image; pulling back equations along the faithfully flat cover \(H\times(N_1\rtimes N_2)\to H\times(N_1N_2)\) detects their vanishing. Thus their product is a smooth connected normal closed subgroup.

This product is unipotent. In any nonzero finite-dimensional representation \(W\), AG-RG-01, Lemma 2.A makes \(W^{N_1}\ne0\). Normality makes this subspace \(N_2\)-stable, so AG-RG-01, Lemma 2.A supplies a nonzero vector fixed by both groups, and hence by their product: the latter equality follows faithfully flatly from the surjective multiplication map. Applying the same argument to successive quotients gives a trivial-quotient full flag. A faithful representation of the affine image is therefore unitriangular.

Choose a smooth connected normal unipotent subgroup of maximal dimension, possible since the dimensions are bounded by \(\dim H\). Its product with any other such subgroup is again of this type. Maximal dimension forces that product to equal it: a proper integral closed subgroup of an integral finite-type group has strictly smaller dimension, by the strict-specialization and dimension proofs in AG-CA, \emph{Krull dimension and Noether normalization}, Lemma 4.1 and Theorem 4.2. This proves greatestness and uniqueness. Automorphisms preserve its defining property, so preserve the subgroup.

For a Borel \(B\) and such a normal \(N\), the product \(NB\) is similarly the smooth connected closed image of \(N\rtimes B\). It is solvable directly on all test rings. Projection to the solvable \(B\) makes every sufficiently iterated commutator word in \(N\rtimes B\) take values in \(N\). The unitriangular entry-distance filtration, with its polynomial commutator identities proved in RG01 Lemma 2.J, makes finitely many further derived commutators equal to the identity. Every tuple of points in the image lifts fppf locally through the multiplication map; hence the same commutator identities hold for \(NB\). Thus maximality of \(B\) gives \(NB=B\), and \(N\) lies in \(B\).

If \(K\) is normal in \(H\), every conjugation by \(H(k)\) gives an automorphism of \(K\) and preserves its unique \(R_u(K)\). The whole conjugation morphism \(H\times R_u(K)\to H\) factors through that closed subgroup: the source is reduced by AG-RG-S08, Lemma G.4.1, and its defining equations vanish at all closed points. To justify the required detection, a nonzero element \(a\) of a reduced finite-type \(k\)-algebra has a nonzero localization at \(a\), since it is not nilpotent. That localization is still finite type and has a maximal ideal, whose residue field is \(k\) by the weak Nullstellensatz. It gives a rational point where \(a\) is invertible. Therefore an element vanishing at every rational point is zero. Apply this calculation to the affine source of conjugation. This proves scheme normality in \(H\). In the solvable \(K\), the decomposition constructed in AG-RG-01, Theorem 2.K, \(K=U\rtimes T\), identifies its radical with \(U\): every smooth connected unipotent subgroup, including one not assumed normal in \(K\), projects trivially to \(T\) by AG-RG-01, Lemma 2.A and is contained in \(U\). \(\square\)

\textbf{Lemma 1.0 (components of an affine group over an algebraically closed field).} Let \(J\) be an affine group scheme of finite type over an algebraically closed field \(k\). Its irreducible components are pairwise disjoint and open and closed. In particular a connected such group is irreducible. No smoothness or reducedness hypothesis is needed for this topological assertion.

\textbf{Proof.} The Hilbert basis theorem, proved in AG-CA, \emph{Noetherian and Artinian rings}, Theorem 2.1, makes \(k[J]\) Noetherian. Its spectrum has finitely many irreducible components: if a closed subset failed to be a finite union of irreducible closed subsets, choose a minimal such subset using the descending chain condition on closed sets. It is reducible, hence the union of two proper closed subsets, both finite unions by minimality, a contradiction.

If \(C_1,C_2\) are components containing the identity, give them their reduced closed structures. They are integral finite-type schemes, so their product is integral by the complete coefficient-and-Nullstellensatz proof in the earlier S08 Lemma G.4.1. The closure of its multiplication image in \(J\) is irreducible and contains both \(C_1\) and \(C_2\), by multiplication with the identity in either factor. It is contained in a component, and maximality of \(C_1\) and \(C_2\) forces them to be that same component. Thus exactly one component contains the identity.

If two different components met, their closed intersection would contain a \(k\)-point by the earlier Nullstellensatz, AG-CA Theorem 2.1 of \emph{The Nullstellensatz and Jacobson rings}. Translation by the inverse of that point is a scheme automorphism of \(J\). It would carry the two distinct components to two distinct components containing the identity, contradicting the preceding paragraph. Hence all components are disjoint. There are only finitely many, so each has closed complement and is open as well as closed. Connectedness leaves exactly one component, proving irreducibility. This is the finite-type algebraically closed case of the earlier AG-GS, \emph{Group schemes over a field}, Section 1 and Theorem 2.2; the proof just given supplies precisely the case consumed here. \(\square\)

\textbf{Lemma 1.1.} Let \(H\) be a smooth connected affine group of finite type over an algebraically closed field \(k\), and let \(A\subset H\) be a torus. Its schematic centralizer \(C_H(A)\) is smooth and connected.

\textbf{Proof.} The complete fixed-subgroup proof in AG-GS, \emph{Diagonalizable groups and groups of multiplicative type}, Theorem 3.4 supplies smoothness. We give explicitly the cocharacter reduction needed for connectedness. Over the algebraically closed \(k\), the torus \(A\) is split. Indeed its étale splitting cover, given by that lesson's Theorem 7.7, has a nonempty finite-type affine chart; the earlier Nullstellensatz supplies a \(k\)-point, and pulling the splitting back along that point splits \(A\). Write \(A=\mathbf G_m^r\) and its character lattice as \(\mathbf Z^r\).

Choose finitely many algebra generators of \(k[H]\) and replace them by all their finitely many homogeneous components for conjugation by \(A\). The complete weight decomposition of AG-GS Theorem 3.1 shows that the resulting homogeneous list still generates. Let \(\Xi\subset\mathbf Z^r\) be its finite set of nonzero weights. If \(r>0\), associate to \(\chi=(a_1,\ldots,a_r)\in\Xi\) the nonzero polynomial

\[
p_\chi(Z)=a_1+a_2Z+\cdots+a_rZ^{r-1}\in\mathbf Q[Z].
\]

Each has only finitely many roots: division by \(Z-c\) removes a root, and induction on the degree bounds the number of distinct roots by that degree. This is also the earlier explicit polynomial calculation in S02 Lemma 4.A. Choose a positive integer \(M\) outside the finite union of their root sets, and put \(\lambda(t)=(t,t^M,\ldots,t^{M^{r-1}})\). Its pairing with every member of \(\Xi\) is nonzero. For an empty weight list choose \(M=1\), and for \(r=0\) use the unique cocharacter of the trivial torus.

The centralizers \(C_H(A)\) and \(C_H(\lambda)\) are equal as schemes, including on nonreduced test algebras. To check this, use the universal conjugation action on each homogeneous algebra generator \(f\) of weight \(\chi\). A test point fixed by \(A\) must satisfy \(f(h)(e^\chi-1)=0\) in its group algebra. The distinct basis monomials force \(f(h)=0\) when \(\chi\ne0\), and impose no condition when \(\chi=0\). The corresponding condition for \(\lambda\) is \(f(h)(t^{\langle\chi,\lambda\rangle}-1)=0\) in the Laurent polynomial algebra. Our choice makes its exponent nonzero precisely for the nonzero weights on this generating list, so coefficient comparison imposes exactly the same equations. Checking the algebra generators checks the full action on every function. Thus the two represented fixed subgroups have the same defining ideal over \(k\) and the same points on every test algebra.

Use the general cocharacter construction proved in the preceding lesson, Lemma 3.3. Its proof is a grading and smoothness argument for arbitrary smooth affine groups and uses no reductive centralizer theorem. Multiplication gives an open immersion

\[
U_H(-\lambda)\times C_H(\lambda)\times U_H(\lambda)\longrightarrow H.
\]

The domain contains the triple of identity elements. Lemma 1.0 makes the connected finite-type \(H\) irreducible, so the nonempty open image, and hence the domain, is irreducible. Its projection onto \(C_H(\lambda)\) is surjective: insertion of the identity in the two unipotent factors gives a section. The centralizer is therefore irreducible and connected. Together with the fixed-subgroup smoothness proof and the schematic equality already established, this proves the lemma. \(\square\)

The cocharacter lemma and the classical fixed-point arguments are independent of the root classification and of the reductive centralizer theorem proved below.

\textbf{Lemma 1.B (fixed unipotent groups are smooth connected).} Let a diagonalizable \(D\) act on \(U\) as in AG-RG-01, Lemma 2.C. Then \(U^D\) is smooth connected. Moreover the sequence \[
1\longrightarrow U_1^D\longrightarrow U^D
\longrightarrow (U/U_1)^D\longrightarrow1
\] is exact as fppf sheaves.

\textbf{Proof.} Fixed subschemes are affine finitely presented and smooth by the coordinate and infinitesimal proofs in AG-GS-05, Proposition 3.2 and Theorem 3.4, including a nonreduced \(D\). Let x be a \(D\)-fixed quotient section on any test algebra. Choose a lift u fppf locally. The defect \[
c(d)=u^{-1}d(u)
\] lies in \(U_1\) and is a regular crossed homomorphism. Write it fppf locally as \(c(d)=v d(v)^{-1}\) by AG-RG-01, Lemma 2.C. Then u v is fixed, since \(d(u v)=u c(d)d(v)=u v\). This proves surjectivity of the last map of the displayed sequence, with the kernel equality evident on every test scheme. Differences of two fixed lifts belong uniquely to \(U_1^D\); consequently its action identifies \(U_1^D\times U^D\) with \(U^D\times_{(U/U_1)^D}U^D\) on every test scheme. A local fixed lift translates this torsor into the product with \(U_1^D\).

For a vector line of character \(\chi\), its \(D\)-fixed subgroup is the whole line if \(\chi=0\), and is zero otherwise: comparison of the two distinct basis monomials \(e^\chi\) and 1 forces the vector coordinate to vanish, including over nonreduced tests. We induct on the given filtration length, simultaneously after every algebraically closed extension of \(k\); the length-zero group is the identity. The fixed kernel in the displayed sequence is smooth and geometrically connected by induction, and the quotient \(Q\) is either \(\mathbf G_a\) or 1. On a geometric fibre the torsor has a point by the earlier Nullstellensatz, and translation identifies it with that connected kernel. Hence all geometric fibres of \(q:U^D\to Q\) are connected.

Here is an explicit descent proof that the source is connected. Both source and target are affine. Write \(A=k[Q]\), \(B=k[U^D]\). On each affine fppf trivializing chart \(\operatorname{Spec}A'\to\operatorname{Spec}A\), the algebra \(B\otimes_A A'\) is flat over \(A'\): it is the base change of the coordinate algebra of the smooth \(k\)-group \(U_1^D\), and AG-CA, \emph{Smooth algebras over a field and the Jacobian criterion}, Theorem 6.1 proves smooth flatness, with the flat base-change proof in the flat-module lesson, Proposition 3.2. For any prime \(\mathfrak p\) of \(A\), choose such a chart and a prime \(\mathfrak p'\) above it. The flat local map \(A_{\mathfrak p}\to A'_{\mathfrak p'}\) is faithfully flat by AG-CA, \emph{Faithful flatness and the local criterion for flatness}, Theorem 2.1. For an injection of \(A_{\mathfrak p}\)-modules, its tensor map with \(B_{\mathfrak p}\) becomes injective after this faithfully flat extension, because the extended algebra is flat. Flatness of the extension and faithful detection make the original tensor map injective. Thus \(B_{\mathfrak p}\) is flat, and local flatness detection in the flat-module lesson, Theorem 3.3, proves \(B\) flat over \(A\). The local torsor sections give a point above every prime; hence \(A\to B\) is faithfully flat by the same faithful-flatness Theorem 2.1.

A partition of the source into open and closed pieces is an idempotent \(e\in B\): glue the function equal to one on one piece and zero on the other. Conversely an idempotent gives these pieces, since in every local ring one of \(e\) and \(1-e\) is a unit and their product is zero.

Let \(e_1,e_2\in B\otimes_A B\) be the pullbacks of \(e\) from the two factors. On each geometric fibre of \(q\), connectedness makes that idempotent constant, so \(e_1\) and \(e_2\) have equal values at every geometric point of the fibre product. Their difference therefore belongs to every prime ideal and is nilpotent. Here is the required nilradical argument for any ring \(C\). If \(z\in C\) is not nilpotent, the powers \(1,z,z^2,\ldots\) avoid zero. An ideal maximal among those avoiding these powers exists by the union-of-chains argument. It is prime: if \(ab\) lies in it but neither \(a\) nor \(b\) does, both larger ideals obtained by adjoining \(a\) and \(b\) meet the powers; multiplying the two resulting equations puts a power of \(z\) in the original ideal, a contradiction. This prime avoids \(z\). Conversely a nilpotent belongs to every prime. Apply this to \(C=B\otimes_A B\). Two idempotents with nilpotent difference are equal: \(e_1(1-e_2)\) and \(e_2(1-e_1)\) are both idempotent and nilpotent, hence zero; thus \(e_1=e_1e_2=e_2\).

The faithfully flat equalizer proved in the earlier S04 Lemma A1.1 now descends \(e\) to \(A\). The map \(A\to B\) is injective, so the descended element is also idempotent. But \(A\) is \(k[x]\) or \(k\), both domains, and has only the idempotents zero and one. Hence \(e\) was trivial. This proves connectedness, and the same argument after every algebraically closed extension proves geometric connectedness. The torsor and kernel equalities were identities on all test schemes, so the entire lemma retains the stated schematic exactness. \(\square\)

For \(A\subset T\subset B=U\rtimes T\), these proofs give \[
C_B(A)=U^A\rtimes T,
\] so this centralizer is smooth connected and solvable.

\textbf{Lemma 1.2.} A unipotent group acting on an affine variety has closed orbits, with their full scheme structures. No smoothness or connectedness assumption on the group or the schematic stabilizer is needed.

\textbf{Proof.} We first prove closedness for a smooth connected unitriangular group \(L\). Give the closure \(Y\) of one point orbit its reduced structure. It is integral. S08 Theorem G.4.2 makes the orbit open in \(Y\), and makes both \(Y\) and its reduced boundary \(D\) invariant under \(L\), using reducedness of the products and the strong Nullstellensatz. If \(D\ne\varnothing\), choose a nonzero function in its ideal. AG-GS-01 Lemma 5.1 puts that function in a finite-dimensional \(L\)-stable subspace of the ideal: in the coefficient construction all coefficient functions stay in the ideal, since its coaction maps into \(k[L]\otimes I_D\). RG01 Lemma 2.A gives a nonzero invariant function in this subspace. Its values are constant on the dense point orbit and hence on \(Y\). It vanishes on the nonempty \(D\), so the constant is zero, a contradiction. Thus the orbit is closed. S08 Theorem G.4.C represents the full quotient by its possibly nonreduced stabilizer as this reduced locally closed orbit. Since its support is closed, it is a closed immersion in the affine target and is affine.

Now embed the given unipotent group \(N\) as a closed subgroup of the smooth connected group \(L=U_m\) of upper unitriangular matrices. Its coordinate ring is the polynomial ring in the entries above the diagonal, and the matrix formulas give its group operations. Fix \(x\) in the affine variety and retain the entire schematic stabilizer \(K=N_x\subset N\subset L\). The RG01 detecting-line construction supplies an \(L\)-representation and a line \(kv\) with full stabilizer \(K\). RG01 Lemma 2.A makes the character of \(K\) on this line trivial, including its infinitesimal points. The vector stabilizer is consequently \(K\) as well. The first paragraph and S08 Theorem G.4.C now construct an affine closed vector orbit \(P\), with an fppf \(K\)-torsor \[
 q:L\longrightarrow P,\qquad
 L\times K\simeq L\times_P L.
\] All these identities hold on arbitrary test algebras.

The closed subscheme \(N\subset L\) descends along this torsor. Indeed, in the displayed relation the two projections are \((l,k)\mapsto l\) and \((l,k)\mapsto lk\). The inverse images of \(N\) coincide as schemes: right multiplication by any section of \(K\subset N\) preserves \(N\), and its inverse does too. This is the descent datum for its defining ideal. The module, ideal and algebra effectivity proofs of S04 Lemmas A1.1, A1.2 and A1.5 give a closed subscheme \(Z\subset P\) with \[
 q^{-1}(Z)=N,\qquad N\longrightarrow Z
 \text{ an fppf }K\text{-torsor}.
\] For clarity, ideal descent applies on the affine cover \(L\to P\): the compatible ideal descends as a submodule of \(\mathcal O_P\), multiplication preserves it after faithful pullback and hence before pullback, and its quotient algebra pulls back to \(\mathcal O_N\). Thus \(Z\) retains any nilpotents of \(N/K\); no reduction has been taken here. The torsor identity is the restriction of that for \(L\).
