If semisimplicity is instead specified by diagonalizability of \(\operatorname{ad}(X)\), it gives the same conclusion. RG01 Lemma 4.K makes its nilpotent part \(\operatorname{ad}(X_n)\), so this is zero. S08 Theorem G.3.4 makes \(C_G(X_n)\) smooth with Lie algebra the whole \(\mathfrak g\), hence with dimension \(\dim G\). The proper-closed-subset dimension proof of AG-CA-09 and irreducibility proved in Theorem 3.1 force \(C_G(X_n)=G\). In particular \(X_n\) commutes with the maximal torus. Theorem 2.2 puts it in \(\operatorname{Lie}T\), whose matrices are diagonal in a torus weight basis. A diagonal nilpotent matrix is zero, so \(X_n=0\). General SGA-regular Lie sections in small characteristic need not meet the fibre condition; the characteristic-two example above explains that restriction.

For a general smooth connected affine group over a field, a \textbf{Cartan subgroup} is \(C_G(T)\) for a geometrically maximal torus. The complete field centralizer proof of Lemma 1.1 gives smoothness and geometric connectedness. Over an algebraic closure \(T\) is central and still maximal in this centralizer, so the entire central-maximal-torus proof of Lemma 1.C gives \(C_G(T)=T\times U_C\) with \(U_C\) smooth connected unipotent. Here nilpotence is explicit. Embed \(U_C\) in upper unitriangular \(m\)-by-\(m\) matrices by RG01 Lemma 2.A. Let \(I_h\) be the matrices whose entries vanish unless column minus row is at least \(h\). Matrix multiplication gives \(I_hI_j\subset I_{h+j}\), and \(I_m=0\). The inverse of \(1+X\) is the finite geometric series, since \(X^m=0\). Modulo \(I_{h+j}\) the products of an \(I_h\) and an \(I_j\) entry vanish in either order, so \([1+I_h,1+I_j]\subset1+I_{h+j}\) on every test algebra. Intersecting these subgroups with \(U_C\) makes its lower central series vanish by step \(m\). The central product with \(T\) is therefore nilpotent as well. These nested commutator identities descend through the faithful field extension, so the original Cartan group is nilpotent. Conjugacy of maximal tori, proved in RG01 Theorem 2.2, conjugates their entire centralizers. In a reductive group Theorem 2.1 makes that centralizer the torus itself. Thus Cartan subgroups are precisely the maximal tori in the reductive case. We make no additional general-base Cartan representability assertion here.

\section{6. Exercises}\label{AG-RG-02-exercises}

\textbf{Exercise 6.1 (first steps).} Compute the centralizer of a diagonal matrix with distinct eigenvalues in \(\operatorname{GL}_n\). If its eigenvalues have multiplicities \(m_1,\ldots,m_a\), compute the dimension of its centralizer.

\textbf{Exercise 6.2 (centralizers).} In characteristic different from two, prove \(C_{\operatorname{SL}_2}(u)=\mu_2\times U\) for the upper unipotent element displayed above. Determine its component group. Explain what changes in characteristic two.

\textbf{Exercise 6.3 (universal equations).} Over an arbitrary base scheme, prove that the centralizer of the diagonal torus in \(\operatorname{GL}_n\) is that torus. Why is checking only the base field's rational points insufficient?

\textbf{Exercise 6.4 (geometry).} Show that the regular semisimple locus of \(\operatorname{GL}_n\) is exactly the nonvanishing locus of the discriminant of its characteristic polynomial, and is dense over every algebraically closed field.

\section{Solutions}\label{AG-RG-02-solutions}

\subsection{Solution 6.1}\label{AG-RG-02-solution-6.1}

The equations \((a_j-a_i)a_{ij}=0\) allow matrix entries only between equal-eigenvalue subspaces. The centralizer is \(\prod_i\operatorname{GL}_{m_i}\) and has dimension \(\sum_i m_i^2\). For distinct eigenvalues all \(m_i=1\), giving the diagonal torus and dimension \(n\).

\subsection{Solution 6.2}\label{AG-RG-02-solution-6.2}

Multiplying out gives \(c=0\), \(a=d\) and \(a^2=1\). The map \((a,x)\mapsto\begin{pmatrix}a&ax\\0&a\end{pmatrix}\) is an isomorphism of group schemes. In characteristic different from two, \(\mu_2\) is étale with two points, so the component group is the constant group of order two. In characteristic two \(\mu_2\) is connected and nonreduced, and the centralizer has one geometric component and a two-dimensional tangent space despite having dimension one.

\subsection{Solution 6.3}\label{AG-RG-02-solution-6.3}

Use the universal diagonal matrix with independent Laurent coordinates \(z_i\). The equation \(a_{ij}(z_i-z_j)=0\) forces \(a_{ij}=0\) for \(i\ne j\) by independence of Laurent monomials over every ring. The diagonal entries are units since the matrix is invertible. Over a finite field the rational points of a torus may not separate all its characters, and over nonreduced algebras rational-point equations may miss infinitesimal conditions; the universal computation avoids both problems.

\subsection{Solution 6.4}\label{AG-RG-02-solution-6.4}

If the roots are \(a_i\), the discriminant is \(\prod_{i<j}(a_i-a_j)^2\), a symmetric polynomial in them. The complete lexicographic elementary-symmetric reduction of S06 Section 1 proves that it is a polynomial in the characteristic coefficients, including in positive characteristic. It is nonzero precisely when all eigenvalues are distinct. A matrix with this property is diagonalizable, and Exercise 6.1 gives its torus centralizer. Conversely a semisimple matrix with repeated eigenvalues has larger centralizer, so is not regular semisimple. The polynomial does not vanish identically: choose distinct nonzero elements in the infinite algebraically closed field and take their diagonal matrix. Its nonvanishing locus in the irreducible variety \(\operatorname{GL}_n\) is therefore open dense. No assertion that this locus has a rational point over every finite field is needed.

The \href{prerequisites.html}{course prerequisite guide} records the exact supporting statements, their full proof routes, and the hypotheses needed in their applications.

\setcounter{chapter}{2}
\chapter{Roots and reductive groups of rank one}\label{AG-RG-03-roots-and-reductive-groups-of-rank-one}

\emph{Written by GPT-6.1 Sol (OpenAI) in Codex, Ultra setting, October 2026. Self-checked by the writing AI, GPT-6.1 Sol (OpenAI). Original text: public domain (CC0). The normalization lemma in Section 5 follows the Stacks Project's proof, cited at the end.}

The diagonal entries of a matrix act on its off-diagonal entries through ratios. Those ratios are the roots of a general linear group. For an arbitrary reductive group, roots are still characters of a maximal torus, but their one-dimensional spaces need not be globally trivial over the base. This lesson constructs the corresponding groups without using a power-series exponential, and shows why every root carries a copy of the rank-one geometry of \(\operatorname{SL}_2\).

We use torus conjugacy, torus deformation, and the centralizer theorem from the preceding two lessons. A reductive \(S\)-group is smooth affine of finite presentation with connected reductive geometric fibres. A semisimple \(S\)-group has semisimple geometric fibres. Statements about line bundles and subgroup schemes are made over arbitrary schemes, including nonreduced ones.

\section{1. The centre and the two ranks}\label{AG-RG-03-the-centre-and-the-two-ranks}

Let \(T\) be a split maximal torus of \(G\), and, on an open set where the ranks are constant, write

\[
\mathfrak g=\mathfrak t\oplus\bigoplus_{\alpha\in\Phi}\mathfrak g_\alpha.
\]

For now \(\Phi\) means the nonzero weights; we will prove that they form a reduced root system. Put

\[
Z=\bigcap_{\alpha\in\Phi}\ker(\alpha:T\to\mathbf G_m).
\]

\textbf{Lemma 1.A (the torus weight kernel is central).} Let \(G/R\) be smooth affine of finite presentation with connected geometric fibres, let \(T=D_R(X)\subset G\) be a split torus, and let \(\Phi\) be the finite set of nonzero \(T\)-weights occurring in \(\operatorname{Lie}(G)\). Put \(L=\mathbf Z\Phi\subset X\). Then \(D_R(X/L)\subset T\) is central in \(G\), is of finite presentation, and commutes with arbitrary base change as a specified subgroup of \(T\).

\textbf{Proof.} The ideal of the displayed intersection of character kernels in \(R[X]\) is generated by the finitely many elements \(e^\alpha-1\). Its quotient is \(R[X/L]\): these relations identify exactly the exponent basis elements in the same coset of \(L\), and the distinct cosets remain an \(R\)-basis. The Hopf operations preserve the relations. This gives the indicated diagonalizable subgroup \(Z\), including any torsion in \(X/L\); no smoothness of \(Z\) is assumed. Finite presentation follows by adjoining these finitely many equations to the Laurent presentation of \(T\). This description also proves arbitrary base-change compatibility.

For conjugation by \(Z\), put \(H=G^Z=C_G(Z)\). AG-GS-05, Proposition 3.2 and Theorem 3.4, prove that this is a closed smooth subgroup of finite presentation and that \(\operatorname{Lie}(H)=\operatorname{Lie}(G)^Z\), even for a nonreduced diagonalizable \(Z\). Every nonzero \(T\)-weight restricts trivially to \(Z\) by construction, and the zero-weight part does too. Thus this Lie inclusion is an isomorphism. Translation by points of \(H\), after each residue-field extension, makes the relative tangent map of \(H\hookrightarrow G\) an isomorphism at every point. S02 Lemma 3.A consequently makes this closed immersion étale.

Here is the scheme argument turning that conclusion into equality. A closed immersion of finite presentation which is étale is open. Indeed, locally write it as \(\operatorname{Spec}(A/J)\hookrightarrow\operatorname{Spec}A\) with \(J\) finitely generated. Formal smoothness applied to \(A/J^2\to A/J\) lifts the identity of \(A/J\) as an \(A\)-algebra map. Compatibility with \(A\) forces every element of \(J\) to vanish in \(A/J^2\), so \(J=J^2\). At any prime containing \(J\), Nakayama's lemma gives \(J_{\mathfrak p}=0\); finite generation makes \(J\) zero on a neighbourhood of that prime. Hence the closed image is also open. Apply this to \(H\hookrightarrow G\). On every geometric fibre its image is open and closed and contains the identity. Connectedness of that fibre makes its image the whole fibre. Its open complement in \(G\) therefore has no point, so \(H=G\) as schemes. This says exactly that \(Z\) is central on every test algebra. \(\square\)

For a maximal \(T\), the displayed intersection \(Z\) is precisely the scheme-theoretic centre. Lemma 1.A proves its centrality. Conversely, on every test algebra a central point belongs to \(C_G(T)=T\) by the preceding lesson, Theorem 2.2. Its action on each \(\mathfrak g_\alpha\) is multiplication by \(\alpha\). On the present rank-constant open this summand is locally free of positive rank; choose a local basis to see that a scalar acting as the identity is one. Thus \(\alpha=1\) for each \(\alpha\in\Phi\), and the point lies in \(Z\). This proves the equality of functors, including nilpotent test algebras. On splitting-cover overlaps these subgroup schemes represent the same centrality condition, so their ideals and maps descend by S04 Lemmas A1.2 and A1.5. The resulting equality and the coefficient presentations commute with every base change.

The centre need not be smooth: \(Z(\operatorname{SL}_n)=\mu_n\), including when the characteristic divides \(n\). Its largest subtorus is called the \textbf{radical}, denoted \(\operatorname{Rad}(G)\). For a group of multiplicative type with finitely generated character sheaf \(M\), it is \(D(M/M_{\mathrm{tors}})\subset D(M)\). Indeed the quotient is a finite free lattice by S04 Lemma P0.10, and the group-algebra quotient gives this closed torus inclusion. Any homomorphism from a torus into \(D(M)\) induces a character map from \(M\) into its torsion-free lattice, so kills \(M_{\mathrm{tors}}\) and factors through this inclusion, by the anti-equivalence proved in AG-GS-05 Theorem 2.2. These character maps agree on splitting-cover overlaps. Thus the construction descends, its rank is locally constant, and it commutes with every base change. The \textbf{rank} of \(G\) is the dimension of a maximal torus; its \textbf{semisimple rank} is

\[
\operatorname{rank}(G)-\dim\operatorname{Rad}(G).
\]

Over an algebraically closed field, every smooth connected solvable normal subgroup \(P\) of \(G\) is a central torus. RG01 Theorem 2.K writes \(P=U\rtimes D\) and makes \(U\) characteristic in \(P\). Rational conjugations by \(G\) preserve \(U\); the reducedness of \(G\times U\) and the Nullstellensatz make the whole conjugation morphism preserve it. Thus \(U\) is normal in \(G\) and is trivial by reductivity. Hence \(P\) is a torus. The integer-matrix description of torus automorphisms in RG01 Lemma D.1 makes the conjugation map from connected \(G\) locally constant, with identity value at the identity; it is the identity everywhere. Therefore \(P\) is central and belongs to the radical constructed above. Conversely that radical is smooth connected solvable and normal. Its quotient \(Q\) is reductive by the independent central-quotient construction in Theorem 1.1 below. To prove semisimplicity, let \(N\subset Q\) be smooth connected solvable and normal and put \(P=q^{-1}(N)\). The torsor \(P\to N\) has the split radical torus as kernel. The diagonalizable-torsor algebra calculation in AG-GS-05 Theorem 4.7 and Corollary 4.8 gives local trivializations: trivialize the finitely many degree modules for a basis of its character lattice, whose homogeneous units identify the torsor algebra with a Laurent algebra. Thus \(P\) is smooth and this map is open with connected geometric fibres. The finitely many disjoint open components of smooth \(P\) have disjoint open images: a connected fibre lies in only one component. These images partition connected \(N\), so \(P\) is connected. It is solvable on all test algebras: a sufficiently long derived commutator word maps to one in \(N\) and hence into the central radical, and the next commutator is one. It is normal as the inverse image of \(N\). The preceding argument gives \(P\subset\operatorname{Rad}(G)\), while the reverse inclusion holds by construction; the quotient torsor therefore gives \(N=1\). This proves that \(Q\) is semisimple. The same inverse-image argument shows that a torus in \(Q\) lifts to a torus in \(G\). Its inverse image is smooth connected and solvable by the preceding torsor and commutator arguments. Write it \(U\rtimes D\) using RG01 Theorem 2.K. Every character of unitriangular \(U\) is trivial by RG01 Lemma 2.A, so its map into the quotient torus is trivial and \(U\) lies in the radical torus. Its inclusion into that torus is itself trivial by the same character calculation, giving \(U=1\). The inverse image is therefore a torus. Conversely the image of a torus in \(G\) is a torus, by the character-lattice quotient calculation of AG-GS-05 Theorems 4.1--4.2. Hence maximal tori correspond under the radical quotient, and their dimensions decrease by the dimension of its torus kernel. In particular the rank of \(Q\) is the stated semisimple rank of \(G\).

The derived group will be constructed for arbitrary bases after the pinned existence theorem in \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/main/docs/courses/AG-RG/AG-RG-05.md\#the-derived-group}{Pinnings and the classification of split reductive groups}. It is semisimple and the multiplication map

\[
\operatorname{Rad}(G)\times G_{\mathrm{der}}\longrightarrow G
\]

is a central isogeny. Its construction uses the root groups established here. We do not assume a relative derived group in constructing these groups. Central quotients are constructed by graded invariant algebras in Theorem 1.1 below, without using coroots. In rank one we will construct the simply connected cover explicitly below.

\subsection{Central quotients before the rank-one argument}\label{AG-RG-03-central-quotients-before-the-rank-one-argument}

The rank-one argument below needs the affine quotient even when the centre is not smooth. The invariant-algebra construction is independent of coroots and root groups. We first supply the field-differential calculation used to check its geometric fibres.

\textbf{Lemma 1.B (differentials over a perfect field).} Let \(k\) be perfect, let \(t_1,\ldots,t_d\) be algebraically independent over \(k\), and let \(K\) be a finite extension of \(F=k(t_1,\ldots,t_d)\). Then \(\dim_K\Omega_{K/k}=d\). No separability assumption on \(K/F\) is required.

\textbf{Proof.} This is S02 Lemma 3.F. Its complete field-differential calculation proves the assertion in both characteristics, including finite inseparable extensions. \(\square\)

\textbf{Lemma 1.C (reduced groups over an algebraically closed field).} A reduced affine group scheme \(E\) of finite type over an algebraically closed field \(k\) is smooth. Its finitely many irreducible components are open and closed translates of its identity component. That component is a smooth connected normal subgroup.

\textbf{Proof.} First prove uniqueness of the component through the identity, without presupposing smoothness. If \(Z_1,Z_2\) are two such components with their reduced structures, S08 Lemma G.4.1 makes \(Z_1\times Z_2\) irreducible. The closure of its multiplication image is contained in a component of \(E\) and contains both \(Z_1\) and \(Z_2\), because the identity belongs to both. Maximality of components forces them to be equal. If two components met elsewhere, their nonempty closed intersection would have a \(k\)-point by the Nullstellensatz. Translation of that point to the identity would give two components there. Thus components are disjoint. They are finite in number by Noetherianity, so each is open as well as closed. Each contains a \(k\)-point, whose translation identifies it with the identity component. In particular they have one dimension \(d\). The identity component is a subgroup: its product with itself is irreducible, and its multiplication image contains the identity; inversion also preserves the component. Both maps factor through this open and closed component.

The restriction of \(E\) to each open component has its reduced closed structure. Indeed, at any point of that component all other minimal primes disappear under localization. The sole remaining minimal prime is the nilradical, which is zero because \(E\) is reduced. Thus the component's defining prime localizes to zero there. AG-GS-03, \emph{Lie algebras and smoothness}, Proposition 2.7, gives \(\Omega_{E/k}\simeq\mathcal O_E\otimes_k\omega_E\), of rank \(r=\dim_k\omega_E\). At a component's generic point the local ring is a field \(K\), since it is reduced with only one prime. Noether normalization and Theorem 4.2 of AG-CA, \emph{Krull dimension and Noether normalization}, make \(K\) finite over a rational function field on \(d\) variables. Localization of differentials and Lemma 1.B give \(r=\dim_K\Omega_{K/k}=d\). At the identity, Corollary 4.4 of the dimension lesson gives local dimension \(d\). AG-CA-18, Proposition 3.1, identifies the identity cotangent space with \(\omega_E\), so its embedding dimension is also \(d\) and its local ring is regular. The same proposition makes \(E\) smooth at that rational point. Translations give smoothness at every \(k\)-point. The smooth locus is open by AG-CA-18, Corollary 2.2; its closed complement, if nonempty, would have a \(k\)-point. Thus \(E/k\) is smooth everywhere.

Finally conjugation by every \(k\)-point preserves the identity component. The source of the conjugation map from \(E\) times that component is reduced by S08 Lemma G.4.1. The equations of the component therefore pull back to functions vanishing at every \(k\)-point, and hence to zero by the Nullstellensatz. This proves normality of the entire group-scheme morphism. \(\square\)

\textbf{Theorem 1.1 (affine central quotient).} Let \(G\) be a reductive group over a scheme \(S\), and let \(H\subset Z(G)\) be a closed subgroup of multiplicative type of finite presentation. The fppf quotient \(G/H\) is an affine reductive \(S\)-group. Formation of the quotient commutes with arbitrary base change.

\textbf{Proof.} Work étale locally on \(S=\operatorname{Spec}R\), with \(H=D_R(M)\). Such splitting neighbourhoods are proved in AG-GS-05, Theorem 7.7. On a nonempty affine chart \(M\) is finitely generated: a finite algebra generating set for \(R[M]\) contains only finitely many exponents; its polynomial expressions contain only the subgroup generated by those exponents, and independence of the exponent basis forces that subgroup to be \(M\). Right translation gives the grading \(A=\Gamma(G,\mathcal O_G)=\bigoplus_{m\in M}A_m\). Put \(B=A_0\) and \(Q=\operatorname{Spec}B\). These degree projectors prove exactness of invariants and arbitrary base-change compatibility. Since smooth algebras are flat over arbitrary rings by AG-CA-18, Theorem 6.1, the direct summand \(B\) is flat over \(R\) too.

Here is finite presentation directly over \(R\). Choose finitely many homogeneous algebra generators of \(A\), of weights \(m_1,\ldots,m_n\), and a graded surjection \(P=R[z_1,\ldots,z_n]\to A\). For \(d\in M\) let \(E_d=\{v\in\mathbf N^n:\sum_i v_i m_i=d\}\). Every such subset has finitely many minimal elements under coordinatewise order. Indeed, every infinite sequence in \(\mathbf N\) has an infinite nondecreasing subsequence: either a value repeats infinitely, or the tails are unbounded and one chooses successive larger values. Extract such a subsequence successively in each of the finitely many coordinates. An infinite antichain is impossible. A minimal element below a prescribed vector exists in the finite box below it. The minimal nonzero vectors in \(E_0\) generate that monoid by repeated subtraction, which decreases the coordinate sum. For any \(d\), its finitely many minimal vectors generate \(P_d\) as a \(P_0\)-module, because subtraction from a comparable vector of the same weight leaves a vector of weight zero.

The monoid algebra \(P_0=R[E_0]\) is finitely presented over \(R\). Choose the just-proved finite monoid generators. They give a surjection from a finite polynomial ring onto \(\mathbf Z[E_0]\); its kernel ideal is finitely generated because the polynomial ring over \(\mathbf Z\) is Noetherian, by S02 Lemma 3.N. Tensor this presentation with \(R\). Tensor product preserves its cokernel, and the monomial basis identifies \(R\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Z[E_0]\) with \(R[E_0]\), giving the required finite presentation.

The kernel \(I\) of \(P\to A\) is finitely generated: compare this generating set with a fixed finite presentation of \(A\) by adjoining both finite sets of variables and the equations for their mutual expressions, then eliminate the old variables. This is the affine presentation calculation of AG-MO-02, Theorem 3.1. Since \(I\) is graded, replace its finite generators by all their homogeneous components, obtaining homogeneous generators \(r_j\) of weights \(d_j\). Taking weight zero in an expression in these generators gives \(I_0=\sum_j P_{-d_j}r_j\). Each coefficient module is finite over \(P_0\) by the preceding minimal-vector calculation. Thus \(I_0\) is a finite ideal of \(P_0\), and \(B=P_0/I_0\) is finitely presented over \(R\). This also supplies the whole invariant-algebra finiteness argument of AG-GS-05, Theorem 3.5 in the present application.

Centrality first makes \(Q\) a group, directly on its algebra. For \(b\in B\), the function \(b(g_1g_2)\) is invariant under right translation by \(H\) in either variable: for the first variable move the central element past \(g_2\), and for the second use the original invariance. The double grading of \(A\otimes_R A\) therefore puts \(\Delta(b)\) in \(B\otimes_R B\). Likewise \((gh)^{-1}=g^{-1}h^{-1}\) proves that inversion preserves \(B\), and the counit restricts to \(B\). The Hopf identities restrict because all the relevant inclusions are split degree-summand inclusions, even after tensoring. Thus \(Q\) is an affine group and \(q:G\to Q\) a homomorphism. It is finitely presented by the affine-pair presentation calculation, since \(A\) and \(B\) are finitely presented over \(R\). It is surjective: the degree-zero projector is a \(B\)-linear retraction of \(B\hookrightarrow A\), so \(A\otimes_B\kappa(y)\) is nonzero for every prime \(y\) of \(B\), and prime existence gives a point above \(y\).

The closed embedding \(H\hookrightarrow G\) gives a graded surjection \(A\to R[M]\). For each of finitely many generators \(m_i\) of \(M\), choose \(a_i\in A_{m_i}\) and \(b_i\in A_{-m_i}\) restricting to \(e^{m_i}\) and \(e^{-m_i}\). Put \(f=\prod_i a_i b_i\in B\). Its restriction to \(H\), and hence its value at the identity, is one. In \(A_f\) all these factors are units. Products of their powers provide a unit \(u_m\) in every weight \(m\). Multiplication by \(u_m\) identifies \((A_f)_m\) with the free rank-one \(B_f\)-module \(B_f u_m\). The torsor algebra map

\[
A_f\otimes_{B_f}A_f\longrightarrow A_f\otimes_R R[M],
\qquad a\otimes c_m\longmapsto ac_m\otimes e^m
\]

is an isomorphism: its inverse on each exponent basis element sends \(a\otimes e^m\) to \(a u_m^{-1}\otimes u_m\). The forward map is an algebra map and the displayed inverse makes it bijective, so its inverse is an algebra map as well. Also \(A_f=\bigoplus_m B_f u_m\) is faithfully flat over \(B_f\). Hence \(q\) is an \(H\)-torsor over the principal open \(U=D(f)\subset Q\), which contains the identity.

To cover the entire quotient over the original ring, form the principal open \(W=\{(g,y)\in G\times_R Q:q(g)^{-1}y\in U\}\). Its projection to \(Q\) is smooth of finite presentation, being a principal open in the base change of \(G/R\). It is surjective. For a geometric point \(y:\operatorname{Spec}\Omega\to Q\), the same module retraction makes \(A\otimes_B\Omega\) nonzero. This is a finite-type \(\Omega\)-algebra, so the proved weak Nullstellensatz supplies \(g\in G(\Omega)\) above \(y\). Then \(q(g)^{-1}y=1\in U\), giving a point of \(W\) above \(y\). Thus \(W\to Q\) is an fppf cover, over arbitrary nonreduced bases as well.

On \(W\), its first coordinate is an actual section \(g\) of \(G_W\). Left translation \(x\mapsto g^{-1}x\) identifies the pullback of \(q\) with the pullback of the already constructed torsor over \(U\), through the map \((g,y)\mapsto q(g)^{-1}y\). This translation commutes with the right \(H\)-action. S04 Lemma A1.3 descends flatness through the affine faithfully flat cover \(W\to Q\), and finite presentation of \(q\) was already proved. The torsor isomorphism \(G\times H\to G\times_QG\) and its inverse descend by S04 Lemma A1.5. Consequently \(q\) is an fppf \(H\)-torsor globally. Every section of \(Q\) lifts fppf locally through \(q\), and two lifts differ by a unique section of \(H\) by this isomorphism. This identifies \(Q\) with the fppf quotient sheaf \(G/H\).

On overlaps of the splitting cover the quotient sheaf is the same, so these affine representing groups are canonically isomorphic, with the cocycle identity forced by their quotient maps. The affine effectivity proof in S04 Appendix A1 descends their algebras, and Lemma A1.5 descends the group laws and torsor isomorphisms. Lemmas A1.3 and A1.3a descend flatness and finite presentation. The degree-zero projector on each splitting chart commutes with every scalar extension, so this descended quotient and its torsor identity commute with arbitrary base change.

We check geometric smoothness directly. Over an algebraically closed field \(k\), smoothness of \(G\) makes \(A\) reduced: AG-CA-18, Theorem 2.1, makes its local rings regular, and the regular-local-domain proof makes them reduced. The inclusion \(B\hookrightarrow A\) therefore makes \(B\) reduced. Lemma 1.C proves \(Q/k\) smooth. It is connected because \(G\to Q\) is surjective.

Let \(U\subset Q\) be any smooth connected normal unipotent subgroup, and put \(P=q^{-1}(U)\). This is a closed normal subgroup of finite type, and \(P\to U\) is the pullback of the surjective \(H\)-torsor. Over \(k\), the product of reduced finite-type schemes is reduced, by S08 Lemma G.4.1. Multiplication and inversion therefore factor through \(P_{\mathrm{red}}\): nilpotent functions pull back to zero on their reduced sources. Thus \(P_{\mathrm{red}}\) is a group. Lemma 1.C makes it smooth with open and closed irreducible components. Put \(K=(P_{\mathrm{red}})^0\). In particular \(K\) is smooth connected and closed in \(G\).

Here normality is a statement about morphisms, including their infinitesimal points. For each \(g\in G(k)\), conjugation preserves \(P\), its reduction and its identity component. Every defining equation of \(K\subset G\) consequently pulls back under conjugation \(G\times K\to G\) to a function vanishing at all \(k\)-points. The source is reduced by S08 Lemma G.4.1, and the Nullstellensatz makes that function zero. Hence the whole conjugation morphism factors through \(K\), proving \(K\triangleleft G\) schematically. Also \(K\) is solvable. Indeed \(U(k)\) is unitriangular and hence nilpotent: commuting matrices with vanishing entries below distances \(a\) and \(b\) gives vanishing entries below distance \(a+b\), as follows by multiplying their strictly upper triangular parts. A sufficiently long derived commutator word in \(P(k)\) therefore lands in \(H(k)\); the next derived commutator is one because \(H\) is commutative. The corresponding word map on a power of the reduced \(K\) is identically one by the same Nullstellensatz argument. This proves solvability as an algebraic group.

The preceding lesson, Theorem 2.K, writes \(K=V\rtimes T\) with \(V\) smooth connected unipotent and \(T\) a torus and proves that \(V\) is the largest smooth connected normal unipotent subgroup. Thus every conjugation automorphism of \(K\) preserves \(V\). Reducedness of \(G\times V\) and the preceding equation argument then give \(V\triangleleft G\). Reductivity of \(G\) forces \(V=1\). Consequently \(K\) is a torus.

There are only finitely many components of \(P_{\mathrm{red}}\). Each contains a \(k\)-point and is a translate \(p_iK\): translation carries the identity component to the component containing \(p_i\). Let \(J\) be the topological closure of the image of \(K\to U\). Surjectivity of \(P\to U\), and equality of the underlying spaces of \(P\) and \(P_{\mathrm{red}}\), imply \(U=\bigcup_i q(p_i)J\). The smooth connected \(U\) is reduced and hence irreducible by Lemma 1.C. One of these finitely many closed translates is all of \(U\), hence \(J=U\). But the homomorphism \(K\to U\) is trivial. To see this directly, pull back a faithful unitriangular representation of \(U\). Its coordinate flag has trivial successive quotients. Exact torus weight projections split every term of this flag, so the whole representation of \(K\) is trivial. Faithfulness of the representation of \(U\) then makes \(K\to U\) the identity-valued morphism. Thus \(J=\{e\}\) and \(U\) is the trivial smooth group. This proves that every geometric fibre of \(Q\) is reductive. Flatness, finite presentation and these smooth geometric fibres prove smoothness of \(Q/S\) by AG-FSE-05, Theorem 3.1.

\(\square\)

\section{2. Why rank one has only two moving directions}\label{AG-RG-03-why-rank-one-has-only-two-moving-directions}

We first prove the geometric rank-one statement, rather than assuming a root classification. Work over an algebraically closed field \(k\).

\textbf{Lemma 2.1.} If a torus acts linearly on an irreducible projective variety \(X\), it has at least \(\dim X+1\) fixed points.

\textbf{Proof.} Put \(d=\dim X\) and let \(T\) be the acting torus. Since \(k\) is algebraically closed, an étale splitting cover of \(T\) has a \(k\)-point: take a nonempty finite-type affine chart and apply the earlier Nullstellensatz. Pulling the splitting back along this point gives \(T\simeq\mathbf G_m^r\). The weight decomposition proved in the preceding lesson, \emph{Diagonal actions and their descent}, applies to the finite-dimensional representation defining the linear action. Choose homogeneous coordinates in which the action on points has the form \[
 t\cdot[c_0:\cdots:c_N]
       =[\chi_0(t)c_0:\cdots:\chi_N(t)c_N],
 \qquad \chi_j\in X^*(T)=\mathbf Z^r.
\] Delete any coordinates vanishing identically on \(X\), thereby restricting to an invariant projective linear subspace.

Here is an explicit cocharacter separating all distinct characters in this finite list. If \(r>0\), write \(\chi=(a_1,\ldots,a_r)\). For distinct characters \(\chi,\psi\), the integer polynomial \[
 \sum_{i=1}^r(a_i-b_i)M^{i-1}
\] is nonzero. The polynomial root bound proved in S02 Lemma 4.A, applied over \(\mathbf Q\), makes its set of integer roots finite. Choose a positive integer \(M\) outside the union of these finitely many sets and put \[
 \lambda(u)=(u,u^M,\ldots,u^{M^{r-1}}):
                  \mathbf G_m\longrightarrow T.
\] The integers \(w_j=\langle\chi_j,\lambda\rangle\) are equal only for equal characters. For \(r=0\), the unique cocharacter has this property since there is only the trivial character. Reorder the coordinates so that \(w_0\) is minimal. By the deletion step, \(c_0\) does not vanish identically on \(X\). The coordinate hyperplane \(H=V(c_0)\) is \(T\)-invariant.

We induct on \(d\). For \(d=0\), the reduced irreducible finite-type \(X\) has one point. An affine neighborhood is a zero-dimensional domain, hence a field; the Nullstellensatz makes it \(k\). Thus \(X=\operatorname{Spec}k\), and its point is fixed.

Suppose \(d>0\). The section \(X\cap H\) is nonempty. Otherwise \(X\) would be closed in the affine complement of \(H\) and hence affine. S01 Theorem 8.4 and its closed-immersion cohomology calculation prove that \(H^0(X,\mathcal O_X)\) is finite-dimensional over \(k\). It is a domain because \(X\) is integral. Multiplication by a nonzero element is an injective endomorphism of a finite-dimensional vector space and therefore surjective, so this algebra is a field. Algebraic closedness makes it \(k\). Affineness would then give \(X=\operatorname{Spec}k\), contradicting \(d>0\).

Every irreducible component of \(X\cap H\), with its reduced structure, has dimension \(d-1\). To check the dimension rather than assume it, take a standard projective affine chart meeting the component and intersect it with \(X\). Its algebra \(A\) is a finite-type domain of dimension \(d\), by the function-field dimension formula in AG-CA \emph{Krull dimension and Noether normalization}, Theorem 4.2. In a local frame the hyperplane section is defined by a nonzero element \(f\in A\); its component corresponds to a prime \(\mathfrak p\) minimal over \((f)\). This prime is nonzero. The principal ideal theorem in AG-CA \emph{Dimension theory of Noetherian local rings}, Theorem 3.1, gives \(\operatorname{ht}\mathfrak p\le1\), while \((0)\subsetneq\mathfrak p\) gives the reverse inequality. The height formula, Theorem 4.3 of the former lesson, yields \[
 \dim(A/\mathfrak p)=\dim A-\operatorname{ht}\mathfrak p=d-1.
\] Passing between nonempty affine opens of this integral component preserves its function field and hence its dimension by that same Theorem 4.2.

Choose one such reduced component \(Y\). It is \(T\)-stable. Indeed, \(T\times Y\) is integral: on affine charts of \(Y\) its algebra is the domain \(A[t_1^{\pm1},\ldots,t_r^{\pm1}]\), and these charts have nonempty intersections. The closure of its image under the action is therefore irreducible, lies in \(X\cap H\), and contains \(Y\) through the identity of \(T\). Maximality of the irreducible component forces this closure to be \(Y\). The action factors through its reduced structure, since pullbacks of its defining ideal vanish at every point of the reduced source and therefore vanish. The restriction is a linear action on the projective variety \(Y\). Induction supplies at least \(d\) distinct \(T\)-fixed points in \(Y\subset H\).

There is one more fixed point outside \(H\). Choose \(a\in(X\setminus H)(k)\), using the Nullstellensatz on this nonempty affine chart, and normalize its coordinates so that \(c_0(a)=1\). Its \(\lambda\)-orbit on the same chart has coordinates \[
 c_j(\lambda(u)a)/c_0(\lambda(u)a)
       =u^{w_j-w_0}c_j(a),\qquad j>0.
\] All exponents are nonnegative integers, so these polynomials define a morphism \(\mathbf A^1_k\to\mathbf P^N_k\setminus H\). It lands in \(X\): the equations of the closed affine subscheme \(X\setminus H\) vanish after substitution in \(k[u,u^{-1}]\), hence in its subring \(k[u]\). At \(u=0\), every coordinate of weight greater than \(w_0\) is zero; the remaining coordinates have character \(\chi_0\) by the separating property. Every element of \(T\), over every \(k\)-algebra, scales these remaining coordinates by the same unit \(\chi_0(t)\). Thus the resulting projective point is \(T\)-fixed. Its zeroth coordinate is still one, so it lies outside \(H\) and differs from all \(d\) points obtained inside \(H\). This proves the bound \(d+1\). \(\square\)

\subsection{The curve duality used in rank one}\label{AG-RG-03-the-curve-duality-used-in-rank-one}

\textbf{Lemma (curve duality).} If \(C\) is a smooth projective pure one-dimensional curve over a field \(k\) and \(L\) is invertible, then naturally

\[
H^1(C,L)^*\simeq
H^0(C,\Omega_{C/k}\otimes L^{-1}).
\]

\textbf{Proof.} Embed \(i:C\hookrightarrow P=\mathbf P^N_k\), and put \(c=N-1\). The regular-immersion calculation in \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/main/docs/courses/AG-RG/AG-RG-S02.md}{Projective cohomology and smooth affine models}, Lemma 6.1, proves over the original field, including imperfect fields, that \(I/I^2\) is locally free of rank \(c\), that the ideal is locally generated by a regular sequence, and that \[
0\longrightarrow I/I^2\longrightarrow i^*\Omega_{P/k}
\longrightarrow\Omega_{C/k}\longrightarrow0
\] is exact. Its proof first calculates at geometric closed points, then descends the conormal module and the exact Koszul complex by faithful field extension.

Dualizing that Koszul resolution, with a local frame of \(L\), gives \[
\mathcal E xt^q_P(i_*L,\omega_P)=0\quad(q\ne c),
\qquad
\mathcal E xt^c_P(i_*L,\omega_P)
=i_*(L^{-1}\otimes i^*\omega_P\otimes\det(I/I^2)^*).
\] Here \(\omega_P=\det\Omega_{P/k}=\mathcal O_P(-N-1)\). Taking determinants of the conormal sequence identifies the sheaf in degree \(c\) with \(i_*(L^{-1}\otimes\Omega_{C/k})\). The finite-cover Hom double complex written in S02 Theorem 6.2 has only this nonzero sheaf-Ext row, and therefore gives \[
\operatorname{Ext}^c_P(i_*L,\omega_P)
=H^0(C,L^{-1}\otimes\Omega_{C/k}).
\] S02 Ambient Theorem 6.B proves projective-space duality by the monomial trace, a two-stage twist presentation and dimension shifting; it identifies the same Ext group with \(H^{N-c}(P,i_*L)^*=H^1(C,L)^*\). Its trace sends the class of \(T_0^{-1}\cdots T_N^{-1}\) to one. All the Koszul, determinant, finite-cover and trace comparisons are natural. This proves the asserted isomorphism. \(\square\)

\textbf{Lemma 2.2 (the curve argument).} Over an algebraically closed field, a smooth projective curve dominated by \(\mathbf P^1\) is isomorphic to \(\mathbf P^1\).

\textbf{Proof.} Write \(C\) for the dominated curve. The dense image of the irreducible \(\mathbf P^1_k\) is irreducible. Smoothness gives reducedness, so \(C\) is integral and connected. If domination is initially given by a rational map, the homogeneous-coordinate DVR extension in the earlier S03 Theorem 2.2 makes it a morphism. Thus the hypotheses of \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/main/docs/courses/AG-RG/AG-RG-S02.md}{S02 Proposition 6.5} hold: its complete separable differential calculation and inseparable-subfield reduction prove \(g=\dim_kH^1(C,\mathcal O_C)=0\) in every characteristic. Its proof is earlier in the programme; no unproved external form of Lüroth's theorem is used.

We supply explicitly the concluding rational-function calculation from that proposition. Choose a closed point \(q\in C(k)\), which exists by the earlier Nullstellensatz. S02 Lemma 6.3 proves \(H^0(C,\mathcal O_C)=k\), divisor Euler characteristics, the canonical degree \(\deg\Omega_{C/k}=2g-2=-2\), and vanishing for negative-degree line bundles. Its earlier Theorem 6.2 gives duality. For every integer \(m\ge0\), these results yield \[
 H^1(C,\mathcal O_C(mq))^*
   =H^0(C,\Omega_{C/k}(-mq))=0,
 \qquad
 h^0(C,\mathcal O_C(mq))=m+1.
\] The first vanishing uses degree \(-2-m<0\); the second is the proved Euler characteristic formula with \(g=0\).

Take \(x\) in \(H^0(C,\mathcal O_C(q))\) independent of the constants. In the divisor description of this sheaf, it is a rational function regular away from \(q\) with pole order at most one at \(q\). It has a pole: otherwise it would be a global regular function and belong to \(k\). Its pole order is therefore exactly one. The functions \(1,x,\ldots,x^m\) belong to \(H^0(C,\mathcal O_C(mq))\) and have distinct pole orders. A nonzero linear combination has the pole order of its highest nonzero power, since all coefficients lie in \(k\) and that term cannot be canceled by terms of smaller order. They are independent, and their number \(m+1\) is the dimension just computed. They form a basis.

Let \(h\in k(C)\) be any nonzero rational function. The earlier divisor proof shows that it has finitely many poles. List its poles \(a_1,\ldots,a_r\) outside \(q\). The function \(x\) is regular at each of them, and \(x(a_i)\in k\). Each nonzero function \(x-x(a_i)\) has positive valuation at \(a_i\) and no pole outside \(q\). Choose integers \(N_i\ge0\) large enough that \[
 P(x)h,\qquad P(T)=\prod_{i=1}^r(T-x(a_i))^{N_i},
\] has no pole outside \(q\). Multiplying cannot introduce a pole at another such point. Its remaining pole order at \(q\) is finite, so the product is a section of \(\mathcal O_C(mq)\) for some \(m\ge0\). By the basis calculation, it equals a polynomial \(Q(x)\). The polynomial \(P\) is nonzero and \(x\) is transcendental over the algebraically closed \(k\), so \(P(x)\ne0\). Consequently \(h=Q(x)/P(x)\in k(x)\). The empty pole list gives \(P=1\), and the zero function is already in \(k(x)\). Hence \(k(C)=k(x)\).

This equality gives inverse rational maps between \(C\) and \(\mathbf P^1_k\): on a nonempty affine chart, send its finitely many coordinate generators to their rational functions in the other function field and clear their denominators; their equations remain satisfied. Both targets are projective and both sources are smooth curves. The earlier S03 Theorem 2.2 extends these maps at every DVR by homogeneous coordinates. Their composites are the identity on the common function field and hence on a dense open. The closed-diagonal equalizer argument for the reduced integral sources makes the composites the identity everywhere. The resulting morphisms are inverse isomorphisms. This argument needs no degree formula for an unchecked inseparable map. \(\square\)

\textbf{Proposition 2.3.} A semisimple group of rank one has exactly two Borel subgroups containing a maximal torus, its Borel quotient is \(\mathbf P^1\), and the action on that quotient has image \(\operatorname{PGL}_2\) and kernel its centre.

\textbf{Proof.} Fix a maximal torus \(T\subset B\) and put \(X=G/B\). RG01 Lemma 2.1 constructs it as a closed orbit with a linear equivariant projective embedding and the full fppf \(B\)-torsor \(G\to X\). The complete orbit proof S08 Theorem G.4.C makes this actual quotient smooth. It is integral, being reduced and the surjective image of the irreducible smooth connected \(G\). RG02's complete torus-fixed-coset proof makes \(X^T\) a finite disjoint union of reduced \(k\)-points. Its following transitivity argument identifies this set with \(N_G(T)/C_G(T)\). RG02 Theorem 2.1 gives \(C_G(T)=T\), so this quotient acts faithfully on the rank-one character lattice \(\mathbf Z\), whose automorphisms are precisely multiplication by \(1\) or \(-1\). Hence \(X^T\) has at most two points. It has at least one, the coset \(B\). If \(\dim X=0\), integrality and the Nullstellensatz make \(X=\operatorname{Spec}k\), so the torsor stabilizer forces \(G=B\), contradicting nontrivial semisimplicity. Lemma 2.1 now gives \(|X^T|\ge\dim X+1\ge2\). Therefore there are exactly two fixed points and \(\dim X=1\). The Borel-normalizer theorem already proved in RG02 identifies these with exactly two Borels containing \(T\).

Let \(K\) be the schematic kernel of the action on \(X\). It is the intersection of the conjugates of \(B\). This retains the full kernel on every test algebra: in the equivariant projective embedding the fixed-point equations are the coordinate two-by-two minors. If they vanish on every constant \(k\)-point of the reduced \(X\), each of their finitely many linearly independent scalar coefficients vanishes on every such point, hence vanishes identically by the Nullstellensatz. Thus these equations vanish after arbitrary scalar extension as well. Its reduced identity component is a smooth connected normal solvable subgroup, hence is trivial by semisimplicity. Normality here holds schematically: conjugation by the smooth connected \(G\) preserves that component, and its reduced source factors through its reduced structure, as in S08 Lemma G.4.1. Thus \(K\) is zero-dimensional. It is finite: its affine algebra is Noetherian, has finitely many minimal primes, and in dimension zero they are maximal, with residue fields \(k\). The nilradical is generated by finitely many nilpotent elements and hence is nilpotent, by the bound on monomial exponents. The reduced algebra is a finite product of copies of \(k\); the successive nilradical quotients are finite modules over it. This gives a finite-dimensional algebra for \(K\). A positive-dimensional Borel consequently has a nonconstant orbit map to \(X\). Otherwise all its point orbits would be points, and density of rational points in the reduced \(B\times X\) would make the action trivial schematically, contradicting \(B\subset K\).

We supply the rational coordinates required for restricting such an orbit map to a line. For a smooth connected solvable group \(B=U\rtimes T\), RG01 Lemma 2.B gives \[
 U=U_0\supset U_1\supset\cdots\supset U_a=1,
 \qquad U_i/U_{i+1}\simeq\mathbf G_a.
\] The quotients \(U/U_i\) are smooth connected and affine by the complete earlier RG01 Lemma 2.G: each \(U_i\) is a closed normal unitriangular subgroup of the smooth connected \(U\). The resulting quotient maps are fppf torsors. The map \[
 U/U_{i+1}\longrightarrow U/U_i
\] is explicitly a \(U_i/U_{i+1}\simeq\mathbf G_a\)-torsor. Pull it back along the fppf cover \(U\to U/U_i\). If two local representatives have the same \(U_i\)-coset, their ratio belongs to \(U_i\); its \(U_{i+1}\)-coset is unchanged on replacing either representative by its \(U_{i+1}\)-equivalent lift. Multiplication and division therefore give inverse maps between this pullback and \((U_i/U_{i+1})\times U\). This is a local trivialization with the translation action, and its equality relation gives the asserted torsor on every test scheme. All these subgroups are normal, so either coset convention gives these quotient groups. Every such torsor over an affine algebra has a section by the explicit vector-line module-descent calculation in RG01's solvable-structure proof: the translation cocycle descends \(0\to A\to E\to A\to0\), and a lift of \(1\) gives the section. This calculation works over any affine \(A\). Translation by a section identifies the torsor with its base times \(\mathbf A^1\). Starting with \(U/U_0=1\) and repeating gives \(U\simeq\mathbf A^a\) as varieties. The torus is split over the algebraically closed field, by the splitting argument in Lemma 2.1. Thus \[
 B\simeq\mathbf A^a\times\mathbf G_m^r,
 \qquad k(B)=k(z_1,\ldots,z_d),\quad d=a+r.
\] These are scheme coordinates; no assertion about abstract group coordinates is needed.

Choose a nonconstant orbit map \(b\mapsto bx\) and a nonconstant \(h\in k(X)\). The map is dominant because its image has positive dimension in the integral curve, so its pullback \(f\in k(B)\) is nonconstant. Choose the least \(j\ge1\) for which \(f\in k(z_1,\ldots,z_j)\). Then \(f\notin k(z_1,\ldots,z_{j-1})\). Write, after clearing finitely many coefficient denominators, \[
 f=P(z_j)/Q(z_j),\quad
 P=\sum_i A_i z_j^i,\quad Q=\sum_i B_i z_j^i,
 \quad A_i,B_i\in k[z_1,\ldots,z_{j-1}].
\] Some coefficient minor \(A_iB_l-A_lB_i\) is nonzero. If they all vanished, choosing \(B_l\ne0\) would give \(P=(A_l/B_l)Q\), contradicting the choice of \(j\).

The inverse image of the domain where \(h\) is regular contains a nonempty principal open of our coordinate chart. Choose a nonzero polynomial \(F\) defining such an open, multiplying by torus coordinates to clear Laurent denominators if necessary. Viewed as a polynomial in \(z_j\), it has a nonzero coefficient in the other variables. Specialize every other coordinate so that this coefficient, the selected minor, and all fixed torus coordinates stay nonzero. Such a specialization exists: their product is a nonzero polynomial over the infinite field \(k\), and repeated use of the univariate root bound in S02 Lemma 4.A supplies a point where it does not vanish. For no remaining variables the product is already a nonzero scalar. On the resulting coordinate line, \(P/Q\) stays nonconstant and \(F\) does not vanish identically. If \(z_j\) is a torus coordinate, restrict also to \(z_j\ne0\). We have obtained a nonconstant rational map \(\mathbf A^1\dashrightarrow X\), since its composition with \(h\) is this nonconstant rational function. The explicit DVR extension calculation in S03 Theorem 2.2 extends it to \(\mathbf P^1\to X\). Lemma 2.2, which includes inseparable domination, identifies \(X\) with \(\mathbf P^1\).

The natural map \(\operatorname{PGL}_2\to\operatorname{Aut}(\mathbf P^1)\) is an isomorphism on all test algebras. An automorphism sends \(0,1,\infty\) to three sections that remain pairwise disjoint on every fibre. Locally trivialize their quotient lines. A change of basis sends \(0,\infty\) to the first and third; the two nonzero coordinates of the middle section are units, so diagonal scaling also sends \(1\) to it. For uniqueness, an automorphism fixing \(0\) and \(\infty\) preserves both Cartier divisors. The ratio of its pulled-back coordinate to that coordinate is therefore an invertible regular function on all of \(\mathbf P^1\). S01 Theorem 7.2 gives \(H^0(\mathbf P^1_R,\mathcal O)=R\), so that ratio is a base unit. Fixing \(1\) makes it one. The local projective matrices consequently agree on overlaps and glue in the represented projective linear group. This proves the assertion even over rings with nilpotents.

Construct the schematic image \(H\) directly from the image of the coordinate Hopf algebra of \(\operatorname{PGL}_2\) in the domain \(k[G]\). Its finitely generated image algebra is a domain; the kernel is a Hopf ideal because tensoring inclusions over a field is injective. Thus \(H\) is a closed integral affine group. The full integral-target monic-division and translation proof in AG-GS-04 Lemma 11.1c makes \(G\to H\) faithfully flat and of finite presentation. The kernel identity gives its torsor relation. Lemma 1.C above makes reduced \(H\) smooth, and integrality makes it connected. The orbit-dimension calculation of S08 Lemma G.4.D applied to the left action on \(H\) gives \(\dim H=\dim G-\dim K\). Its kernel \(K\) is finite. Its torus image has dimension one, and maximal-torus conjugacy in RG01 conjugates it to the diagonal torus of \(\operatorname{PGL}_2\). If \(H\) were proper, it would have dimension at most two. In every characteristic, \(\operatorname{Lie}\operatorname{PGL}_2=\mathfrak{gl}_2/kI\) has the diagonal line of weight zero and two distinct root lines of weights \(1,-1\) for the cocharacter represented by \(\operatorname{diag}(t,1)\). The \(T\)-stable Lie algebra of \(H\) contains the diagonal line and at most one root line. Choose that cocharacter or its inverse so that all its weights on \(\operatorname{Lie}H\) are nonnegative. The general limit-subgroup proof already given in RG01 Lemma 3.3 makes \(P_H(\lambda)\) smooth with this entire Lie algebra, hence of dimension \(\dim H\). A closed subgroup of that dimension in the connected smooth \(H\) is all of \(H\). But \[
 P_H(\lambda)=H\cap P_{\operatorname{PGL}_2}(\lambda),
\] and the ambient limit subgroup is triangular. Thus \(H\) would be solvable. The finite group \(K(k)\) is central in \(G(k)\): each conjugation orbit is the image of the connected reduced \(G\) in a finite set and is the identity translate. Every \(H(k)\)-point lifts through the faithfully flat finite-type image map by the Nullstellensatz. Hence \(G(k)\) is a central extension of a solvable group and is solvable. Its finite derived-word identities hold on the dense rational points of each reduced finite Cartesian power of \(G\), so they hold schematically, making \(G\) solvable. This contradicts semisimplicity. Therefore \(H=\operatorname{PGL}_2\).

In particular \(\dim G=3\). Since \(\dim X=1\), each of the two Borels \(B_+,B_-\) has dimension two and unipotent radical of dimension one. The one-dimensional unipotent classification proved in S03 Section 4 identifies each radical with \(\mathbf G_a\). Its image has dimension one because the kernel is finite. Projection of the corresponding point stabilizer onto its diagonal torus gives a character of the radical, trivial by RG01 Lemma 2.A. Thus its reduced closed image lies in the ambient unipotent line; dimension one makes it that entire line. Its torus character \(\alpha_+\) or \(\alpha_-\) is nonzero, since the induced diagonal-torus map is an isogeny and the ambient root character is nonzero. The normalizer element interchanging the two fixed points acts by inversion on \(T\), so \(\alpha_-=-\alpha_+\).

The Lie algebra of \(K\) lies in both \(\mathfrak b_+\) and \(\mathfrak b_-\). Their nonzero-weight lines have these distinct opposite characters, while the shared torus has weight zero. Thus \(\operatorname{Lie}K\) has no vector in either unipotent root line. Each finite intersection \(K\cap R_u(B_\pm)\) is torus-stable. Since \(\alpha_\pm\ne0\), its polynomial ideal is homogeneous for the distinct weights \(i\alpha_\pm\), hence is \((x^n)\) for some \(n\ge1\). The Hopf identity requires every intermediate binomial coefficient in \((X+Y)^n\) to vanish. In characteristic zero the coefficient \(n\) excludes \(n>1\). In characteristic \(p\), write \(n=p^e m\) with \(p\nmid m\). If \(m>1\), the coefficient \(m\) of \(X^{p^e}Y^{n-p^e}\) in \((X^{p^e}+Y^{p^e})^m\) is nonzero, a contradiction. Thus \(n=p^e\). Any \(n>1\) gives nonzero tangent space at the identity, already excluded. Both intersections are therefore trivial. The image maps of the two radicals are faithfully flat with trivial kernel, hence isomorphisms onto the ambient unipotent subgroups, by their full torsor relations.

For a point of \(B_+\cap B_-\) over any test algebra, write it \(tu_+\) by the solvable decomposition. Its image lies in the diagonal intersection of the two ambient point stabilizers, so the image of \(u_+\) is trivial. The just-proved isomorphism gives \(u_+=1\). Therefore \(B_+\cap B_-=T\) schematically and \(K\subset T\). A finite normal multiplicative-type subgroup of a smooth connected group is central: over \(k\) it has a finite character group, and the earlier coefficient proof for diagonalizable groups represents its automorphisms by that finite constant étale character-automorphism group. The conjugation map from connected \(G\) to this discrete group has value the identity automorphism at the identity of \(G\), hence is constant with that value as a scheme morphism. Thus \(K\subset Z(G)\). Conversely \(Z(G)\) maps to the centre of \(\operatorname{PGL}_2\), which is trivial schematically. Indeed a central automorphism of \(\mathbf P^1\) commutes with the diagonal torus and preserves its fixed sections \(0,\infty\); interchanging them would invert the universal torus parameter and cannot commute with it. It is therefore a scaling by a base unit, and commuting with every translation forces that unit to be one. Thus \(Z(G)\subset K\), proving \(K=Z(G)\) and every assertion. \(\square\)

For a reductive group of semisimple rank one, the radical-quotient proof in Section 1 produces a semisimple group \(Q\) of rank one. The inverse image of a Borel of \(Q\) is smooth connected and solvable by that same central-torus torsor argument; maximality and the inverse-image comparison make it a Borel of \(G\). It has the same projective-line quotient, by the equality of its fppf cosets. Conversely a Borel of \(G\) contains the radical: their product is smooth connected and solvable, since the radical is central, and maximality forces equality with the Borel. Its image in \(Q\) is a Borel by the inverse-image comparison. In its decomposition \(B=U\rtimes T\), the radical belongs to \(T\) by RG01 Lemma 2.N and centrality, and \(U\cap\operatorname{Rad}(G)=1\) schematically by the unitriangular character calculation in RG01 Lemma 2.A. Quotienting the product gives \(B/\operatorname{Rad}(G)=U\rtimes(T/\operatorname{Rad}(G))\) as fppf sheaves, hence as the represented groups. Thus its two unipotent radicals map isomorphically to the additive radicals of \(Q\), with their opposite characters pulled back to \(T\). The action kernel is \(q^{-1}(Z(Q))\). A point of this kernel lies in both opposite Borel inverse images, whose intersection is \(T\) by the displayed product descriptions and \(B_+\cap B_-=T\) for \(Q\). It acts trivially on both root lines. The centre formula in Section 1, now with those two nonzero weights, makes it central. The reverse containment follows from the trivial centre of the projective linear image. Thus its centre is precisely the kernel of the action on that same projective line.

Now let \(\alpha\) be any nonzero weight of a maximal torus of an arbitrary reductive \(k\)-group. Define the codimension-one torus

\[
T_\alpha=(\ker\alpha)^0_{\mathrm{red}}.
\]

The centralizer \(G_\alpha=C_G(T_\alpha)\) is reductive by the preceding lesson. Its weights are precisely the weights of \(G\) that are rational multiples of \(\alpha\), since these and only these vanish on \(T_\alpha\). Its maximal central torus has codimension one in \(T\): the nonzero characters on \(T/T_\alpha\) span a rank-one lattice. Thus its semisimple rank is one. Proposition 2.3 proves

\[
\Phi\cap\mathbf Q\alpha=\{\alpha,-\alpha\},\qquad
\dim\mathfrak g_\alpha=1.
\]

This proves both the reducedness along each root line and the one-dimensional root-space assertion without appealing to a general root-system classification.

\section{3. Subgroups obtained by taking a limit}\label{AG-RG-03-subgroups-obtained-by-taking-a-limit}

The definitions and full grading, smoothness, connectedness and open-cell proof for these subgroups are in \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/main/docs/courses/AG-RG/AG-RG-01.md\#subgroups-obtained-by-taking-a-limit}{Tori, maximal tori and their conjugacy, Lemma 3.3}, an earlier lesson. In this lesson Lemma 3.1 denotes that already proved general lemma; it applies to every smooth affine group of finite presentation, without reductivity or a root classification.

For \(\operatorname{SL}_2\) and \(\lambda(t)=\operatorname{diag}(t,t^{-1})\), conjugation sends \(\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}\) to \(\begin{pmatrix}a&t^2b\\t^{-2}c&d\end{pmatrix}\). Thus \(P(\lambda)\) is upper triangular, \(U(\lambda)\) is upper unipotent, and \(L(\lambda)\) is diagonal. This calculation works in characteristic two because the group character \(t^2\) remains nontrivial.

\section{4. Root groups over the base}\label{AG-RG-03-root-groups-over-the-base}

Let \(T=D_S(M)\) be a split maximal torus. Locally the nonzero weights are a fixed finite set \(\Phi\subset M\), and each \(\mathfrak g_\alpha\) is a line bundle by Proposition 2.3 on geometric fibres. Define \(T_\alpha\) by the torsion-free quotient of \(M/\mathbf Z\alpha\). Then

\[
G_\alpha=C_G(T_\alpha),\qquad
\operatorname{Lie}(G_\alpha)=\mathfrak t\oplus\mathfrak g_\alpha\oplus\mathfrak g_{-\alpha}.
\]

Choose a cocharacter \(\lambda\) of \(T\) with \(n=\langle\alpha,\lambda\rangle>0\), and set \(U_\alpha=U_{G_\alpha}(\lambda)\). It is a smooth connected one-dimensional unipotent group, with Lie algebra \(\mathfrak g_\alpha\).

For a line bundle \(L\), write \(\mathbf V(L)=\operatorname{Spec}_S\operatorname{Sym}(L^*)\) for its additive group.

\textbf{Theorem 4.1.} There is a unique \(T\)-equivariant homomorphism

\[
\exp_\alpha:\mathbf V(\mathfrak g_\alpha)\longrightarrow G
\]

whose differential is the inclusion of the root line. It is a closed immersion, with image \(U_\alpha\), and commutes with every base change. Moreover

\[
U_{-\alpha}\times T\times U_\alpha\longrightarrow G_\alpha
\]

is an open immersion.

\textbf{Proof.} The earlier RG01 Lemma 3.3, used as Lemma 3.1 here, gives the smooth affine subgroup \(U_\alpha=U_{G_\alpha}(\lambda)\) of finite presentation, its action extending to \(\mathbf A^1\) with zero equal to the identity, and its Lie module \(\mathfrak g_\alpha\). On that line \(\lambda(t)\) acts by \(t^n\), with the positive integer \(n=\langle\alpha,\lambda\rangle\). The earlier RG01 Lemma 3.D therefore constructs a unique normalized equivariant group isomorphism

\[
\mathbf V(\mathfrak g_\alpha)\xrightarrow{\sim}U_\alpha.
\]

Its entire graded-algebra, differential and gluing proof works over the original base, even if \(n\) is zero in some residue fields. Since \(T\) commutes with \(\lambda\), the last assertion of that lemma makes this isomorphism \(T\)-equivariant on every test algebra. Compose it with the closed immersion \(U_\alpha\subset G_\alpha\subset G\) to obtain \(\exp_\alpha\).

For uniqueness as a homomorphism into \(G\), let \(h\) be any \(T\)-equivariant homomorphism with the required differential. The subtorus \(T_\alpha\) acts trivially on its source, so the equality expressing equivariance makes every value of \(h\) commute with \(T_\alpha\), including its universal points. Hence \(h\) factors through the represented centralizer \(G_\alpha\). Moreover

\[
\lambda(t)h(x)\lambda(t)^{-1}=h(t^n x).
\]

The right side extends regularly to \(t=0\) and there equals \(h(0)=1\). The defining orbit-limit equations from RG01 Lemma 3.3 therefore force \(h\) to factor through \(U_{G_\alpha}(\lambda)\). In a local Lie-line frame, compose with the inverse of the preceding isomorphism. The result is a weight-\(n\) equivariant endomorphism of an affine line with identity differential. The Laurent-coefficient calculation in RG01 Lemma 3.D makes it the identity. These equalities hold on overlaps, proving global uniqueness.

We also verify the equality needed for the open cell over the original base. The centralizer theorem of the preceding lesson makes the geometric fibres of \(L=L_{G_\alpha}(\lambda)\) connected. The two opposite nonzero weights established in Section 2 and RG01 Lemma 3.3 give \(\operatorname{Lie}(L)=\mathfrak t\). On a geometric fibre the closed torus \(T\) thus has the same dimension as the smooth connected \(L\), and is all of it: a proper closed subset of the irreducible smooth connected group has smaller dimension. Over \(S\), both groups are smooth, and the inclusion \(T\to L\) has invertible differential at the identity and hence everywhere by translation. S02 Lemma 3.A makes it étale; S04 Lemma A1.9 makes this monomorphism an open immersion. Its image contains every geometric fibre by the equality just proved, so it is all of \(L\). Thus \(L=T\) as schemes over \(S\). Applying the open-cell assertion of RG01 Lemma 3.3 inside \(G_\alpha\), with the cocharacters \(\lambda\) and \(-\lambda\), gives the displayed open immersion. Formation of these centralizers and limit subgroups commutes with every base change by their defining equations. So do their Lie modules and the uniquely normalized isomorphism of RG01 Lemma 3.D. All the asserted constructions are therefore compatible with every base change. \(\square\)

The notation \(\exp_\alpha\) denotes this algebraic map, not the analytic exponential series. No division by factorials occurs. A root-group parameterization \(x_\alpha:\mathbf G_a\simeq U_\alpha\) is exactly a trivializing section of the root line.

\textbf{Example 4.2.} In \(\operatorname{GL}_n\), conjugation by \(\operatorname{diag}(t_i)\) sends \(E_{ij}\) to \((t_i/t_j)E_{ij}\). Thus

\[
\alpha_{ij}=e_i-e_j,\quad
\mathfrak g_{\alpha_{ij}}=\mathcal O_SE_{ij},\quad
x_{ij}(u)=I+uE_{ij}.
\]

\textbf{Example 4.3.} Let \(E=\mathcal O_S\oplus L\) for a line bundle \(L\). Define \(\mathrm{SL}(E)\) by the automorphisms whose action on \(\bigwedge^2E=L\) is the identity. On opens trivializing \(L\) this is exactly the determinant-one matrix group of RG01 Lemma 1.M. If two frames differ by a unit \(\ell\), their matrix coordinates differ by conjugation with \(\operatorname{diag}(1,\ell)\); these conjugations satisfy the same cocycle as the frames and preserve determinants. The complete affine algebra/morphism descent of S04 Lemmas A1.2, A1.3a and A1.5 therefore glues these local affine smooth finite-presentation groups into \(G=\mathrm{SL}(E)\). Each geometric fibre is the already proved reductive \(\mathrm{SL}_2\). The local diagonal maps \((t,t^{-1})\) commute with the transitions, so glue to a closed split maximal torus, maximality being checked on those fibres.

The off-diagonal endomorphism modules are \(\operatorname{Hom}(L,\mathcal O)=L^{-1}\) above and \(\operatorname{Hom}(\mathcal O,L)=L\) below. Conjugation gives their full weights \(t^2\) and \(t^{-2}\), and the trace-zero diagonal tangent module has weight zero. For an upper entry \(u:L\to\mathcal O\), its square as an endomorphism of \(E\) is zero. Consequently \(I+u\) has determinant one, inverse \(I-u\), and \((I+u)(I+v)=I+(u+v)\) on every test scheme. This identifies the upper subgroup with \(\mathbf V(L^{-1})\); the same calculation gives \(\mathbf V(L)\) below. They are the root groups of Theorem 4.1 because their equivariant tangent maps are the displayed identities, whose uniqueness that theorem proves. Here \(\mathbf V(M)\) means the additive group whose local sections are sections of the line module \(M\). Its Lie module is \(M\), by the same square-zero calculation. A group-scheme isomorphism with \(\mathbf G_a\) would induce an isomorphism \(M\simeq\mathcal O_S\) on Lie modules. Thus when \(L\) is nontrivial neither displayed root group is globally isomorphic to \(\mathbf G_a\). Over a field every line is trivial, by choosing a nonzero vector. Having a split maximal torus is therefore weaker than having globally parameterized root groups.

\section{5. A projective quotient and its rank-one form}\label{AG-RG-03-a-projective-quotient-and-its-rank-one-form}

We use the general algebraic-space tool proved before this lesson in \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/main/docs/courses/AG-RG/AG-RG-S04.md}{Affine descent, Zariski Main and recognition of spaces}, Theorems E8.1 and E9.1. The proof there includes the finite flat affine quotient, the off-diagonal induction, separated locally quasi-finite scheme effectivity, and relative integral closure with its étale base change. It applies over every base and on every test scheme.

\textbf{Quasi-finite normalization lemma.} Let \(S\) be a scheme and let \(f:X\to Y\) be a quasi-finite separated morphism of algebraic spaces over \(S\). Let \(Y'\) be the relative integral closure of \(Y\) in \(X\). Then the factorization \(X\xrightarrow{f'}Y'\xrightarrow{\nu}Y\) has \(f'\) a quasi-compact open immersion and \(\nu\) integral. In particular \(f\) is quasi-affine.

\textbf{Proof.} Theorem E9.1 of the preceding supporting lesson proves the full factorization, after Theorem E8.1 establishes recognition and Corollary E8.2 establishes representability on every scheme test. Its integral algebras are descended using the proved affine faithfully flat equalizer, and Corollary D4.3 supplies their étale base-change compatibility. Thus for every affine scheme \(Z\to Y\), the pullback \(Z\times_YX\) is a quasi-compact open subscheme of the affine integral scheme \(Z\times_YY'\). This is quasi-affineness. All these input proofs precede the present application in the programme. \(\square\)

The relative integral closure retains nilpotents; a reduced normalization is not substituted for it. The full argument is in the preceding supporting lesson, rather than being delegated to a source citation.

The following construction will also be used for flag varieties. It makes explicit why a fibrewise projective quotient is a scheme, even before we have classified the group over the base.

\textbf{A flat-source fibre criterion.} A finitely presented closed immersion \(Y\hookrightarrow Z\) over \(S\), with \(Y\) flat over \(S\), is an isomorphism if it is so on every geometric fibre. Locally write its ideal as \(I\subset C\). Flatness of \(C/I\) makes \(I\otimes k(s)\to C\otimes k(s)\) injective. Fibre equality makes this module zero. Since \(I\) is finitely generated as an ideal, Nakayama at every prime of \(C\) gives \(I=0\). No flatness assumption on \(Z\) is needed.

\subsection{Formal separation and normalizers}\label{AG-RG-03-formal-separation-and-normalizers}

We first justify identity-neighbourhood detection over bases with nilpotents, and then prove the full finite-jet normalizer assertion.

\textbf{Formal separation lemma.} Let \(R\) be Noetherian and let \(H/R\) be a smooth affine group of finite presentation with geometrically connected fibres. Write \(C=\mathcal O(H)\) and let \(J\) be its augmentation ideal. Then

\[
\bigcap_{n\geq 1}J^n=0.
\]

\textbf{Proof.} The entire affine smooth-field component proof of AG-RG-S02 Lemma 4.1 makes every geometric fibre integral. For a prime \(\mathfrak p\subset R\), flatness embeds \(C/\mathfrak pC\) into its generic fibre over the fraction field of \(R/\mathfrak p\): multiplication by any nonzero base element stays injective. That generic fibre is integral by geometric connectedness and smoothness, so \(C/\mathfrak pC\) is a domain. Its augmentation onto \(R/\mathfrak p\) also shows that it is nonzero.

We give the prime-filtration argument used here. In any nonzero finite module over a Noetherian ring choose a maximal annihilator of a nonzero element. It is prime: if \(ab\) annihilates that element and \(b\) does not, the nonzero element obtained by multiplying by \(b\) has a larger annihilator unless \(a\) already belongs to the first annihilator. Insert this cyclic prime-annihilator submodule and repeat in the quotient. The ascending chain condition on submodules makes the process stop. Apply it to the finite \(R\)-module \(R\) and tensor its filtration with the flat \(C\). Its factors are \(C/\mathfrak pC\). For any \(j\in J\), the element \(1-j\) has augmentation one in each factor, so is nonzero in that domain and acts injectively. Induction through the finite filtration makes it a nonzerodivisor on \(C\).

The algebra \(C\) is Noetherian by the full Hilbert-basis calculation of AG-RG-S01 Lemma 1.3. Put \(I=\bigcap_nJ^n\). The complete Artin--Rees proof of AG-RG-S02 Lemma 1.1 gives \(I=JI\) by applying it to the finite submodule \(I\subset C\) and taking \(n=c+1\). With finite generators of \(I\), write this equality as \(v=Mv\), with entries of \(M\) in \(J\). The adjugate identity gives \(\det(1-M)I=0\), with \(\det(1-M)=1-j\) for a \(j\in J\). The just-proved nonzerodivisor property gives \(I=0\). This proves the stated separation, including when \(R\) is nonreduced. \(\square\)

\textbf{Normalizer lemma.} If \(H\) is a smooth closed subgroup with geometrically connected fibres of a smooth affine group \(K\) of finite presentation over any scheme \(S\), then its scheme-theoretic normalizer is a closed subgroup of finite presentation in \(K\). Its formation commutes with every base change.

\textbf{Proof.} First suppose \(S=\operatorname{Spec}R\) is Noetherian. We justify the finite locally free identity neighbourhoods used for the equations. For a smooth affine group \(F/R\) with augmentation ideal \(J_F\), the identity conormal bundle \(J_F/J_F^2=\operatorname{Lie}(F)^*\) is finite locally free. On a base neighbourhood where it is free of rank \(d\), lift a basis to functions \(y_1,\ldots,y_d\in J_F\). They define \(F\to\mathbf A_R^d\), sending the identity to zero and with invertible differential there. The complete differential proof of AG-RG-S02 Lemma 3.A makes it etale on a neighbourhood of that section. The full formal-etale lifting theorem of AG-FSE, \emph{Infinitesimal lifting and invariance under thickenings}, Theorem 4.1, constructs its unique inverse on successive zero thickenings. At each step the kernel \((y)^n/(y)^{n+1}\) is square-zero; both composites are the identity by lifting uniqueness. The thickenings are supported on the identity and stay in the chosen etale neighbourhood. Hence, locally on the base, \[
 \mathcal O(F)/J_F^{n+1}\simeq
 R[y_1,\ldots,y_d]/(y_1,\ldots,y_d)^{n+1}.
\] This proves finite local freeness of every identity neighbourhood and the intrinsic associated graded identity \[
 \operatorname{gr}_{J_F}\mathcal O(F)
       =\operatorname{Sym}(\operatorname{Lie}(F)^*).
\] The monomial descriptions agree through the natural graded maps, so the latter identity is independent of coordinates and glues.

Apply this to \(K_n,H_n\), the \(n\)th identity neighbourhoods of \(K,H\). They are finite locally free schemes, without a claim that these thickenings are subgroup schemes. The closed immersion \(H\subset K\) induces a surjection on augmentation ideals: lift a zero-augmentation function using the coordinate-algebra surjection. Thus its augmentation powers are also the induced powers, and \(H_n=H\times_KK_n\). Conjugation preserves the identity and all these powers. It acts by invertible linear maps on the finite locally free coordinate module of \(K_n\).

Write \(D=\mathcal O(K)\) and choose finite generators \(f_i\) of the ideal of \(H\). Restrict their universal conjugates to \(H_n\), for conjugation by both \(g\) and \(g^{-1}\). A section in \(D\otimes_R\mathcal O(H_n)\) vanishes exactly when all its coefficients vanish: locally use a free basis, or globally a finite generating list of its projective dual. The dual and its evaluation commute with arbitrary base change by finite local freeness. These are finitely many equations in \(D\) and define the closed finite-presentation stabilizer \(N_n\subset K\) of the closed subscheme \(H_n\subset K_n\). They represent the stabilizer on every test ring, including nonflat and nonreduced tests. Its two conjugation conditions make it a subgroup.

Its ideals \(L_n\subset D\) increase: preserving the \((n+1)\)st thickening preserves the \(n\)th. Since \(D\) is Noetherian, their union is \(L_N\) at one finite index \(N\). Over the universal Noetherian quotient \(A=D/L_N\), both conjugation restrictions vanish on every identity neighbourhood of \(H_A\). The formal separation proof above applies to the smooth geometrically connected \(H_A\), so each restricted defining equation is zero in its whole coordinate algebra. Both conjugations therefore preserve the entire \(H_A\). Pulling back these actual zero equations proves sufficiency over every \(R\)-algebra. Conversely an automorphism preserving \(H\) preserves its augmentation powers, giving necessity. Thus \(N_K(H)=N_N\) as full scheme functors. This finite universal description proves arbitrary base change, rather than assuming that an infinite intersection commutes with it.

For an arbitrary affine base, first descend \(K,H\) simultaneously to a finitely generated \(\mathbf Z\)-algebra, retaining smoothness, the closed immersion and group-law identities by the complete smooth-model proof AG-RG-S02 Proposition 3.2. Then the entire connected-fibre model argument of its Theorem 4.5 enlarges that coefficient stage so that \(H\) has geometrically connected fibres; the already retained smoothness and finite identities of \(K\) survive that base change. No connectedness hypothesis is imposed on \(K\). Apply the preceding universal Noetherian construction there. Its pullback represents the original normalizer on every test scheme. The unique represented subgroup identifications agree on overlaps and glue. This proves closedness, finite presentation and every asserted base change over the original \(S\). \(\square\)

\subsection{Cohomology of a projective completion}\label{AG-RG-03-cohomology-of-a-projective-completion}

The preceding supporting lesson \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/main/docs/courses/AG-RG/AG-RG-S02.md}{Projective cohomology and smooth affine models}, Theorem 2.3, proves the precise formal-functions statement used here. If \(A\) is Noetherian, \(X/A\) projective, \(F\) coherent and \(I\subset A\), then \[
H^q(X,F)^\wedge_I
\simeq\varprojlim_nH^q(X,F/I^nF).
\] Here is the mechanism of that written proof. Over the Rees algebra \(B=\bigoplus I^nt^n\), the sheaf \(\bigoplus I^nF\) is finite on the projective base change \(X_B\); projective Serre finiteness therefore makes \(\bigoplus H^q(X,I^nF)t^n\) finite over \(B\). If \(M^q=H^q(X,F)\), \(J_n^q=\operatorname{im}(H^q(X,I^nF)\to M^q)\) and \(K_n^q\) is its kernel, finite homogeneous generators give constants \(a_q,b_q\) with \[
I^nM^q\subset J_n^q\subset I^{n-a_q}M^q,
\qquad K_m^q\longrightarrow K_n^q=0\quad(m\ge n+b_q).
\] The sheaf exact sequence consequently gives \[
0\longrightarrow M^q/J_n^q\longrightarrow H^q(X,F/I^nF)
\longrightarrow K_n^{q+1}\longrightarrow0.
\] Its compatible kernel coordinates vanish by the displayed transition bound; the remaining quotient filtration is cofinal with \(I^nM^q\). This proves the inverse-limit comparison, without an unexplained exchange of cohomology and inverse limit.

S02 Lemmas 1.2--1.3 prove exact finite-module completion, Noetherianity and faithful flatness of local completion. Thus a finite module over a complete local Noetherian ring is complete. S02 Lemma 1.4 proves unique lifting of idempotents through nilpotent ideals, and Corollary 2.4 turns the compatible thickened idempotents into an actual section of a projective scheme. These are precisely the two completion operations in the quotient proof below.

\phantomsection\label{AG-RG-03-ag-rg-03-grassmannian}

\textbf{Lemma 5.A (Grassmannians).} The scheme \(\operatorname{Gr}_d(V)\) of locally free rank-\(d\) quotients of a finite locally free \(V/S\) is smooth and projective, commutes with arbitrary base change, and its Plücker line bundle is \(\det Q\), for its universal quotient \(Q\).

\textbf{Proof.} Trivialize \(V=\mathcal O^n\). On the open where columns \(I\) give a basis of a quotient, its unique normalized matrix has those columns equal to the identity and \(d(n-d)\) free entries. A second basis \(J\) gives the transition \(M_J=(M_I|_J)^{-1}M_I\). These open affine charts represent the quotient functor on all tests and glue. The determinant quotient \(\bigwedge^dV\twoheadrightarrow\det Q\) defines the Plücker map to \(\mathbf P(\bigwedge^dV)\), with the quotient convention. Over the target chart \(p_I\ne0\), the ratios of minors containing a single replacement of an identity column recover, with their determinant signs, every free matrix entry. The corresponding map of coordinate rings is surjective. These target charts cover the projective bundle, so the Plücker map is a closed immersion, and its \(\mathcal O(1)\) pulls back to \(\det Q\). The construction glues for general \(V\) and uses only invertible minors, hence works over nonreduced bases. The subbundle convention follows by dualizing. \(\square\)

\subsection{Projective homogeneous quotients}\label{AG-RG-03-projective-homogeneous-quotients}
