\textbf{Lemma 5.1.} Let \(H\) be a smooth closed subgroup with geometrically connected fibres of a smooth affine \(S\)-group \(K\) with geometrically connected fibres. Suppose \(N_K(H)=H\), and suppose every geometric quotient \(K_{\bar s}/H_{\bar s}\) is proper. Then the fppf quotient \(X=K/H\) is a smooth projective \(S\)-scheme, locally on \(S\). Its universal conjugate subgroup \(\mathcal H\subset K_X\) supplies a canonical relatively ample line bundle \(\det(\operatorname{Lie}\mathcal H)^*\).

\textbf{Proof.} The claim is local on the base, so work on affine pieces with fixed smooth relative dimensions. If \(\dim H=0\), its connected smooth geometric fibres are the identity points. The identity section into \(H\) is an etale monomorphism by the entire differential and open-monomorphism proofs of AG-RG-S02 Lemma 3.A and AG-RG-S04 Lemma E7.2. It is surjective on geometric fibres and hence an isomorphism. Thus \(H=1\). Its normalizer is \(K\), so the hypothesis gives \(K=1\) and \(X=S\). The asserted line bundle is then relatively ample through \(\mathbf P(\mathcal O_S)=S\). We may treat the positive-dimensional pieces below.

The entire finite-model theorem of AG-RG-S02 Theorem 4.5 descends \(K,H\) and their finite equations to a finite-type Noetherian base \(S_0\), retaining smoothness and geometrically connected fibres. The full normalizer theorem just proved commutes with every base change. The equality \(N_K(H)=H\) descends at a later coefficient stage: both are finitely presented closed subschemes of the affine group, and equality of their finite ideal generators uses finitely many relation witnesses. Work on the open-and-closed model rank pieces for the finite locally free modules below. Their pullbacks cover the original base, so this introduces no additional hypothesis.

The complete free-action proof of AG-RG-S07 Corollary 8.3 constructs \(X_0=K_0/H_0\) as an algebraic space and the full fppf \(H_0\)-torsor \(K_0\to X_0\), with every base change. Flatness and local finite presentation of \(X_0/S_0\) descend on etale scheme charts by the complete AG-RG-S07 Lemma 5.2. Here is the smoothness argument in full. Choose an etale scheme chart \(W\to X_0\). For any \(s\in S_0\) and any field extension \(L/\kappa(s)\), the scheme \(K_L\times_{X_L}W_L\) is etale over the smooth \(L\)-group \(K_L\), hence smooth over \(L\) by the square-zero composition proof of AG-CA-17 Theorem 1.2 and finite-presentation permanence. Its local rings are regular by AG-CA-18 Theorem 2.1. Its map to \(W_L\) is surjective and flat, being the base change of the torsor. At each point of \(W_L\), a point above it gives a faithfully flat local map from its local ring into a regular local ring. The full regularity descent in \emph{Descending properties}, Proposition 1.1, applies: the residue-field resolution acquires a projective syzygy upstairs by AG-CA-14 Theorem 2.2, that finite projectivity descends by AG-RG-S04 Lemma A1.3 and AG-CA-07 Theorem 5.3, and the same residue-field criterion proves regularity downstairs. Thus every \(W_L\) is regular. To turn this into fibre smoothness without an omitted geometric-regularity converse, fix \(w\in W_s\) and choose an algebraically closed field \(L\) containing \(\kappa(w)\) by AG-RG-S07 Lemma 2.3. Evaluation gives a rational closed point \(z\in W_L\) above \(w\). The cotangent calculation of AG-CA-18 Proposition 3.1 identifies its differential fibre with its maximal ideal modulo its square. Regularity makes its dimension equal to \(\dim\mathcal O_{W_L,z}\), which is \(\dim_zW_L\) by AG-CA-09 Theorem 6.1. AG-RG-S07 Lemma 3.1 identifies this point dimension with \(\dim_wW_s\). Differential base change, AG-CA-15 Theorem 2.2, gives the same cotangent dimension at \(w\). The full field Jacobian criterion AG-CA-18 Theorem 2.1 now makes \(W_s\) smooth at \(w\). Flatness, finite presentation and the complete arbitrary-base fibrewise criterion of \emph{Smooth morphisms}, Theorem 3.1, make \(W/S_0\) smooth. This proves smoothness of \(X_0\) on its etale charts. Geometric connectedness follows from the surjective image of each connected \(K_{\bar s}\). Quasi-compactness follows from the quasi-compact surjective source. The quotient is separated: the pullback of its diagonal to \(K_0\times K_0\) is the inverse image of the closed \(H_0\) under \((g,g')\mapsto g^{-1}g'\). Apply the whole ideal/closed-immersion descent of AG-RG-S04 Corollary A3.2 on etale scheme charts. Thus \(X_0\) is a separated finite-presentation space over \(S_0\).

Choose the finite jet index \(n\geq1\) that detects the full normalizer on this model. The whole preceding coordinate proof makes \(\mathcal O(K_n)\) and its quotient \(\mathcal O(H_n)\) finite locally free. Their ranks are fixed on the pieces chosen above. Conjugation gives a section of the Grassmannian of quotients of \(\mathcal O(K_n)\) of rank \(\operatorname{rank}\mathcal O(H_n)\), with stabilizer exactly \(H\). Its orbit map factors through the quotient sheaf. It is a monomorphism on all tests: lift two cosets locally to \(g_1,g_2\); equality of their Grassmannian quotients says that \(g_2^{-1}g_1\) stabilizes \(H_n\), and the full stabilizer theorem puts this element in \(H\). The cosets are equal. Thus we have a finite-type monomorphism \[
 \theta:X_0\longrightarrow\operatorname{Gr}.
\] It is separated and quasi-finite. The full space recognition and normalization proofs of AG-RG-S04 Theorems E8.1--E9.1, as stated in the preceding quasi-finite normalization lemma, make \(X_0\) a scheme. On each affine Grassmannian chart its pullback is an open subscheme of the represented affine integral closure; these scheme opens cover it.

We now construct the compactification needed below. The Grassmannian is qcqs and projective by the complete Lemma 5.A. The full scheme finite-factorization theorem AG-RG-S04 Theorem D7.1 applies to \(\theta\) and gives \[
 X_0\lhook\joinrel\longrightarrow\overline X_0
                \xrightarrow{\pi}\operatorname{Gr},
\] with first map a quasi-compact open immersion and \(\pi\) finite. We supply the full universal closed-image calculation for projective space used here. Over an arbitrary affine base \(\operatorname{Spec}R\), a closed subset \(C\subset\mathbf P_R^N\) is cut out by a homogeneous ideal \(I\subset R[T_0,\ldots,T_N]\). Indeed on the chart \(T_i\ne0\) its closed subset is cut out by an ideal \(J_i\) in the ratio coordinates. Homogenize every \(f\in J_i\) and multiply its homogenization by \(T_i\). These homogeneous polynomials vanish on \(C\) also outside this chart because of that last factor. If a point is outside \(C\), choose a chart containing it and an \(f\in J_i\) nonzero at that point; its homogenization times \(T_i\) is still nonzero there. The ideal generated by all these polynomials consequently cuts out exactly \(C\). Put \(D=R[T]/I\). A fibre over \(p\in\operatorname{Spec}R\) is empty precisely when \(\operatorname{Proj}(D\otimes_R\kappa(p))\) is empty. For such an empty fibre each \(T_i\) is nilpotent in this graded algebra: otherwise its nonzero localization has a nonzero degree-zero subring, whose spectrum gives a point in the \(T_i\ne0\) chart by the prime-existence proof. A sufficiently large degree \(m\) therefore has \((D_m)\otimes_R\kappa(p)=0\), since every degree-\(m\) monomial contains one of those vanishing powers. The module \(D_m\) is finite over \(R\), being a quotient of the finite free degree-\(m\) polynomial module. Local Nakayama gives \((D_m)_p=0\). Its finitely many generator images are killed by denominators outside \(p\), so one \(a\notin p\) gives \((D_m)_a=0\). Every higher graded piece is generated from degree \(m\), since \(D\) is generated in degree one; hence all those pieces also vanish over \(R_a\). Every projective fibre over \(D(a)\) is empty. The complement of the image of \(C\) is thus open. This argument works for every ring and every closed subset, so it proves universal closedness after every base change, affine locally on the new base. The finite affine projective charts give finite type and the diagonal calculation of AG-RG-S01 Section 7 gives separatedness. Therefore projective space, and every closed subscheme of it, is proper. Apply this to the actual Plucker closed immersion of the Grassmannian from Lemma 5.A. The scheme \(\overline X_0\) is now proper over \(S_0\): finite maps are finite type and separated on affine charts, and the integral closed-image calculation of AG-RG-S04 Lemma P0.4 proves universal closedness after every base change. Properness is preserved by composition. We use this constructed finite-over-projective compactification, and require no assertion that it is itself projective.

Let \(p\) be in the image of the original base in \(S_0\). Its quotient fibre is proper: after an algebraically closed extension of a residue field of a point above \(p\), it is the given proper geometric quotient. Properness descends under a field extension here directly. Finite type and separatedness are already known; for any base-change test and closed subset, its image becomes closed after the faithfully flat field cover. The images commute with that cover because nonempty field fibres remain nonempty under extension. The full fpqc quotient-topology proof of AG-RG-S04 Lemma A1.4 therefore makes the original image closed. This proves universal closedness on every test.

Localize \(S_0\) at \(p\) and pass to its complete local Noetherian ring \(A\), faithfully flat by the entire AG-RG-S02 Lemma 1.3. Write \(X,\overline X,\operatorname{Gr}\) for these base changes. Its proper special fibre \(X_s\) is open and closed in \(\overline X_s\): it is open by the constructed immersion, and its map to the separated \(\overline X_s\) is proper by the closed-graph/projection argument, so its image is closed. It corresponds to an idempotent. The full nilpotent idempotent-lifting proof AG-RG-S02 Lemma 1.4 lifts it uniquely through all maximal-ideal thickenings of \(\overline X\); local lifts glue by uniqueness.

Here formal functions is applied to an actual projective scheme. Put \(F=\pi_*\mathcal O_{\overline X}\) on \(\operatorname{Gr}_A\). This is coherent since \(\pi\) is finite and the target is Noetherian. On every affine target chart, the finite module quotient calculation gives \[
 F/\mathfrak m_A^rF=\pi_{r*}\mathcal O_{\overline X_r}.
\] Finite pushforward also identifies their global sections. To apply projective-space finiteness precisely, take the Plucker closed immersion \(i:\operatorname{Gr}_A\hookrightarrow\mathbf P_A^M\) supplied by Lemma 5.A. The sheaf \(i_*F\) is coherent: on an affine target chart it is the same finite module, now over the ambient ring through its quotient. By the definition of pushforward, its global sections are \(H^0(\operatorname{Gr}_A,F)\). Thus AG-RG-S01 Theorem 8.4, applied to \(i_*F\) on \(\mathbf P_A^M\), makes this module finite over \(A\). The full completion and formal-functions proofs AG-RG-S02 Lemma 1.2 and Theorem 2.3 then give the canonical ring isomorphism \[
 \Gamma(\overline X,\mathcal O_{\overline X})
   =H^0(\operatorname{Gr}_A,F)
   \simeq\varprojlim_r\Gamma(\overline X_r,\mathcal O_{\overline X_r}).
\] It is multiplicative because each comparison is the restriction map of the finite algebra. Thus the compatible formal idempotents give an actual idempotent and a proper open-and-closed component \(Z\subset\overline X\) with \(Z_s=X_s\).

The closed subset \(Z\setminus X\) has empty special fibre. Its image in the local base is closed by properness; any nonempty closed subset of a local spectrum contains its closed point, so this subset is empty. Hence \(Z\subset X\). The image of \(Z\to\operatorname{Spec}A\) is open by the whole flat-openness proof for its smooth restriction from \(X\), and it contains the closed point. Any such open is the entire local spectrum. In every geometric fibre \(Z\) is now a nonempty open-and-closed subset of the connected \(X_{\bar s}\), and is all of that fibre. The open immersion \(Z\subset X\) is therefore surjective and is an isomorphism. This proves that \(X\) is proper over \(A\).

The monomorphism \(\theta_A\) to the separated Grassmannian is proper by its closed graph and the proper source projection. It is quasi-finite, so the whole AG-RG-S04 Corollary D7.3 makes it finite. A finite monomorphism is closed: on an affine target chart \(R'\to B\) its field fibre algebra has dimension \(e\), and its monomorphism diagonal gives \(e^2=e\), so it is zero or the residue field. The coordinate map is therefore fibrewise surjective. Its finite cokernel is zero by the complete local Nakayama proof in AG-RG-S01 Lemma 1.2. Thus the ring map is surjective. Consequently \(\theta_A\) is a closed immersion.

Closed-immersion descent AG-RG-S04 Corollary A3.2 gives the same assertion over \(\mathcal O_{S_0,p}\). The whole eventual-property proof of AG-MO-03 Theorem 4.2 spreads it to an open neighbourhood of \(p\): the local spectrum is the inverse limit of principal neighbourhoods and these are the given finite-presentation models. The union of these neighbourhoods contains the entire image of the original base. Pulling back proves that its orbit map is a closed Grassmannian immersion locally on \(S\). This proves the original scheme and projectivity assertion; no properness condition has been imposed on unrelated model fibres.

\subsection{The canonical Plücker line and its exponent}\label{AG-RG-03-the-canonical-pluxfccker-line-and-its-exponent}

The full Grassmannian proof in Lemma 5.A makes its Plücker line the determinant of the universal quotient. Its pullback here is \(\det\mathcal O(\mathcal H_n)\), where \(\mathcal H\) is the universal conjugate subgroup. The entire finite-jet coordinate argument above identifies the augmentation filtration quotients with \(\operatorname{Sym}^i((\operatorname{Lie}\mathcal H)^*)\) for \(0\leq i\leq n\). These are finite locally free; their short exact sequences split locally because the quotient is projective. An adapted basis proves multiplicativity of the determinant in such a sequence: the matrix is block triangular, so its signed permutation determinant is the product of the two diagonal-block determinants. More generally the top exterior power of a composition is the composition of its top exterior powers; its coefficient in a wedge basis is the signed permutation determinant. This proves the determinant composition identity, including the conjugation calculation below, over every ring. Hence this line is \[
 \bigotimes_{i=0}^n\det\bigl(\operatorname{Sym}^i((\operatorname{Lie}\mathcal H)^*)\bigr).
\] We prove its exponent over every ring. For a rank-\(d\) free module the monomials of total degree \(i\) form a basis of its symmetric power, as follows directly from its presentation. Tensor words in a chosen basis form a free basis before the symmetric relations are imposed. Those relations exchange adjacent letters, so they identify exactly the words having the same multiplicity list. Within each such class, the coefficient-sum map has kernel generated by word differences: subtract one chosen representative from each other word. Its quotient is one free rank-one summand. The multiplicity classes consequently give precisely the asserted monomial basis over every ring. A diagonal matrix with entries \(t_1,\ldots,t_d\) has determinant on that power equal to \[
 \prod_{a_1+\cdots+a_d=i}t_1^{a_1}\cdots t_d^{a_d}
       =(t_1\cdots t_d)^{c_i},\qquad
 c_i=\binom{i+d-1}{d}.
\] All coordinate exponent sums are equal by permuting the coordinates; their total is \(i\binom{i+d-1}{d-1}\), since the separator-position bijection counts the weak compositions. Division of this integer identity by \(d\) gives the displayed binomial coefficient. For \(i=0\) the exponent is zero.

This determinant identity holds for every matrix, including in positive characteristic. Both sides are universal integer polynomials in its entries. We prove the density calculation used to compare them. For the monic degree-\(d\) characteristic polynomial \(\chi\), the Sylvester determinant is the determinant of \[
 (u,v)\longmapsto u\chi+v\chi',
 \qquad \deg u\leq d-2,\quad\deg v\leq d-1,
\] with target the polynomials of degree at most \(2d-2\). Both spaces have dimension \(2d-1\); for \(d=1\) the first summand is zero. Over a characteristic-zero field this determinant is nonzero exactly when \(\chi\) and \(\chi'\) are coprime. If they are coprime, their Bezout identity makes \(\chi\mid v\), and the degree bound gives \(v=u=0\). If a nonconstant \(h\) divides both, the pair \((\chi'/h,-\chi/h)\) is a nonzero kernel vector within those bounds. These are the full earlier polynomial division and Bezout calculations of AG-RG-S04 Lemma P0.4a. In an algebraic closure the factored derivative at a root is the product of its differences from the other roots, so coprimality is exactly distinct eigenvalues. A diagonal matrix with distinct integer entries makes this determinant nonzero, proving it is a nonzero polynomial. On that open, the eigenbasis calculation is explicit. For each of the \(d\) distinct roots \(\lambda\) of \(\chi\), the matrix \(X-\lambda I\) has determinant zero; the finite Gaussian reduction of AG-RG-S06 Section 1 gives a nonzero vector in its kernel. Eigenvectors for distinct roots are independent: applying \(\prod_{\mu\ne\lambda}(X-\mu I)\) to a relation kills every other term and multiplies the chosen vector by the nonzero scalar \(\prod_{\mu\ne\lambda}(\lambda-\mu)\). Thus all coefficients are zero. The \(d\) independent vectors are a basis by that same finite matrix calculation. Conjugation now reduces the determinant identity to the diagonal one. If its difference polynomial is \(g\) and this nonzero Sylvester polynomial is \(\delta\), then \(g\delta\) vanishes at every field-valued matrix. The multivariable root bound follows by induction on the number of matrix entries: view the polynomial as a polynomial in the last entry; for every tuple of the other entries, the univariate root bound over the infinite characteristic-zero field makes each coefficient zero, and induction kills those coefficient polynomials. It makes \(g\delta\) the zero polynomial; the polynomial domain and \(\delta\ne0\) give \(g=0\). Its integer coefficients are zero since \(\mathbf Z\) injects into the characteristic-zero field. Specializing proves the universal identity over arbitrary rings. Applying it to the transition matrices gives the identity of line bundles \[
 \det\mathcal O(\mathcal H_n)
   =\bigl(\det(\operatorname{Lie}\mathcal H)^*\bigr)^c,
 \qquad c=\sum_{i=0}^n\binom{i+d-1}{d}>0.
\] The inequality follows from \(n\geq1\) and its \(i=1\) summand equal to one, for \(d>0\).

This positive power is relatively very ample through the actual closed Plücker immersion. The line itself is relatively ample, with the defining section criterion verified directly. Work over an affine base piece trivializing the finite Plücker bundle, so \(L^c\) is the pullback of \(\mathcal O(1)\) from a closed immersion into \(\mathbf P^N\). Its coordinate nonvanishing opens are affine. At any point and inside any chosen open neighbourhood, choose a principal open \(D(f)\) in one such affine chart contained in that neighbourhood, by the full affine principal-basis proof of AG-RG-S01 Section 2. Express \(f\) as a polynomial in the coordinate ratios and homogenize to a polynomial \(h\) of degree \(a\). Multiplying \(h\) by that chart coordinate gives a global section of \(L^{c(a+1)}\) whose nonvanishing locus is exactly this affine principal open. These loci form a basis, and all their exponents are positive. This is the entire ample-section criterion proved in AG-RG-S01 Sections 8--9, so \(L\) is relatively ample. The zero-dimensional case was treated at the start. All finite-jet quotients, character actions, determinants and quotient-sheaf identities commute with arbitrary base change. Their unique comparisons descend the canonical line and the stated quotient to the original base. \(\square\)

The quotient proof is the complete earlier AG-RG-S07 Theorem 8.2 and Corollary 8.3. Recognition and the finite compactification use AG-RG-S04 Theorems E8.1--E9.1 and D7.1. Formal functions is used on the projective Grassmannian with its coherent finite algebra, by AG-RG-S02 Theorem 2.3. The scheme and ample-line arguments are written here under the original hypotheses.

\subsection{A universal finite cohomology complex}\label{AG-RG-03-a-universal-finite-cohomology-complex}

\textbf{Lemma (finite projective replacement).} Let \(A\) be Noetherian and let \(C\) be a complex of flat \(A\)-modules concentrated in degrees \([a,b]\), with finite cohomology modules. There is a complex \(K\) of finite projective modules in \([a,b]\) and a quasi-isomorphism \(K\to C\) that remains a quasi-isomorphism after tensoring with any \(A\)-module.

\textbf{Proof.} Construct a bounded-above complex \(P\) of finite free modules and a map \(f:P\to C\), descending from degree \(b\). Once the terms above \(j\) are chosen, its cone has terms

\[
D^i=C^i\oplus P^{i+1},\qquad
d(c,p)=(d_Cc+f(p),-d_Pp).
\]

Its cohomology is finite: the cone long exact sequence uses the finite cohomology of \(C\) and of the already chosen finite free portion of \(P\). Choose finitely many cocycles \((c_\ell,p_\ell)\) generating \(H^j(D)\). Take \(P^j\) free on \(e_\ell\), and set \(f(e_\ell)=c_\ell\), \(d_P(e_\ell)=-p_\ell\). The cocycle equations give \(d_P^2=0\) and \(d_Cf=fd_P\). In the new cone, \(d(0,e_\ell)=(c_\ell,p_\ell)\), so this kills \(H^j\) without changing higher cohomology. Continue to the left. Each degree stabilizes, giving a quasi-isomorphism \(P\to C\).

Its cone is acyclic, bounded above and flat termwise. Such a complex stays acyclic after every tensor: start at its last degree and descend through

\[
0\longrightarrow Z^i\longrightarrow D^i\longrightarrow Z^{i+1}\longrightarrow0.
\]

The quotient is flat; hence the kernel is flat and the sequence stays exact under tensor. Thus \(H^i(P\otimes_AM)=H^i(C\otimes_AM)\) for every \(M\).

Put \(Q=\operatorname{coker}(P^{a-1}\to P^a)\). The left tail is a free resolution of \(Q\), and

\[
\operatorname{Tor}_1^A(Q,M)=H^{a-1}(P\otimes_AM)=0
\]

for every \(M\), since \(C\otimes_AM\) starts in degree \(a\). The module \(Q\) is finitely presented, so it is flat and finite projective. Take \(K^a=Q\) and \(K^i=P^i\) for \(a<i\leq b\). The map to \(C\) factors through \(Q\) because \(C^{a-1}=0\). Truncation preserves cohomology, and the same acyclic flat-cone argument proves the assertion after every tensor. \(\square\)

Apply this to the finite section complex of a line bundle \(L_0\) on a smooth projective scheme over a Noetherian ring \(A_0\). Choose a finite affine cover. Separatedness makes its intersections affine, and S01 Sections 4--5 prove that its ordered section complex computes quasi-coherent cohomology. On each intersection the line bundle is a projective module over its chart algebra; smoothness makes that algebra \(A_0\)-flat, so every term is \(A_0\)-flat. S01 Theorem 8.4 and its closed-immersion passage prove that all cohomology modules are finite. Under every algebra base change, affine module-sheaf correspondence and localization, proved in S01 Section 2, identify the new section complex with its tensor product over \(A_0\). The finite projective replacement just proved therefore computes the line bundle cohomology after every base change.

\subsection{Sections in a vanishing family}\label{AG-RG-03-sections-in-a-vanishing-family}

\textbf{Lemma (sections in a vanishing family).} Let \(f:X\to S\) be smooth and projective of finite presentation, and let \(L\) be an invertible sheaf on \(X\). Suppose that \(H^q(X_{\bar s},L_{\bar s})=0\) for every geometric point \(\bar s\) and every \(q>0\). Then \(f_*L\) is finite locally free, all its positive higher direct images vanish, and these statements commute with every base change. In particular the canonical map \(g^*f_*L\to f'_*L'\) is an isomorphism for any \(g:S'\to S\). The base may be nonreduced.

\textbf{Proof.} Work with \(S=\operatorname{Spec}A\). Choose a projective embedding, a finite affine cover trivializing \(L\), and finite affine covers of the pairwise and triple overlaps. Write \(A\) as the filtered union of its finitely generated \(\mathbf Z\)-subalgebras. The embedding, chart opens and overlap maps descend at a finite stage by \href{https://github.com/KokunoYumeto/open-math-courses/blob/main/docs/courses/AG-MO/AG-MO-03.html\#4-descending-objects-maps-and-properties}{finite-presentation descent}, Theorems 4.1--4.2. Retain the closed immersion, so the model \(X_0\) is projective.

Retain smoothness at a finite stage by S02 Lemma 3.1 and Proposition 3.2. In a finite polynomial presentation, Lemma 3.0 identifies formal smoothness with a left inverse of the conormal differential map. The left inverse uses finitely many coefficients; its equations on the finitely many relation generators have finite polynomial witnesses. Descend these coefficients and witnesses to one stage. The same left inverse then proves formal smoothness there, and the retained finite presentation proves smoothness. Apply this on a finite affine cover, retaining the cover and the projective closed immersion by the finite-presentation limit proof. The line-bundle transition units, their inverses and the finitely many overlap and cocycle witnesses descend at the same stage, as in S02 Proposition 3.2. Gluing these descended transition units defines the invertible sheaf \(L_0\) on the smooth projective model \(X_0/A_0\).

The preceding finite-projective-replacement lemma gives a bounded finite projective complex \(K_0\) such that

\[
H^q(K_0\otimes_{A_0}B)
\simeq H^q(X_0\times_{A_0}\operatorname{Spec}B,L_0\otimes_{A_0}B)
\]

for every \(A_0\)-algebra \(B\), compatibly with the canonical comparison maps. Its proof uses the finite affine-cover complex and projective Serre finiteness; ordinary tensor of \(K_0\) computes its derived tensor. This finite argument supplies the universal comparison before pullback to the original base.

Put \(K=K_0\otimes_{A_0}A\). Near any \(s\in\operatorname{Spec}A\), trivialize its terms. Whenever a differential has an entry invertible at \(s\), shrink the neighbourhood and perform row and column operations to put that entry in an identity block. The equation \(d^2=0\) makes the adjacent differentials zero on that block, so it splits off a contractible pair \(A\xrightarrow{1}A\). After finitely many cancellations, all remaining differential entries vanish in \(\kappa(s)\). The remaining complex therefore has

\[
K^q\otimes_A\kappa(s)=H^q(X_s,L_s).
\]

For \(q>0\) the right side is zero by the hypothesis and field extension; for \(q<0\) it is zero because \(L_s\) is a sheaf. Thus every remaining free term except degree zero has rank zero and disappears on a neighbourhood of \(s\). The degree-zero term is finite free. Every cancelled identity pair stays contractible after any tensor. The universal comparison consequently proves the direct-image assertions and every base-change assertion, including nonflat changes involving nilpotents. The canonical comparisons glue. Notice that vanishing was imposed only on the original family, not on unrelated fibres of its Noetherian model. \(\square\)

\textbf{Lemma 5.B (the automorphism sheaf of a projective line).} Over every base scheme \(T\), the sheaf of \(T\)-automorphisms of \(\mathbf P^1_T\) is represented by \(\operatorname{PGL}_{2,T}\). This identification holds on all schemes over \(T\) and includes nonreduced tests.

\textbf{Proof.} Work locally on a test base, and write \(p:\mathbf P^1_T\to T\). For an automorphism \(a\), put \(M'=a^*\mathcal O(1)\otimes\mathcal O(-1)\). On every geometric fibre this line is trivial. Indeed \(\mathcal O(1)\) is the divisor line of any rational point: a linear homogeneous form cuts that point simply, and the two affine coordinate frames identify its divisor line with \(\mathcal O(1)\). Pullback by an automorphism cuts the inverse-image point simply and gives the same line. The whole sections-in-a-vanishing-family lemma applies to \(M'\), since the explicit projective-line cohomology of AG-RG-S01 Theorem 7.2 gives \(H^q(\mathcal O)=0\) for \(q>0\) and \(H^0(\mathcal O)\) of rank one. Hence \(M=p_*M'\) is a line bundle with every base change. The evaluation \(p^*M\to M'\) is an isomorphism: on every geometric fibre it is the constant-section isomorphism, and on local line-bundle frames its coefficient is therefore outside every maximal ideal of the local ring, hence a unit. Thus \(a^*\mathcal O(1)=\mathcal O(1)\otimes p^*M\). Trivialize \(M\) locally. Pullback of the two coordinate sections, together with this trivialization, gives a linear map on the rank-two module of sections of \(\mathcal O(1)\), whose standard linear-form basis is again the explicit AG-RG-S01 Theorem 7.2 calculation. Its geometric-fibre maps are invertible because \(a\) is an automorphism. Its determinant is a unit on the base, by the same local residue test, so the matrix belongs to \(\operatorname{GL}_2\). The quotient-functor construction of projective space identifies the corresponding projective transformation with \(a\): its coordinate quotient sections are precisely these pulled-back coordinate sections. A different trivialization of \(M\) multiplies the matrix by a unit. The kernel of the projective action consists exactly of scalar matrices on all tests. A matrix acting identically preserves the points \([1:0]\) and \([0:1]\), so its off-diagonal entries are zero and its diagonal entries are units; preserving \([1:1]\) makes the two entries equal. Conversely scalar matrices act identically. Finally the fppf quotient \(\operatorname{GL}_2/\mathbf G_m\) is the actual scheme open \(D_+(\det)\subset\mathbf P^3_T\): on each projective coordinate chart a line of four entries is locally a matrix, and its determinant section being nowhere vanishing means an invertible determinant after this frame is chosen. Changing the frame is exactly scalar multiplication. These local coordinates, their unique scalar comparisons and line-bundle frame gluing represent the quotient sheaf on every test, by the full local-coordinate sheaf construction of AG-RG-S04 Lemma A1.7. Matrix multiplication and inversion descend and give the group scheme \(\operatorname{PGL}_2\). The local matrix descriptions just proved therefore identify its functor with the automorphism sheaf, compatibly with composition and every base change. \(\square\)

\textbf{Proposition 5.2.} If \(G\) has trivial centre and geometric semisimple rank one, and has a split maximal torus \(T\), then Zariski locally \((G,T)\) is isomorphic to \((\operatorname{PGL}_2,D)\).

\textbf{Proof.} Its geometric fibres are \(\operatorname{PGL}_2\) by Proposition 2.3: the action on the projective line has trivial kernel. Choose a root \(\alpha\) locally. It is an isomorphism \(T\to\mathbf G_m\), with the following full base-ring check. Locally identify the rank-one split torus with \(\mathbf G_m\). A character is a finite Laurent polynomial \(\sum_n a_nt^n\). Its coproduct and identity equations give \(a_n^2=a_n\), \(a_ma_n=0\) for \(m\ne n\), and \(\sum_n a_n=1\), by comparing the independent Laurent coefficients. Thus its finitely many nonzero coefficient idempotents split the affine base into open-and-closed pieces on which it is \(t^n\). Its geometric-fibre character is primitive, so on every nonempty piece \(n=1\) or \(n=-1\). The inverse there is respectively \(t\) or \(t^{-1}\), and these inverses glue over the idempotent pieces. Put \(B=P_G(\alpha^{-1})\). It is smooth and on each geometric fibre is an upper triangular Borel subgroup of \(\operatorname{PGL}_2\).

Its scheme-theoretic normalizer equals \(B\). The normalizer lemma makes it closed of finite presentation and proves that its formation commutes with arbitrary base change. On geometric fibres the point stabilizer in \(\mathbf P^1\) is self-normalizing. Infinitesimally, use the diagonal class of \(\operatorname{diag}(1,0)\) in \(\mathfrak{pgl}_2\). Its bracket with the lower off-diagonal class is the negative of that class, nonzero in every characteristic. Thus the normalizer has exactly the two-dimensional tangent space of \(B\) at the identity. Its local dimension is at least two because it contains the smooth closed \(B\), and is at most the dimension of that tangent space by the embedding-dimension bound. It is therefore a regular local ring of dimension two. The rational-point cotangent calculation and field Jacobian criterion of AG-CA-18 Proposition 3.1 and Theorem 2.1 make it smooth at the identity. Every closed point of the geometric normalizer is in \(B\): a normalizing element must preserve the unique fixed point of the upper triangular group on \(\mathbf P^1\), as is checked using its translations on the other affine chart. Translation carries the smooth identity neighbourhood through every such point. The open smooth locus consequently covers the fibre, since any nonempty closed complement in a finite-type scheme over an algebraically closed field contains a closed point by the full Zariski lemma. The closed inclusion \(B\to N\) is now a map between smooth groups with identical tangent spaces, so AG-RG-S02 Lemma 3.A makes it etale. The full etale-monomorphism proof of AG-RG-S04 Lemma E7.2 makes it an open immersion; all geometric points belong to it, so it is an isomorphism. This proves equality on the entire geometric fibres, including nilpotent tests. The flat-source criterion above, applied with source \(B\), proves the equality over the base without assuming the normalizer flat.

Lemma 5.1 makes \(f:X=G/B\to S\) a smooth projective curve whose geometric fibres are \(\mathbf P^1\), and it has the section \(e=1B\). A section of a separated smooth relative curve is an effective Cartier divisor, with the following local calculation. Near the section over a chosen base point, take an etale coordinate \(q\) by AG-RG-S02 Lemma 3.A and subtract its pullback along the section, so it vanishes there. It is a nonzerodivisor: multiplication by the affine-line coordinate is injective over every base ring, and the etale coordinate algebra is flat. The zero scheme \(Z(q)\) is etale over the base and the section factors through it. The base and \(Z(q)\) are both smooth of relative dimension zero; AG-RG-S02 Lemma 3.A therefore makes the section etale. It is a monomorphism because it is a section, so the full etale-monomorphism proof makes it an open immersion. It is also closed because the curve is separated. Its complement in \(Z(q)\) is consequently closed also in the ambient coordinate neighbourhood. Remove that complement; on the resulting neighbourhood the section is cut out exactly by \(q\). Its ideal is thus locally free of rank one. Its reciprocal defines the divisor line bundle, and on each geometric curve fibre this coordinate cuts its point simply, giving degree one. Put \(L=\mathcal O_X(e)\); it has degree one on every geometric fibre. The sections-in-a-vanishing-family lemma applies to \(L\), since \(H^1(\mathbf P^1,\mathcal O(1))=0\), and gives \(E=f_*L\) locally free of rank two, with arbitrary base change. The evaluation \(f^*E\to L\) is surjective: its cokernel is finite locally, its geometric fibres vanish by generation of \(\mathcal O(1)\), and local Nakayama kills that cokernel. With the quotient convention it defines \(j:X\to\mathbf P(E)\), and \(j_{\bar s}\) is the usual isomorphism given by the two sections of \(\mathcal O(1)\). Both schemes are smooth over \(S\), and the differential of \(j\) is an isomorphism on all geometric fibres, hence locally an isomorphism of their cotangent bundles. The étale differential criterion makes \(j\) étale. Its geometric fibres are isomorphisms, so it is universally injective and surjective; an étale universally injective morphism is an open immersion, and surjectivity makes it an isomorphism. Trivializing \(E\) Zariski locally now gives \(G/B\simeq\mathbf P^1_S\).

Lemma 5.B identifies the automorphism sheaf of this projective line with the actual group scheme \(\operatorname{PGL}_2\), so the action gives a morphism \(G\to\operatorname{PGL}_2\) on all base tests. It is an isomorphism on every geometric fibre. Both groups are smooth of finite presentation; their differential is an isomorphism on those fibres, hence locally an isomorphism of differential bundles by the finite matrix and Nakayama calculations. AG-RG-S02 Lemma 3.A makes the morphism etale. Its geometric fibres are single reduced points, so it is universally injective and surjective. AG-RG-S04 Lemma E7.2 then makes it a surjective open immersion, hence an isomorphism. It carries \(B\) to the point stabilizer. Here is the full Zariski-local pair calculation. In that stabilizer, every projective matrix has a unique scalar-normalized representative \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}v&u\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), with \(v\) invertible; this gives its group law \((v,u)(v',u')=(vv',u+vu')\). The diagonal character on \(T\) is an isomorphism to \(\mathbf G_m\), since its geometric-fibre character is the primitive root already identified above. Use its value \(t\) as the torus coordinate. The homomorphism \(T\to B\) has the form \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}t&u(t)\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\) for a finite Laurent polynomial \(u(t)\). Commutativity gives \((1-s)u(t)=(1-t)u(s)\) in \(R[t^{\pm1},s^{\pm1}]\). For each exponent \(m\notin\{0,1\}\), its coefficient in \(t\) says \((1-s)a_m=0\); independence of Laurent coefficients gives \(a_m=0\). The coefficient at \(t\) then gives \(u(s)=a_1(s-1)\). Conjugation by \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&a_1\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\) replaces \(u(t)\) by \(u(t)+a_1(1-t)=0\). Thus it takes \(T\) to the diagonal torus over the affine base itself. This calculation uses no division or reducedness and finishes the Zariski-local pair assertion. \(\square\)

\section{6. Splitting a central extension of the rank-one cover}\label{AG-RG-03-splitting-a-central-extension-of-the-rank-one-cover}

We need an integral result, including characteristic two. The following splitting argument is due to Gabber; we give the argument for a separated commutative group scheme \(Z\), which includes the multiplicative-type centres used here.

\textbf{Theorem 6.1.} Every fppf central extension

\[
1\longrightarrow Z\longrightarrow E\longrightarrow\operatorname{SL}_{2,S}\longrightarrow1
\]

has a unique homomorphic section.

\textbf{Proof.} We first record the full scheme calculation behind the cell covers. The group \(\operatorname{SL}_2\) is cut out by \(ad-bc=1\). The opens \(a\ne0\) and \(b\ne0\) cover it. On the first, elimination of \(d\) gives the algebra \(R[a,a^{-1},b,c]\); on the second, elimination of \(c\) gives \(R[b,b^{-1},a,d]\). Both are polynomial localizations, so are smooth over every ring by the square-zero lifting and finite-presentation proofs. Over every field both charts are integral and their intersection is nonempty, containing \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\). Their union is therefore reduced and irreducible, hence integral. The identity cell is the first chart: the matrix factorization \(y(v)h(t)x(u)\) gives \(a=t\), \(b=tu\), \(c=vt\) and \(d=vtu+t^{-1}\), uniquely. Thus it is an open dense cell in every geometric fibre. In \(\operatorname{SL}_2\) use

\[
x(u)=\begin{pmatrix}1&u\\0&1\end{pmatrix},\quad
y(v)=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\v&1\end{pmatrix},\quad
h(t)=\operatorname{diag}(t,t^{-1}).
\]

Let \(D',U',V'\) be their inverse images in \(E\). A central extension of a commutative group has a commutator pairing on its quotient, on all tests. Indeed any two lifts differ by a central-kernel element, so replacing a lift leaves the commutator unchanged. Local lifts consequently glue the commutator through the represented fppf sheaf \(Z\). Every such commutator lies in \(Z\), hence is central; the identities \([ab,c]=a[b,c]a^{-1}[a,c]\) and \([a,bc]=[a,b]b[a,c]b^{-1}\) therefore make the pairing additive in each variable. This constructs the pairing as a natural map of sheaves, hence as a scheme morphism by its values on every test.

For \(D'\), the pairing \(\mathbf G_m\times\mathbf G_m\to Z\) is trivial. The \(n\)th-power map of \(\mathbf G_m\), for every \(n\geq1\), is an fppf epimorphism over every ring: above a unit \(u\in R^*\) its root algebra is \(R[z]/(z^n-u)\), with free basis \(1,z,\ldots,z^{n-1}\). The element \(z\) is already invertible, with inverse \(z^{n-1}/u\). This free positive-rank algebra is faithfully flat, and its monic equation is a finite presentation. Restrict the first pairing argument to \(\mu_n\). Bilinearity makes the pairing there killed by \(n\) in that argument. Locally write the second argument as an \(n\)th power using this cover, and bilinearity makes the pairing the identity. Faithful sheaf descent removes the cover. The union of the \(\mu_n\) is universally schematically dense in \(\mathbf G_m\), with the following actual ideal test. On an affine test base, write a Laurent polynomial as a finite sum with coefficients in the base ring (or in the Laurent ring of the second coordinate). Choose \(n\) greater than every difference of two exponents present. Reduction modulo \(t^n-1\) then leaves those exponents in distinct residue classes, whose images are independent in the free basis \(1,t,\ldots,t^{n-1}\). A polynomial vanishing on every \(\mu_n\) therefore has all coefficients zero. Since \(Z\) is separated, equality of the pairing with the identity is a closed subscheme of the product; this ideal test kills its entire ideal on every affine base chart. Thus the pairing is the identity and \(D'\) is commutative.

The conjugation action on \(E\) factors through \(\operatorname{SL}_2\): two local lifts differ by \(Z\), which is central, so give identical conjugation maps; their maps glue by the sheaf property. The commutator pairing on \(U'\) is invariant under simultaneous multiplication of its arguments by \(t^2\). The square-power cover just proved makes it invariant under simultaneous multiplication by every unit. For given \(u,v\) over any test, the morphism \(a\mapsto c(au,av)\) from \(\mathbf A^1\) to \(Z\) is constant on \(\mathbf G_m\). This equality extends to zero on nonreduced tests too. Its equalizer with the constant morphism is closed by separatedness; on an affine test chart the equalizer ideal becomes zero in \(R[a,a^{-1}]\). The map \(R[a]\to R[a,a^{-1}]\) is injective because multiplication by \(a\) is injective on the polynomial basis, so that ideal was zero. At zero the pairing is the identity, and at one it is \(c(u,v)\). Hence \(c(u,v)=1\). Thus \(U'\) is commutative; the same argument proves it for \(V'\).

We construct a unique \(D\)-equivariant section of \(U'\to U\). Fppf locally choose a unit \(t\) with \(t^2-1\) invertible and a lift \(\tilde h\) of \(h(t)\). The first choice is the actual finite-presentation cover \(R[t,1/(t(t^2-1))]\): it is a smooth polynomial localization and its geometric fibres are nonempty. An algebraically closed field is infinite, since a finite field's polynomial \(\prod_a(T-a)+1\) would have no root; the nonzero degree-three polynomial \(t(t^2-1)\) therefore cannot vanish at all its elements by the univariate root bound. Smoothness gives flatness by the earlier arbitrary-base smooth-flatness proof. Thus this open is surjective, flat and finitely presented. The extension's fppf epimorphism supplies the second local choice. In the commutative group \(U'\), the endomorphism

\[
\varphi(a)=\tilde h a\tilde h^{-1}a^{-1}
\]

kills \(Z\) and induces multiplication by \(t^2-1\) on \(U=\mathbf G_a\). The factorization through \(U\) is explicit: locally lift a section of \(U\) to \(U'\) and apply \(\varphi\). Changing the lift multiplies by \(Z\) and leaves its value unchanged, so these values glue uniquely. This defines a homomorphism of represented sheaves \(U\to U'\). Dividing its input by the unit \(t^2-1\) gives a section. It is \(D\)-equivariant because all lifts in the commutative \(D'\) commute with \(\tilde h\). Any two such equivariant sections differ by a \(D\)-invariant homomorphism \(U\to Z\). Square-power surjectivity gives scalar invariance under every unit, and the same injective-polynomial equalizer argument used above extends that invariance to the zero scalar, where the homomorphism is the identity. The difference is consequently zero. This uniqueness descends the local sections, giving \(x':\mathbf G_a\to E\) and similarly \(y'\).

Set

\[
w'(t)=y'(-t^{-1})x'(t)y'(-t^{-1}),\qquad
h'(t)=w'(t)w'(1)^{-1}.
\]

Their images are \(\begin{pmatrix}0&t\\-t^{-1}&0\end{pmatrix}\) and \(h(t)\). Thus \(h'(t)\in D'\). Equivariance gives

\[
h'(s)w'(t)h'(s)^{-1}=w'(s^2t).
\]

Divide by the instance \(t=1\). Since \(D'\) is commutative, this gives \(h'(t)=h'(s^2t)h'(s^2)^{-1}\). The square map being fppf surjective, \(h'\) is a homomorphism. Its definition then gives \(h'(s)w'(t)=w'(st)\).

Expand the identity \(h'(s)w'(t)=w'(st)\) and move \(h'(s)\) across the first \(y'\) using \(h'(s)y'(v)h'(s)^{-1}=y'(s^{-2}v)\). Multiply on the left by \(y'(1/(st))\) and on the right by \(y'(1/t)\). Additivity of \(y'\) gives the actual intermediate equality \(x'(st)y'((s-1)/(st))=y'((s-1)/(s^2t))x'(s^2t)h'(s)\). Move the final \(h'(s)\) to the left of this \(x'\) using its conjugation identity, obtaining \(x'(st)y'((s-1)/(st))=y'((s-1)/(s^2t))h'(s)x'(t)\). Set \(u=st\) and \(v=(s-1)/(st)\). Conversely every pair for which \(u\) and \(1+uv\) are units has this form with \(s=1+uv\) and \(t=u/s\). Thus we have

\[
x'(u)y'(v)=y'\left(\frac{v}{1+uv}\right)
h'(1+uv)x'\left(\frac{u}{1+uv}\right)
\tag{1}
\]

when \(u\) and \(1+uv\) are units. The restriction that \(u\) be a unit can be removed on all tests. Fppf locally write \(u=a+b\) with \(a,b,1+bv\) units, by adjoining \(b\) on the open \(b(u-b)(1+bv)\ne0\). This is a smooth polynomial localization. In every geometric fibre its defining polynomial is nonzero (of degree two when \(v=0\), and degree three otherwise), so the infinite-field root bound makes its image surjective; the same smooth-flatness argument makes it an fppf cover. Apply (1) first to \(x'(b)y'(v)\), then to \(x'(a)y'(v/(1+bv))\). Write \(q=1+bv\) and \(p=1+uv\). The second denominator is \(p/q\), so its result is \(y'(v/p)h'(p/q)x'(aq/p)h'(q)x'(b/q)\). The rule \(x'(c)h'(q)=h'(q)x'(q^{-2}c)\) and multiplicativity of \(h'\) combine the two torus factors into \(h'(p)\). The resulting \(x'\) parameter is

\[
\frac{a}{(1+bv)(1+uv)}+\frac{b}{1+bv}
=\frac{u}{1+uv}.
\]

This proves (1) in its full domain.

These identities, the additivity of \(x',y'\), the multiplicativity of \(h'\), and its two conjugation identities are exactly the multiplication rules on the open cell \(\Omega=U_-DU_+\) of \(\operatorname{SL}_2\). Define a section there by

\[
y(v)h(t)x(u)\longmapsto y'(v)h'(t)x'(u).
\]

It is multiplicative whenever both factors and their product are in \(\Omega\): reorder their factors with (1). Write \(s_\Omega:\Omega\to E\) for this cell section. For any test scheme \(R\to S\) and finite list \(g_1,\ldots,g_m\in\operatorname{SL}_2(R)\), the open \[
\Omega_R\cap\bigcap_i\Omega_Rg_i^{-1}
\] is nonempty in every geometric fibre: the two-chart calculation above makes that fibre integral, each translate of the identity cell is a nonempty dense open, and irreducibility makes every finite intersection of these opens nonempty. The intersection is a smooth open of \(\operatorname{SL}_2\) and is surjective over \(R\). On an affine test base, the cell translates are principal opens, their finitely many defining functions giving a polynomial localization of the finite-presentation group algebra. Thus it is locally finitely presented; smoothness gives flatness, and affine refinements supply an actual fppf local point \(c\) with \(c,cg_i\in\Omega\).

In particular, for one \(g\), use the nonempty open \[
\Omega_R\cap\Omega_R^{-1}\cap\Omega_Rg^{-1}.
\] Then \(g=c^{-1}(cg)\) is a product of two points of \(\Omega\). Assign to a word in cell points the corresponding product of their \(s_\Omega\)-values. This is independent of the word. For two words with the same endpoint \(g\), choose \(c\) so that \(c\) and its translates by every partial product of both words lie in \(\Omega\). Successive cell multiplicativity says that multiplying either lifted word on the left by \(s_\Omega(c)\) gives \(s_\Omega(cg)\). Cancellation proves equality. In particular a word representing the identity has lift one; concatenation therefore respects multiplication and inverses. These word values agree after further fppf pullbacks, so descend through the sheaf property of \(E\). They define a homomorphism of represented fppf sheaves, hence a scheme homomorphism \(\operatorname{SL}_2\to E\). Its composite with \(E\to\operatorname{SL}_2\) is the identity on generating words. It is the required homomorphic section on all test schemes.

Finally any homomorphism \(\operatorname{SL}_2\to Z\) kills \(x(u)\), since

\[
[h(t),x(u)]=x((t^2-1)u),
\]

and one may choose \(t^2-1\) invertible fppf locally. It kills \(y(v)\) similarly, and then \(h(t)=w(t)w(1)^{-1}\). It kills the open cell, hence the group. The difference between two central sections is such a homomorphism, proving uniqueness. \(\square\)

\section{7. Coroots from multiplication}\label{AG-RG-03-coroots-from-multiplication}

\textbf{Theorem 7.1.} For every root \(\alpha\) there is a canonical coroot \(\alpha^\vee:\mathbf G_m\to T\), with \(\langle\alpha,\alpha^\vee\rangle=2\). There is a canonical perfect pairing \(\mathfrak g_\alpha\otimes\mathfrak g_{-\alpha}\to\mathcal O_S\) such that, writing its value as \(XY\),

\[
\exp_\alpha(X)\exp_{-\alpha}(Y)
=\exp_{-\alpha}\left(\frac{Y}{1+XY}\right)
\alpha^\vee(1+XY)
\exp_\alpha\left(\frac{X}{1+XY}\right)
\tag{2}
\]

whenever \(1+XY\) is a unit. This unit condition is precisely membership in the open cell \(U_{-\alpha}TU_\alpha\).

\textbf{Proof.} Work in \(G_\alpha\), whose scheme-theoretic centre is \(Z=\ker\alpha\subset T\), by Section 1. Theorem 1.1 constructs \(q:G_\alpha\to Q=G_\alpha/Z\) as an affine reductive quotient and an fppf \(Z\)-torsor, compatible with every base change. The torus quotient has character group \(\mathbf Z\alpha\subset X^*(T)\), so \(T/Z\simeq\mathbf G_m\) via the descended character \(\alpha\). It is a closed subgroup of \(Q\): its pullback under \(q\) is \(T\subset G_\alpha\), and closed immersions descend through the fppf torsor. On geometric fibres Proposition 2.3 identifies this quotient with \(\operatorname{PGL}_2\), so \(T/Z\) is a maximal torus.

The open cell \(U_{-\alpha}TU_\alpha\) is right \(Z\)-stable; centrality makes \(Z\) act only on its torus coordinate. Its quotient is the open subscheme \[
U_{-\alpha}\times(T/Z)\times U_\alpha\subset Q,
\] as follows by invariant-open descent and the product torsor. At the identity this gives the two nonzero torus weights \(\alpha,-\alpha\), with their root lines, in \(\operatorname{Lie}Q\). The centre formula of Section 1, applied to \(Q,T/Z\), is consequently \(Z(Q)=\ker(\alpha:T/Z\to\mathbf G_m)=1\), as a scheme over the original base. Proposition 5.2 therefore identifies the pair \(Q,T/Z\), Zariski locally, with \(\operatorname{PGL}_2\) and its diagonal torus. Choose the identification so \(\alpha(\operatorname{diag}(t,1))=t\).

The map \(\operatorname{SL}_2\to\operatorname{PGL}_2\) used next is an fppf epimorphism over the original base, with the following integral proof. Lemma 5.B represents \(\operatorname{PGL}_2\) by the invertible-matrix open in \(\mathbf P^3\), so a section has a matrix representative \(M\) after locally trivializing its coordinate line. Its determinant \(d\) is a unit. The finite-free square-root cover \(R[z]/(z^2-d)\) from Theorem 6.1 has an invertible \(z\); the matrix \(z^{-1}M\) has determinant one and lifts the section. The kernel consists on every test of scalar matrices \(zI\) with \(z^2=1\), hence is \(\mu_2\), even in characteristic two. On the upper and lower additive matrix groups the map is the identity on their parameters. Pull back \(G_\alpha\to\operatorname{PGL}_2\) along this map. Theorem 6.1 splits the resulting central extension by \(Z\), giving a homomorphism \(\rho:\operatorname{SL}_2\to G_\alpha\). We verify its full \(T\)-equivariance. For any test point \(t\in T\), put \(a=\alpha(t)\). Conjugation of matrices by \(\operatorname{diag}(a,1)\) defines an automorphism \(c_a\) of \(\operatorname{SL}_2\), scaling the upper parameter by \(a\) and the lower by \(a^{-1}\). Its adjoint-quotient action equals conjugation by \(q(t)\). Thus \(g\mapsto t\rho(c_a^{-1}(g))t^{-1}\) is another homomorphic lift of the same map \(\operatorname{SL}_2\to Q\). Together with its \(\operatorname{SL}_2\) coordinate it is a section of the same pullback extension; uniqueness in Theorem 6.1 makes it \(\rho\). This proves equivariance on every test. The quotient-cell coordinates above make \(dq\) an isomorphism on both root lines, and the matrix cover has the same property. Consequently \(d\rho\) is an isomorphism on those lines. Apply Theorem 4.1 to the upper map after identifying its tangent basis with \(d\rho(e)\), and likewise to the lower map: their images are exactly \(U_\alpha,U_{-\alpha}\) and they identify the respective additive lines. The diagonal cocharacter of \(\operatorname{SL}_2\) therefore defines \(\alpha^\vee\).

Direct multiplication gives

\[
\begin{pmatrix}1&x\\0&1\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\y&1\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\y/(1+xy)&1\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}1+xy&0\\0&(1+xy)^{-1}\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}1&x/(1+xy)\\0&1\end{pmatrix}.
\]

The quotient cell is saturated: its pullback along the \(Z\)-torsor is exactly \(U_{-\alpha}TU_\alpha\), since on that open the torsor acts only in the torus factor and the product torsor gives its whole inverse image. In the projective invertible-matrix model the cell is precisely the locus where the upper-left coordinate is invertible in a local coordinate-line frame. Indeed the lower-diagonal-upper matrix factorization determines its parameters uniquely; changing the frame multiplies that coordinate by a unit. For the displayed product that coordinate is \(1+xy\). Thus the product lies in the cell exactly when \(1+xy\) is a unit, on all tests. Transporting the matrix identity through \(\rho\) gives (2). The chosen root-line tangent bases have pairing one, which supplies a perfect pairing, and the diagonal image gives \(\alpha\circ\alpha^\vee(t)=t^2\).

The pairing and coroot are unique, including over nonreduced bases. Work in paired root-line frames and let an alternative perfect pairing have coefficient \(c\in R^*\). Its coroot still has adjoint image \(\operatorname{diag}(t^2,1)\), since its pairing with \(\alpha\) is two. Set \(Y=F\) and \(X=xE\), and compare the upper-root coordinates in (2) after passing to the adjoint quotient. On \(R[x,1/((1+x)(1+cx))]\) the two coordinates are \(x/(1+x)\) and \(x/(1+cx)\). Equality gives \((c-1)x^2=0\). The factors \(1+x\) and \(1+cx\) are monic up to an invertible leading coefficient, so multiplication by their product is injective on \(R[x]\); the localization is injective. Independence of the polynomial basis therefore gives \(c=1\). With the pairing fixed, uniqueness of the three actual coordinates in the open cell of \(G_\alpha\) fixes the actual torus value \(\alpha^\vee(1+x)\), not only its adjoint image. On any test ring every unit \(u\) occurs by taking \(x=u-1\) and \(Y=F\). Thus the coroot itself is fixed on all tests. This also rules out a possible difference by a cocharacter into \(Z\). The constructions on different local identifications consequently agree, so the morphisms and pairing glue; the same characterization proves arbitrary base-change compatibility. \(\square\)

For \(\operatorname{SL}_2\), use \(T\simeq\mathbf G_m\) via \(\operatorname{diag}(t,t^{-1})\). Its root is \(\alpha(t)=t^2\), and \(\alpha^\vee(t)=\operatorname{diag}(t,t^{-1})\). For \(\operatorname{PGL}_2\), parameterize its diagonal torus by the class of \(\operatorname{diag}(t,1)\). Its root is \(t\mapsto t\), and its coroot is the class of \(\operatorname{diag}(t^2,1)\). In both cases the pairing is two, but the root and coroot occupy different sublattices.

For \(\operatorname{GL}_2\), the roots are \(e_1-e_2\) and its negative, and the positive coroot is \(t\mapsto\operatorname{diag}(t,t^{-1})\). These explicit formulas remain valid over \(\mathbb Z\).

\section{8. The three rank-one groups}\label{AG-RG-03-the-three-rank-one-groups}

\subsection{A lattice calculation with pairing two}\label{AG-RG-03-a-lattice-calculation-with-pairing-two}

\textbf{Lemma 8.A.} Let \(X\) be a finite free abelian group of rank \(r+1\). Let \(a\in X\) and \(b\in X^*=\operatorname{Hom}(X,\mathbf Z)\) be nonzero and satisfy \(b(a)=2\). Up to an isomorphism of \(X\) preserving this pair, exactly one of the following descriptions occurs:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \(X=\mathbf Z e_0\oplus\mathbf Z^r\), \(a=2e_0\), \(b=e_0^*\).
\item
  \(X=\mathbf Z e_0\oplus\mathbf Z^r\), \(a=e_0\), \(b=2e_0^*\).
\item
  \(r\geq1\), \(X=\mathbf Z e_1\oplus\mathbf Z e_2\oplus\mathbf Z^{r-1}\), \(a=e_1-e_2\), \(b=e_1^*-e_2^*\).
\end{enumerate}

In these formulas \(b\) is zero on the displayed extra summand.

\textbf{Proof.} Choose a basis of \(X\). For a nonzero vector the positive greatest common divisor of its coordinates is its divisibility; division by it gives a primitive vector. The same calculation applies to the coordinate list of a nonzero integral functional. Integer division, Bezout and the Smith basis operations are proved in S02 Lemma 3.M. In particular a primitive vector extends to an integral basis: the Euclidean row operations reduce its coordinate list to \((1,0,\ldots,0)\) and their inverses give that basis. A kernel of an integral functional is finite and torsion-free, hence free by that lemma. Write \(a=m a_0\) and \(b=n b_0\), with \(a_0,b_0\) primitive and \(m,n>0\). Then

\[
mn\,b_0(a_0)=2.
\]

Consequently \((m,n)\) is \((2,1)\), \((1,2)\), or \((1,1)\).

In the first case \(b(a_0)=1\). Every \(x\in X\) has the unique expression

\[
x=b(x)a_0+\bigl(x-b(x)a_0\bigr),
\qquad x-b(x)a_0\in\ker b.
\]

Thus \(X=\mathbf Z a_0\oplus\ker b\); choose a basis of the free kernel. This gives case 1. In the second case apply the same expression using \(b_0(a)=1\). It gives case 2.

Suppose now that both \(a\) and \(b\) are primitive. Extend \(a\) to a basis \(a,c_1,\ldots,c_r\). At least one \(b(c_i)\) is odd: otherwise every value of \(b\), including \(b(a)=2\), would be even, contradicting primitivity of \(b\). Relabel so that \(b(c_1)=2q+1\), and replace \(c_1\) by \(c_1-qa\). This is a basis operation and makes its value under \(b\) equal to one. Call the new vector \(c\). Replace each remaining \(c_i\) by \(c_i-b(c_i)c\); their values become zero. Finally set

\[
e_1=c,\qquad e_2=c-a.
\]

These replace the basis pair \(a,c\) by another unimodular basis pair. They satisfy \(a=e_1-e_2\), \(b(e_1)=1\) and \(b(e_2)=-1\), giving case 3. If \(r=0\), both primitive elements would pair to \(\pm1\), so this case cannot occur.

The divisibilities \((m,n)\) of \(a\) and \(b\) are invariant under lattice isomorphisms. They distinguish all three cases. \(\square\)

\subsection{Extending a map from the rank-one cell}\label{AG-RG-03-extending-a-map-from-the-rank-one-cell}

\textbf{Lemma 8.B.} Let \(K/S\) be a smooth group with geometrically connected fibres. Let \(\Omega\subset K\) be a fibrewise dense open containing the identity. Let \(H/S\) be a group scheme. Suppose \(f:\Omega\to H\) sends the identity to the identity and satisfies

\[
f(xy)=f(x)f(y)
\]

on the open where \(x,y,xy\in\Omega\). Then \(f\) extends uniquely to a homomorphism \(K\to H\).

\textbf{Proof.} We spell out irreducibility without a quasi-compactness assumption on \(K\). In a geometric fibre, every local ring of a smooth scheme is a regular local domain, by AG-CA-18 Theorem 2.1 and the regular-local-domain proof of AG-CA-14 Theorem 1.1. Each affine smooth chart is Noetherian. Its finitely many irreducible components cannot meet: two distinct minimal primes at a meeting point would remain distinct in the local ring, contradicting that it is a domain. The components on that chart are consequently disjoint closed-and-open subsets, each reduced and irreducible. Thus every point of the fibre has an irreducible open neighbourhood. Form equivalence classes of such neighbourhoods under chains of nonempty intersections. A finite union along a chain is irreducible, since the union of two intersecting irreducible open subsets is irreducible; this follows by testing two nonempty opens in their union. Any two members in one class lie in such a finite union, so the whole class union is irreducible. These class unions are disjoint opens covering the fibre. Connectedness leaves only one, proving irreducibility. This is the local form of the calculation in S02 Lemma 4.1. For any test scheme \(R\to S\) and any finite list \(g_1,\ldots,g_d\in K(R)\), the open

\[
\Omega_R\cap\bigcap_{i=1}^d\Omega_R g_i^{-1}
\]

has a nonempty open in every geometric fibre of \(K_R\): each translate is a dense nonempty open in the irreducible fibre and finite intersections remain nonempty. Its map to \(R\) is a smooth surjection. Smoothness gives flatness over arbitrary rings by AG-CA-18 Theorem 6.1, and local finite presentation is part of the proved smooth-chart criterion. Refine by affine smooth charts above affine base opens; these are finitely presented, flat maps and jointly cover \(R\). They give an actual fppf covering family and therefore a local point \(c\) with \(c\) and all \(cg_i\) in the cell. No rational-point choice over the original residue fields and no flatness of \(H\) are required.

In particular, for \(g\in K(R)\), choose \(c\in\Omega_R\cap\Omega_R^{-1}\cap\Omega_Rg^{-1}\) locally. Then \(g=c^{-1}(cg)\) is a product of two cell points. Assign to any word in cell points the corresponding product of \(f\)-values.

This assignment is independent of the word. For two words \(x_1\cdots x_d\) and \(y_1\cdots y_e\) with the same endpoint \(g\), choose \(c\) so that it and every translated partial product of both words lie in the cell. Repeatedly apply the given identity. The first image word multiplied on the left by \(f(c)\), and the second image word multiplied by the same element, both equal \(f(cg)\). Cancellation proves equality. The assignment also respects inverses: for \(x\in\Omega(R)\), choose \(d,d^{-1},dx^{-1}\in\Omega\). The identities \((dx^{-1})x=d\) and \(d^{-1}d=1\) then give \(f(d^{-1})f(dx^{-1})=f(x)^{-1}\). The word \(d^{-1}(dx^{-1})\) represents \(x^{-1}\), as required.

The assignments agree after fppf pullback, so the sheaf property of \(H\) descends them. Concatenation of words proves multiplicativity. Yoneda makes this map of represented fppf sheaves a scheme morphism. Every extension must have these values on generating words, proving uniqueness. \(\square\)

\subsection{The three rank-one models}\label{AG-RG-03-the-three-rank-one-models}

\textbf{Theorem 8.1.} A split reductive group of rank \(r+1\) and semisimple rank one over a field is isomorphic to exactly one of

\[
\mathbf G_m^r\times\operatorname{SL}_2,
\qquad
\mathbf G_m^r\times\operatorname{PGL}_2,
\qquad
\mathbf G_m^{r-1}\times\operatorname{GL}_2\quad(r\geq1).
\]

For a reductive group over a scheme with a split maximal torus and semisimple rank one, the same description holds Zariski locally on fixed-type loci. Trivial root lines with chosen frames give a global isomorphism to the corresponding base change from \(\mathbf Z\).

\textbf{Proof.} The root and coroot construction in Theorem 7.1 gives two roots \(\pm\alpha\), their additive root lines, the coroot \(\eta=\alpha^\vee\), and \(\langle\alpha,\eta\rangle=2\). Apply Lemma 8.A to \(X=X^*(T)\), \(a=\alpha\), \(b=\eta\). The three resulting pairs are precisely those computed for the three displayed matrix groups: in \(\operatorname{SL}_2\) the root is twice the primitive character and the coroot is primitive; in \(\operatorname{PGL}_2\) the root is primitive and the coroot twice primitive; in \(\operatorname{GL}_2\) they are respectively \(e_1-e_2\) and \(e_1^*-e_2^*\).

Let \(G_0\) be the indicated matrix model. The lattice isomorphism gives a torus isomorphism \(f_T:T\to T_0\) carrying root characters and coroots to those of the model. Choose a nonzero positive-root frame \(E\in\mathfrak g_\alpha\). The perfect pairing of Theorem 7.1 gives a unique negative-root frame \(F\) with pairing one. Define \(x(u)=\exp_\alpha(uE)\) and \(y(v)=\exp_{-\alpha}(vF)\), and match these to the upper and lower matrix parameters \(x_0,y_0\) of \(G_0\).

The matrix model has a smooth geometrically connected underlying scheme over every base. For \(\operatorname{SL}_2\) the two polynomial-localization charts and their nonempty intersection were calculated in Theorem 6.1. For \(\operatorname{GL}_2\) it is the principal determinant open of affine four-space, smooth by the polynomial lifting proof and geometrically integral because a localization of a polynomial domain is a domain. For \(\operatorname{PGL}_2\) it is the determinant open of \(\mathbf P^3\) from Lemma 5.B, smooth on its affine coordinate charts and geometrically integral as a nonempty open of integral projective space. The latter integrality follows from the polynomial domains on its affine charts, whose pairwise intersections are nonempty. A product with the extra split torus stays smooth; its affine fibre charts have Laurent polynomial algebras over these domains and remain integral, with nonempty chart intersections. Thus both the model and \(G\) satisfy the hypotheses of Lemma 8.B. The open cell theorem gives \(\Omega=U_-TU_+\). On it define

\[
f\bigl(y(v)t x(u)\bigr)=y_0(v)f_T(t)x_0(u).
\]

This is an isomorphism of schemes from \(\Omega\) to the model cell. The group law on the torus, the additivity of \(x,y\), and the conjugation identities \(t x(u)t^{-1}=x(\alpha(t)u)\), \(t y(v)t^{-1}=y(\alpha(t)^{-1}v)\), agree under this map. The remaining multiplication rule is

\[
x(u)y(v)=y\left(\frac{v}{1+uv}\right)
\eta(1+uv)x\left(\frac{u}{1+uv}\right),
\qquad 1+uv\in\mathcal O^\times,
\]

proved in Theorem 7.1 by the arbitrary-base central-extension argument and the explicit \(2\times2\) matrix identity.

For two cell points \(y(v)t x(u)\) and \(y(v')t'x(u')\), their product is in the cell exactly when \(x(u)y(v')\) is: left multiplication by \(U_-T\) and right multiplication by \(TU_+\) preserve the cell, as do their inverses. The preceding rule and its unit criterion therefore give every multiplication of cell points whose product remains in the cell. It follows that \(f\) satisfies Lemma 8.B. The lemma extends it to a group homomorphism \(G\to G_0\). The inverse cell map satisfies the same identities and extends in the other direction. Uniqueness in the lemma makes their compositions the identity. Thus \(G\simeq G_0\).

Any group isomorphism carries a maximal torus to a maximal torus. Over an algebraic closure the torus conjugacy theorem then identifies its root/coroot pair with the pair for the fixed torus. It can interchange the signs of both elements, but does not change either divisibility. The three invariant pairs \((2,1),(1,2),(1,1)\) distinguish the models in all characteristics, including characteristic two. This proves uniqueness without a forward reference to the derived group.

Over a scheme, restrict to an open where the root/coroot lattice pair is constant and the positive root line is trivial. Its paired negative line is then also trivial. The same torus map, cell formula and fppf word argument work over every test scheme, so give the asserted local isomorphism. When the lattice pair and frames are fixed globally, these constructions are global. All maps commute with base change because the displayed formulas and their character pairings do. \(\square\)

\section{9. Exercises}\label{AG-RG-03-exercises}

\textbf{Exercise 9.1 (first steps).} Compute all roots and root spaces of \(\operatorname{GL}_n\) with respect to its diagonal torus. Determine the zero-weight space and the positive coroot for \(e_i-e_j\).

\textbf{Exercise 9.2 (rank-one multiplication).} Compute \(U_{\pm\alpha}\) and \(\alpha^\vee\) for \(\operatorname{SL}_2\). Verify the factorization (2), and explain why the character differential in characteristic two does not change this factorization.

\textbf{Exercise 9.3 (infinitesimal information).} In characteristic different from two, show that \(\mathfrak{sl}_2\simeq\mathfrak{pgl}_2\) as Lie algebras, while the groups are not isomorphic. What happens to the differential of \(\operatorname{SL}_2\to\operatorname{PGL}_2\) in characteristic two?

\textbf{Exercise 9.4 (classification).} List the rank-two split reductive groups of semisimple rank one. Distinguish them by their centres and derived groups, including characteristic two.

\textbf{Exercise 9.5 (families).} For \(G=\operatorname{SL}(\mathcal O\oplus L)\), identify the two root groups and their pairing. Give a condition on \(L\) necessary for a pinning of this pair with its displayed torus.

\section{Solutions}\label{AG-RG-03-solutions}

\subsection{Solution 9.1}\label{AG-RG-03-solution-9.1}

The diagonal matrix units have weight zero and form \(\mathfrak t\). For \(i\ne j\), \(E_{ij}\) has weight \(e_i-e_j\), each once. The corresponding root group is \(I+uE_{ij}\). Its coroot has diagonal entries \(t\) in position \(i\), \(t^{-1}\) in position \(j\), and \(1\) elsewhere. Evaluating \(e_i-e_j\) gives \(t^2\), so the root--coroot pairing is two.

\subsection{Solution 9.2}\label{AG-RG-03-solution-9.2}

The two groups are the upper and lower unipotent matrices. Their parameters are \(x,y\) in the displayed matrix identity, and \(\alpha^\vee(t)=\operatorname{diag}(t,t^{-1})\). Multiplication of the three factors gives \(\begin{pmatrix}1+xy&x\\y&1\end{pmatrix}\), equal to \(x_\alpha(x)x_{-\alpha}(y)\). The character on the upper group is \(t^2\), so its pairing with this coroot is two. Although its differential is zero in characteristic two, the Laurent character and all polynomial matrix identities remain valid; no division by two was used.

\subsection{Solution 9.3}\label{AG-RG-03-solution-9.3}

The projective affine charts and scalar torsor constructed over \(\mathbf Z\) in RG02 Lemma 4.P compute \(\operatorname{Lie}(\mathrm{PGL}_2)=\mathfrak{gl}_2/kI\) in every characteristic: an infinitesimal scalar changes \(I+\epsilon X\) to \(I+\epsilon(X+qI)\). The derivative of the determinant is the trace, so \(\operatorname{Lie}(\mathrm{SL}_2)=\{X:\operatorname{tr}X=0\}\). Inclusion followed by quotient is bracket preserving, with scalar kernel defined by \(2q=0\). When two is invertible it has zero kernel and both spaces have dimension three, so it is an isomorphism. In characteristic two the scalar line lies in the trace-zero space, giving exactly a one-dimensional kernel.

To compute the group kernel on every test algebra, a scalar determinant-one matrix is \(qI\) with \(q^2=1\), giving \(\mu_2\). Every projective class lifts locally to an invertible matrix \(M\). After the cover \(R[z]/(z^2-\det M)\) it has the determinant-one representative \(z^{-1}M\). This is a finite free rank-two faithfully flat cover (basis \(1,z\) and nonzero fibres); \(z\) is a unit because its square is a unit. Thus \(\mathrm{SL}_2\to\mathrm{PGL}_2\) is the fppf central quotient by \(\mu_2\) in every characteristic, and Theorem 1.1 supplies reductivity of this quotient as well. Its centre is trivial: a central element centralizes the diagonal torus and hence lies in it by RG02 Theorem 2.1; writing its ratio as \(q\), commutation with the universal upper root matrix gives \((q-1)u=0\) in \(R[u]\), whence \(q=1\). For \(\mathrm{SL}_2\) the same diagonal-centralizer calculation makes a central element \(\operatorname{diag}(q,q^{-1})\), and the universal root equation gives \(q^2=1\). Hence its entire centre is \(\mu_2\). This is nontrivial as a scheme even in characteristic two, whereas the projective centre is trivial, so the groups are not isomorphic.

\subsection{Solution 9.4}\label{AG-RG-03-solution-9.4}

Put \(r=1\) in Theorem 8.1. The list is \(\mathbf G_m\times\operatorname{SL}_2\), \(\mathbf G_m\times\operatorname{PGL}_2\), and \(\operatorname{GL}_2\). Their centres are respectively \(\mathbf G_m\times\mu_2\), \(\mathbf G_m\), and \(\mathbf G_m\). The first centre is not a torus: in characteristic two it is nonsmooth, and otherwise it has two geometric components. We compute the indicated derived groups directly. The extension \(R\to R[t,t^{-1},(t^2-1)^{-1}]\) is faithfully flat and finitely presented: it is a localization of the polynomial algebra, is \(R\)-flat, and every field fibre is a nonzero localization at a nonzero polynomial. Each such fibre has a prime by AG-CA-01 Lemma 1.1, so the map on spectra is surjective and flatness is faithful by AG-CA-07 Theorem 2.1. Thus fppf locally we can choose \(t\) with \(t^2-1\) invertible, including in characteristic two. The identities \([h(t),x(u)]=x((t^2-1)u)\) and \([h(t),y(v)]=y((t^{-2}-1)v)\) put both root groups of \(\operatorname{SL}_2\) in its commutator subgroup. The open cell word argument of Theorem 6.1 shows that these root groups generate \(\operatorname{SL}_2\) as an fppf sheaf, since \(h(t)=w(t)w(1)^{-1}\). Their images generate \(\operatorname{PGL}_2\), because \(\operatorname{SL}_2\to\operatorname{PGL}_2\) is fppf surjective; hence its derived group is itself. For \(\operatorname{GL}_2\), determinant kills all commutators, and conjugation by \(\operatorname{diag}(t,1)\), with \(t-1\) invertible fppf locally, puts both determinant-one root groups in the commutator subgroup. The same generation argument gives its derived group \(\operatorname{SL}_2\). The central \(\mathbf G_m\) factors contribute no commutators. Thus the last two models have derived groups \(\operatorname{PGL}_2\) and \(\operatorname{SL}_2\); the first and third have the same derived group but different centres. These computations are scheme-theoretic and remain valid in characteristic two.

\subsection{Solution 9.5}\label{AG-RG-03-solution-9.5}

An upper off-diagonal entry is a map \(L\to\mathcal O\), so its line is \(L^{-1}\); a lower entry is a map \(\mathcal O\to L\), so its line is \(L\). Composition gives \(L^{-1}\otimes L\to\mathcal O\), the perfect pairing in Theorem 7.1. A pinning chooses a nowhere-vanishing section in the simple root line. It therefore requires \(L^{-1}\), equivalently \(L\), to be trivial. This illustrates the global hypothesis absent from the field case.
